# 📗 Arif's Pathology & Haematology (15th ed., 2025) — Complete Extracted Text

> **Single-file edition.** All 57 chapter files of the two-volume OCR extraction merged, in book order, into one document.
> Source PDFs are photo-scans; text produced via Tesseract OCR at 250 dpi. Every page is preserved verbatim with its page anchor.
> The individual chapter files remain in this folder unchanged — this file is a merge of them, not a replacement.
>
> - Volume 1: General Pathology + Haematology (pp. 1–492)
> - Volume 2: Systemic Pathology + Clinical Pathology (pp. 1–512)
> - Quality flags: see `_QA_REPORT.md` · File index: see `_INDEX.md`

> **Source:** `Arif Pathology guide 2025(1).pdf` · **Pages 23–51** (29 extracted) · **UNIT-I : GENERAL PATHOLOGY**

GENERAL PATHOLOGY

Introduction to Pathology

Pathology literally translates as the study of suffering (Greek pathos = suffering, logos = study); more
prosaically, and as applied to modern medicine, it is the study of disease.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1)

Q. Define pathology. What are the divisions of pathology?
Ans

Pathology: Pathology is the study of the structural, biochemical, and functional changes in cells, tissues, and
organs that underlie disease.

Division of pathology: Traditionally the study of pathology is divided into general pathology and systemic pathology.

* General pathology is concemed with the common reactions of cells and tissues to injurious stimuli.

Such reactions are often not tissue specific: thus acute inflammation in response to bacterial infections
produces a very similar reaction in most tissues.

Systemic pathology (on the other hand), examines the alterations and underlying mechanisms in
diseases of particular organ systems, such as ischemic heart disease.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/33)

Q. Who is called the father of modern pathology & why? (Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Father of modern pathology: Virtually all diseases start with molecular or structural alterations in cells
This concept of the cellular basis of disease was first put forth in the nineteenth century by Rudolf Virchow,
known as the father of modern pathology.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/34)

Cell Injury

Q. Define cell injury. (DU-08Ja, BUP-22Nv,21Nv/M, RU-20Nv,19M, SU-20Nv/M, CU-05Ja)
(Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Cell injury: If the limits of adaptive responses are exceeded or if cells are exposed to damaging insults,
deprived of critical nutrients, or compromised by mutations that affect essential cellular functions, a
sequence of events follows that is termed cell injury.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/35)
Or,
When cells are stressed so severely that they are no longer able to adapt or when cells are exposed to
inherently damaging agents, cell injury results.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. What are the causes of cell injury? (DU-10Ja, RU-20Nv,17M,12Ja, SU-22Nv,20M,15Ja,12Ju,
CU-11Ja) (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Causes of cell injury: The major causes of cell injury can be grouped into the following categories:
1. Oxygen deprivation:

i. Hypoxia: Hypoxia is a deficiency of O, to the tissue, which causes cell injury by reducing aerobic
oxidative respiration. Causes include inadequate oxygenation of the blood due to cardio-
respiratory failure; and decreased oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, as in anaemia or CO
poisoning and severe blood loss.

ii. Ischemia: It means loss of blood supply from impeded arterial flow or reduced venous drainage ina
tissue.
2. Physical agents: It includes mechanical trauma, extremes of temperature (burn and deep cold), sudden
changes in atmospheric pressure, radiation, and electric shock etc.

3. Chemical agents and drugs: Glucose or salt in hypertonic concentrations; oxygen in high
concentration; trace amount of poisons e.g. arsenic, cyanide, or mercury; environmental pollutants,
insecticides, and herbicides; industrial and occupational hazards, such as carbon monoxide and
asbestos; recreational drugs such as alcohol; variety of therapeutic drugs (toxic side effects).

4. Infectious agents: Virus, rickettsiae, bacteria, fungi, and higher forms of parasites.

5. Immunologic reactions: Immune reactions to foreign bodies (such as viruses and environmental
substances), and autoimmune diseases (injurious reactions to endogenous self-antigens).

6. Genetic abnormalities: Genetic injury may result in congenital malformations to anemias e.g. Down

syndrome, sickle cell anemia etc.

7. Nutritional imbalances: such as protein-calorie deficiency, vitamin deficiency, nutritional excess

(atherosclerosis, obesity) etc.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/36)

Q. What are the causes of cellular swelling? (Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.
Causes of cellular swelling: Cellular swelling is the earliest manifestation of almost all forms of injury to cells
which results from influx of water. It occurs when cells are incapable of maintaining ionic and fluid
homeostasis and is the result of failure of the ATP-dependent Na‘-K* plasma membrane pump due to
depletion of ATP resulting from oxygen deficiency, which interferes with mitochondrial oxidative
phosphorylation, or mitochondrial damage by radiation or toxins.

(Ref: Robbins/10°/37)

Q. Mention the morphological pattern of cell death. (DU-05Ja)

Q. What are the morphological types of irreversible cell injury? (DU-13Ja)

Ans.

Morphological pattern of cell death: Irreversibly injured cells invariably undergo morphologic changes that
are recognized as cell death. (** Irreversible cell injury = Cell death)

A. There are two principle types of cell death:

1. Necrosis
2. Apoptosis

B. Other mechanisms of cell death:
1. Necroptosis

2. Pyroptosis

3. Ferroptosis

(Ref: Robbins/10"/38,47)

Reversible & Irreversible Cell Injury

Q. Define reversible cell injury. (CU-09Ja)
Q. What are the hall marks / criteria of reversible cell injury? (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Reversible cell injury: When the injury to the cells or tissues occurred in such extent or up to certain limit
that all of these disturbances are reversible if injurious stimulus is withdrawn.

Hall marks / criteria of reversible cell injury: The hall marks of reversible cell injury are-

* Reduced oxidative phosphorylation
«= ATP depletion
= Cellular swelling caused by changes in ion concentration and water influx.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/37 + 9"/38 + 8/11)

Q. Define irreversible cell injury. (CU-09Ja)

Q. What are the hall marks / criteria of irreversible cell injury? (SU-15Ju, CU-12Ju) (Very
Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Irreversible cell injury: If the injurious stimulus persists or is severe enough from the beginning, the cells or

tissues are damaged to such extent that it become unable to recover when injurious stimulus is withdrawn, is
called irreversible cell injury.

Hall marks / criteria of irreversible cell injury: Irreversible cell injury occurs due to irreversible damage
of cell membrane, mitochondria and nucleus. It is characterized by-

» Increasing swelling of the cell

* Swelling and disruption of lysosomes

*  Vacuolization of mitochondria with reduced capacity to generate ATP

= Disruption of cellular membranes

= Profound nuclear changes.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/35,37 + 8""/11)

(N.B: Cellular swelling is one of the hall marks of reversible cell injury, whereas increasing swelling of the
cell is one of the hall marks of irreversible cell injury.)

---

#### 📄 Page 29

GENERAL PATHOLOGY | 29

Cell injury is reversib/e up to a point, but if the injurious stimulus is persistent or severe, the cell suffers
irreversible injury and ultimately undergoes cell death,

Q. How reversible cell injuries become irreversible? (Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Transformation of reversible cell injury to irreversible cell injury: Although the “point of no return,” at
which the reversible damage becomes irreversible, is still largely undefined, Mvo phenomena consistently
characterize irreversibility-

1. Inability to reverse mitochondrial dysfunction (lack of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP
generation) even after resolution of the original injury.
2. Profound disturbances in membrane function (of cell and cellular organelles), especially injury to

lysosomal membranes results in the enzymatic dissolution of the injured cell that is characteristic of
necrosis or cell death.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/40)

Mechanisms of Cell Injury

Q. What are the targets in cells for injurious stimuli? (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Targets in cells for injurious stimuli: Cell injury results from abnormalities in one or more essential cellular
components. The principal targets of injurious stimuli are:

1. Mitochondria
2. Cell membranes
3. The machinery of protein synthesis and secretion
4. DNA.

Ans.

Mechanisms of cell injurv: Injurious stimuli causes cell injury by the following three principle mechanisms-

1. Mitochondrial damage
2. Membrane damage
3. Damage to DNA

Other biochemical alterations involved in mechanisms of cell injury:
4. Oxidative stress: Accumulation of oxygen-derived free radicals
5. Disturbance in calcium homeostasis
6. Endoplasmic reticulum stress: the unfolded protein response.

1) Mitochondrial damage: Mitochondria are critical players in all pathways leading to cell injury and death.
Mitochondna can be damaged by-

a. Increases of cytosolic Ca**

b. Reactive oxygen species (ROS)

c. Oxygen deprivation (including hypoxia and toxins)
d. Mutations in mitochondnal genes.

There are three major consequences of mitochondrial damage:
a. ATP depletion: Decreased ATP synthesis and ATP depletion are frequently associated with both

hypoxic and chemical (toxic) injury. ATP depletion leads to- (Very Important for VIVA)

* | Activity of plasma membrane energy-dependent Na pump (Na*-K*-ATPase pump) — {
Influx of Ca’*, HO & Na’ & f efflux of K* — ER swelling, cellular swelling, loss of microvilli,
appearance of blebs.

= f Anaerobic glycolysis — f Production of lactic acid + |]pH — Clumping of nuclear chromatin.

= Detachment of ribosomes from the rough ER — | Protein synthesis — Lipid deposition.

Ultimately, there is irreversible damage to mitochondrial and lysosomal membranes, and the cell
undergoes necrosis.

Fig: Functional and morphological consequences of decreased intracellular ATP in ischemic cell injury.

GENERAL PATHOLOGY | 31

b. Incomplete oxidative phosphorylation — formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) — cell death
by necrosis.

c. Leakage of mitochondrial proteins into the cytosol due to formation of high-conductance channel
in the mitochondrial membrane (called mitochondrial permeability transition pore) \eading to cell
death by apoptosis.

NECROSIS APOPTOSIS

Fig: Role of mitochondria in cell injury and death.

Membrane damage: It is a consistent feature of most forms of cell injury (except apoptosis). Membrane
damage may affect the integrity and functions of all cellular membranes.

Damage to different cellular membranes has diverse ffects on cells.

a. Mitochondrial membrane damage: Damage to mitochondrial membranes —> opening of the

mitochondrial permeability transition pore > | ATP generation and release of proteins that rigger
apoptotic death.

b. Plasma membrane damage: Plasma membrane damage — loss of osmotic balance and influx of fluids
and ions, as well as loss of cellular contents. The cells may also leak metabolites (e.g. glycolytic
intermediates) that are vital for the reconstitution of ATP, thus further depleting energy stores.

c. Injury to lysosomal membranes: It results in leakage of their enzymes into the cytoplasm and
activation of acid hydrolases in the acidic intracellular pH of the injured cell. These lysosomal
hydrolases include RNases, DNases, proteases, phosphatases, and glucosidases, which degrade RNA,
DNA, proteins, phosphoproteins, and glycogen, respectively, and push cells into necrosis.

Damage to DNA: Cells have mechanisms that repair damage to DNA, but if this damage is too severe to
be corrected (e.g. after exposure to radiation, chemotherapeutic [anticancer] drugs, and ROS, or may occur

spontaneously as a part of aging), the cells initiate a suicide program that results in death by apoptosis
triggered by p53 gene.

Oxidative stress (accumulation of oxygen-derived free radicals): Cell injury induced by free radicals
(particularly ROS) is an important mechanism of cell damage in many pathologic conditions, such as
chemical and radiation injury, ischemia-reperfusion injury, cellular aging, and microbial killing by
phagocytes.

Disturbance in calcium homeostasis: Excessive intracellular Ca’* causes cell injury by several

mechanisms-

a) Accumulation of Ca** in mitochondria results in opening of the mitochondrial permeability
transition pore and failure of ATP generation.

32 arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

b) Increased cytosolic Ca*’ activates a number of enzymes that damage cellular components and me,
also trigger apoptosis.
These enzymes include- (Very Important for VIVA)

* Phospholipases > causing membrane damage.
Protease — causing breakdown of both membrane and cytoskeletal proteins.

* Endonucleases — responsible for DNA and chromatin fragmentation.
* ATPase — leading to ATP depletion.

6) Endoplasmic reticulum stress: the unfolded protein response: Accumulation of misfolded proteins jy
the ER activates adaptive mechanisms that help the cell to survive, but if their repair capacity is exceede
they trigger apoptosis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/49-54

Nice to Know: Bi gk ¢
Endoplasmic reticulum stress: ‘the unfolded protein response:

. Unfolded _protein response: If the unfolded or misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER, they
trigger a number of alterations that are collectively called the unfolded protein response.

« Endoplasmic reticulum stress: If the cytoprotective.response is unable to cope with the
accumulation of misfolded proteins, the cell activates caspases and induces apoptosis. This process
is called ER stress.

Intracellular accumulation of misfolded proteins may be caused by an increased rate of misfolding or a
reduction in the cell’s ability to repair or eliminate them.

Diseased caused by misfolded proteins are cystic fibrosis, familial hypercholesterolemiass pisyeSachs
disease, a)-antitrypsin deficiency, Creutzfeldt-Jacob disease, Alzheimer disease etc.

(Ref: Robbins/10/54-55)

Q. How ATP is produced?
Ans.
ATP production: ATP is produced in two ways:
1) Oxidative phosphorylation (the major pathway in mammalian cells, particularly those that are non-
dividing e.g. brain and liver).

2) Glycolytic pathway (which can generate ATP in the absence of oxygen using glucose derived either
from body fluids or from the hydrolysis of glycogen).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/49)

(N.B: ATP is required for virtually all synthetic and degradative processes within the cell. These include
membrane transport, protein synthesis, lipogenesis, and the deacylation-reacylation reactions necessary for
phospholipid turnover. Hence, depletion of ATP to 5% to 10% of normal levels has widespread effects on many
critical cellular systems.)

(Ref: Robbins/10"/50)

Q. What are the causes of ATP depletion? (RU-18M,17Ju)

Q. How does ATP depletion occur? (CU-18Nv)

Ans.

Causes of ATP depletion: The major causes of ATP depletion are-
1. Mitochondrial damage

2. Reduced supply of oxygen and nutrients (because of ischemia and hypoxia)
3. Actions of some toxins (e.g. cyanide).

#### 📄 Page 33

GENERAL PATHOLOGY 33

nial —_ —

Mitochondrial damage often results in the formation of a high-conductance channel in the mitochondrial
membrane, called the mitochondrial permeability transition pore. The opening of this conductance channel
leads to the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, resulting in failure of oxidative phosphorylation
and progressive ATP depletion that culminates in necrosis (cell death).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/50)

Q. Describe the biochemical mechanisms leading to cell membrane damage. (DU-10Ju, RU-10Ju)
Ans.
Biochemical_mechanisms leading to_cell_ membrane damage: Several biochemical mechanisms may

contribute to membrane damage-

1. Reactive oxygen species: Oxygen free radicals cause injury to cell membranes by lipid peroxidation,
oxidative modification of proteins and lesions in DNA.

2. Decreased phospholipid synthesis: Decreased phospholipid synthesis as a consequence of defective
mitochondnial function or hypoxia may affect all cellular membranes, including those of mitochondria.

3. Increased phospholipid breakdown: Severe cell injury is associated with increased degradation of
membrane phopholipids, probably due to activation of endogenous phospholipases by increased levels
of cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca’. Phospholipid breakdown leads to accumulation of /ipid
breakdown products including unesterified free fatty acids, acyl carnitine, and lysophospholipids,
which have a detergent effect on membranes. They also either insert into the lipid bilayer of the
membrane or exchange with membrane phospholipids, potentially causing changes in permeability and
electrophysiologic alterations.

4. Cytoskeletal abnormalities: Activation of proteases by increased cytosolic Ca** may cause damage
to elements of the cytoskeleton. In the presence of cell swelling, particularly in myocardial cells, this
damage leads to detachment of the cell membrane from the cytoskeleton, rendering it susceptible to
stretching and rupture.

MEMBRANE DAMAGE
Fig: Mechanisms of membrane damage in cell injury.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/51)

Q. What is reperfusion injury? Discuss the mechanism of reperfusion injury. (DU-05Ja)
Q. Short note: Ischemia-reperfusion injury. (Important for VIVA for Honours Gainer)

Ans.

Reperfusion injury / Ischemia-reperfusion injury: Restoration of blood flow to ischemic tissues can
promote recovery of cells if they are reversibly injured, but can also paradoxically exacerbate the injury and
cause cell death.

Depending on the intensity and duration of the ischemic insult, in some cases, after restoration of blood flow to
ischemic tissue causes further death to cells by necrosis and apoptosis, is called ischemia-reperfusion injury.

Mechanisms of reperfusion injury:

Oxidative stress: New damage may be initiated during re-oxygenation by increased generation of
reactive oxygen and nitrogen species produced by damaged mitochondria, or because of the action of
oxidases in leukocytes, endothelial cells, or parenchymal cells.

Intracellular calcium overload: Influx of calcium into re-perfused cells damages various organelles
including mitochondna, and increases the production of free radicals, which in turn causes further cell
injury.

Inflammation: Ischemic injury is associated with inflammation as a result of the production of
cytokines and increased expression of adhesion molecules by hypoxic parenchymal and endothelial
cells, which recruit circulating neutrophils to re-perfused tissue. The inflammation causes additional
tissue injury.

Activation of the complement system: For unknown reasons, some IgM antibodies have a propensity

to deposit in ischaemic tissues, and when blood flow is resumed, complement proteins bind to the
deposited antibodies, are activated, and exacerbate cell injury and inflammation.

ical ortance: It is clinically important because it contributes to tissue damage during-

Myocardial infarction
Cerebral infarction
Following therapies that restore blood flow.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/56)

Q. Short note: Free radical. (SU-20Nv,19M,11/06/04Ja, RU-19Nv,18Nv/Ja, 12Ju,10Ja, CU-12Ju)
Ans.
Free radicals: Free radicals are chemical species that have a single unpaired electron in an outer orbit.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/52)
Types of free radicals:
1. Oxygen derived free radicals: Superoxide anion (02°), hydrogen peroxide (H;O;), hydroxyl ions (‘OH).
2. Carbon derived free radicals: CCl,-.
3. Nitrogen derived free radicals: NO-, ONOO,, NO;-, NO;.

Sources of free radicals: (Important for MCQ) The free radicals may be generated within cells in
several ways-

1. Reduction-oxidation reactions that occur during normal metabolic processes.

Example: During normal respiration small amounts of partially reduced free radicals are produced in
which different numbers of electrons have been transferred from O, e.g. superoxide anion (O2":, one
electron), hydrogen peroxide (H2O,, two electrons), hydroxyl ions (OH, three electrons).

2. Absorption of radiant energy (e.g. UV light, X-rays)
H,O (ionizing radiation) + -OH +H:

3. Rapid bursts of ROS are produced in activated leukocytes during inflammation. In addition, some
intracellular oxidases (such as xanthine oxidase) generate O;°.

Enzymatic metabolism of exogenous chemicals or drugs (e.g. CCl, can generate CCl)°).

5. Transition metals (e.g. Fe & Cu) donate or accept free electrons during intracellular reactions and
catalyze free radical formation, as in Fenton reaction.

H,0, + Fe’* > Fe** + -OH+ OH

6. Nitric oxide (NO) generated by endothelial cells, macrophages, neurons, and other cell types can act
as a free radical and can also be converted to highly reactive peroxynitrite anion (ONOO-) as well as
NO, and NO;.

Role of free radicals: Free radical-mediated damage contributes to various processes, such as:
* Chemical and radiation injury
* Ischemic reperfusion injury (induced by restoration of blood flow in ischemic tissue)
* Cellular ageing
* Microbial killing by phagocytes.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/52)

Spontaneous destruction: Free radicals are inherently unstable and generally decay spontancously,

Cellular mechanism:

a) Antioxidants: They either block the initiation of free radical formation or inactivate (eg
scavenge) them. Examples are the lipid soluble vitamins E & A as well as ascorbic acid (vitamin
C) and glutathione in the cytosol.

b) Binding with storage and transport proteins: Iron and copper can catalyze the formation of
ROS. The levels of these reactive metals are minimized by binding of the ions to storage and
transport proteins (e.g. transferrin, ferritin, lactoferrin, and ceruloplasmin), thereby minimizing the

formation of ROS.

Ans.
Necrosis: Necrosis refers to a spectrum of morphologic changes that follow cell death in living tissue,
largely resulting from the progressive degradative action of enzymes on the lethally injured cell.

(Ref: Robbins/7"/21)

Necrosis is a pathologic process that is the consequence of severe injury which is characterized by
denaturation of cellular proteins, leakage of cellular contents through damaged membranes, local
inflammation, and enzymatic digestion of the lethally injured cell.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/39)

Ans.

Morphology of necrotic cell: (Very Very Important for VIVA)

Nuclear changes in necrosis: Nuclear changes in necrosis appear in the form of one of three patterns, all dy.
to non-specific breakdown of DNA.

1. Karyolysis: Nuclear fading (i.e. basophilia gradually fades) due to dissolution of chromatin by the
action of DNAases & RNAases.

2. Pyknosis: Nuclear shrinkage with increased basophilia. Here the chromatin condenses into a solid
shrunken basophilic mass

3. Karyorrhexis: Fragmentation of pyknotic nucleus.

With the passage of time (1 or 2 days), the nucleus in the necrotic cell totally disappears.

Q. Define autolysis and heterolysis. (RU-13Ju) (V.V.1. for VIVA)
Ans.
Autolysis: When enzymatic digestion of a cell occurs by its own lysosomal enzyme, is called autolysis.

Heterolysis: When enzymatic digestion of a cell occurs by the lysosomal enzymes of immigrant leukocytes

during inflammatory reaction, is called heterolysis.
(Ref: Robbins/7"/21)

Or,
Heterolysis refers to cellular degradation by enzymes derived from sources extrinsic to the cell (e.g. bacteria

and Jeukocytes).
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5'"/6)

Ans.
Sequele of necrosis / cell death:

1. When small number of cells is involved, the cellular debris is removed by phagocytosis,

2. With large numbers of dead cells, there is an inflammatory response with organization and fibrous
repair.

3. When the necrotic tissue cannot be completely removed or organized, deposition of calcium may be
an additional feature, for example in tuberculous caseous necrosis. This feature is important in
radiological diagnosis. It is sometimes described as ‘dystrophic’.

4. Gangrene duc to putrefaction.

Description of each type of necrosis: (Very Very Important Topic for VIVA)

1. Coagulative necrosis (most_ common e): It is a form of necrosis in which the basic cellular

shape, outline & architecture is preserved for a span of at least some days. The cell takes
acidophilic stain. The localized area of coagulative necrosis is called an infarct.

Examples: Occurs in solid organs, except brain, ¢.g. ischaemic necrosis of heart (myocardial
infarction), kidney, liver, adrenal gland and other solid organs, gumma of tertiary syphilis etc.

Fig: Coagulative necrosis (A wedge-shaped kidney infarct).

---

#### 📄 Page 42

42 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Morphology:

*  Macroscopic- The affected tissues exhibit a firm, dry, opaque, homogenous texture.

* Microscopic- Preservation of basic outline of cells, nucleus shows pyknosis, karyorthexis or
karyolysis; cytoplasm becomes opaque and acidophilic.

2. Liquefactive necrosis: Liquefactive necrosis, in contrast to coagulative necrosis, is characterized by
digestion of dead cells, resulting in transformation of the tissue into a liquid viscous mass. There is
complete loss of cellular architecture.

Example:
* Focal bacterial or fungal infections (e.g. abscess, boil)
* Ischaemic necrosis of brain tissue.

Morphology: The necrotic material is frequently creamy yellow because of the presence of dead
leukocytes and is called pus.

-_~ -

Fig: Liquefactive necrosis (An infarct in the brain).

3. Gangrenous necrosis:
* It is a distinctive pattern of coagulative necrosis usually occurs in lower limb due to loss of

blood supply (dry gangrene)
» When bacterial infection is superimposed, this transforms into liquefactive necrosis (wet gangrene).
4. Caseous necrosis: It is a distinctive form of coagulative necrosis. It occurs most commonly in foci of

tuberculous infection (& brucellocis). The term “caseous” (cheese-like) is derived from the friable
white appearance of the area of necrosis.

ae. otto

Fig: Caseous necrosis.

Example: Granuloma of tuberculosis, cat scratch disease, brucellosis.

Morphology:

* Macroscopic- White and cheesy appearance of the area of necrosis.

« Microscopic- The necrotic area appears as a collection of fragmented or lysed cells and
amorphous granular debris enclosed within a distinctive inflammatory border known as a
granuloma. The tissue architecture is lost & the cell outline is not preserved.

5. Fat necrosis: It occurs in adipose tissue due to action of lipase. It is two types-

a) Enzymatic fat necrosis: Enzymatic fat necrosis of pancreas & omental tissue occurs in acute
pancreatitis. Activated pancreatic lipase goes into the pancreatic tissue & peritoneal cavity and
liquefies fat cell membranes & split triglyceride esters. The released fatty acids combine with
calcium to produce grossly visible chalky white areas (fat saponification).

— -—~ de —-
Morphology:
= Macroscopic: Chalky white saponification.
® Microscopic: Foci of shadowy outlines of necrotic fat cells, with basophilic calcium deposits,
surrounded by an inflammatory reaction.

b) Traumatic fat necrosis: c.g. in breast.

Fig: Fat necrosis.

6. Fibrinoid necrosis: It is a special form of vascular damage usually seen in immune reactions
involving blood vessels. This pattern of necrosis typically occurs when complexes of antigens and
antibodies are deposited in the walls of arteries, along with fibrin.

Example: Rheumatic fever, vasculitis (e.g. polyarteritis nodosa), malignant hypertension, rheumatoid
arthritis, SLE etc.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/40; Reid & Roberts/6""/5-8)

Q. Define apoptosis. (DU-08/07Ju,05Ja, BUP-22M, CMU-21INv, 1 0Ju, RU-20M,09/08Ju,07Ja, SU-1 1 Ja)
Q. What is the significance of apoptosis? (DU-24Nv)

Q. What are the causes of apoptosis? (DU-05Ja, CU-10Ju,05Ja)

Q. Give examples of apoptosis in physiological condition. (DU-17Nv)

Q. Give 4 examples of apoptosis. (CMU-21Nv)

Q. Give two examples of apoptosis in pathological condition. (DU-09Ju)

Q. Short note: Apoptosis. (DU-21Ja,20Nv/M, SU-19Nv)

Ans.

Apoptosis: Apoptosis is a type of cell death that is induced by a tightly regulated suicide program in which
cells destined to die activate intrinsic enzymes that degrade the cells’ genomic DNA and nuclear and
cytoplasmic proteins.

Because it is genetically regulated, apoptosis is sometimes referred to as programmed cell death.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/42)

Importance of apoptosis:
« It serves to remove unwanted, aged, or potentially harmful cells

* Removal of cells having irreversible DNA damage (from viruses, free radicals, chemicals etc.)
* Protect against neoplastic transformation.

Causes of apoptosis: (Important for VIVA)

Physiological causes: Death by apoptosis is a normal phenomenon that serves to eliminate cells that are no
longer needed. Apoptosis is important in the following physiologic situations:

---

#### 📄 Page 46

46 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY _

1. Removal of supernumerary cells (in excess of the required number) during development.

2. Involution of hormone-dependent tissues on hormone withdrawal, such as endometrial ej
breakdown during the menstrual cycle, ovarian follicular atresia in the menopause, the regression of
the lactating beast after weaning, and prostatic atrophy after castration.

3. Cell turnover in proliferating cell populations, such as immature lymphocytes in the bone marrow
and thymus, B-lymphocytes in germinal centers, and epithelial cells in intestinal crypts, so as to
maintain a constant cell number (homeostasis).

4. Elimination of potentially harmful self-reactive lymphocytes to prevent immune reactions against
one’s own tissues.

5. Death of host cells that have served their useful purpose, such as neutrophils in an acute
inflammatory response, and lymphocytes at the end of an immune response.

=,

Pathological causes: Apoptosis eliminates cells that are injured beyond repair without eliciting a host
reaction, thus limiting collateral tissue damage. Death by apoptosis is responsible for loss of cells in a variety
of pathologic states:

1. DNA damage: Radiation, cytotoxic anticancer drugs and hypoxia can damage DNA, either directly or
via production of free radicals.

2. Accumulation of misfolded proteins: Excessive accumulation of these proteins (because of gene
mutation or damaged caused by free radicals) in the ER leads to a condition called ER stress, which
culminates in apoptotic cell death.

3. Cell death in certain infections, particularly viral infections, such as in viral hepatitis or adenovirus
and HIV infections.

4. Pathologic atrophy in parenchymal organs after duct obstruction, such as occurs in the pancreas,
parotid gland & kidney.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/42,43)

‘). Give the morphologic features of apoptosis. (CMU-23M,16/12Ju, RU-11Ju,07Ja)
ins.
Morphologic features of apoptosis: (Very Important for VIVA)
1. Cell shrinkage: The cell is smaller in size; the cytoplasm is dense; and the organelles are more tightly packed.

2. Chromatin condensation: This is the most characteristic feature of apoptosis. The chromatin
aggregates peripherally, under the nuclear membrane, into dense masses of various shapes and sizes.

3. Formation of cytoplasmic blebs & apoptotic bodies: The apoptotic cell first shows extensive surface
blebbing, then undergoes fragmentation into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies composed of
cytoplasm and tightly packed organelles, with or without nuclear fragments.

4. Phagocytosis of apoptotic cells or cell bodies, usually by macrophages: The apoptotic bodies are
rapidly ingested by phagocytes and degraded by the phagocyte’s lysosomal enzymes.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/43)

Pathogenesis / mechanism of anontsle? Apoptosis is the regulated “rine haifa of cell death that serves to

eliminate unwanted and irreparably damaged cells, with the least possible host reaction. It results from the

activation of enzymes called caspases (Which causes enzymatic degradation of proteins and DNA) and

recognition and removal of dead cells by phagocytes.

A. Caspases activation: The process of caspases activation may be divided into an initiation phase, during
which some caspases become catalytically active and unleash a cascade of other caspases, and an
execution phase, during which the terminal caspases trigger cellular fragmentation.

1. Initiation phase: Two distinct pathways converge on caspase activation:
a) The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway- It is the major mechanism of apoptosis which is the
result of increased mitochondrial permeability with consequent release of death-inducing (pro-
apoptotic) molecules into the cytoplasm.

b) The extrinsic (death receptor-initiated) pathway- This pathway is initiated by engagement of
plasma membrane death receptors (members of TNF receptor family) on a variety of cells.

2. Execution phase: The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge to activate a caspase cascade that
mediates the final phase of apoptosis, called execution phase.
B. Recognition and removal of dead cells: By phagocytosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/44-46)

resembles necrosis morphologically, but like apoptosis is a genetically controlled form of cell death.

| The following features characterize necroptosis:

= Morphologically, and to some extent biochemically, it resembles necrosis, as both are characterized
__ by loss: of ATP, swelling of the cell. and organelles, generation. of reactive, oxygen species (ROS),
__ release of lysosomal enzymes, and ultimately rupture of the plasma membrane.

* Mechanistically, it is triggered by signal transduction pathways that culminate in cell death, a feature
similar to apoptosis.

| Because of these overlapping features, necroptosis is sometimes called programmed necrosis to
distinguish it from forms of necrosis driven passively by toxic or ischemic injury to the’cell: In sharp
‘contrast to apoptosis, the signals leading to necroptosis do not result in caspase activation, apd hence a
is also sometinics referredito as “‘caspase-independent” programmedicell death.

Q. Write about dry gangrene & wet gangrene.
Q. Give the pathogenesis of dry & wet gangrene. (CU-04Ja)
Ans.
Dry gangrene: Dry gangrene occurs due to lack of arterial blood supply, which may occur in:
1. Changes in arterial wall, e.g. atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis and thromboangitis obliterans
(Buerger’s disease). Commonest example is diabetic gangrene
2. Spasm of artery, e.g. Raynaud’s disease, ergot poisoning
3. Obstruction of the lumen of artery, e.g. thrombosis, embolism
4. Pressure from outside by tumour, tight plaster.

Pathogenesis and pathology: Dry gangrene occurs due to lack of arterial blood supply in the extremities,
particularly lower extremity. Usually gangrene starts at the great toe. The area is cold, dry, shriveled,
mummified, black due to iron sulphide, and foul smelling. Iron is derived from haemolysed red blood cells and
hydrogen sulphide is produced due to putrefaction by invaded saprophytes. Iron and hydrogen sulphide react
and form black iron sulphide. Dry gangrene usually occurred in distal part of extremity but the area of

gangrene may gradually extend proximally.

Wet gangrene: When bacterial infection is superimposed there is more liquefactive necrosis, and then it is
called as wet gangrene.

Sites:
1. Intestine is the commonest site. In strangulated hernia, intussusception, volvulus & thrombosis in

mesenteric artery

2. Bed sores
3. Lungs
4. Other sites: Vulva, scrotum, anterior abdominal wall, thigh etc.

Q. Explain the mechanism of left ventricular hypertrophy.

Ans.

Mechanism of left _ventricular hypertrophy: Increased mechanical work due to pressure or volume
overload (c.g. systemic hypertension or aortic stenosis), or trophic signals (e.g. those mediated through the
activation of B-adrenergic receptors) causes myocytes to increase in size (hypertrophy). Hypertrophy is
dependent upon increased cellular protein synthesis, which enables the assembly of additional sarcomeres.

The pattern of hypertrophy reflects the nature of the stimulus. In response to increases in pressure (c.g.
hypertension or aortic stenosis), ventricles develop pressure overload hypertrophy, which usually causes a
concentric increase in wall thickness. In pressure overload, new sarcomeres are predominantly assembled in

parallel to the long axes of cells, expanding the cross-sectional area of myocytes. In contrast, volume overload
hypertrophy is characterized by ventricular dilatation.

Q. A 70 years old man has hypertension for prolonged period. What type of adaptive change

Q. A 40 years old male presented with high blood pressure for prolonged period. What will
be the effect on myocardium? State its interpretation. (DU-09Ju)
Ans.

Effect on myocardium due to high blood pressure for prolonged period: Hypertrophy (left ventricular

hypertrophy).

(Note: In systemic hypertension there is pressure over-load causing myocardial stretch to the myocytes
leading to their hypertrophy. Pressure over-load hypertrophy, which usually causes a concentric increase
in wall thickness, and new sarcomeres are predominantly assembled in parallel to the long axes of cells
expanding the cross-sectional area of myocytes. As myocardial fibers are permanent (non-dividing) cells
so, hyperplasia ts impossible here, and due to increased work load, hypertrophy occurs. }

Interpretation: Left ventricular hypertrophy changes the structure and working ability (pumping action)
of the heart. The enlarged left ventricle may become weak or stiffen and may loss the elasticity.

Depending on severity, duration and underlying basis of hypertension, the patient may enjoy normal
longevity, or progressively may develop some complications, like-

Ischaemic heart disease (due tinsufficient supply of oxygen to the heart)

Heart failure (inability of the heart to pump enough blood to the body)

Arrhythmia (abnormal heart rhythm)

Stroke (due to insufficient supply of oxygen to the brain)

Sudden cardiac death (sudden, unexpected loss of heart function, breathing and consciousness)

Q. A 50 years old male has a blood pressure of 150/100 mm Hg. If this condition remains
untreated, what type of cellular adaptation will be seen in the heart? Write the
complications of that type of cellular adaption? (DU-08Ju)

Ans.

Cellular adaptation in the heart in response to long term systemic hypertension: Hypertrophy (left
ventricular hypertrophy)

(Note: Chronic haemodynamic overload like hypertension causes mechanical stretch, which causes
hypertrophy of cardiac muscle (as cardiac muscles cannot divide). }

Complications of LVH:
Ischaemic heart disease (due to insufficient supply of oxygen to the heart)
Heart failure (inability of the heart to pump enough blood to the body)
Arrhythmia (abnormal heart rhythm)
Stroke (duce to insufficient supply of oxygen to the brain)
Sudden cardiac death (sudden, unexpected loss of heart function, breathing and consciousness)

Q. A male of 70 years has a history of long standing essential systemic hypertension. What

Ans.
Cellular adaptation: Hypertrophy / pressure overload hypertrophy.

Organ: Heart (left ventricle).

Ans.

Atrophy: Atrophy is defined as a reduction in the size of an organ or tissue due to a decrease in cell size

and number.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/59)

Ni -<— Normal as (OQ Loss of structure
Ti Ov. | ene and shrinkage

Fig: Atrophy.

Types of atrophy: (Very Important for VIVA)
1. Physiologic atrophy:
a) Atrophy during early fetal development e.g. atrophy of notochord or thyroglossal duct.
b) The uterus decreases in size shortly after parturition (delivery).

2. Pathologic atrophy:
a) Localized: e.g. denervation atrophy, disuse atrophy, pressure atrophy.
b) Generalized: e.g. due to starvation, senile atrophy etc.

Common causes of atrophy:

1. Decreased workload (disuse atrophy) e.g. skeletal muscle atrophy in a patient restricted to complete
bed rest or when a broken limb is immobilized in a plaster cast.

2. Loss of innervations (denervation atrophy) e.g. Atrophy to the muscle fibers due to damage of the
supplying nerves.

3. Diminished blood supply: In late adult life, the brain may undergoe progressive atrophy, mainly
because of reduced blood supply (ischemia) as a result of atherosclerosis in cerebral vessels. This is
called senile atrophy which is seen in the brain and heart (tissues containing permanent cells).

4. Inadequate nutrition e.g. marked muscle wasting in profound protein-calorie malnutrition
(marasmus), chronic inflammation, cancer (cachexia).

5. Loss of endocrine stimulation e.g. loss of estrogen stimulation after menopause results in physiologic
atrophy of the endometrial, vaginal epithelium & breast.

6. Pressure atrophy: Atrophy occurs due to tissue compression for a long time e.g. an enlarging benign

tumor can cause atrophy in the surrounding compressed tissues.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/59)

(N.B: In chronic starvation, all organs are atrophied, except brain as it takes metabolic fuel from ketone
bodies.) **** For VIVA

Q. Describe the mechanism of atrophy. (DU-16Ju, SU-12Ju) (Important for ITEM)
Ans.

---

#### 📄 Page 60

60 arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

===
Mechanism of atrophy: Atrophy results from decreased protein synthesis and increased protein degradation
in cells.

1. Decreased protein synthesis: Protein synthesis decreases because of reduced trophic signals (c.y.
those produced by growth receptors), which enhance uptake of nutrients and increase mRNA
translation.

2. Increased protein degradation:
Example:

* Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases (e.g. cathepsins) and other enzymes that degrade endocytosed
proteins from the extracellular environment and the cell surface as well as some cellular
components.

* Ubiquitin-proteasome pathway is responsible for the degradation of many cytosolic and nuclear
proteins e.g. in cancer cachexia.

* Increased number of autophagic vacuoles: These are membrane-bound vacuoles within the cell
that contain fragments of cell components (e.g. mitochondria, ER) that destined for destruction and
into which the lysosomes discharge their hydrolytic contents. The cellular components are then digested.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/60)

Q. What is brown atrophy? (/mportant for VIVA for Honours Gainers)

Q. Short note: Brown atrophy. (RU-16Ju)

Ans.

Brown atrophy: Atrophy is accompanied by marked increase in number of autophagic vacuoles. The cellular
components in it are digested. Some of the cellular debris may resist digestion and persists as residual body.

An example of this is lipofuscin granules, when present in sufficient amount, impart a brown discoloration of
tissue that is termed as brown atrophy. Heart shows it in chronic starvation.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/60)

Q. Why metaplasia is called double edged sword? (DU-24M) (Very Important for VIVA)

Q. Why “Epithelial metaplasia is a double edged sword”? - Explain. (DU-17M,11/08Ja)

Ans.

Metaplasia is a two edged sword: Metaplasia is a two-edged sword, because it causes Ovo harmful effects at
the same time. They are-

1. Alteration of the normal physiological function: Due to squamous metaplasia in the respiratory
tract, an important protective mechanism-mucus seeretion-is lost.

2. Malignant transformation: The influences that predisposes to metaplasia, if present may induce
malignant transformation in metaplastic epithelium, e.g. squamous cell carcinoma can occur in
respiratory tract from metaplastic squamous cell.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/61)

Q. What are the merits and demerits of metaplasia? (DU-19Nv,18Nv/Ja)

Q. Mention the advantage and disadvantage of metaplasia. (RU-19Nv,09Ju) (Very Important
for VIVA)

Ans.

Advantage of metaplasia: (Survival of the cells in adverse environment).

The most common epithelial metaplasia is columnar to squamous, as occur in respiratory tract in response to
chronic imitation, and excretory ducts of the salivary glands, pancreas and bile duct due to stone. In all these
instances, the more rugged stratified squamous epithelium is able to survive under circumstances in which the
more fragile specialized columnar epithelium most likely would have succumbed.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/61)
Disadvantage of metaplasia: Metaplasia is a two-edged sword, because it causes two harmful effects at the
same time. They are-

1. Alteration of the normal physiological function: Due to squamous metaplasia in the respiratory
tract, an important protective mechanism-mucus secretion-is lost.

2. Malignant transformation: The influences that predisposes to metaplasia, if present may induce
malignant transformation in metaplastic epithelium, e.g. squamous cell carcinoma can occur in
respiratory tract from metaplastic squamous cell.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/61)

Intracellular Accumulation

Q. What do you mean by intracellular accumulations?

Q. What are the intracellular accumulations? (CU-03Ja)

Ans.

Intracellular_accumulations: It is one of the manifestations of metabolic derangements in cells which is
characterized by intracellular accumulation of abnormal amounts of various substances.

Intracellular accumulations are-
1. Normal cellular constituents: Watcr, lipids, protein & carbohydrates that accumulates in excess.
2. Abnormal substance:
i. Exogenous: Minerals or products of infectious agents. Such as-

* Carbon particles (in coal miners)
* Silica (silica factory workers)

ii. Endogenous: Product of abnormal synthesis of metabolism. Such as storage diseases, e.g.
* Glycogen storage disease
* Haemochromatosis (iron)
* Willson’s disease (copper)

3. Pigments: (Very Important for VIVA)
a. Exogenous: Carbon or coal dust, e.g. anthracosis (accumulation of C-particles in lungs)
b. Endogenous: Lipofuscin, melanin, hemosiderin, bilirubin etc.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/62-65)

Q. Mention the mechanisms of intracellular accumulations.
Ans

Mechanisms of intracellular_accumulations: There are four main pathways of abnormal intracellular
accumulations-

1. Inadequate removal of a normal substance (secondary to defects in mechanisms of packaging and
transport): e.g. fatty change (steatosis) in the liver.

2. Accumulation of an abnormal endogenous substance (as a result of genetic or acquired defects in
its folding, packaging, transport, or secretion): e.g. certain mutated forms of a,-antitrypsin.

3. Failure to degrade a metabolite (duc to inherited enzyme deficiencies): The resulting disorders are
called storage diseases.

4. Deposition and accumulation of an abnormal exogenous substance (when the cell has neither the

enzymatic machinery to degrade the substance nor the ability to transport it to other sites): e.g.
accumulation of carbon or silica particles.

(Ref: Robbins/10""/62)

Q. What are the gross and microscopic findings in a case of fatty liver? (CU-14Ja)

Morphology of fatty liver:
Gross:
= Enlarged liver with a tense, glistening capsule and rounded margins.

Microscopic: Characteristic feature is the presence of numerous lipid vacuoles in the cytoplasm of
hepatocytes.

* The vacuoles are initially small and are present around the nucleus (microvesicular).
* With progression of the process, the vacuoles become. larger pushing the nucleus to the periphery of
the cells (macrovesicular).
= Occasionally contiguous cells rupture, and the enclosed fat globules coalesce, producing so-called
fatty cysts.

Pathologic calcification: Pathologic calcification 1s the abaorenl tissue deposition of calcium salts,

Types: There are two forms of pathologic calcification-

Q. Define dystrophic calcification. (DU-05S) Give an account of dystrophic calcification. (SU-03Ja)

Q. Short note: Dystrophic calcification. (DU-06M, SU-13Ju,09Ja,08Ju)

Ans.

Dystrophic calcification: Deposition of calcium salts locally in dead or dying tissue is called dystrophic

calcification. It occurs despite normal serum levels of calcium and in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/65)

It is encountered in areas of necrosis, whether they are of coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive type, and in foci
of enzymatic necrosis of fat.

sites / examples of dystrophic calcification:
Aged or damaged heart valves
« Atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis
Tuberculous lymph node, Ghon focus
Area of necrosis, thrombus, infarct
Fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis
Papillary carcinoma of thyroid (Psammoma bodies).

Pathogenesis: The final common pathway is the formation of crystalline calcium phosphate mineral in the
form of an apetite. The process has two major phases-

1. Initiation (or nucleation): Formation of microcrystal, which can then propagate and perforate the
membrane.
Intracellularly- occurs in mitochondria of dead or dying cells

Extracellularly- occurs in phospholipid found in membrane bound vesicles, cartilage, and bone
(matrix vesicles).

2. Propagation: It depends on the concentration of Ca™ and PO, and the presence of inhibitors and other
proteins in the extracellular space.

Morphology:
* Macroscopic: The calcium salts appear macroscopically as fine, white granules or clumps, often felt

as gritty deposits. Sometimes a tuberculous lymph node is virtually converted to stone.

* Histologically: With the usual haematoxylin and eosin stain, the calcium salts have a basophilic
(blue), amorphous granular, sometimes clumped appearance. They can be intracellular, extracellular or
in both locations. Heterotrophic bone may form in the focus of calcification. The progressive
acquisition of outer layers may create lamellated configurations, called psamoma bodies.

Clinical significance:
« Itis a sign of previous cell injury

* Accelerated bone tumover (c.g. Paget disease)
* Immobilization

3. Vitamin D-related disorders, e.g.
* Vitamin-D intoxication
* Sarcoidosis
* Idiopathic hypercalcaemia of infancy (Williams syndrome)

4. Renal failure (CKD) — causes retention of phosphate, leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism

Cellular Aging

Q. What do you mean by cellular aging?

Q. Short note: Cellular aging.

Ans.

Cellular aging: Cellular aging is the result of a progressive decline in cellular function and viability caused
by genetic abnormalities and the accumulation of cellular and molecular damage due to the effects of exposure
to exogenous influences.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/67)

Individuals age because their cells age. Aging has important health consequences, because age is one of the
strongest independent risk factors for many chronic diseases, such as cancer, Alzheimer disease, and ischemic
heart disease.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/67)

Causes / mechanisms of cellular aging: Cellular aging results from a combination of following factors-

1. Accumulation of DNA damage (e.g. by free radicals)

2. Reduced capacity of the cell to divide (replicative senescence)
3. Defective protein homeostasis

4. Dysregulated nutrient sensing

Inflammation

Q. Define inflammation. (DU-06M, RMU-24M, SUST-21Nv,20Nv/M,19Nv/M,17M,15Ju,14/10Ja,
CU-08Ju,07Ja) (***Very Important for VIVA***)
Ans.
Inflammation: Inflammation is a response of vascularized tissues that delivers leukocytes and molecules of
host defense from the circulation to the sites of infection and cell damage in order to eliminate the offending agents.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/71)
Or,
Inflammation is a complex response of vascularized tissues to infections and damaged tissues that brings
cells and molecules of host defense from the circulation to the sites where they are needed, in order to
eliminate the offending agents.
(Ref: Robbins/9'"/69)
Or,
Inflammation is a complex reaction in tissues that consists mainly of responses of blood vessels and
leukocytes.
(Ref: Robbins/8'"/44)
Or,
Inflammation is a complex reaction to injurious agents such as microbes and damaged, usually necrotic,
cells that consist of vascular responses, migration and activation of leukocytes, and systemic reactions.
(Ref: Robbins/7"/48)

(N.B: The suffix -itis after an organ denotes inflammation in that site, such as appendicitis, conjunctivitis, or
meningitis etc., but there are exceptions, e.g. boil, abscess, pneumonia etc.)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/71)

Q. What are the major components of inflammation? (***Very Important for VIVA***)
Ans

Major components of inflammation: Inflammation has 2 main components:
1. Vascular - Blood vessels

2. Cellular - Leukocytes (White Blood Cells).

Vascular (exudative) component involves dilatation of blood vessels (causing redness and heat) and
movement of fluid containing many selected proteins such as fibrin and immunoglobulins (antibodies) from
the intravascular space into the extravascular damaged tissue / site of infection (vascular leakage) giving

rise to edema (exudative edema) or swelling. The swelling distends the tissues, compresses nerve endings, and
So causes pain.

Cellular component involves the movement of leukocytes (White Blood Cells) from blood vessels into the
site of infection / focus of injury (leukocyte extravasation), and act as phagocytes, picking up microbes, dead
cells, foreign bodies and other unwanted materials in the tissues.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/72; Shahzad G. Raja/258)

Introduction to Acute & Chronic Inflammation

Q. Define acute inflammation. (***Very Important for VIVA***)

Ans.

Acute inflammation: Acute inflammation is a rapid, often self-limited response to offending agents that are
readily eliminated (such as many bacteria & fungi, and dead cells), typically develops within minutes or
hours and is of short duration (lasting for several hours to a few days), characterized by the exudation of
fluid and plasma proteins (edema) and the emigration of leukocytes, predominantly neutrophils (also
called polymorphonuclear leukocytes).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/73)

If the offending stimulus is eliminated, the reaction subsides, and residual injury is repaired.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/73)

Q. Write down the causes of inflammation / acute inflammation. (V.V.4 for VIVA)
Q. What are the stimuli for acute inflammation? (SU-13Ju)

Ans.
Causes of inflammation / acute inflammation: Acute inflammatory reactions are triggered by a variety of
stimuli-

1. Infections (bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic) and microbial toxins

2. Tissue necrosis from any cause, including-

= ischemia (reduced blood flow)

® trauma

* physical and chemical injury (c.g. thermal injury, as in burs or frostbite; irradiation; exposure to
some environmental chemicals)

Foreign bodies (splinters, dirt, sutures)

4. Immune reactions (hypersensitivity reactions), in which the normally protective immune system
damages the individual’s own tissues.

Components of acute inflammation: Acute inflammation has three major components-

1. Dilatation of small blood vessels leading to an increase in blood flow
2. Increased permeability of the microvasculature enabling plasma proteins and leukocytes to leave

3. Emigration of leukocytes from the microcirculation, their accumulation in the focus of injury,
and their activation to eliminate the offending agent.

Q. What are the fates / outcomes of acute inflammation? (DU-15Ju, CMU-23M,06S, RMU-
21M,17Ju)

Q. Short note: Fates of acute inflammation. (CMU-22Nv, RU-18M) (V.V./. for VIVA)

Ans.

Fates / outcomes of acute inflammation: All acute inflammatory reactions typically have one of three
outcomes-

1. Complete resolution (restoration of the site of acute inflammation to normal)

= When the injury is limited or short-lived
= When there has been little tissue destruction
= When the damaged parenchymal cells can regenerate.

Resolution involves removal of cellular debris and microbes by macrophages and resorption of
edema fluid by lymphatics, followed by regeneration of the damaged tissue.

2. Healing by connective tissue replacement (scarring, or fibrosis). This occurs when the injured
tissue cannot regenerate.

3. Progression to chronic inflammation. This occurs owing to the persistence of the injurious agents or
to some interference of the normal process of healing (e.g. pneumonia to chronic lung abscess).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/95)

(N.B: Most of the time, when the acute inflammation fulfills it’s goals, that is to stop or contain the offending
agent and also to remove the damaged tissue, usually acute inflammation subsides, However if the acute
inflammatory reaction fails to remove the offending agent, the reaction may progress to a further prolonges
Phase, and that is known as chronic inflammation.)

Q. Define chronic inflammation. (RMU-21Nv,18Nv/Ja,17M,16Ju,13Ja) (*Very Important for

VIVA*)

Ans.

Chronic inflammation: Chronic inflammation is a response of prolonged duration (weeks or months) in
which inflammation, tissue injury and attempts at repair coexist in varying combinations.

Example: Rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, tuberculosis, and chronic lung diseases.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/96)

Q. What are the causes of chronic inflammation? (RU-21/19Nv,17M, 1 6Ju, 12/08Ja)

1. Persistent infections by microorganisms those are difficult to cradicate, such as mycobacteria & certain
viruses, fungi, and parasites.

2. Hypersensitivity diseases {e.g. autoimmune (such as rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis) and
allergic diseases (such as bronchial asthma) }.

Acute Inflammation

Q. What are the morphological patterns of acute inflammation? (RMU-23M, CU-15/14Ju,06S)
Q. Write the morphological types of acute inflammation with example of each. (CMU-21Nv)
Q. Classify acute inflammation morphologically. (SU-14Ju, RU-13Ja)

Ans.

Morphological types of acute inflammation:

1. Serous inflammation: It is marked by the exudation of cell poor fluid into spaces created by cell
injury or into body cavities lined by the peritoneum, pleura, or pericardium. Accumulation of fluid
in these cavities is called an effusion (e.g. pleural effusion). The skin blister resulting from a burn or
viral infection is another example.

2, Fibrinous inflammation: Fibrinous exudate develops when the vascular leaks are large enough to
pass large molecules such as fibrinogen out of the blood, e.g. fibrinous pericarditis after acute
myocardial infarction; also occur in meninges, pleura etc.

3. Purulent (suppurative) inflammation and abscess:

* Purulent (suppurative) inflammation is characterized by the production of pus or purulent
exudates consisting of neutrophils, the liquefied debris of necrotic cells, and edema fluid. It is
caused by pyogenic (pus-producing) bacteria e.g. staphylococci. A common example of an acute
suppurative inflammation is acute appendicitis.

« Abscesses are localized collections of pus caused by suppuration buried in a tissue, an organ, or
a confined space. They are produced by seeding of pyogenic bacteria into a tissue.

4. Ulcers: An ulcer is a local defect, or excavation, of the surface of an organ or tissue that is produced
by the sloughing (shedding) of inflamed necrotic tissue e.g. peptic ulcer of stomach or duodenum (in

which acute and chronic inflammation coexist), pressure sore, leg ulcer etc.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/93)

Q. What are the vascular changes / vascular events occur in acute inflammation? (DU-
15/14Ju, 12Ja,08Ju, RMU-23M, 13/12Ju, CMU-21 Nv, 16/07Ja, SU-15Ju)
Q. Describe the vascular changes occur in acute inflammation. (SU-20Nv)
Q. Briefly narrate reactions of blood vessels in acute inflammation. (RU-19M, 1 1Ju)
Ans,
1) Vascular events:
a) Change in vascular flow and caliber:
i) Vasodilation (induced by several chemical madiators, particularly histamine & nitric oxide acting
on vascular smooth muscle)

ii) Increased arterial blood flow {results in heat & redness (erythema) at the site of inflammation}

b) Increased vascular permeability of the micro-vasculature leading to the escape of a protein-rich
fluid (exudate) into the extra-vascular tissue (vascular leakage), causing edema.

c) Slowing of blood flow or stasis (combined effect of vasodilation and increased vascular permeability).

{loss of fluid due to vascular leakage and increased vessel diameter results in (i) concentreation of red
cells in small vessels (ii) increased viscosity of blood (iii) slowing of the blood flow — engorgement of
small vessels with slowly moving red cells (stasis)}.

2) Cellular events:
a) Emigration of leukocytes from the micro-circulation (leukocyte extravasation) and their
accumulation in the focus of injury.
b) Phagocytosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/75)

(N.B: Increased vascular permeability is a hallmark of acute inflammation.) (*V.V.I. for VIVA*)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/76)

Q. Write the mechanism of increased vascular permeability in inflammation. (CU-10Ja)
Q. How increased vascular permeability occurs in acute inflammation? (SU-15Ja)

Q. Briefly outline the process of vascular leakage. (SU-14/10Ja)

Q. How blood vessels become leaky in acute inflammation? (SU-13Ju)

Ans.
Mechanism _of_ increased _vascular_permeability (vascular leakage) in acute inflammation: Several

mechanisms are responsible for the increased permeability of microvasculature with the outpouring of
protein-rich fluid into the extravascular tissues:

1. Contraction of endothelial cells: It results in increased gap between the endothelial cells & through
these widened pores the fluid escapes.

= It is the most common mechanism of vascular leakage.

= Occurs rapidly/immediately (also called immediate transient response) and is usually short-lived
(15 to 30 minutes)

» Elicited by the chemical mediators e.g. histamine, bradykinin & leukotrienes.

2. Endothelial injury (direct damage to the endothelium): Endothelial cells are damaged & broken
down by severe injuries (such as thermal burns, microbes & microbial toxins etc.). Through these
damaged endothelial cells, the fluid escapes out of the vascular lumen. It occurs immediately after
injury and is sustained for several hours (long-lived) until the damaged vessels are thrombosed or
repaired.

3. Leukocyte-mediated endothelial injury: The leukocytes (neutrophils) adhering to endothelium,
they themselves can injure the endothelium by releasing toxic oxygen species and proteolytic

4. Transcytosis (transport of fluids and proteins through the endothelial cells): This process involves
intracellular channels. Increased transport of fluids and proteins through these intracellular channels
stimulated by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) which promotes vascular leakage
(leakage through the endothelial cells).

Q. Define extravasation. (SU-18M) What are the steps of extravasation of leukocytes in

inflammation? (DU-11Ju)

Ans.

Cellular events in acute inflammation: (Very Important for VIVA)

A. Leukocyte extravasation: The sequence of events in the journey of leukocytes (neutrophils &

monocytes) from the vessel lumen to the interstitial tissue, called extravasation is a multi-step
process that is mediated and controlled by adhesion molecules and cytokines called chemokines.

This process can be divided into the following steps:

1. In the lumen:

* Margination: Early in inflammation, as stasis develops, the leukocytes which normally are in
the centre assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface. This process of
leukocyte accumulation is called margination.

Margination is basically a redistribution of leukocytes along the margins of the blood vessels.

* Rolling: Immediately after margination, the leukocytes adhere transiently (loose adhesion) to
the endothelium; detach and bind again, and then detach and bind again; and this particular
process is referred to as rolling. This rolling interaction is mediated by a family of proteins
called selectins.

" Adhesion: Firm attachment of leukocytes to the endothelium is called adhesion which is
mediated by a family of leukocyte surface of proteins called integrin.

2. Across the endothelium: Transmigration (also called diapedesis) (migration of the leukocytes
through the inter-endothelial spaces by squeezing themselves is called transmigration or diapedesis).

which is mediated by chemo-attractants).

B. Phagocytosis {ingestion & destruction of the injurious agents (microbes/necrotic tissue/foreign
bodies) by the leucocytes, mostly neutrophils and macrophages}.

Q. Short note: Chemokines. (DU-04M)
Ans.
Chemokines: Chemokines are chemo-attractant cytokines which play a very crucial role in leukocyte
migration.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/90)
Types: About 40 different chemokines have been identified. They are classified into four major groups,
according to the arrangement of the conserved cytokine (C) residues in the mature proteins.

1. C-X-C chemokines (also called a-chemokines)
2. C-C chemokines (also called B- chemokines)
3. C chemokines (also called y-chemokines)

4. CX,C chemokines.

Functions of chemokines: Chemokines have two main functions-

1. Stimulate leukocyte recruitment in inflammation
2. Control the normal migration of cells through various tissues.

Q. What are the acute inflammatory cells? (RMU-24M)
Q. Enumerate the functions of acute inflammatory cells.
Ans.’
Acute inflammatory cells: (Very Important for VIVA)
1. Neutrophil (within 6-24 hours)
2. Macrophages (within 24-48 hours)
3. Eosinophil (in case of parasitic infection)
4. Lymphocyte (in case of viral infection)

Functions of acute inflammatory cells:
Neutrophil:
1. Phagocytosis (within 6-24 hours) & killing of the ingested organism by intracellular killing
mechanism, that is by formation of phagolysosome.

2. Extracellular release of granules or cytotoxic substances by neutrophil can also occur.

Macrophage:
1. Initiation and amplification of the inflammatory response
2. Phagocytosis (within 24-48 hours)
3. Antigen presentation to the helper T-cell (antigen presenting cell)
4. Production of cytokines
« IL-1 that activates the CD4+ T cells
« TNF-a that takes part in inflammatory reaction.

Eosinophil:
1. Can phagocytose & kill the microorganisms by intracellular killing mechanism.
2. They have granules that contain major basic proteins that are toxic to parasites, so beneficial in
controlling parasitic infection.
3. Eosinophil secretes histaminase, which inactivates histamine released by basophil & mast cell.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/80,81 + 8'"/72)

* Attach more firmly to adhesion molecules.

(macrophages), as they survive longer and can proliferate in tissues.

Q. Short note: Phagocytes. (DU-24Nv, CU-19Nv, SU-19M,13Ju, RU-18M, 12/10Ja)
Ans.

Phagocytosis: Phagocytosis is the process by which phagocytic cells, mainly neutrophil and macrophage
recognize and then engulf and dispose off foreign particles (e.g. bacteria).

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Steps of phagocytosis: Phagocytosis involves three sequential steps-

1. Recognition and attachment of the particle to be ingested by the leukocyte
2. Engulfment, with subsequent formation of a phagocytic vacuole
3. Killing of the microbe and degradation of the ingested material.

1. Recognition & attachment: Phagocytosis is initiated by recognition of the particles by receptors
expressed on the leukocytes surface, such as mannose receptors, scavenger receptors etc.

The efficacy of phagocytosis is greatly enhanced when microbes are opsonized by specific opsonin
proteins for which the phagocytes expressed high affinity receptors. Major opsonins are IgG antibodics,
C3b component of complement, and certain plasma lectins (e.g. mannose binding lectin, collectin etc.).

2. Engulfment: Extension of cytoplasm (pseudopods) flows around the particle to be engulfed, eventually
resulting in complete enclosure of the particle within a phagosome, created by the plasma membrane of

the cell. The phagosome fuses with one or more lysosomes of the cell and form bigger vacuole called
phagolysosome.

3. Killing and degradation: (Very Important for VIVA)
Killing:
a. O,-dependent free-radical mediated mechanism: Phagocytosis — ©, consumption —
glycogenolysis — {glucose oxidation via HMP shunt — production of reactive oxygen species.

* Hypochlorite (HOC) is a potent antimicrobial agent, that destroy microbial agents by halogenation

ii. MPO-deficient system: The organisms are killed by virtue of the formation of superoxide,
hydroxyl radicals and singlet-oxygen.

Q. What do you mean by opsonization?
Ans.
Opsonization: Opsonization refers to the attachment of antigen molecules to the surface of phagocytes by the
help of some special molecules (e.g. immunoglobulins & complement).
Or,
Opsonization is the process of coating of microbe to target it for phagocytosis.
Or,
Opsonization is the process of attachment of any substance to antigen (or microorganism) that facilitates
phagocytosis of that antigen (or microorganism), i.e. makes it more easily ingested by phagocytic cells.

Significance of opsonization: Opsonization greatly enhances phagocytosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/80; Lange Microbiology/14"/515; Lecture ShSMC)

Q. Short note: Opsonin. (DU-06/04Ja, RU-19Nv, 14Ju)
Ans.
Onsonins: These are the substances which attach antigens to phagocytes.
Or,
An opsonin is any molecule that acts as a binding enhancer for the process of phagocytosis.

Examples: The opsonins are- (Very Important for VIVA & MCQ)

1. IgG

2. C3b

3. Plasma lectins (e.g. MBL)
4. CRP

5. Fibrinogen.

Significance of opsonins: Facilitate phagocytosis, i.e. cause more effective phagocytosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/80; Lange Microbiology/14"/515; Lecture ShSMC)

Q. Write down the functions of vasoactive amines, (DU-10Ja)
Q. What is the role of histamine in inflammation? (DU-0SM)
Q. Short note: Vasoactive amines.
Ans.
Vasoactive amines:

1. Histamine

2. Serotonin

(N.B: Histamine and serotonin are the two major vasoactive amines, so named because they have important
actions on blood vessels. They are stored as preformed molecules in cells and are therefore among the first
mediators to be released during inflammation.)

Histamine:
Source: Mast cell, basophils, platelets (the mchest source of histamines is the mast cell)

Release of histamine: Histamine is present in mast cell granules and is released by mast cel] degranulation in
response to a variety of stimuli like-

* Physical injury (trauma, cold or heat)

* Binding of antigen to IgE antibodies displayed on the surfaces of mast cells (immediate

hypersensitivity/allergic reactions)

* Anaphylatoxins (C3a and C5a)

= Histamine-releasing proteins derived from leukocytes

= Neuropeptides (substance P)

* Cytokines (IL-1, IL-8)

Role of histamine:

1. Vasodilatation: Histamine causes dilation of arterioles (it, however, constricts large arteries)

2. Increased vascular permeability: Histamine is considered to be the principal mediator of the
immediate transient phase of increased vascular permeability, producing interendothelial gaps in
venules

3. Endothelial activation

4. Bronchoconstriction (due to smooth muscle spasm)

5. Hypersecretory state in nasal, bronchial, and gastric glands.

Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine):

Source: Platelets, certain neuroendocrine cells (such as in the gastrointestinal tract).

Role / functions of serotonin: Similar to those of histamine. But, its primary function is as a neurotransmitter
in the gastrointestinal tract. \t is also a vasoconstrictor, but the importance of this action in inflammation is
unclear.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/86)

Complements

Q. Define complement.

Ans.

Complement: Complement is a collective term used to designate a group of serum proteins, mainly
synthesized by the liver, at least 20 in numbers, which normally remain in inactive form and when activated
they act in concert in an orderly sequence to exert their biological effects.

(Ref: Prof. Akram/4"/222)
Or,
The complement system is a collection of plasma proteins that function mainly in host defense against
microbes and in pathologic inflammatory reactions.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/90)

Q. What are the components of complement system?
Ans.
Components of complement: There are more than 20 components of complement system of which
followings are important:

1. Cl, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7, C8, C9

2. Factor B, Factor D, Factor H, Factor I

3. Properdin, Cl inhibitor

4. C4-binding protein and S-protein.

(Ref: Prof. Akram/4"/223; Robbins/10"/90)

Q. Name the pathways of complement activation.
Ans

Pathways of complement activation: There are 3 pathways of complement activation-
1. Classical pathway (activated by antigen-antibody complex)

2. Alternative pathway {activated by bacterial endotoxin, or lipopolysaccharide (LPS), fungal cell wall,
viral envelope, cobra venom, aggregated IgA}

3. Lectin pathway (activated by plasma mannose binding lectin).
(Ref: LANGE review/15"/537; Robbins/10'/90)

Q. Write the functions of complement in inflammation. (DU-06M, RU-18/17Nv,11Ja, SU-
09Ju,08Ja)
Q. Write the role of complement in acute inflammation. (RU-17/16Ja, SU-14Ju)

Q. Mention the role of anaphylatoxins in vascular changes.
Ans.

Role of complement in inflammation:
1. Vascular phenomena: C3a, C4a and C5a act as anaphylatoxin which causes release of histamine
from mast cells leading to vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.

2. Chemotaxis: CSa acts as chemotactic factor because they can attract neutrophils.
3. Opsonization & phagocytosis: C3b acts as opsonin, which favour phagocytosis.

4. Cell lysis / cytolysis: The deposition of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) on cells makes these
cells permeable to water and ions and results in death (lysis) of the cells.

5. Release of other mediators: CSa activates arachidonic acid metabolism.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/90,91)

Q. State the consequences of complement activation. (DU-09Ja)
Ans.

Consequences of complement activation:

---

#### 📄 Page 98

arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

1. Cell lysis / cytolysis: Insertion of the CSb-9 (membrane attack complex) into the cell membrane lead;
to killing or lysis of many types of cells including RBC, bacteria, enveloped virus, virus infected cells,
malarial parasite and tumor cells.

2. Opsonization & phagocytosis (C3b): C3b (and to a lesser extent C4b) can acts as opsonin, which
favour phagocytosis.

3. Anaphylaxis (C3a, C4a and CSa): C3a, C4a and CSa are anaphylatoxins which cause degranulation
of mast cells with the release of mediators e.g. histamine that cause anaphylaxis (skin rash,
hypotension, bronchoconstriction, diarrhoea & shock).

4. Chemotaxis (CSa): C5a acts as chemotactic factor because they can attract neutrophils.
5. Virus neutralization (C1 & C4): Cl & C4 play a role in neutralization of virus.

6. Stimulation of antibody production: The binding of C3b to its receptors on the surface of activated
B-cells greatly enhances antibody production.
Activation of B lymphocyte: By serving as a 2™ signal.

8. Removal of harmful immune complexes from the body (C3b, C4b): C3b and to a lesser extent of
C4b help to remove harmful immune complexes from the body.
(Ref: Prof. Akram/4"/234; LANGE review/15"/537; Robbins/10"/90,91)

Arachidonic Acid Metabolites

Q. What are the arachidonic acid metabolites? (SU-13Ja)

Q. Describe briefly the generation of arachidonic acid metabolites and their role in
inflammation. (DU-03Ja, RU-03Ja)

Q. Write the role of arachidonic acid metabolites in inflammation. (SU-19M)

Q. Mention role of arachidonic acid derivatives in acute inflammation. (RU-16Ju)

Q. Describe the pathway of synthesis of arachidonic acid metabolites. (SU-12Ja)

Q. Short note: Arachidonic acid metabolites. (RU-08Ja)

Q. Short note: Prostaglandin. (RU-15Ja)

Ans.

Arachidonic acid metabolism: Arachidonic acid (AA) is a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid that is
derived from dietary sources or by conversion from the essential fatty acid linoleic acid. It does not occur free
in the cell but is normally esterified in membrane phospholipids through the action of cellular phospholipases,

mainly phospholipaseA;, which may be activated by mechanical, chemical, and physical stimuli or by other
mediators (e.g. C5a).

Arachidonic acid metabolites (ecosanoides) are synthesized by two major classes of enzymes-

1. Cyclooxygenases (which generates prostaglandin, prostacycline, and thromboxane-A;)
2. Lipoxygenases (which produce leukotrienes and lipoxins)

Pathway of synthesis of arachidonic acid metabolites:
1. Cyclooxygenase pathway: Produces prostaglandin, prostacycline, and thromboxane-A).
2. Lipoxygenase pathway: Produces leukotrienes and lipoxins.

Arachidonic acid metabolites: (Very Important for VIVA)
1. Prostaglandins: PGD,, PGE, PGF2, PGG2, PGH2, PGI, (prostacyclin), thromboxane-A, (TXAz2).
2. Leukotrienes: LTAy, LTBs, LTC,, LTD, LTE.
3. Lipoxins: LXA,, LXBy.

Q. Define exudation (SU-18M) & exudate. (RU-19Nv, 12Ju,09Ja)
Ans.

Exudation: Escape of fluid, proteins, and blood cells from the vascular system into the interstitial tissue or
body cavities is known as exudation. It occurs usually in inflammation.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/75)
Or,
Exudation is the leaking of blood constituents from blood vessels into interstitial tissue with formation of
exudate.

(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/15)

Exudate: An exudate is an inflammatory extravascular fluid that has a high protein concentration,
contains cellular debris, and has a high specific gravity (above 1.020).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/75)

This edema fluid results from increased vascular permeability caused by inflammation.
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/41)

Nice to Know:
Mechanism of formation of exudate:

Acute inflammation
Alteration in vascular caliber

Increase in blood flow

Structural change in the microvasculature

Characteristics of exudate: (Very Important for VIVA)

## Inflammatory edema
Resulting from increased vascular permeability

Types of exudate: Exudate consists of: (1) Fluid exudate, and (2) Cellular exudate.

Importance of exudate: Its presence implies that there is an increase in the permeability of small blood
vessels triggered by some sort of tissue injury and an ongoing inflammatory reaction.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/75; Prof. Khaleque/37; BRS Pathology/5'"/41)

Q. What are the effects of fluid exudate?
Q. Write down the function of fluid exudate in inflammation?
Ans.
Effects of fluid exudate: (V/IVA DMC)
I. Beneficial Effects.
(1) Dilutes the irritant and thus lowers injurious effect
(2) Helps to nourish the greatly increased number of cells
(3) Brings chemical mediators, natural immune products, antibodies, antimicrobial agents (c.g
antibiotics) and anti-enzymes which inhibit proteolytic enzymes
(4) Low pH due to lactic acid, formed by neutrophils inhibits bacterial growth
(5) If fibrin is produced, it acts as barrier against invasion of microorganisms, helps in surface
phagocytosis, and acts as scaffold in repair process
(6) Microorganisms and toxins are carried by the exudate to local lymph nodes where the antigens
stimulate immune response.

II. Harmful Effects:
(1) Acts as a splendid medium for bacterial growth due to high protein content
(2) An excess fibrin may lead to adhesion
(3) Causes pain by chemical mediators like bradykinin and prostaglandins.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/15; Robbins/10"/75)

Q. Define transudate. (RU-19Nv,12Ju)

Q. Short note: transudate.
Ans.
Transudate: A transudate is a fluid with low protein content (most of which is albumin), little or no cellular

material, and low specific gravity (less than 1.012).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/75; BRS Pathology/5”/41)
