Pus, Abscess & Ulcer

Q. Define pus. What is the composition of pus?
Ans,
Pus: Pus is a purulent inflammatory exudate consisting of neutrophils, the liquefied debris of necrot,
cells, and edema fluid.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/94)
Or,

Pus is a purulent inflammatory exudate consisting of profuse healthy leukocytes (mostly neutrophils) and pus
cells (dead leukocytes), protein-rich fluid exudate and fibrin, necrotic cells, tissue debris and, in many cases
microbes (many of which are living).

(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/19)

Composition of pus:
Healthy leukocytes (mostly neutrophils)

Pus cells (dead leukocytes, mostly neutrophils)
Protein-rich fluid exudate (edema fluid) and fibrin
Liquefied debris of necrotic cells

Tissue debris

Organisms (many of which are living).

a

(Ref: Robbins/10"/94; Prof. Khaleque/19)

Q. Define abscess.

Q. Short note: Abscess.

Ans.

Abscess: Abscesses are localized collections of pus caused by suppuration buried in a tissue, an organ, ora
confined space.

Cause: They are produced by deep seeding of pyogenic bacteria into a tissue.

Histology:
1. A central region that appears as a mass of necrotic leukocytes & tissue cells.

2. There is a zone of preserved neutrophils around this necrotic focus.

3. Outside this region vascular dilation & parenchymal & fibroblastic proliferation occur, indicating the
beginning of repair.

4. In time it may become walled off and ultimately replaced by connective tissue.

Example: Skin abscess (boil or furuncle), dental abscess, perianal abscess, breast abscess, liver abscess,
splenic abscess, cold abscess in TB, lung abscess etc.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/94)

Q. Define ulcer.

Ans.

Ulcer: An ulcer is a local defect, or excavation, of the surface of an organ or tissue that is produced by the
sloughing (shedding) of inflamed necrotic tissue.

Common sites: It is most commonly encountered in-
1. The mucosa of the mouth, stomach, intestines, or genitourinary tract, and
2. The skin and subcutaneous tissue of the lower extremities in older persons who have circulatory
disturbances that predispose to extensive ischemic necrosis.

Example: Peptic ulcer of the stomach or duodenum, mouth ulcers (aphthous ulcers or canker sores), pressure
ulcers (bedsores or decubitus ulcers), diabetic foot ulcers, genital ulcers, arterial / venous ulcers, corneal ulcers

etc.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/94)

Chronic Inflammation

Q. What are the types of chronic inflammation?
Ans.
Tvpes of chronic inflammation:
1. Chronic specific inflammation: It is histologically distinctive. Granuloma is the hallmark of
chronic specific inflammation (e.g. tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis etc.).

2. Chronic non-specific inflammation: It is not histologically distinctive. There is non-specific chronic
inflammatory reaction with formation of granulation tissue and healing by fibrosis. Here, there is no
granuloma (e.g. chronic osteomyelitis, chronic ulcer, lung abscess etc.).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/96; Prof. Khaleque/27; Harsh Mohan/7"”135)

Q. What are the chronic inflammatory cells? (RMU-24M) Give their functions.
Ans.
Chronic inflammatory cells:

1. Macrophage (dominant cellular player in chronic inflammation)

2. Lymphocytes

3. Plasma cells

4. Mast cells

5. Eosinophils.

Functions of chronic inflammatory cells:

Macrophage: Please see below.

Lymphocyte:
1. Cell-mediated immunity (by T- lymphocyte)
2. Antibody-mediated (humoral) immunity (by B-lymphocyte)
3. Delayed hypersensitivity reaction.

Mast cells:
1. Anaphylactic reaction (type-I hypersensitivity), by release of histamine
2. Participate in both acute and persistent inflammatory reaction.

Plasma cells: Production of antibodies.

Eosinophils:
1. Phagocytose & kill the microorganisms by intracellular killing mechanism.
2. Beneficial in controlling parasitic infection.
3. Secretes histaminase, which inactivates histamine released by basophil & mast cell.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/97)

Q. Short note: Granuloma. (SU-20M,19Nv,17M, RU-19M,18M/Ja,17M,11Ju)
Ans.
: A microscopic aggregation of epithelioid (epithelial-like) cells, usually surrounded by a collar of
tymphocytes is referred to as granuloma.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/214)
Or,
A granuloma is a focus of chronic inflammation consisting of a microscopic aggregation of activated
macrophages that are transformed into epithelial-like cells (epithelioid cells), surrounded by a collar of
mononuclear leukocytes, principally lymphocytes and occasionally plasma cells.
(Ref: Robbins/8"/73; Lecture SSMC)
Or,
Granuloma is a focus of chronic inflammation consisting of a microscopic aggregation of macrophages and
epithelioid cells which are modified macrophages surrounded by a colar of mononuclear leucocytes,
principally lymphocytes and occasionally plasma cells.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/27)

Common causes of granuloma formation:
® Tuberculosis (granuloma is a hallmark of TB)

Leprosy

Syphilis

Cat-scratch disease
Sarcoidosis

Crohn’s disease

Brucellosis

Fungal infections

Berylliosis
Lymphogranuloma venereum.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/101)

Histological features of granuloma: (Very Important for VIVA)

1. Modified activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) in granulomas have a pink granular cytoplasm
with indistinct cell boundaries, often appearing to merge into one another.

2. The aggregates of epitheloid macrophages are surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes.

Older granulomas develop an enclosing rim of fibroblasts and connective tissue.

4. Frequently, multiple activated macrophages fuse to form multinucleated giant cells in the periphery
or sometimes in the center of granulomas.

5. These giant cells may attain diameters of 40-50 pum. They consists of a large mass of cytoplasm and
many nuclei arranged either peripherally (Langhans-type giant cell) or haphazardly (foreign-body
type giant cell).

»

(Ref: Robbins/10"/100)

Classification of granuloma: (Very Important for VIVA)
A. Pathological (etiological) classification: There are two types of granulomas-

1. Foreign body granulomas: Foreign body granulomas are incited by inert foreign bodies, which
induce inflammation in the absence of T-cell mediated immune responses. Typically, they form
around material such as tale (associated with intravenous drug abuse), sutures or other fibers, wood
splinter etc. that are large enough to preclude phagocytosis by a macrophage and are not

---

#### 📄 Page 110

110 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

a,
immunogenic, so they do not incite any specific immune response. Epithelioid cells & giant ce),
form and are apposed to the surface and encompass the foreign body. The foreign material can usually
be identified in the center of the granuloma.

2. Immune granulomas: They are caused by a variety of agents that are capable of inducing ,
persistent T cell-mediated immune response. This type of immune response usually produce,
granulomas when the inciting agent is difficult to eradicate, such as a persistent microbe. In such
responses, activated Th1 cells produce cytokines such as IFN-y, which activates macrophages and
transforms them into epithelioid cells & multinucleate giant cells.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/100)
B. Morphological classification:

1. Caseating granuloma: Associated with central caseation necrosis, e.g. soft tubercle of tuberculosis
and brucellosis.

2. Non-caseating granuloma: It occurs in hard tubercle of tuberculosis, tuberculoid leprosy,
sarcoidosis, foreign body granuloma, schistosomiasis, syphilis.

3. Suppurative granuloma: Associated with pus formation, e.g. lymphogranuloma venereum, cat-
scratch disease.

4. Diffuse granulomatous inflammation: It is seen in lepromatous leprosy.
(Ref: Lecture DMC; Prof. Khaleque/27)

Q. What is epithelioid cell? (CU-18Nv)

Ans.

Epithelioid cells: Epithelioid cells are modified activated macrophages having abundant cytoplasm
resembling epithelial cells found in certain granulomas (granulomatous inflammation). These cells show little
Phagocytic activity and may fuse with one another to form multinucleated giant cells.

Q. Draw and label the microscopic appearance of tubercular lymph node / TB lymphadenitis.
Ans.

Morphology of granuloma / caseating granuloma / soft tubercle of tuberculosis:

1. A granuloma comprises an organized aggregation of activated macrophages; because they resemble
epithelial cells, they are called epithelioid cells.

2. Epithelioid cells have a pink granular cytoplasm with indistinct cell boundaries, often appearing to
merge into one another

3. The aggregates of epitheloid macrophages are surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes.

4. Frequently, multiple activated macrophages fuse to form multinucleated giant cells in the periphery
or sometimes in the center of granulomas.

5. These giant cells may attain diameters of 40-50 pm. They consists of a large mass of cytoplasm and
many nuclei arranged either peripherally (Langhans-type giant cell) or haphazardly (foreign-body
type giant cell).

6. Caseating granulomas / soft tubercle (the characteristic hallmark of TB) have characteristic central
caseation necrosis (so called because of its dry cheese-like appearance).

7. Older granulomas develop an enclosing rim of fibroblasts and connective tissue (indicates healing by
fibrosis).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/100; Microbiology Lecture, SSMC)

Ans.
Systemic effects of inflammation / acute phase response: Cytokine-induced systemic reactions in

inflammation are collectively called the acute phase response.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/101)
Or,
The systemic changes associated with acute inflammation are collectively called the “acute phase

response”, or the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
(Ref: Robbins/8"/74)

Clinical and pathological changes: The ‘‘acute phase response”’ consists of several clinical and pathological changes.

1. Fever: Fever is produced in response to pyrogens, that stimulate synthesis of prostaglandin in
hypothalamus. Pyrogens may be exogenous or endogenous. Exogenous pyrogens are bacterial
products such as LPS that stimulate leucocytes to release endogenous pyrogens which are cytokines
such as IL-1 and TNF.

2. Production of acute-phase proteins: Acute-phase proteins are plasma proteins mostly synthesized
in the liver in response to cytokines-IL-6 (for CRP and fibrinogen) and IL-1 or TNF (for SAA).
About 12 proteins are produced. Three important ones are-
= (C-reactive protein (CRP)

» Serum amyloid A protein (SAA)
* Fibronogen

3. Leukocytosis: It is a common feature of bacterial infection. Leukocytosis occurs due to accelerated
release of leucocytes from bone marrow reserve pool by IL-1 and TNF and proliferation of leukocyte
precursors in the bone marrow by increased production of colony stimulating factor (CSF) induced by
IL-1 and TNF.

#### 📄 Page 120

arifs representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Regeneration: Some tissues are able to replace the damaged components and essentially return to a norma

state, this process ts called cogeneration
(Ref: Robbins/10"/193)

Example: bpithelia of the skin and intestines, hepatocytes in the liver etc.

Criteria / characteristics: (dmportant for ITEM)
* Regeneration occurs by proliferation of differentiated cells that survive the injury and retain the

capacity to proliferate
* Teesve stem cells may contribute to the restoration of damaged tissues.

* Mammals have a limited capacity to regenerate damaged tissues and organs.
® Only some components of most tissues are able to fully restore themselves.

Connective tissuc deposition (scar formation): If the injured tissues are incapable of regeneration, or if the

supporting structures of the tissue are too severely damaged to support regeneration of the tissue cells, repair
occurs by the laying down of connective (fibrous) tissue, a process that may result in scar formation.

Example: In the lungs, liver, kidney, myocardium (after extensive ischemic necrosis / infarction) etc.

Characteristics: If repair cannot be accomplished by regeneration alone it occurs by:
* Replacement of the injured cells with connective tissue, leading to the formation of a scar, or

* Combination of regeneration of some residual cells & scar formation.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/103)

Q. Describe the steps in scar formation.
Steps_in_scar formation: Repair by connective tissue deposition (scar formation) consists of sequential
processes that follow tissue injury. The subsequent steps are-

1. Inflammation: Breakdown products of complement activation, chemokines released from activated
platelets, and other mediators produced at the site of injury function as chemotactic agents to recruit
neutrophils and then monocytes over the next 6 to 48 hours. These inflammatory cells eliminate the
offending agents, such as microbes that may have entered through the wound, and clear the debris. As
the injurious agents and necrotic cells are cleared, the inflammation resolves.

2. Cell proliferation: In the next stage, which takes up to 10 days, several cell types, including
epithelial cells, endothelial and other vascular cells, and fibroblasts, proliferate and migrate to close the
now clean wound. Each cell type serves unique functions.

* Epithelial cells respond to locally produced growth factors and migrate over the wound to cover it up.

* Endothelial cells and pericytes proliferate to form new blood vessels, a process known as
angiogenesis.

* Fibroblasts proliferate and migrate into the site of injury and lay down collagen fibers that form
the scar.

3. Formation of granulation tissue: Migration and proliferation of fibroblasts and deposition of loose
connective tissue, together with the blood vessels and interspersed mononuclear leukocytes, form
granulation tissue.

4. Deposition of connective tissue: Granulation tissue is progressively replaced by deposition of
collagen. The amount of connective tissue increases in the granulation tissue, eventually resulting in

the formation of a stable fibrous scar.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/105)

Types of Cells on the Basis of Regenerative Capacity

Q. Mention the types of cells on the basis of regenerative capacity.
Ans.

Types of cells on the basis of regenerative capacity: The cells of the body are divided into three groups op

the basis of their proliferative / regenerative activity-

A. Labile (continuously dividing) cells: Proliferate actively throughout life, replacing those that ar
destroyed. They are capable of regeneration after injury.

Example:

* Hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow;

* Stratified squamous epithelia of the skin, oral cavity, vagina, and cervix;

* Cuboidal epithelia of the ducts draining exocrine organs (e.g. salivary glands, pancreas, biliary
tract);

= Columnar epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract, uterus, and fallopian tubes;

* Transitional epithelium of the urinary tract.

B. Quiescent (stable) cells: (in the Gp stage of the cell cycle). Normally have a /ow level of replication,
however can undergo rapid division in response to stimuli.

Example:

* Parenchymal cells of liver, kidney, and pancreas;
* Vascular endothelial cells;

* Fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells;

* Cartilage, connective tissue, and osteoblasts.

C. Non-dividing (permanent) cells: These cells have been considered to be incapable of division and
regeneration.

Example: Neurons, skeletal & cardiac muscle cells.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/103; BRS Pathology/5"/26)

Stem Cells

Q. Define and classify stem cells. Give the importance of stem cells.

Q. Short note: Stem cells.

Ans.

Stem cells: Stem cells are those characterized by their self-renewal properties and their capacity to give rise
to differentiated cells and tissues.

Under conditions of homeostasis, stem cells are maintained by self-renewal, which can involve two types of
cell division:
1. Asymmetric division, occurs when one daughter cell enters a differentiation pathway and gives rise to
mature cells, while the other retains its self-renewal capacity.

2. Symmetric division, occurs when both daughter cells retain self-renewal capacity.

Types of stem cells with importance: Fundamentally there are two varieties of stem cells:

1. Embroyonic stem cells (ES cells): The inner cell mass of the blastocysts in early embryonic
development contains pluripotent cells known as the embroyonic stem (ES) cells.

2. Tissue stem cells (adult stem cells): Many tissues in adult (bone marrow and other tissues as well)
have been shown to contain reservoirs of stem cells, which are known as adult stem cells. The adult
stem cells in any given tissue can usually produce only those cells normally found within that tissue.

Fig: A, Skin stem cells are located in the bulge area of the hair follicle, in sebaceous glands, and in the

Paneth cells.

Importance:

= Bone marrow: The bone marrow contains hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) that can generate all
the blood cell lineages.

= Liver: Liver contains stem cells/ progenitor cells in the canals of Hering, can give rise to oval cells
which are capable of differentiating into hepatocytes and biliary cells.

= Brain: Neural stem cells (known as neural precursor cells) capable of generating neurons,
astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes.

= Skin: Stem cells are located in three different areas of the epidermis that produce all of the cell
lineages of the hair follicle.

= Intestinal epithelium: Stem cells in small intestine crypts regenerate the crypt in 3 to 5 days.

* Skeletal and cardiac muscle: Growth and regeneration of injured skeletal muscle occur by
replication of satellite cells. The heart may contain progenitor-like cells with the capacity to
regenerate progeny after injury.

Q. What do you mean by angiogenesis? (RMU-22Nv) Write down the steps that occur in
angiogenesis. (RU-13Ja)
Q. Write down the mechanism of angiogenesis in secondary wound healing. (CU-19M)
Q. Short note: Angiogenesis. (RU-07Ja)
Ans.
Angiogenesis: Angiogenesis is the process of new blood vessel development from existing vessels.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/106)

Steps of angiogenesis: It involves sprouting of new vessels from existing ones, and consists of the following steps:

Quiescent Vasodilation
vessel (VEGF)

Fig: Angiogenesis.

= Vasodilation in response to nitric oxide and increased permeability induced by vascular endothelial
growth factor (VEGF)

* Separation of pericytes from the abluminal surface (outer aspect of lumen) and breakdown of the
basement membrane to allow formation of a vessel sprout

= Migration of endothelial cells toward the area of tissue injury
= Proliferation of endothelial cells just behind the leading front (“tip”) of migrating cells
= Remodeling into capillary tubes

Granulation Tissue
(Very Very Important for VIVA both in Pathology & Surgery)

Q. Define granulation tissue. (DU-24Nv, RMU-22M,17Ja, CU-17M,09/08Ja) How a surgeon can
recognize it? (RU-17Ja)
Q. State the functions of granulation tissue. (RU-13Ja)
Q. Write briefly about the granulation tissue. (CU-18Nv)
Q. Short note: Granulation tissue. (DU-11Ju,06Ja, RMU-23/20M,18/17Nv,16/15Ja,14/ 13/09Ju,
SU-20Nv)
Ans.
Granulation tissue: Migration and proliferation of fibroblasts and deposition of loose connective tissue,
together with the vessels and interspersed leukocytes, form granulation tissue.

Or,
Granulation tissue may be defined as the “immature mesenchymal tissue with proliferation of fibrovascular
tissue with inflammatory infiltrates mainly lymphocytes may be plasma cells”.

The term granulation tissue derives from its pink, soft, granular gross appearance, such as that seen beneath
the scab of a skin wound.

(N.B: Granulation tissue is not related to granulomas or granulomatous inflammation).

Composition of granulation tissue: Fibroblast + newly formed blood vessels + ECM + Neutrophil +
Macrophage + Plasma cell + Lymphocytes.

Histology of granulation tissue:
* Proliferation of fibroblasts (deposit type 3 collagen)

= Presence of new thin-walled, delicate capillaries (angiogenesis), in a loose extracellular matrix, often
with admixed inflammatory cells, mainly macrophages

= The new vessels are leaky, allowing the passage of plasma proteins and fluid into the extravascular
space. Thus, new granulation tissue is often edematous.

Characteristics of granulation tissue: (Must be Asked in VIVA)
It is a hallmark of tissue repair

Pink, soft, granular gross appearance of the surface of the wound
Easily bleed on touch due to rupture of new capillaries
Insensible due to lack of nerve supply

Resistant to infection as monocytes form a coat on the surface
New granulation tissue is often edematous

It progressively fills the site of injury

Amount of granulation tissue that is formed depends on the size of the tissue defect created by the
wound and the intensity of inflammation.

i. It is much more prominent in healing by secondary union.

Functions of granulation tissue:
a. Resorption (e.g. resorption of the necrotic tissue, thrombi or fibrin)

b. Tissue replacement (e.g. replacement of defects in the skin or mucous membrane)

c. Localization (e.g. walling of an abscess).

Q. Give an account of healing by primary union / first intention. (DU-07Ja, SU-16Ja,10Ju)
Q. Mention the sequential steps involved in healing by first intention. (DU-24Nv)

Q. Write down the steps of primary wound healing. (RU-20Ju)

Q. Short note: Healing of clear incised wound. (CU-12Ju)

Ans.

Healing by primary union / first intention: When the injury involves only the epithelial layer, the principal
mechanism of repair is epithelial regeneration, also called primary union or healing by first intention.

Example: Healing of a clean, uninfected surgical incision approximated by surgical sutures.

Sequence of events in primary healing:
1. Immediately: Wounding causes the rapid activation of coagulation pathways, which results in the
formation of a blood clot on the wound surface. The clot serves to stop bleeding and supports
migrating cells, which are attracted by growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines released into the area.

2. Within 24 hours: Neutrophils are seen at the incision margin, migrating toward the fibrin clot.
They release proteolytic enzymes that begin to clear the debris.

3. Within 24-48 hours: Epithelial cells from both edges have begun to migrate and proliferate along the
dermis yielding a thin but continuous epithelial layer that closes the wound.

3. By day 3:

* Neutrophils have been largely replaced by macrophages, which are the key cellular constituen,
of tissue repair clearing extracellular debris, fibrin, and other foreign material, and promotin
angiogenesis and ECM deposition :

* Formation of granulation tissue which progressively invades the incision space

4. By day 5:
* Formation of new blood vessels (neovascularization) which are leaky, allowing the passage of
plasma proteins and fluid into the extravascular space
» Considerable production of granulation tissue (which is often edematous) that fills the incisiona|
space.
* Fibroblasts progressively migrate into the granulation tissue, where they proliferate and lay down
collagen and ECM.

5. During the second week:
* There is continued collagen accumulation and fibroblast proliferation
= Leukocytic infiltrate, edema & increased vascularity are substantially diminished.

6. By the end of the first month:
* Formation of scar by the cellular connective tissue largely devoid of inflammatory cells ang
covered by an essentially normal epidermis
* Tensile strength of the wound increases thereafter, but it may take months for the wounded area to
obtain its maximal strength.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/108)

Q. Short note: Healing by second intention. (CU-12Ja)

Ans.

Healing by second intention: When cell or tissue loss is more extensive, such as in large wounds, abscesses,
ulceration, and ischemic necrosis (infarction) in parenchymal organs, the repair process involves a combination
of regeneration and scarring. This is called secondary union or healing by second intention.

Criteria of wound healing by second intention:

1. It occurs in extensive injury or complicated wound |

Large tissue defects generate a larger fibrin clot that fills the defect (hematoma formation)

There is more intense inflammatory reaction (because large tissue defects have a greater volume of
necrotic debris, exudate, and fibrin that must be removed)
There is development of abundant granulation tissue to fill a bigger gap caused by the large area of deficit.
Accumulation of ECM and formation of a large scar
Wound contraction (by the action of myofibroblasts) - generally occurs in large surface wounds. The

contraction helps to close the wound by decreasing the gap between its dermal edges and by reducing
the wound surface area.

Q. Narrate the stages of healing in fracture of bone. (RU-13Ju)

Ans,
Stages of bone repair:

Stage-1: Haematoma formation: Immediately following the injury there is a variable amount of bleeding

from torn vessels.

Stage-2: Traumatic inflammation: Due to trauma. Fluid exudate & neutrophil infiltration occurs.

Stage-3: Macrophage activity (Demolition phase): Neutrophils are replaced by monocyte infiltration g
macrophage activity.

Stage4: Formation of granulation tissue: By the end of the 1" week, haematoma is organizing. This js
called procallus. Neovascularization & fibrogenesis occur from the periosteum & endosteum.

Stage-S: Woven bone & cartilage formation: Osteoblasts & chondroblasts are derived from periosteum &
endosteum. The calcified hard tissue is called callus.

Stage-6: Formation of lamellar bone: Woven bone & cartilage are removed. Progressive calcification &
Haversian system formation occurs.

Stage-7: Remodeling: The original structure of bone is formed by remodeling process by osteoclastic
removal & osteoblastic lying down of bone. The intermediate callus is converted into compact bone, the
external callus is removed & the internal callus is hollowed out into marrow cavity.

(Ref: Walter & Israel/7""/182-185)

Factors Influencing Wound Healing

Q. Name the factors responsible for wound healing / tissue repair. (RMU-24M, BUP-22Nv,19M,
RU-20Nv)
Q. Mention the factors affecting / controlling wound healing. (RU-17/12Ju,10Ja, SU-09Ju, CU-
11Ju)
Q. Discuss the factors influencing wound healing. (SU-14Ja)
Q. What are the local and systemic factors that influence wound healing? (RMU-23M)
Q. What are the systemic factors that influence healing? (RU-18M,13Ju)
Q. Mention the general factors which influence healing. (SU-10Ju)
Q. Write down the factors delaying wound healing. (DU-21Oct/M)
Q. Short note: Factors controlling wound healing. (RU-17M)
Ans.
Factors influencing wound healing: (****V.V./**** for VIVA)
A. Systemic factors:
1. Nutrition: Protein deficiency & particularly vitamin C deficiency inhibit collagen synthesis and retard
wound healing.
2. Metabolic status: Can change wound healing, e.g. diabetes mellitus is associated with delayed healing.
3. Circulatory status: Inadequate blood supply (poor perfusion), usually caused by arteriosclerosis and
diabetes or by obstructed venous drainage (e.g. in varicose veins), also impairs healing.

4. Hormones: Such as glucocorticoids (steroids), have well-documented anti-inflammatory effects that
influence various components of inflammation & fibroplasias. These agents also inhibit collagen synthesis.

B. Local factors:

1. Infection: Causes delay in healing because of persistent tissue injury and inflammation.

2. Mechanical factors: Such as early motion, or increased local pressure or torsion may cause wounds
to pull apart and ultimately delay healing.

3. Foreign bodies: Such as unnecessary sutures or fragments of steel, glass or even bone impede healing.

4. Size, location & type of wound: Influence healing. Wounds in richly vascularized areas, such as the
face, heal faster than those in poorly vascularized ones, such as foot. Small incisional injuries heal
faster and with less scar formation than large excisional wounds or wounds caused by blunt trauma.

(Ref: Robbins/9"/106)

Q. Write in brief about the complications of wound healing. (DU-19/18M,17Ja, CU-
1ONv,16Ju/Ja, RU-17/10Ju)

CMU-22M, 16Ju/Ja, RU-20Nv,17/10Ju)

Q. State the complications of cutaneous wound healing. (SU-13/11Ja)

Q. Mention conditions resulting from abnormal wound healing.

Q. Short note: Complications of wound healing. (DU-14Ja, SUST-21Nv)

Ans.

Complications of wound healing: The complications of wound healing can be grouped into three general categories:
1. Deficient scar formation
2. Excessive formation of the repair components
3. Formation of contractures

A. Deficient scar formation (Defects in healing: Chronic wounds):
1. Wound dehiscence: When a surgical incision reopens internally or externally it is called wound
dehiscence. The risk factors for such an occurrence are obesity, malnutrition, infections, and vascular

insufficiency. In abdominal wounds it can be precipitated by vomiting and coughing.

2. Ulceration: Wounds can ulcerate because of inadequate vascularization during healing. The following
are some common examples-

= Venous leg ulcers develop most often in elderly people as a result of chronic venous hypertension,
which may be caused by severe varicose veins or congestive heart failure. These ulcers fail to heal
because of poor delivery of oxygen to the site of the ulcer.

## Arterial ulcers develop in individuals with atherosclerosis of peripheral arteries, especially
associated with diabetes.

" Diabetic ulcers affect the lower extremities, particularly the feet. There is tissue necrosis and
failure to heal as a result of vascular disease causing ischemia, neuropathy, systemic metabolic
abnormalities, and secondary infections.

« Pressure sores are areas of skin ulceration and necrosis of underlying tissues caused by prolonged
compression of tissues against a bone, e.g. in elderly patients with numerous morbidities lying in
bed without moving. The lesions are caused by mechanical pressure and local ischemia.

_ get —

(A) Venous leg ulcer; (B) arterial ulcer; (C) diabetic ulcer; (D) pressure sore.

---

#### 📄 Page 134

134 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

B. Excessive formation of the repair components (Excessive scarring):

1. Hypertrophic scar: Accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen may give rise to raised scar tha
remains within the boundaries of the original wound is known as hypertrophic scar. It regresse;
within 6 months.

2. Keloid: If the scar tissue grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound and does not regress,
it is called a keloid.

3. Exuberant granulation (proud flesh): Formation of excessive amounts of granulation tissue, which
protrudes above the level of the surrounding skin and blocks re-epithelialization.

4. Desmoids / aggressive fibromatoses: If the exuberant proliferation of fibroblast and other connective

tissue recur after excision, it is called desmoids. These lie in the interface between benign
proliferations and malignant tumours.

Fig: (A) Hypertrophic scar. (B) Keloid.

C. Contracture: Contraction in size of a wound is an important part in normal healing process. An
exaggeration of this process is called a contracture and results in deformities of the wound & the
surrounding tissues. Contractures are particularly prone to develop on palms, soles & anterior aspect of
the thorax. Contractures are commonly seen after various bums and can compromise the movement of joints.

(Ref: Robbins/10°/110,111)

Q. Write down the role of hydrostatic pressure in edema formation. (RU-1 7Ju, 1 lJa)

Ans.

Role of hydrostatic pressure in edema formation: Hydrostatic pressure of blood always tends to push the
fluid outside the capillary. On the other hand colloidal osmotic pressure always opposes to extravasate fluid.
When hydrostatic pressure rises in such extent that it exceeds the colloidal osmotic pressure, then extravasation
of fluid occurs. As a result fluid is accumulated in interstitial space, causing edema.

(Ref: Lecture RMC)

Q. Define pulmonary edema. Mention the mechanism of pulmonary edema.

Q. What are the causes of pulmonary edema? (SU-19Nv,17M)

Ans.

Pulmonary edema: Leakage of excessive interstitial fluid which accumulates in alveolar spaces.

Mechanism of pulmonary edema: Pulmonary edema can result from hemodynamic disturbances
(hemodynamic or cardiogenic pulmonary edema) or from direct increases in capillary permeability, as a
result of microvascular injury.

Classification and causes of pulmonary edema:
1. Haemodynamic pulmonary edema:
i) Increased hydrostatic pressure (increased pulmonary venous pressure):
= Left-sided congestive heart failure (common)
=» Volume overload
* Pulmonary vein obstruction

ii) Decreased oncotic pressure (less common):
* Hypoalbuminaemia
* Nephrotic syndrome
* Liver disease
*  Protein-losing enteropathies

iii) Lymphatic obstruction (rare)

2. Edema due to alveolar wall injury (microvascular or epithelial injury):
i) Direct injury
= Infections: Bacterial pneumonia
* Inhaled gases: High concentration oxygen, smoke

* Liquid aspiration: Gastric contents, near-drowning
* Radiation
* Lung trauma

ii) amare injury
Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (c.g., associated with sepsis, bums, pancreatitis,
extensive trauma)
* Blood transfusion-related
* Drugs and chemicals: chemotherapeutic agents (bleomycin), other medications (methadone,
amphotericin B), heroin, cocaine, kerosene, paraquat
* Shock, trauma

3. Edema of undetermined origin:
i) High altitude
ii) Neurogenic (central nervous system trauma).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/675)

Q. Write about clinical consequences of pulmonary edema. (RU-16Ja)

Ans.

Clinical consequences _of pulmonary edema: Whatever the clinical setting (either hemodynamic or
cardiogenic pulmonary edema or edema due to microvascular injury), pulmonary congestion and edema
produce heavy, wet lungs.

1. Clinical consequences of hemodynamic or cardiogenic pulmonary edema:
s Presence of hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart failure” cells) in abundance.
= Fibrosis and thickening of the alveolar walls cause the soggy lungs to become firm and brown
(brown induration).
= Impairment of normal respiratory function
* Infection.

2. Clinical consequences of edema caused by microvascular (alveolar) injury:
* Pneumonia (when localized edema)
* Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (when diffuse edema).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/675)

Q. Write down the mechanism / pathogenesis of edema / ascites in cirrhosis of liver. (CMU-

23M, 13Ja, RU-19Nv,17Ja, SU-12Ja)

Q. Mention the causes of edema in liver cirrhosis. (RU-14Ja)

Q. How ascites develop in cirrhosis of liver? (DU-09Ja)

Ans.

Mechanism of ascites in liver cirrhosis:

1. Sinusoidal hypertension: Cirrhosis of liver — Fibrosis of liver —> Sinusoidal hypertension —

Driving of fluid into the space of Disse > Removed by hepatic lymphatics > Excess amount of
lymph in peritoneal cavity — Ascites.

2. Percolation of hepatic lymph into the peritoneal cavity: Cirrhosis — Hepatic lymphatic flow (20
L/day in exchange of normal 800-1000 ml/day) exceeding thoracic duct capacity — Percolation of
excess amount of hepatic lymph (rich in proteins) into the peritoneal cavity — Ascites.

3. Intestinal fluid leakage: Cirthosis of liver — Portal hypertension — Increased perfusion pressure in

intestinal capillaries + Movement of additional out of intestinal capillanes into the abdomen — Ascites.

4. Secondary hyperaldosteronism: Cirthosis of liver — Impaired hepatic metabolism of aldosterone +
Increased Na’ and H;0 retention by the kidney — Increased plasma hydrostatic pressure — Increased
transudation of fluid into the peritoneal cavity — Ascites.

§. Hypoalbuminaemia: Cirthosis of liver — Impaired function of liver —+ Decreased synthesis of
albumin — Hypoalbuminaemia — Decreased plasma colloidal osmotic pressure ++ Oedema (Ascites).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/117,828)

Hyperaemia & Congestion

Q. Define hyperaemia. (CU-03Ja)
Ans.

Hyperaemia: Hyperemia is an active process in which arteriolar dilation leads to increased blood flow.

Affected tissues turn red (erythema) because of increased delivery of oxygenated blood.

Example: At sites of inflammation or in skeletal muscle during exercise.

Q. Define congestion. (CU-03Ja)

Q. Short note: Congestion.
Ans.

Congestion: Congestion is a passive process in which there is a local increased blood volume resulting from

reduced outflow of blood from a tissue.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/117)

Example: It can be systemic as in cardiac failure, or localized, as in isolated venous obstruction.

Types:
1. According to site of involvement:

* Localized congestion: Isolated venous obstruction

* Systemic congestion: Cardiac failure

2. According to duration of onset:
a. Acute congestion
* Lung (Acute left ventricular failure)
= Liver (Acute right sided heart failure)

b. Chronic congestion
= Lung (Rheumatic mitral stenosis)
= Liver (Chronic right sided heart failure)

Effects of congestion:

1. Congested tissues take on a dusky reddish-blue colour (cyanosis) due to red cell stasis and the

accumulation of deoxygenated Hb.

2. Development of edema as a result of the increased volumes and pressure.

3. In long-standing chronic passive congestion, the lack of blood flow causes chronic hypoxia,

potentially resulting in ischemic tissue injury and scarring.
4. Capillary rupture in chronic congestion can also cause small haemorrhagic foci.

5. Subsequent breakdown and phagocytosis of the extravasated red cell debris can eventually result in

small clusters of haemosiderin-laden macrophages.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/117,118; Prof. Khaleque/40)

Haemostasis and Thrombosis

Q. Describe brief the role of platelets in normal haemostasis. (DU-04M)
Ans.

---

#### 📄 Page 151

GENERAL PATHOLOGY | 151
ee == —=== =

Role of platelet in normal hemostasis: Platelets play important role in every aspects of hemostasis-

1. Vasoconstriction: When a blood vessel is cut or ruptured, platelets secrete serotonin and
thromboxane A, which cause vasoconstriction and thus reduce flow of blood outside the vessel.

2. Platelet plug formation: Platelets adhere to extracellular matrix collagen at sites of endothelial injury
by vWF. On activation, they secrete ADP & TxA; — Further platelet recruitment — Formation of
primary hemostatic plug.

3. Coagulation: Platelets also express phospholipid complexes on which clotting pathway activation
occur — Formation and deposition of fibrin + Secondary hemostatic plug.

4. Colt retraction: Thrombosthenin of platelet in presence of ADP & Mg” helps in clot retraction.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/118-124; Lecture SSMC)

Q. Write the ani-thrombotic role of endothelium. (SU-20Nv,19M, 13Ju,05/04Ja)

Q. What are the ani-thrombotic factors? (DU-23M)

Ans.

Anti-thrombotic properties of endothelium: Endothelial cells are resistant to the thrombogenic influence of
platelets and coagulation proteins. Intact endothelial cells act to modulate several aspects of hemostasis and
oppose coagulation after injury by thrombo-resistance.

The antithrombotic properties of endothelium can be divided into activities directed at platelets, coagulation
factors, and fibrinolysis.

1) Platelet inhibitory effects:

= An intact endothelium prevents platelets from engaging the highly thrombogenic subendothelial
collagen and vWF.

= Normal endothelium also releases a number of factors that inhibit platelet activation and
aggregation, e.g.
- Prostacyclin (PGI)
- Nitric oxide
- Adenosine diphophatase etc.

= Finally, endothelial cells bind and alter the activity of thrombin, which is one of the most potent
activators of platelets.

2) Anticoagulant effects: Normal endothelium shields coagulation factors from tissue factor in vessel
walls and expresses multiple factors that actively oppose coagulation, e.g.
* Thrombomodulin
= Endothelial protein C receptor
= Heparin-like molecules, and
= Tissue factor pathway inhibitor

3) Fibrinolytic effects: Normal endothelial cells synthesize tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA), a
protease that cleaves plasminogen to form plasmin; plasmin, in turn, cleaves fibrin to degrade thrombi.
(Ref: Robbins/10°/119; BRS Pathology/5"/35)

13Ju)
Q. What are the prothrombotic factors? (DU-23M)

Ans.
Prothrombotic role of endothelium in thrombus formation:
1. Platelet effects: Severe endothelial injury may trigger thrombosis by exposing ECM, vWF and tissue
factor (factor IID to platelets.

2. Procoagulant changes: Endothelial cells activated by inflammatory cytokines downregulate the
expression of thrombomodulin (a key modulator of thrombin activity). In addition, inflamed
endothelium also down-regulates the expression of other anticoagulants, such as protein C and tissue
factor protein inhibitor, changes that further promote a procoagulant state.

3. Anti-fibrinolytic effects: Activated endothelial cells secrete plasminogen activator inhibitors
(PAIs), which limit fibrinolysis, and down-regulate the expression of t-PA, alterations that also favor
the development of thrombi.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/126)

Q. What are the causes of endothelial activation?
Ans.
Causes of endothelial activation: Endothelial activation or dysfunction and can be produced by diverse
exposures, including-
* Physical injury
Infectious agents
Abnormal blood flow
Inflammatory mediators
Metabolic abnormalities, such as hypercholesterolemia or homocystinemia
Toxins absorbed from cigarette smoke

Endothelial activation is believed to have an important role in tiggenng arterial thrombotic events.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/126)

Ans.
Source of vWF: Endothelium.

Function of vWF: Acts as a glue between platelet and ECM (collagen).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/126)

Q Name different types of thrombus. (CU-04Ja)
Ams
Different types of thrombus:
A. Based on site:
1. Arterial thrombus
a) Thrombus on ulcerated atheromatous plaque — in coronary artenes
b) On atheroma of abdominal aorta
c) Thrombus in thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)
d) Laminated thrombus - in aneurism
ec) Trauma

2. Venous thrombus:
a) Phicbothrombosis
b) Thrombophlebitis
c) Other types — thrombophlebitis migrans, ileofemoral thrombosis

3. Thrombosis in the heart:
a) Vegetations (e.g. infective endocarditis)
b) Mural thrombus
c) Laminated thrombus (in aneurism of heart)
d) Ball thrombus.

(N.B: Vegetation: Thrombus on the cardiac valve.)

B. Based on occlusion of lumen:
1. Occlusive thrombus — Completely occludes the lumen
2. Maral thrombus - It is attached to the wall but does not completely occlude the lumen

C. Based on presence of infection:
1. Bland / aseptic thrombus

2. Septic / infected thrombus.

(Ref: Robbins/10°/128; Prof. Khaleque/41)

Fig: The Virchow triad in thrombosis.

1. Endothelial injury: This is the dominant influence. It is particularly important for thrombus formation in
the heart or the arterial circulation, where the high rates of blood flow impede clot formation.

Causes of endothelial injury:

* Myocardial infarction (MI)
Vasculitis
Hypertension
Dyslipidemia
Smoking
Homocystinuna
Endotoxins

Process: Endothelial injury > Exposure of subendothelial ECM — Adhesion of platelets, release of
tissue factor, and local depletion of prostacyclin (PGI,) and plasminogen activators (PAs) — This leads
to platelet adhesion and aggregation and the end result is the formation of platelet plug and thrombus.

2. Alteration in normal blood flow (stasis or turbulence):
Causes of stasis and turbulence:
* Ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques

Acute myocardial infarctions

Aortic aneurysms

Q. Short note: Fate of thrombus. (RU-07Ja) (Very ****** Important for VIVA)

Ans.
Fates of the thrombus: Thrombi undergo some combination of the following four events-

1. Propagation: The thrombi may accumulate additional platelets and fibrin and eventually leading to
vessel obstruction.
2. Embolization: Thrombi may dislodge and travel to other sites in the vasculature.

3. Dissolution: Dissolution is the result of fibrinolysis, which can lead to the rapid shrinkage and total
disappearance of recent thrombi.

4. Organization and recanalization: Older thrombi become organized by the ingrowth of endothelial
cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts; and may eventually become recanalized; that is, may re-

establish vascular flow, or may be incorporated into the vessel wall.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/129)

Q. Short note: Lines of Zahn. (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Lines of Zahn: Thrombi often have grossly and microscopically apparent laminations called lines of Zahn;
these represent pale platelet and fibrin deposits alternating with darker red cell-rich layers.

Significance of lines of Zahn: Such laminations signify that a thrombus has formed in flowing blood; there

presence can therefore distinguish antemortem clots from the bland non-laminated clots that occur
postmortem.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/128)

Ans.

Different types of embolism:

1. Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary emboli originate from deep venous thromboses and are the most
common form of thromboembolic disease.

Pathogenesis:
Venous emboli originating from deep leg vein thrombi (>95% instances)

L

They are carned through progressively larger channels and usually pass through the right side of the heart

into the pulmonary vasculature
L
Depending on the size of the embolus, it may occlude the main pulmonary artery, impact across the
bifurcation (saddle embolus) or pass out into the smaller, branching arteries

Frequently, there are multiple emboli from a single large mass. Patient who has had one pulmonary
embolus, is at high risk of having more.

Rarely, a venous embolus may pass through an inter-atrial or inter-ventricular septal defect to gain access
to the systemic arterial circulation (paradoxical embolism).

Clinical effects / outcome:
i) Most pulmonary emboli (60% to 80%) are clinically silent (because they are small)

ii) Sudden death, right heart failure (cor pulmonale), or cadiovascular collapse occurs when emboli
obstruct 60% or more of the pulmonary circulation

iii) Embolic obstruction of medium-sized arteries with subsequent vascular rupture can result in
pulmonary haemorrhage

iv) Embolic obstruction of small end-arteriolar pulmonary branches often does produce hemorrhage or infarction

v) Multiple emboli over time may cause pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure.

(Remember: Embolic obstruction of medium-sized arteries never causes pulmonary infarction due to
dual blood supply of lungs, rather it results in haemorrhage.)

Fig: Pulmonary thromboembolism.

Systemic thromboembolism: It refers to emboli traveling within the arterial circulation.

Pathogenesis: Most systemic emboli (80%) arise from intracardiac mural thrombi, two thirds of which
are associated with left ventricular wall infarcts and another one fourth with left atrial dilation and
fibrillation. The remainder originates from aortic aneurysms, atherosclerotic plaques, valvular
vegetations, or venous thrombi (paradoxical thrombi); 10-15% are of unknown origin.

Sites of lodgment & clinical effects:

i) Lower extremities (75%) - peripheral vascular disease, gangrene may develop.
ii) Brain (10%) - if in middle cerebral artery is may cause death.

iii) Infarction of intestine, kidneys, spleen.

iv) Upper extremities (lesser extent).

Fat embolism:
Causes: Fracture of long bones, soft tissue trauma and bum.

Pathogenesis:
After fracture of long bones (which have fatty marrow) or, rarely, soft tissue trauma and burns
Fat enters the circulation by rupture of the marrow vascular sinusoids or of venules
|
Occlusion of the pulmonary and cerebral microvasculature
{

Release of FFA from the fat globules, causing local toxic injury to endothelium

i) Nosymptoms in 90% individuals of traumatic fat embolism.

fi) Fat embolism syndrome occurs in 10% of cases, characterized by- (For VIVA)
- Pulmonary insufficiency (tachypnea, dyspnea, and tachycardia)
- Neurological symptoms (iritability, restlessness, delirium, coma)
- Anaemia
- Thrombocytopenia
- Death (5-15% of cases).

Air embolism: It ccurs when air is introduced into venous or arterial circulation.

Causes:

* Obstetric or laparoscopic procedure

* Chest wall injury

® Underwater construction workers (decompression sickness)
* During haemodialysis.

Q. Briefly discuss decompression sickness. (For Honours Gainers)

Q. Short note: Decompression sickness. (RMU-23M)

Ans.

Decompression sickness: It is a particular form of gas embolism which occurs when individuals are exposed
to sudden changes in atmospheric pressure. It is commonly seen in scuba and deep sea divers, under
water construction workers, and individuals in unpressurized aircraft in rapid ascent. When air is
breathed at high pressure (e.g. during a deep see dive) increased amount of gas (particularly nitrogen) become
dissolved in the blood and tissues. If the diver then ascends (depressurizes) too rapidly, the nitrogen comes out of
solution in the tissues and the blood.

Clinical features:
* Skeletal muscles and supporting tissues around the joints: Painful condition called the bends (due
to rapid formation of gas bubbles)

---

#### 📄 Page 165

GENERAL PATHOLOGY | 165

« Lungs: Pulmonary oedema, haemorthage, and focal atelectasis or emphysema leading to a form of
respiratory distress called the chokes (due to gas bubbles in the vasculature)

* In chronic form of decompression sickness (caisson disease): Persistence of gas emboli in the
skeletal system leads to multiple foci of ischemic necrosis, commonly in the femoral heads, tibia,
and humeri.

Treatment: Individuals affected by acute decompression sickness are treated by being placed in a chamber
under sufficiently high pressure to force the gas bubbles back into solution. Subsequent slow decompression
permits gradual resorption and exhalation of the gases, which prevents the obstructive bubbles from reforming.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/128)

Q. What do you mean by “Bends & chokes” in patients with decompression sickness? (RMU-
21M)

Ans.

Bends: Rapid formation of gas bubbles within skeletal muscles and supporting tissues in and about joints
leading to the painful condition called the ‘bends’.

Chokes: Pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage, and focal atelectasis or emphysema leading to a form of
respiratory distress called the ‘chokes’ (due to accumulation of gas bubbles in the pulmonary vasculature).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/128; Harsh Mohan/7"/126)

Q. What is caisson disease? (For VIVA)
Ans.
Caisson disease: Chronic form of decompression sickness is called caisson disease.

Clinical effects of caisson disease: Persistence of gas emboli in the skeletal system leads to multiple foci of
ischemic necrosis, commonly in the femoral heads, tibia, and humeri.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/128)

Q. Give an account of morphology of an infarct. (SU-10Ja)
Ans.
Morphology of an infarct:

A) Macroscopic:
* Shape: Wedge-shaped, with the occluded vessel at the apex and the periphery of the organ
forming the base.

* Margin: Hyperaemic (due to inflammation).
* Consistency: Firmer than the surrounding tissue.

* Colour: After 24 to 48 hours, the colour of the infarct is red (in case of red infarct); yellow white
/ pale (in case of white infarct).

B) Microscopic: (Very Important For VIVA)

* Allinfarcts (except brain):
Coagulative necrosis.
Inflammatory reaction & fibroblastic response at periphery.

* Septic infarction: Liquefactive necrosis (formation of abscess which is replaced by scar tissue).

RU-14Ja)

Q. What are the factors that play role in infarction? (RU-07Ja)

Ans.

Factors contributing in development of an infarct: (For VIVA)

1. Anatomy of the vascular supply: Organs having dual blood supply (e.g. lungs, liver, extremities)
are less vulnerable to ischemia in contrast to organs having end arterial supply (e.g. kidney, spleen).

2. Rate of development of occlusion: Slowly developing occlusions are less likely to cause infarction
because they provide time for the development of alternative perfusion pathways (e.g. collateral
coronary circulation).

3. Tissue vulnerability to hypoxia: Neurons undergo irreversible damage after 3 to 4 minutes of
ischemia; Myocardial cells are also quite sensitive and die after only 20 to 30 minutes of ischemia. In
contrast, fibroblasts within myocardium remain viable even after many hours of ischemia.

4. Hypoxemia: Abnormally low blood O; content (regardless of cause) increases both the likelihood and
extent of infarction.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/134)

Stages of shock: (****Y.V./ For VIVA)

1.

Initial nonprogressive stage: Reflex compensatory mechanisms, including increased heart rate and
increased peripheral resistance, maintain perfusion of vital organs.

Following neurohumoral mechanisms help to maintain cardiac output and blood pressure:

metabolic imbalance, including metabolic acidosis from lactic acidemia. Compensatory mechanisms
are no longer adequate.

Features:

* Lactic acidosis
* | Urine output
* Confusion

Irreversible stage: In this stage, organ damage and metabolic disturbances are so severe that even if
the hemodynamic defects are corrected, survival is not possible.

Features:

Multiorgan failure

DIC

Renal shutdown.

Q. Mention the clinical consequences of shock. (V.V./ For VIVA both in Pathology &

Ans.

Clinical consequences of shock:

1. In hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock: The patient presents with hypotension, a weak rapid pulse,
tachypnea, and cool, clammy, cyanotic skin.

2. In septic shock: The skin may be warm and flushed owing to peripheral vasodilation (in anaphylactic
shock also).

3. The primary threat to life is the underlying initiating event (e.g., myocardial infarction, severe
hemorrhage, bacterial infection). However, the cardiac, cerebral, and pulmonary changes rapidly
aggravate the situation.

4. If patients survive the initial insult, worsening renal function can provoke a phase dominated by
progressive oliguria, acidosis, and electrolyte imbalances.

5. Prognosis varies with the origin of shock and its duration.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/138)

## Arif's Pathology & Haematology — Genetic Disorders

CHAPTER ¢

“GENETIC DISORDERS

Mutation

Q. What is mutation? (CU-19Nv,17M) Mention its types and consequences with example.
Q. Short note on: Mutation / Genetic mutation. (DU-19M, CU-15Ja)
Ans.
Mutation: A mutation is defined as a permanent change in the DNA.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/142)

Types of mutation: Based on the extent of genetic change, mutations may be classified into three categories:

1. Genome mutation: Loss or gain of whole chromosomes, giving rise to monosomy or trisomy.

2. Chromosomal mutation: Rearrangement of genetic material and give rise to visible structural
changes in the chromosome.

3. Gene mutation: Partial or complete deletion of a gene or, most often, affect a single base. It is of 2 types-

(a) Frame-shift mutation: This type of mutation occurs when one or two base pairs may be inserted
into or deleted from the DNA, leading to alterations in the leading frame of the DNA strand.

(b) Point mutation: In this type of mutation a single nucleotide base may be substituted by a
different base. Consequences of point mutation are-

i) Missense mutations: A point mutation (single base substitution) may alter the codon ina
triplet of bases and lead to the replacement of one amino acid by another. Because this
mutation alters the meaning of the genetic code, they are often termed missense mutations.

Example: Sickle cell anemia.

ji) Nonsense mutations: A point mutation may change an amino acid codon to a chain
terminator, or stop codon.

Example: B°-thalassemia.

iii) Silent mutations: Silent mutations are those that cause no change in the final protein product
and can only be detected by sequencing the gene. (This type not included in Robbin’s
Pathology)

(Ref: Robbins/10°/142 + 7°/138-140)

= Autosomal dominant disorders: Von Willebrand disease
= Autosomal recessive disorders: Thalassaemia
« X-linked recessive disorders: Haemophilia A & B
s X-linked dominant disorders: Very rare; such as Vitamin D resistant rickets.

interactions between variant forms of genes and environmental factors. Such as-

Cleft lip or cleft palate
Congenital heart disease
Pyloric stenosis
Diabetes mellitus
Hypertension

Coronary heart disease

3. Cytogenic disorders / chromosomal disorders: They include diseases resulting from chromosomal

and genomic mutation and are therefore associated with numerical or structural changes in
chromosome.

Examples:

a. Involving autosomes:
= Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
= Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)

Q. Short note: Features of autosomal dominant inheritance. (DU-13/10Ju)

Ars.

Autosomal dominant disorders: Autosomal dominant disorders are the Mendelian disorders involving
mutation in the autosomes that are manifested in the heterozygous state, so at least one parent of an index
case is usually affected; both males and females are affected, and both can transmit the condition.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/144)

Examples of autosomal dominant disorders: (Very Important for VIVA)

System Disorder

Neurofibromatosis
Myotonic dystrophy

Marfan syndrome

Achondroplasia

_ Acute intermittent porphyria

(Ref: Robbins/10"/144)

Features of autosomal dominant inheritance:

1. Autosomal dominant disorders are manifested in the heterozygous state, so at least one parent of an
index case is usually affected.

2. Both males and females are affected, and both can transmit the condition.

3. No carrier state.

4. When an affected person marries an unaffected one, every child has one chance in two of having the
disease (50% chance).

5. Risk remains the same for each successive pregnancy.

6. Clinical features can be modified by reduced penetrance and expressivity.

7. In many conditions, the age at onset is delayed; symptoms and signs do not appear until adulthood (as
in Huntington disease).

8. Rare and usually less severe than autosomal recessive disorder.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/144)

Ans.

Autosomal recessive disorders: Autosomal recessive disorders are the largest category of Mendelian
disorders involving mutation in the autosomes, that are manifested only in the homozygous state.

Autosomal recessive disorders occur when both alleles at a given gene locus are mutated. The trait dose not
usually affect the parents of the affected individual, but siblings may show the disease. Siblings have one
chance in four of being affected (i.e. the recurrence risk is 25% for each birth).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/145)

Examples of autosomal recessive disorders: Autosomal recessive disorders include almost all inborn errors
of metabolism. (Very Important for VIVA)

Features of autosomal recessive inheritance:

1. Both sexes are equally affected.
Only manifests in homozygous state.
Heterozygotes are phenotypically unaffected.
Does not usually affect the parents of the affected individual, but siblings may show the disease.
Siblings have one chance in four of being affected (i.e. the recurrence risk is 25% for each birth).
There is increased risk of disease among offspring of consanguineous marriage.
The expression of the defect tends to be more uniform than in autosomal dominant disorders.
Complete penetrance is common.
Onset is frequently early in life.

CHNINAA Rw

(Ref: Robbins/10'/145)

Q. Short note: X-linked dominant disorders. (DU-13/10Ju)

Ans.

X-linked dominant disorders: There are only a few X-linked dominant conditions. They are caused by
dominant disease-associated alleles on the X chromosome.

Examples; Vitamin D-resistant rickets and Alport syndrome.
Features of X-linked dominant inheritance:

* Affects both sexes, but more in females

* All children of affected females are affected

* All daughters of affected males are affected but none of their sons (no male to male transmission).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/146)

Ans.
Marfan syndrome: Marfan syndrome is a disorder of connective tissues, manifested principally by changes
in the skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system.

Pathogenesis: Marfan syndrome results from an inherited defect in an extra-cellular glycoprotein calleg
fibrillin-1, which is the major component of microfibrils found in the extra-cellular matrix.

Skeletal abnormalities in Marfan syndrome:
1]. The patient is unusually tall with exceptionally long extremities and long, tapering fingers and toes.
2. The joint ligaments in the hands and feet are lax, suggesting that the patient is double-jointed; typically
the thumb can be hyperextended back to the wmist.
3. The head is commonly dolichocephalic (long-headed) with bossing of the frontal eminences and
prominent supraorbital ridges.

4. A variety of spinal deformities may appear, including kyphosis, scoliosis or rotation or slipping of the
dorsal or lumbar vertebrae.

5. The chest is classically deformed, presenting either pectus excavatum (deeply depressed sternum) ora
pigeon-chest deformity.

Ocular changes in Marfan syndrome: Most characteristic is bilateral subluxation or dislocation (usually
outward and upward) of the lens referred to as ectopia lentis.

Cardiovascular lesions:
1. Mitral valve prolapse
2. Dilation of the ascending aorta owing to cystic medionecrosis
3. Loss of medial support results in progressive dilation of the aortic valve ring and the root of the aorta,
giving rise to severe aortic incompetence.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/148)

6- phosphatase.

2. Myopathic form (McArdle disease): Lacking of muscle phosphorylase gives rise to storage in
skeletal muscles and cramps after exercise.

3. Pompe disease: there is lack of lysosomal acid maltase, and all organs are affected, but hear
involvement is predominant.

Q. Short note: Karyotyping. (DU-12Ju)

Q. Short note: Karyotype. (DU-17M)

Ans.

Karyotyping: The study of chromosomes is called karyotyping.
Or,

Karyotyping is the presentation of a cellular chromosome profile.

It is the basic tool for cytogeneticist.

Normal karyotype: Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes; these comprise 22 homologous pairs of
autosomes and two sex chromosomes, XX in the female and XY in the male.

Procedure of karyotyping: A karyotype is a standard arrangement of a photographed or imaged stained
metaphase spread in which chromosome pairs are arranged in order of decreasing length.

1. Mitosis in dividing cells is arrested in metaphase by use of mitotic spindle inhibitors (e.g. colcemid)

2. Then to stain the chromosomes (commonly Giemsa stain)

3. In a metaphasic spread, the individual chromosomes to take the form of two chromatids connected at
the centromere.

4. A karyotype is obtained by arranging each pair of autosomes according to length, followed by sex
chromosomes.

Way of karyotype presentation: Karyotypes are usually described using a shorthand system of notations in
the following order: total number of chromosomes is given first, followed by the sex chromosome
complement, and finally the description of abnormalities in ascending numerical order. For example, a male
with trisomy 21 is designated 47,XY,+21/.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/164)

Introduction

Immunity: The classic definition of immunity is protection from infectious pathogens.
| (Ref: Robbins/10"/190)

Types of immunity:
1. Innate immunity (also called natural, or native, immunity)

2. Adaptive immunity (also called acquired, or specific, immunity).
(Ref: Robbins/10'/190)

Components of immunity:
1. Innate immunity: The major components of innate immunity are-
* Epithelial barriers
* Dendritic cells
* Natural killer (NK) cells
* Several plasma proteins (including the proteins of the complement system).

2. Adaptive immunity: The adaptive immune system consists of lymphocytes and their products,
including antibodies.

Types of adaptive immunity: There are two types of adaptive immunity:

1. Humoral immunity, which protects against extracellular microbes and their toxins, and
2. Cell-mediated (or cellular) immunity, which is responsible for defense against intracellular
microbes.

Humoral immunity is mediated by B (bone marrow-derived) lymphocytes and their secreted products,
antibodies (also called immunoglobulins, Ig), and cellular immunity is mediated by T (thymus-derived)

lymphocytes.

Both classes of lymphocytes express highly specific receptors for a wide variety of substances, which are

called antigens.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/190)

Tissues of the immune system: The tissues of the immune system consist of-

---

GENERAL PATHOLOGY 189

1. Primary (also called generative, or central) lymphoid organs: Thymus & bone marrow.
2. Secondary (or peripheral) lymphoid organs: Lymph nodes, spleen, and the mucosal and cutaneous
lymphoid tissues.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/196)

Q. What are the common disorders of immune system?
Ans.

Immunological disorders:

= Hypersensitivity reactions: Here, there is altered exaggerated immune reaction to an antigen, e.g.
anaphylactic reaction, acute glomerulonephritis etc.

* Autoimmune diseases: These are caused by immune reactions against self antigen, e.g. SLE,
rheumatoid arthritis.

* Immuno-deficiency syndromes: These result from genetically determined or acquired defects in
some components of normal immune system, e.g. severe combined immune deficiency disease
(SCID), acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS).

* Rejection of tissue transplants

* Amyloidosis: A poorly understood disorder having immunologic association.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/189 + 8"/197,226,230,249)

Q. Short note: Type-I hypersensitivity. (BUP-21Nv/M)

Ans.

Type I hypersensitivity: Immediate, or type I, hypersensitivity is a rapid immunologic reaction occurring in
a previously sensitized individual that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface
of mast cells.

These reactions are often called allergy, and the antigens that elicit them are allergens.

Anaphylaxis: Anaphylaxis may be defined as an immediate hypersensitivity response triggered by IgE-
mediated mast cell degranulation, leading to anaphylactic shock due to vasodilation and smooth muscle
contraction. It may be caused by drugs, bee sting, food etc.

Anaphylactic shock: Systemic anaphylaxis (anaphylactic shock) is a potentially fatal reaction characterized
by rapid onset of urticaria, bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, and shock after exposure to an offending antigen.

(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/70)

Q. Classify graft on the basis of animal of origin.

Classification of graft on the basis of animal of origin:

1. Autograft: A graft or transplant from one area to another area of the same individual, ©.g.
transplantation of skin from one area of an individual to another area of the same individual.

2. Isograft: A graft between two genetically identical individuals, as in identical twins, ©¢.8-
transplantation of kidney or any other organ.

---

3. Allograft: The graft between two genetically dissimilar individuals of same species cy.
transplantation of kidney from one person to another HLA mismatched person. The graft is usually
rejected.

4. Xenograft or heterograft: A graft between a donor and a recipient from different species e.g.
transplantation of heart from monkey to human.
(Ref: Prof. Akram/3"/189,190; Robbins/10"/234)

Q. What is transplant rejection? What are the types? How prolonged survival of a transplant
can be achieved?
Q. Short note: Transplant rejection.

Ans.
Transplant_rejection: A major barrier to transplantation is the process of rejection, which is an
immunological reaction in which the recipient’s immune system recognizes the graft as being foreign and
attacks it.
Or,

Rejection is a process in which T lymphocytes and antibodies produced against graft antigens react against and
destroy tissue grafts.

(Ref: Robbins/10'/234)

Classification of transplant rejection: On the basis of the morphology and the underlying mechanism,
rejection reactions are classified as-
1. Hyperacute: Occurs within minutes or hours after transplantation.
2. Acute: Occurs within days after transplantation but suddenly.
3. Chronic: Progressive over a period of 4 to 6 months.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/235)

Measures to be taken to prevent transplant rejection:
1. Tissue matching-
= HLA typing and matching
* Blood grouping and cross matching
* Cross matching of patients serum with donors leukocytes

2. Immune suppression of the host by-
* Total body irradiation by x-ray
* Cytotoxic drug therapy e.g. corticosteroids, azathioprine, cyclosporine

3. Others: Such as injection of excessive amounts of antigens like those antigens shed from the grafted
tissue in the circulation. These injected antigens will neutralize the host antibody or T-cell.
(Ref: Prof. Akram/3"/193,194)

Q. What are the routes of transmission of AIDS?
Ans

(Ref: Robbins/10"/247)

Routes of transmission of AIDS: There are three major routes of transmission of AIDS-

1. Sexual transmission

2. Parenteral transmission:
= Intravenous drug abuser
* Hemophiliacs who received factor VIII concentrates
= Random recipients of blood transfusion

3. Mother to infant transmission:
= In utero by transplacental spread

Q. What is amyloid?

Ans.

Amyloid: Amyloids are misfolded proteins that accumulate in extracellular space and damages tissue.
(Ref: Pathoma Lecture Notes)

Q. Short note: Amyloidosis.
Ans.
Amyloidosis: Amyloidosis is a condition associated with a number of inherited and inflammatory disorders
in which extracellular deposits of fibrillar proteins are responsible for tissue damage and functional
compromise.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/259)
Or,
Amyloidosis is a disorder characterized by the extracellular deposits of misfolded proteins that aggregate to
form insoluble fibrils.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/265)
Or,
Amyloidosis is a group of disorders which is characterized by the deposition of amyloid, a proteinaceous
material with certain physicochemical features.

(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/80)

Organs involved:
* Kidney (most common)

Heart

Liver, spleen

Adrenal

Pancreas

Lymph node

Peripheral nerves, skin, tongue
Thyroid, pituitary.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/259; BRS Pathology/5"/80)
Classification of amyloidosis:

1. Systemic (generalized) amyloidosis
* Primary amyloidosis (immunocyte dyscrasias with amyloidosis), e.g. multiple myeloma,
Waldenstrém macroglobulinemia.
* Secondary amyloidosis (reactive systemic amyloidosis), e.g. chronic inflammatory conditions.
* Hemodialysis associated amyloidosis, e.g. chronic renal failure.

* Hereditary or familial amyloidosis, ¢.g. familial Mediterranean fever, systemic senile
amyloidosis.

2, Localized amyliodosis
* Senile cerebral, e.g. Alzheimer disease

* Endocrine
- Medullary carcinoma of thyroid

> **Source:** `Arif Pathology guide 2025(1).pdf` · **Pages 199–261** (63 extracted) · **UNIT-I : GENERAL PATHOLOGY**

GENERAL PATHOLOGY

Q. Define neoplasm / neoplasia (DU-24Nv, RMU-22Nv,21/20Nv, CMU-22Nv, 1 5Ja, 14Ju/Ja,13/12/
11/10/07Ja, SU-22M, 19Nv,16Ja) with example. (DU-24Nv)

Q. Give modern definition of neoplasm. (CMU-23Nv/M)

Q. Define tumour (Willis definition). (SU-06Ja, CU-04S,03Ja, RU-03Ja)

Ans. (Very**** Important for V/VA)

Neoplasm / tumour: Neoplasia means “new growth,” and the collection of cells and stroma composing new

growths are referred to as neoplasms.

In the pre-molecular era, the eminent British oncologist Willis defines neoplasm / tumour (Willis
definition): “A neoplasm is an abnormal mass of tissue, the growth of which exceeds and is uncoordinated
with that of the normal tissues and persists in the same excessive manner after cessation of the stimuli which
evoked the change.”

(Ref: Robbins/9""/266)

In the modern era, a neoplasm is defined as a genetic disorder of cell growth that is triggered by acquired or
less commonly inherited mutations affecting a single cell and its clonal progeny.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/268)

Example:
* Benign neoplasm arising from fibrous tissue is called fibroma; whereas malignant neoplasm is

called fibrosarcoma.

« Benign neoplasm arising from bone is called osteoma; whereas malignant neoplasm is called
osteosarcoma.

* Benign neoplasm arising from cartilage is called chondroma; whereas malignant neoplasm is called
chondrosarcoma.

* Benign neoplasm arising from glandular tissue is called adenoma; whereas malignant neoplasm is
called adenocarcinoma.

Q. Short note: Lipoma. (CMU-21/20Nv)

Ans.

Lipoma: Lipoma is the benign tumour of adipose tissue. It is the commonest soft tissue tumour, which
appears as a solitary, soft, movable and painless mass which may remain stationary or grow slowly. A lipoma
rarely ever transforms into /iposarcoma (malignant tumours of adipose tissue).

Age of incidence: Lipomas occur most often in 4" to 5" decades of life and are frequent in females.

Site: They may be found at different locations in the body but most common sites are the subcutaneous tissues
in the neck, back and shoulder.

Variants of lipoma:
* Fibrolipoma (admixture with fibrous tissue)

Angiolipoma (combination with proliferating blood vessels)

Myelolipoma (admixture with bone marrow elements as seen in adrenals)

Infiltrating or intramuscular lipoma (benign lipoma infiltrating into the striated muscle)
Spindle cell lipoma

Pleomorphic (atypical) lipoma.

Morphology:
* Grossly, a subcutaneous lipoma is usually small, round to oval and encapsulated mass. The cut surface
is soft, lobulated, yellowish-orange and greasy.
* Histologically, the tumour is composed of lobules of mature adipose cells separated by delicate fibrous
septa. A thin fibrous capsule surrounds the tumour.

Ans.
Mixed tumours: Mixed tumors have more than one neoplastic cell type, usually derived from one germ cell layer.
Example:

* Salivary gland: Pleomorphic adenoma (mixed tumor of salivary gland) - mostly benign and rarely

malignant
* Fibroadenoma of breast (benign tumour)

* Wilm’s tumour (malignant tumour).
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/S0)

Q. Write about teratoma. (RU-12/10Ju) (Very Important For VIVA)
Q. Short note: Teratoma. (RU-20Nv,08Ja, CU-05Ja)

Ans.
Teratoma: Teratoma refers to a group of complex tumors arise from totipotential cells, composed of
recognizable mature or immature cells or tissues belonging to more than one germ cell layer (and

sometimes all three).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/269)

Characteristics of teratoma: (V\V.I. For VIVA)

=  Teratomas originate from totipotent cells which are normally present in the gonads (ovary and
testis), and sometimes abnormally present in sequestered embryonic cell rests in midline locations
(extra-gonadal) such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, head, neck, and sacrococcygeal region.

= Teratoma is made up of a variety of parenchymal cells or tissues representing more than one germ
cell layer and often all three:

a) Ectoderm such as stratified squamous epithelial cells, skin, sebaceous glands, hair, tooth.
b) Endoderm such as gut epithelium.
c) Mesoderm such as muscle, fat, bone, cartilage.

* Skin and its appendages, tooth, gut epithelium, muscle, fat and any other tissue of the body may be
present in a teratoma.

s They may occur at any age from infancy to adult life.

s Teratomas may be benign or malignant. When all the components are well differentiated it is a
benign or mature teratoma, e.g. ovarian dermoid cyst (cystic teratoma). When a component is less
well-differentiated it is a malignant or immature teratoma.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/476,477; Prof. Khaleque/50)

Q. What is hamartoma? (RU-15/13Ja)

Q. Short note: Hamartoma. (RU-18M/Ja,14/10Ja) (Very Important For VIVA)
Ans.
Hamartoma: Hamartomas are disorganized masses composed of cells indigenous to the involved tissue.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/269)
Or,
The term hamartoma refers to an excessive, focal overgrowth of cells and tissues native to the organ in which
it occurs.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/475)
Or,
Hamartoma is a tumour-like developmental malformation formed by local tissue or tissues which are
arranged haphazardly.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/50)

Characteristics of hamartoma:
* It is a focal overgrowth of mature, normal tissues in abnormal proportions.
Usually there is an excess of one or more of its components
There is no capsule around a hamartoma
In any event, they are considered totally benign.
Although these might be considered neoplasms, the complete resemblance of the tissue to normal
cartilage or blood vessels and the occasional admixture of other elements suggest that the lesions
reflect anomalous development.

Example: A hamartoma in the lung may contain islands of cartilage, blood vessels, bronchial-type structures,
and lymphoid tissue. Sometimes the lesion is purely cartilaginous or purely angiomatous. But they do not form

organoid structure of lung tissue.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/269,475; Prof. Khaleque/50)

(Ref: Robbins/10"/270)

in abnormal locations.

neoplasms. Rarely, they are sites of origin of true neoplasms, producing paradoxes such as an adrenal

carcinoma arising in the ovary.

Q Define latent cancer.

Ags.

Latent cancer: These tumours show histological characteristics of malignancy but are clinically silent and
have very less chance of metastasis.

Example: Carcinoma of prostate in elderly people.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. Define dormant cancer. (CU-03Ja)
ABS.
Dermant cancer: It is the late appearance of metastasis after the successful removal of primary tumour.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. What is occult cancer?
Ans.
Occult cancer: These are also clinically silent carcinoma but diagnosed first from metastasis. Such as,
papillary carcinoma of thyroid may be first detected from metastatic lymph node.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. What is desmoplasia? (CU-03S) (For VIVA)

Ans.

Desmoplasia: When the parenchymal cells stimulate the formation of an abundant collagenous stroma, it is
referred to as desmoplasia.

Example: Scirrhous (stony hard) carcinoma of the female breast.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/268)

Q. What are the familial cancers? Name three familial cancers. (SU-10Ju)

Q. Short note: Familial cancers.

Ans.

Familial cancers: Besides the inherited syndromes of cancer susceptibility, cancer may occur at higher

frequency in certain families without a clearly defined pattem of transmission. These cancers are known as
familial cancers.

Examples:
* Breast cancer
* Ovarian cancer
* Pancreatic cancer

Features of familial cancers:
Early age at onset

Two or more primary relatives with the cancer
Multiple or bilateral tumors
Not associated with specific marker phenotypes
Transmission pattern is unclear
In general, siblings have a risk between two and three times greater than unrelated individuals.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/281 + 8"/275)

Q. Short note: Sacrococcygeal teratoma. (For VIVA)
