Ans.
Sacrococcygeal teratoma: Sacrococcygeal teratomas are the most common teratomas of childhood
accounting for 40% or more of cases.

Characteristics:
1. They occur with a frequency of 1 in 20,000 to 40,000 live births, four times more commonly in girls
than in boys.

2. Approximately 10% of sacrococcygeal teratomas are associated with congenital anomalies, primarily
defects of the hindgut and cloacal region and other midline defects (e.g. meningocele, spina bifida),
3. Approximately 75% of these tumors are mature teratomas, and about 12% are unequivocally
malignant and lethal. The remainders are immature teratoma.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/476)

Fig: Sacrococcygeal teratoma.

Benign & Malignant Tumour

Q. Define benign tumour. (V.V.I. for VIVA)
Ans.
Benign tumour: A tumor is said to be benign when its gross and microscopic appearances are considered
relatively innocent, implying that it will remain localized at its site of origin and is generally amenable to
surgical removal.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/268)

Predictably, the patient generally survives. However, “benign” tumors may cause significant morbidity and
are sometimes even fatal, when it occurs in vulnerable locations such as the brain.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/268)

Q. Mention the characteristics of benign tumour / neoplasm. (DU-22Nv)
Ans.

Characteristics of benign tumour / neoplasm: (V.V.I. for VIVA)
1. Differentiation: Benign tumours are well-differentiated. An example- leiomyoma resembles normal
smooth muscle. There is no undifferentiation (anaplasia). Mitotic figures are normal and rare.

2. (a) Rate of growth: The growth of most benign tumours is slow, (b) Size: Benign tumours are usually
small in size. But leiomyoma of the uterus and ovarian cystadenomas may be very large in size, (¢c)
Stroma: Well-formed.

3. (a) Capsule: Most benign tumours form capsule composed of surrounding rim of compressed
connective tissue. Capsule separates the tumour from the host tissue. Encapsulation leads to a discrete,
readily palpable and easily movable mass and can be surgically enucleated. But leiomyoma of the
uterus, haemangioma and surface growths (papilomas and adenomas) are not encapsulated, (b) No
local invasion in the surrounding tissue. Remain localized at the site of origin and do not have the
capacity to invade or infiltrate. \

5,

Clinical effects: Mostly innocent but may be harmful. They do not recur after complete removal.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/51)

Features of malignant tumour: (V.V.I. for VIVA)
1.

Differentiation and anaplasia: Malignant tumours exhibit variable differentiation ranging from
well differentiated (e.g. adenocarcinoma of thyroid) to poorly differentiated to anaplastic /

undifferentiated (most of the malignant tumours). Anaplasia is considered as a hallmark of
malignancy.

Anaplasia or lack of differentiation is marked by morphologic changes of anaplastic cells:

= Pleomorphism: Cancer cells & their nuclei often display pleomorphism (i.e. variation in cell size
and shape).

* Abnormal nuclear morphology: The nuclei are hyperchromatic and disproportionately large for
the cell, and the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio is 1 : 1 instead of the normal | : 4 or 1 : 6. The nuclear
shape is also very variable.

* Mitosis: Mitotic figures are often atypical and may show bizarre arrangement producing tripolar,
quadripolar or multipolar spindles.

= Loss of polarity: Architecture, organization and orientation of malignant cells are markedly
disturbed (i.e. they loss normal polarity).

« Other changes:
- Formation of tumour giant cells
- Hemorrhage and necrosis is common.

Rate of growth: Most cancers usually grow rapidly. Malignant tumours grow by invasion and
infiltration.

Local invasion: Malignant cells are locally invasive, infiltrating and destroying the surrounding
tissues, whereas nearly all benign tumors grow as cohesive expansile masses that remain localized to
their site of origin and lack the capacity to infiltrate, invade, or metastasize to distant sites.

Metastasis: Malignant cells may penetrate into blood vessels, lymphatics, and body cavities,
providing the opportunity for spread to a distant site by invasiveness. With few exceptions, all
malignant tumors can metastasize. Metastasis is the most reliable feature that differentiates

malignant from benign tumours.

Q. Classify malignant tumours. (For VIVA)
Ans.
Classification of malignant tumours:
A) On the basis of tissue of origin:
1. Carcinoma (malignant tumour of epithelial tissue)
2. Sarcoma (malignant tumour of solid mesenchymal tissue)

B) On the basis of invasiveness:
1. Carcinoma in situ or pre-invasive carcinoma (there is no local invasion)
2. Locally malignant tumors (these tumors spread locally by invasion but may not produce
metastasis)

C) On the basis of metastasis:
1. Primary malignant tumor

2. Secondary malignant tumor.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/269)

Q. What do you mean by tumours of intermediate malignancy (intermediate tumour /
borderline tumour)? (Very Important For VIVA)
Q. Name some intermediate tumours (borderline tumour). (RMU-24M)
Q. Name four intermediate tumours. (SU-14Ju)
Q. Short note: Intermediate tumours (borderline tumour).
Ans.
Tumours of intermediate malignancy (intermediate tumour / borderline tumour): An intermediate or
borderline tumor refers to a type of tumor that falls between benign (non-cancerous) and malignant
(cancerous).

* They do not fit either into benign or malignant group.

* Have uncertain or limited malignant potential.

= Have many histologic criteria of malignancy.

* No invasion.

= Future behavior is uncertain.
While they may not invade surrounding tissues aggressively like malignant tumors, they have a higher
risk of recurrence and potential to progress into cancer.

Example of intermediate / borderline tumors:
1. Borderline ovarian tumors: These are epithelial ovarian tumors with atypical cell features but
without clear invasion into surrounding tissue.

2. Atypical meningioma (WHO Grade II): A type of brain tumor that is more aggressive than a benign
meningioma but does not meet full criteria for malignancy.

3. Desmoid tumors (aggressive fibromatosis): Locally aggressive soft tissue tumors that do not
metastasize but have a high recurrence rate after removal.

4. Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs) - intermediate risk: Some GISTs have an intermediate
risk of malignancy based on size and mitotic activity.

These tumors require close follow-up as they may behave unpredictably, sometimes remaining stable or

progressing to a more aggressive form.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

LS
* In general benign tumors are well differentiated.

* Malignant tumors range from well differentiated to undifferentiated.

(N.B: Poorly differentiated malignant tumours usually have worse prognosis.)
(Ref: Robbins/10°/270)

Anaplasia: Lack of differentiation is called anaplasia. It is considered a hallmark of malignancy.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/270)

Characteristic features of anaplasia:
1, Pleomorphism: Cancer cells & their nuclei often display pleomorphism (i.e. variation in size and shape).

2. Abnormal nuclear morphology:
* The nuclei are hyperchromatic and disproportionately large for the cell
* Nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio = | : | (instead of the normal 1 : 4 or 1 : 6)
* Nuclear shape is extremely variable and large nucleoli.

3. Mitoses: Atypical, bizarre mitotic figures, sometimes producing tripolar, quadripolar or multipolar spindles.

4. Loss of polarity: Architecture, organization and orientation of anaplastic cells are markedly disturbed
(i.e. they loss normal polarity).

5. Other changes:
= Formation of tumour giant cells
* Hemorrhage and necrosis is common.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/271)

Q. What do you mean by dysplasia? (DU-19M,13Ju, RU-15/11Ja, SU-17M,14Ju) Write down the
features of dysplasia. (DU-16Ju)

Q. Mention the clinical importance of dysplasia. (DU-13Ju)

Q. Short note: Dysplasia. (DU-04Ja, RU-07Ja) (Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Dysplasia: The term dysplasia literally means “disordered growth” which is characterized by a loss of
uniformity of the individual cells as well as a loss in their architectural orientation.

Although dysplasia may be a precursor to malignant transformation, it does not always progress to cancer.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/272)

Characteristics: In dysplasia some but not all of the features of malignancy are present microscopically.
* Pleomorphism of the cells & nuclei (Pleomorphism — variation in size & shape)
* Large hyperchromatic nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio (1 : 4 - 1 : 6)
* Nuclear shape — variable
* Nuclear margin — irregular
* Chromatin — coarsely clumped & distributed along the nuclear membrane
* Mitotic figures are more abundant than usual
* Nucleoli— size and number increased
* The architecture of the tissue may be disordered.

---

#### 📄 Page 218

218 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Sites of dysplasia: Dysplasia is particularly common in squamous and transitional epithelia, such as-
= Cervix of uterus
* Respiratory tract in chronic cigarette smoker
» Adjacent to foci of invasive carcinoma
= Epidermis of skin
= Urinary bladder
=» Larynx
= Gall bladder
= Oral mucosa

} Uncommon

(N.B: Dysplasia is not encountered in connective tissue but in epithelia. It often occurs in metaplastic
epithelium, not all metaplastic epithelium is dysplastic.)

Grading of dysplasia:
= Mild dysplasia: If the changes are in lower 1/3".

= Moderate dysplasia: If features of dysplasia is in lower 2/3".

* Severe dysplasia: If features of dysplasia present in whole layers of the epithelium (also known as
carcinoma in situ).

Clinical importance of dysplasia:

« When dysplasia is severe and involves the full thickness of the epithelium but the lesion does not
penetrate the basement membrane, it is referred to as pre-invasive carcinoma or carcinoma in situ.
Once the tumor cells breach the basement membrane, the tumor is said to be invasive.

* Dysplastic changes are often found adjacent to foci of invasive carcinoma, and in some situations,
such as in the cervix, severe epithelial dysplasia or carcinoma in situ frequently antedates the
appearance of cancer.

= Moreover, some mutations associated with full-blown cancer may be present in even “mild”
dysplasias.

* With removal of inciting causes, even moderately severe dysplasias may be completely reversible.

« Even carcinoma in situ may persist for years before it becomes invasive.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/272,273)

(N.B: Dysplasia often occurs in metaplastic epithelium, but not all metaplastic epithelium is dysplastic).

Nice to Know: (Very Very Important for VIVA)
Dysplasia differs from cancer in two different aspects:

1. Lack of invasiveness
2. Reversibility.

Q. What do you mean by carcinoma in situ (DU-17/15Ja, RMU-24M, RU-17Ju/M,12Ja,09Ju) and
how you are going to diagnose such case? (RU-17Ju)
Q. Write in short about carcinoma in situ (CIS). (CU-08Ja)
Q. Short note: Carcinoma in situ (CIS). (DU-18/05Ja, RU-18Nv,16Ju, CU-11Ju)
Ans.
Carcinoma in situ: When dysplasia is severe and involves the full thickness of the epithelium but the lesion
does not penetrate the basement membrane, it is referred to as carcinoma in situ.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/272)

In situ epithelial cancers display all of the cytologic features of malignancy and unless treated have high
probability of progression to invasive cancers.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/272)
(N.B: Once the tumor cells breach the basement membrane, the tumor is said to be invasive.)

Examples of carcinoma in situ: Carcinoma in situ is often seen in the skin, breast, bladder, and uterine
cervix.
1. Cervical intra-epithelial neoplasia (CIN grade II) — (W.B: Don’t say grade I & Il)
2. Carcinoma in situ in the epidermis of skin (preceding the formation of invasive squamous cell
carcinoma)
3. In-situ carcinoma of the female breast
= Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)
= Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)

4. Severe dysplastic leukoplakia of mouth

5. Bowen’s disease

6. Erythroplasia of Queyrat

7. Carcinoma in situ of the urinary bladder
Importance:

1. From carcinoma in situ, invasive cancer may form
2. It is very early stage of invasive carcinoma and its excision results in complete cure of the cancer
3. Carcinoma in situ may persist for years before it becomes invasive.

Diagnosis: Cytology (by cells smears), confirmed by biopsy.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/52; Robbins/10"/272)

Q. Define tumour invasion. (CU-17M, 13Ja,12Ju)
Q. Define invasive carcinoma. (SU-04M)
Ans.
Tumour invasion: Invasion is aggressive infiltration of adjacent tissues by a malignant tumor.
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5°/90)

It is an active process in which invasion of tumour often occurs along tissue planes offering less resistance to
tumour growth such as surrounding extracellular matrix, peri-neural spaces and vascular lamina.

The invasiveness of cancers permits them to penetrate into blood vessels, lymphatics, and body cavities,
providing the opportunity for spread.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/273)

Invasive carcinoma: Invasive carcinomas are those that invade the surrounding extra-cellular matrix,
peri-neural spaces and vascular lamina.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/54)
Or,
When dysplasia is severe and involves the full thickness of the epithelium and the lesion penetrates the
basement membrane, it is considered as invasive neoplasm.

(Ref: Robbins/10°/272)

---

#### 📄 Page 221

GENERAL PATHOLOGY | 221

Example: Invasion within epithelium (intraepithelial spread) & infiltration of the epidermis of the nipple by
the tumour cells from a ductal carcinoma of the breast leads to Paget’s disease.

(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/54)

Q. Discuss in short the mechanism of tumour invasion. (SU-23M, RU-19M,11Ju,10/08/07Ja, CU-
10/08Ju)

Q. Write in brief the mechanism of malignant tumor invasion. (SU-08Ja)

Ans.

Mechanism of tumour invasion: Invasion of the ECM initiates the metastatic cascade and is an active
process that can be resolved into several steps:

I.

“Loosening up” of tumor cell-tumor cell interactions
Degradation of ECM

Attachment to “remodeled” ECM components
Migration and invasion of tumor cells.

First step: “Loosening up” of tumour cell-tumour cell interactions: Normal epithelial cells are
tightly glued to each other and the ECM by a variety of adhesion molecules. Cell-cell interactions are
mediated by the cadherin family of transmembrane glycoproteins (e.g. E-cadherins). In several
epithelial tumors (e.g. adenocarcinomas of the colon, stomach, and breast) E-cadherin function is
lost. Presumably, this reduces the ability of cells to adhere to each other and facilitates their
detachment from the primary tumor and their advance into the surrounding tissues.

A. LOOSENING OF INTERCELLULAR JUNCTIONS

Cadhenns| Type lV Laminin Fibronectin Laminin Basement
collagen receptor receptor membrane

Second step: Degradation of ECM (extra-cellular matrix): Tumor cells degrade the basement
membrane and interstitial connective tissue by either secreting proteolytic enzymes themselves or
by inducing fibroblasts and inflammatory cells to elaborate proteases (such as type IV collagenase,
matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), cathepsin D, and plasminogen activator etc.).

Type IV collagen cleavage = Plasminogen activator

3" step: Attachment of tumor cells to ECM proteins: After detachment, the malignant cells adhere
to the ECM components like laminin, fibronectin, and collagen via receptors.

Final step: Migration and invasion of tumour cells: Propelling of tumor cells through the degraded
basement membranes is stimulated and directed by several types of factors. These include:

---

#### 📄 Page 222

222 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Tumor cell-derived cytokines including chemokines and growth factors (e.g. insulin-like growth
factors), which act as autocrine motility factors.

= Cleavage products of matrix components (e.g. collagen, laminin).
«= Stromal cell-derived paracrine factors such as hepatocyte growth factor/scatter factor.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/306-308)

Nice to Know:

The invasiveness of cancers permits them to penetrate blood vessels, lymphatics, and body cavities,
providing the opportunity for spread (metastasis).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/274)

Q. Define metastasis. (DU-09Ju, SU-22/21Nv,14/11Ja,09Ju, BUP-22M,21Nv/M, RU-20M,11/07Ja,

CU-20Ju, 17M, | 5Ju,13Ja,12Ju) (Very*** Very*** Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Metastasis: Metastasis is defined as the spread of a tumor to sites that are physically discontinuous with the
primary tumor, an event that unequivocally marks a tumor as malignant.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/273)
Or,
Metastasis are tumour implants discontinuous with the primary tumour.
(Ref: Robbins/8"/269)
Examples:
= Carcinomas of the prostate and breast preferentially spread to bone
* Bronchogenic carcinomas (lung cancers) tend to involve the adrenals and the brain
* Neuroblastomas spread to the liver and bones.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/309)

Nice to Know:

It is evident then that the properties of invasiveness and metastasis are separable. Blood cancers
(leukemias and lymphomas) are a special case. These tumors are derived from cells that normally have
the capacity to enter the bloodstream and travel to distant sites. As a result, leukemias and lymphomas
(sometimes referred to as “liquid tumors”) are often disseminated at diagnosis and are always taken to be

malignant, unlike all other tumors (so-called “solid” tumors), which are derived from cells that do not
_ normally circulate in the bloodstream.

Overall, approximately 30% of solid tumors (excluding skin cancers other than melanomas) present as
| metastatic disease, In general, the likelihood of metastasis of a solid tumor correlates with other
_ features of malignancy, including lack of differentiation, aggressive local invasion, rapid growth, and
large size There are innumerable exceptions, however. Small, well-differentiated, slow-growing lesions
netimes metastasize widely; conversely, some rapidly growing, large lesions remain localized for years.

---

#### 📄 Page 223

GENERAL PATHOLOGY | 223

—_

Metastasis is thus a complex and unpredictable process that involves many factors relating to both invader
and host. Metastatic spread strongly reduces the possibility of cure; hence, short of prevention of cancer,
no achievement would be of greater benefit to patients than an effective means to block metastasis, with the

important caveat that many tumors that kill the patient have already spread by the time of initial diagnosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/274)

Ans.
Pathways / routes of tumour metastasis: Dissemination of cancers occurs through three pathways-
1. Lymphatic spread
2. Haematogenous or blood spread
3. Direct seeding of body cavities or surfaces

A. Lymphatic spread: Transport through lymphatic vessels is the most common pathway for the initial
dissemination of carcinomas. Sarcomas also sometimes use this route.

Example:

* Ca breast arising in the upper outer quadrants, generally disseminate first to the axillary lymph
nodes and then to infraclavicular and supraclavicular lymph nodes.

* Bronchogenic carcinoma metastasizes first to the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes.

* Gastric carcinoma metastasizes to left supraclavicular / Virchow’s node (Troisier’s sign).

(N.B: Local lymph nodes, however, may be bypassed—so-called skip metastasis).

Cancer lung

Cancer breast

tracheal lymph nodes involved by bronchogenic carcinoma.

B. Haematogenous or blood spread: Haematogenous spread is fypical of sarcoma but is also seen with
carcinomas, especially those of the lung, breast, thyroid, kidney, liver, prostate and ovary etc.

and adrenals etc.

C. Seeding of body cavities or surfaces: It occurs whenever a malignant neoplasm penetrates into a natural
“open field” lacking physical barriers. It involves most often the peritoneal cavity, but any other cavity-
pleural, pericardial, subarachnoid and joint spaces—may be affected.

Example:
* Carcinoma of stomach or colon may gravitate and metastasize in one or both ovaries
transperitoneally producing secondary tumors termed “Krukenberg tumors”.

A mucus-secreting appendiceal carcinoma or ovarian carcinoma fills the peritoneal cavity with a
gelatinnous neoplastic mass referred to as “Pseudomyxoma peritonei”.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/274; BRS Pathology/5"/90; Harsh Mohan/7"/193)

walls, are more resistant to penetration by cancer cells.

Q. Briefly discuss about sentinel lymph nodes. (CU-18Nv)

Q. Short note: Skip metastasis (RU-18M,16/14Ju) (For VIVA)

Ans.

Skip metastasis: It is the metastasis bypassing the local lymph nodes due to venous-lymphatic anastomosis
or because inflammation or radiation has obliterated lymphatic channels.

Sentinel lymph node: A sentinel lymph node is defined as “the first node in a regional lymphatic basin that
receives lymph flow from the primary tumor.”

Sentinel lymph node biopsy: Sentinel node mapping can be done by injection of radiolabeled tracers or
colored dyes during surgery — Frozen section biopsy of the sentinel lymph nodes.

Importance of sentinel lymph node biopsy: Biopsy of sentinel nodes is often used to assess the presence or
absence of metastatic lesions in the lymph nodes guiding the surgeon to the appropriate therapy.

Q. Name two most important angiogenic & anti-angiogenic factors. (V.V./ for MD/MS exam)
Q. Short note: Tumour angiogenesis. (DU-10Ju)
Ans.

Tumor angiogenesis: Tumors stimulate the growth of host blood vessels, a process called angiogenesis,
which is essential for supplying nutrients to the tumor.

---

#### 📄 Page 228

228 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY
—__—$__—_—— —_—_— SS SS

Tumour can not grow / enlarge beyond 1-2 mm unless they are vascularized. To grow vascularization is
essential. Beyond this necrosis (death) occur.

Effects of tumour angiogenesis: Neovascularization has a dual effect on tumor growth:

1. Oxygen and nutrition supply & newly formed endothelial cells secrete polypeptide growth factors
(such as insulin-like growth factor and PDGF) which stimulates tumour growth.
2. Provides path for metastasis.

Mechanism of tumour angiogenesis: Recruitment of endothelial cell precursors or by sprouting of existing
capillaries.

Fig: Mechanism of tumour angiogenesis.

Important tumour angiogenic factors: Produced by tumor cells or macrophages-
a. VEGF (Vascular endothelial growth factor)
b. PDGF (Platelet-derived growth factor)
c. bFGF (Basic fibroblast growth factor).

Anti-angiogenic factors produced by tumour cells: Tumor growth is controlled by the balance between
angiogenic & anti-angiogenic factors produced by the tumour cells. Important anti-angiogenic factors are:

a. Thrombospondin-1

b. Angiostatin

c. Endostatin

d. Vasculostatin.

(Ref: Robbins/10'/305)

Tumour Progression & Heterogeneity

Q Shert note on: Tumour progression (SU-05M) and heterogeneity. (DU-04M)

Aas

Twmeur progression: Tumour progression refers to the phenomenon whereby tumours become more
aggressive and acquire greater malignant potential over a period of time.

Example: In some instances (e.g. colon cancer), there is an orderly evolution from pre-neoplastic lesion to
benign tumors and, ultimately, invasive cancers. This phenomenon is referred to as tumour progression.
Angiogenesis and changes in the tumor stroma are also components of tumor progression.

Pre-neoplastic lesion — benign tumors — invasive cancers

This biologic phenomenon is related to the sequential appearance of cells that differ with respect to several
phenotypic attributes such as invasiveness, rate of growth, metastatic ability, karyotype, hormonal
responsiveness, and susceptibility to anti-neoplastic drugs.

Tumour heterogeneity: Transformed cells are genetically unstable due to loss of P® gene or from inherited or
acquired mutations in gene that regulate DNA repair. These and other unidentified factors render tumor cells
prone to a high rate of random, spontaneous mutations during clonal expansion. This phenomenon is called
tamor heterogeneity which begins well before the tumor is clinically evident.

(Ref: Robbins/7"/319)

Tumour Immunity

Q. Name the components of tumour immunity. (/mportant for VIVA)
Q. What is tumour immunity? (CMU-24M)
Ans.

Tumour immunity: Tumor immunity refers to the body’s immune response against cancerous cells.
Components of tumour immunity:
1. Cell-mediated immunity:
= Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+ cells) is protective against virus associated neoplasm.

* NK cells: Capable of destroying tumour cells without prior sensitization. NK cells particularly
effective against cells with reduced MHC expression.

= Macrophages: Activated macrophages have anti-tumour reactivity. They may kill tumour cells by
producing reactive oxygen metabolites or by producing tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-a)

2. Humoral immunity: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) may play a protective role.
NK cells can participate in ADCC.

(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/63)

Etiology of Tumour : Carcinogen & Carcinogenesis

Q. Briefly state the role of environmental factors in the development of cancer. (DU-18M)
Ans.

Esiology / causes of cancer:
1. Environmental factors: It is the dominant risk factors for the development of most cancers. Important
environmental factors implicated in carcinogenesis include-

* Infectious agents: About 15% of all cancers worldwide are believed to be caused directly or
indirectly by infectious agents. For example-

type-1 (HTLV-1) _|

= Gastric lymphoma (MALToma)

Smoking: Smoking particularly of cigarettes, has been implicated in cancer of the mouth,
pharynx, larynx, esophagus, pancreas, bladder, and most significantly, about 90% of lung cancer
deaths.

Alcohol consumption: Alcohol abuse increases the risk of carcinoma of mouth and esophagus
(especially in association with cigarette smoking), and hepatocellular carcinoma (in association
with cirrhosis of liver).

Diet: Colorectal carcinoma, prostate carcinoma, and breast carcinoma has been ascribed to
differences in diet.

Obesity: Approximately 14% of cancer deaths in men and 20% in women can be attributed to
obesity.

Reproductive history: Exposure to estrogen without progesterone, increases the risk of cancers of
the breast and endometrium.

Environmental carcinogens: Individuals may be exposed to carcinogenic factors when they go
outside, e.g.-

- Ultraviolet [UV] rays / excess sun exposure — Squamous cell carcinoma and basal cell
carcinoma of skin; melanoma.

- Drink tube well water (e.g. arsenic, particularly in Bangladesh) — Squamous cell and basal cell
carcinoma of skin.

- Certain medications (e.g. methotrexate)

- Occupational exposure (e.g. asbestos) — Lung Ca, oesophageal Ca, Gastric Ca, Colon Ca,
mesothelioma.

- Taking grilled meat, high-fat & low-fiber diet - Adenocarcinoma of colon, breast carcinoma.

2. Genetic predisposition: In some families cancer is an inherited trait, ¢.g. breast cancer, ovarian
cancer, and pancreatic cancer as well as melanomas and lymphomas.

3. Age: Cancers are most common in adults older than 60 years of age, but occurs in adults at all ages
and in children and infants.

4. Sex: Breast carcinoma is greater in female than male whereas gastric and colorectal cancers are more
in male.

5. Acquired predisposing conditions:

Chronic inflammations: Chronic epithelial injury often leads to metaplasia, and eventually
leading to cancer. Examples include - Barrett esophagus (gastric and colonic metaplasia of the
esophageal mucosa in the setting of gastric reflux); squamous metaplasia of the bronchial mucosa

---

#### 📄 Page 231

GENERAL PATHOLOGY 231

(in response to smoking) and the bladder mucosa (in response to schistosomiasis infection); and
colonic metaplasia of the stomach (in the setting of pernicious anemia and chronic atrophic
gastritis),

* Precursor lesions: Precursor lesions can be defined as localized morphologic changes that are
associated with a high risk of cancer. Virtually all precursor lesions arise in epithelial surfaces and
are associated with an increased risk of various forms of carcinoma.

Such conditions include atrophic gastritis of pernicious anemia, solar keratosis of the skin, chronic
ulcerative colitis, and leukoplakia of the oral cavity, vulva, and penis.

« Immunodeficiency states: Patients who are immunodeficient, and particularly those who have
deficits in T-cell immunity, are at increased risk for cancers, especially those caused by oncogenic
viruses. These virally associated tumors include mainly lymphomas, but also certain carcinomas
and even some sarcomas and sarcoma-like proliferations.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/278; BRS Pathology/5"/93)

Q. Write down the events of chemical carcinogenesis. (BUP-22M,21Nv/M)
Q. Write a note on chemical carcinogenesis. (RU-18/17Ja, SU-10Ju)

Ans.

Chemical carcinogenesis: Chemical carcinogenesis means induction of cancer by chemical carcinogens.

Steps involved in chemical carcinogenesis: Carcinogenesis is a multistep process. Among them initiation anj

promotion are the 2 major steps-

1. Initiation: Initiation results from exposure of cells to a sufficient dose of a carcinogenic agen
(initiator); an initiated cell is altered, making it potentially capable of giving rise to a tumor. It al
causes permanent DNA damage (mutations). Initiation alone, however, is not sufficient for tumor

formation.

Chemicals that can cause initiation of carcinogenesis can be classified into two categories-

* Direct-acting agent: Cancer chemotherapeutic drugs (e.g. alkylating agents).
« Indirect-acting agent: Polycyclic hydrocarbons, benzo[a]pyrene, aromatic amines and azo dyes.

2. Promotion: Promoters can induce tumors in initiated cells, but they are nontumorigenic by
themselves. Furthermore, tumors do not result when the promoting agent is applied before, rather than
after, the initiating agent. This indicates that, in contrasts to the effects of initiators, the cellular

changes resulting from the application of promoters do not affect DNA directly and are reversible.

Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals

Evasion of apoptosis

Limitless replicative potential (immortality)

Ability to evade the host immune response.

Q. Short note: Aneuploidy. (CU-18Nv, SU-18M)

Ans.

Aneuploidy: Normal cells are diploid, containing 46 chromosomes, 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex
chromosomes, XX in females or XY in males.

Aneuploidy is a chromosome number that is not a multiple of 23 (the normal haploid number), for example a
human cell having 45 or 47 chromosomes instead of the usual 46.

Mechanism: It is caused most often by an addition or loss of one or two chromosomes; this change may result
from non-disjunction or anaphase lag.

Non-disjunction:
(1) It is the failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis or mitosis (meiotic non-disjunction is the
most common).
(2) It is responsible for disorders such as trisomy 21 (the most common form of Down syndrome).

Anaphase lag:
(1) It results in the loss of a chromosome during meiotic or mitotic division.
(2) In early embryonic life, this can result in mosaicism, in which an individual develops two lines of
cells, one with a normal chromosome complement and another with monosomy, a single residual

chromosome, for the affected chromosome pair.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/165; BRS Pathology/5"/48)

{N.B: Aneuploidy is remarkably common in cancers, particularly carcinomas (i.e. cancer cells may have

abnormal number of chromosomes)}.
(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/203)

Q. p53 gene is called “guardian of the genome” - Explain.

Q. Short note: p53. (CU-12Ja)

Ans.

p53 gene: p53 (Guardian of the Genome) is a tumor suppressor gene that regulates cell cycle progression,
DNA repair, cellular senescence, and apoptosis, and is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancers.
it is found in more than 50% of cancers.

(The official name of the gene is TP53 and the protein is p53; for the sake of simplicity, we refer to both as
“p53”)

Location of p53 gene: It is located on chromosome 17p13.1.
Functions of p53 gene: Cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage.

p53 acts in G,/S check point of the cell cycle. When cells sustain DNA damage, p53 undergoes conformational
change & includes the expression of genes that causes-

---

#### 📄 Page 242

242 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

* Shut down of cell cycle until DNA damage is repaired. So damaged DNA is not duplicated.
«= When DNA damage repair is not possible, then p53 gene initiates apoptosis of cell.

In view of these activities, p53 has been rightfully called the “guardian of the genome”.

With loss of function of p53, DNA damage goes unrepaired, mutations accumulate in dividing cells, and the
cell marches along a one-way street leading to malignant transformation.

p53 mutations occur in virtually every type of cancer, including carcinomas of the lung, colon, and breast—
the three leading causes of cancer death.

p53 mutation is common in a variety of tumour suggests that p53 acts a critical gatekeeper against the
formation of cancer. Indeed, it is evident that p53 acts as a “molecular policeman” that prevents the
propagation of genetically damaged cells.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/294; BRS Pathology/5"/97)

Clinical Aspects of Neoplasia: Cancer Cachexia & Para-neoplastic Syndrome

Q. Short note: Cancer cachexia. (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Cancer cachexia: Cancer cachexia is a hypercatabolic state defined by a loss of muscle mass (with or
without loss of fat) that cannot be explained by diminished food intake.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/328)

Or,

Cancer cachexia may be defined as progressive loss of body fat and lean body mass, accompanied by profound
weakness, anorexia, and anemia, that is caused by release of factors by the tumor or host immune cells.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/331)

It occurs in about 50% of cancer patients, most commonly in individuals with advanced gastrointestinal,
pancreatic, and lung cancers, and is responsible for about 30% of cancer deaths.

Characteristics: It is a highly debilitating condition characterized by extreme weight loss, fatigue, muscle
atrophy, anemia, anorexia, and edema. Mortality is generally the consequence of atrophy of the diaphragm and
other respiratory muscles.

Causes of cancer cachexia: The precise causes of cancer cachexia are not known, but several inflammatory
mediators appear to have important roles.

=« TNF-a (cachectin), IL-1 (released from macrophage) — promotes catabolism of fatty tissue.
* Proteolysis inducing factors (released from tumour cells) — responsible for loss of muscle mass.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/328; BRS Pathology/5”/91)

21M,20Nv/M, 18M, 16Ju)

Q. Write briefly about tumour grading. (CU-11Ju)

Q. Short note: Cancer grading. (CU-14Ju)

Ans.
Grading of tumour: Grading of a cancer is based on the degree of differentiation of the tumour cells and, in

some cancers, the number of mitoses or architectural features.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/330)
Or,
Grading of a cancer is based on the degree of differentiation of tumour cells and the number of mitoses
within the tumour as presumed correlates to the neoplasm aggressiveness. Thus cancers are classified as

grade-I to grade-IV with increasing anaplasia.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

In general, with a few exceptions, such as soft-tissue sarcomas, grading of cancers has proved of less clinical
value than has staging.

Grading procedure: Cancers are classified as grades I to [TV with increasing anaplasia.
1. Grade-I (Well differentiated): More than 75% cells are differentiated (normal cells)
2. Grade-I] (Moderately differentiated): 50 - 75% cell differentiation
3. Grade-III (Poorly differentiated): 25 - 50 % cell differentiation
4. Grade-IV (Undifferentiated): Less than 25% cell differentiation.

Staging of tumour: The staging of solid cancers is based on the size of the primary lesion, its extent of
spread to regional lymph nodes, and the presence or absence of blood-borne metastases. It has greater
clinical value than grading.

Staging procedure: Two major staging systems are currently in use-

1. UICC (Union Internationale Contre Cancer) employs TNM system, and
2. AJC (American Joint Committee) employs different nomenclature

Q. Short note: Cytology.
Ans

Laboratory diagnosis of tumour / cancer: (V.V./, ********* For VIVA)
1. Cytopathology
2. Histopathology
3. Tumour markers
4. Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
5. Flow cytometry
6. Molecular diagnosis

A. Cytopathology: Cytopathological methods (study of cells) for diagnosis of tumour consist of following
methods:
a) Exfoliative cytology (Study of cells shed off into body cavities): This method is based on

microscopic identification of the characteristics of malignant cells into the sheded or ‘exfoliated’
cells. Here exfoliated cells are used to prepare smears & staining.

Most commonly used smear is Papanicolaou or Pap smear method which is used for detecting
dysplasia, carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma of the uterine cervix, and carcinoma of vagina.
Other materials include - sputum and bronchial washings; pleural, peritoneal and pericardial effusions;
urine, gastric secretions, and CSF.

b) Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC): This method consists of study of cells obtained by a fine
needle introduced into the superficial and deep-seated lesions in the body (which do not shed off cells
freely). It is a less invasive, less expensive, reliable & quick method of diagnosis, e.g. from the breast,
thyroid, lymph nodes, liver and pancreas etc.

c) Others: Brushing cytology, Scrap cytology, imprint cytology etc.

B. Histopathology (gold standard): Microscopic examination of excised tumour mass or biopsy tissue from
the mass.

---

#### 📄 Page 252

EE —

252 | _arif’s representation ¢ on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Specimen:
a) Biopsy. A mass or a piece of tissue is removed for histopathology, e.g. lymph node biopsy by
excision; true cut / core needle biopsy from liver, lung, breast, kidney etc.

b) Large material like whole breast (after mastectomy), part of breast (after lumpectomy) etc.

Examination: A gross or naked eye description is recorded. Then sectioning and staining of the sample
are done for histological / microscopic examination.

C. Tumour markers: Tumour markers are biochemical indicators of the presence of a tumour. They may
be found in the blood, urine, stool, other bodily fluids, or tissues of some patients with cancer. They
cannot be used for definitive diagnosis of cancer; however they contribute to the detection of cancer.

Example: More than 20 tumour markers are currently in use. Examples include AFP (hepatocellular
carcinoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours of the testis), PSA (carcinoma prostate), CEA &
CA-19-9 (cancers of the GI tract & pancreas), CA-125 (carcinoma ovary) etc.

D. Immuno-histochemistry (IHC): This is an immunological method where surface markers or cell
products (called antigens) are identified by using specific antibodies. Examples include -
Pancytokeratin (for carcinoma), desmin & vimentin (for sarcoma), CD markers (for lymphoma), S-100
(for melanoma) etc.

E. Flow cytometry: It is used to measure cell characteristics such as membrane antigens and DNA
content of tumour cells. It can be employed on liquid particles such as blood cells, bone marrow
aspirates, body fluids etc., and this method is most commonly used in diagnosis of leukaemia and
lymphoma.

F. Molecular diagnosis (PCR, DNA sequencing, DNA microarray analysis): Molecular techniques are

used for diagnosis of tumours, like B-cell and T-cell neoplasms, chronic myeloid leukaemia etc. Molecular
techniques are also used in the diagnosis of hereditary predisposition to cancer.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/331; Prof. Khaleque/62; Lecture SSMC)

(Note: For diagnosis of a neoplasia, proper history, clinical examination, biochemical and radiological findings
are necessary prior to cytological or histopathological examination is done.)

Q. What is FNAC? (RU-12Ja) Write down the indications of FNAC. (RMU-22/18M)

Q. Write in brief about FNAC. (RU-10Ja)

Q. Short note: FNAC. (DU-18M, CMU-23/22/21M,20Ju, 1 6Ja, 13Ju,11Ja, RU-20/19M,17Ju/M, 16/
07Ja, SU-17M,06/05Ja)

Ans.

FNAC: FNAC means “fine needle aspiration cytology”. It is the procedure which involves aspiration of a
small amount of fluid and very small pieces of tissue from the tumour with a very thin, small-bore needle
followed by cytological examination of the stained smear.

Procedure:
a) Image guided (USG & CT scan)
b) Non-guided

Staining:
a) Papanicolaou stain (PAP stain)
b) Haematoxylin and eosin (H & E) staining

Application: This method is used most commonly for the assessment of readily palpable lesions in sites such as-

a) Breast

b) Thyroid

c) Salivary glands

d) Superficial lymph nodes

e) Lung, prostate, liver & pancreas (by using modern imaging techniques).

Significance:

Advantages:
* Less invasive, relatively painless and more rapidly performed than needle biopsies.

* Cheaper than needle biopsies.

* Low risk of complication so can be done in outpatient department.
* Highly suitable for debilitated persons.

* Readily repeatable and useful for multiple lesions.

* Aspiration can be done without anesthesia.

* Highly accurate in experienced hand.

Disadvantages:
* Small sample size (sometimes FNA needle can’t remove enough tissue for a definite diagnosis)

Sampling errors
Need experienced hands

May produce complications, e.g. bleeding, infection, shedding of tumour cells.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/331; Lecture DMC)

Q. Mention the role of histopathology in tumour diagnosis. (RU-| 7Nv,12/10Ju)
Q. Short note: Histopathology. (RU-16/15Ju)

Ans.

Histopathology: Microscopic examination of tissue after proper preparation.

Examination: A gross or naked eye description is recorded. Then sectioning and staining of the sample are
done for histological / microscopic examination.

a) Sectioning:

* Paraffin section method: It is the routine method. Steps in preparation of sections of the tissue
are: The tissue is cut into small pieces + fixed in formal-saline fixative — Tissue is dehydrated in
ethyl alcohol and then in xylol — Tissue is casted in paraffin to make a ‘block’ — Sections are
cut from the block and taken on slides for staining.

* Frozen section method: It is a special method and not done as a routine. The sample is frozen
quickly and sections are made. By this method histological examination is done within minutes.
As an example: To decide the nature of a breast lesion during operation.

b) Staining: Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining of sections: It is the routine staining for
histopathological examination. The nucleus takes purple colour and the cytoplasm takes pink colour
in H&E stain.

Role of histopathology in tumour diagnosis: Histopathology (biopsy) results-
* The cells are cancerous or not
= Ifcancerous, then type of cancer & grading as well.

(Ref: Robbins/10'/331; Prof. Khaleque/62)

* 95% ethanol / 95% alcohol
= 95% rectified spirit (90% ethanol + other constituents)
= 100% methanol
* 80% isopropanol or propanol

2. Coating preservatives:
= 2-10% carbowax in 95% ethanol

3. Carnoy’s preservatives: Ideal for bloody specimen.

Aim: Preservatives are used after biopsy to-
1. Process the tissue for microtome sectioning

Q. Short note: Tissue processing. (CU-19M)

Ans.

Tissue processing: Preparation of tissue (animal or human) to visualize under light microscope is called tissue
preparation.

Purpose of tissue processing: The purpose of tissue processing is to demonstrate normal and abnormal
structures of cell.

Steps of tissue processing:

1. Sample / tissue collection - Fresh tissue specimens should be collected and handled carefully and
appropriately fixed as soon as possible after dissection.

2. Fixation - It is a process where tissues are immersed in solution called fixatives (such as 10% formal
saline / formalin) for permanent preservation of tissue structure and protection against subsequent
processing steps.

3. Dehydration - It is the process of removal of extractable or free water from the fixed tissue by
immersing specimens in a series of ethanol (alcohol).

4. Clearing - Clearing is a process by which tissue is allowed to be transparent for well visualization.
Xylene is used as routine ‘clearing agent’.

5. Embedding - Tissues are usually embedded in a solid medium to facilitate sectioning. To obtain thin
sections with the microtome, tissues must be infiltrated after fixation with embedding substances that
impart a rigid consistency to the tissue. Routinely used embedding agent is paraffin wax.

6. Sectioning / cutting - Tissues in paraffin blocks are sectioned at 5-10 micrometer thickness with a rotary
microtome.

7. Preliminary mounting - Sections were placed in hot water bath at 48-50°C. Tissue section is then taken on slide.

8. Staining - To be studied microscopically sections must typically be stained or dyed because most
tissues are colorless. Routinely used dye combination is hematoxyline & eosine (H & E).
Staining procedure:
« Deparaffinization
* Rehydration
» Staining with hematoxylin & eosine (H & E)
= Dehydration
* Clearing
* Final mounting.

Now slide is ready for visualization under light microscope.

Nice to Know:
Classification of stains:

1. Acid stains: Eosin which imparts red color.

2. Basic stains: Hacmatoxilin which imparts blue color
3. Neutral stain: Leishman stain

Q. What is frozen section? Mention its two important uses. (DU-17M)

Q. Write down the indications of frozen section. (DU-17Nv)

Q. Short note: Frozen section biopsy. (BUP-21Nv/M)

Ans.

Frozen section: It is a histological technique to provide intra-operative diagnosis. The technical name for this
procedure is cryosection. In frozen section, there is no use of dehydrating solution, clearing agent and
embedding media.

Importance / use / indications of frozen section:
Urgent histological or ‘On-table’ diagnosis of malignancy (in Operation Theater).

Depending on result, surgeon can plan the next course of operation.

Determine whether margins are free of malignancy.

Determine whether a breast nodule is benign or malignant & decide to perform lumpectomy or

mastectomy.

Determine presence or absence of ganglion cells in case of Hirchsprung’s disease in surgical pathology.

= Special uses:

- Used in enzyme and non-enzyme histochemistry

- Used in immunofluorescence (i.e. to demonstrate deposition of antibody, complement, fibrin &
other antigen)

- Used for detection of amyloid in tissue.

Limitation:
* Adequate clinical information must be needed.
* Adequate and representative sample must be submitted.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/331; Lecture DMC & SSMC)

Q. Why clinical data is important for accurate histopathologic diagnosis? (DU-17M)
Ans.

Role of clinical data for accurate histopathologic diagnosis: Clinical data are invaluable for accurate
pathologic diagnosis, but often clinicians underestimate its value. For example-

* Radiation changes in the skin or mucosa can be similar to those associated with cancer.
* Sections taken from a healing fracture can mimic an osteosarcoma.

So, clinical data is important for accurate histopathologic diagnosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/331)

Q. Discuss the utility of immuno-histochemistry in diagnosis of malignant tumour. (SU-14/13Ju)
Q. Write down the role / importance of immuno-cytochemistry / immuno-histochemistry in
tumour diagnosis. (RU-12Ju, SU-19Nv,17M,11Ju)

Q. Short note: Immunohistochemistry. (CU-19M)

Ans.

Immuno-histochemistry (IHC): This is a technique for identifying cellular or tissue constituents (antigens)
by means of antigen-antibody interaction.

Role of THC in diagnosis of tumour: The utility of IHC in the diagnosis or management of malignant
neoplasms is as follows:

---

#### 📄 Page 259

GENERAL PATHOLOGY | 259

—_—_—_— .
1) Categorization of undifferentiated malignant tumours: For example, presence of cytokeratins

points to an epithelial origin (carcinoma), whereas desmin is specific for neoplasms of muscle cell
origin (sarcoma), and hematologic malignancies lack these cytoskeletal structures.

2) Categorization of leukaemias and lymphomas: For example, detection of CD29, a marker of B-cell
lymphoma.

3) Determination of site of origin of metastatic tumours: For example, prostate-specific antigen
(PSA) and thyroglobulin are markers of carcinomas of the prostate and thyroid, respectively.

4) Detection of molecules that have prognostic or therapeutic significance: For example,
immunohistochemical detection of hormone receptors (estrogen & progesterone receptors) in
breast cancer cells is of prognostic and therapeutic value because these cancers are susceptible to
anti-estrogen therapy (hormone therapy). In general, receptor-positive breast cancers have a better
prognosis than receptor-negative tumors. Moreover, breast cancers with strong immunohistochemical
staining for the protein product of the HER2 generally have a poor prognosis but are amenable to
treatment with antibodies that block the activity of the HER2 receptor.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/332)

Q. What do you mean by small, round, blue-cell tumors? Name 4 of them. (CU-18Nv)

Ans.

Small, round, blue-cell tumors: A group of childhood tumors that are characterized by their primitive
histologic appearance are collectively referred to as small, round, blue-cell tumors.

Under the microscope, these tumors are characterized by small, round cells that stain blue on routine H & E

Example:
= Neuroblastoma

Wilms tumor

Lymphoma

Rhabdomyosarcoma

Ewing sarcoma / peripheral neuroectodermal tumor

Medulloblastoma

Retinoblastoma.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/475 + Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/286)

Q. Short note: Wilm’s tumour. (SU-05Ja)
Ans.
Wilm’s tumour: Please see the Systemic Pathology “Renal System”.

Q. Short note: Retinoblastoma. (SU-05Ja)
Ans.
Retinoblastoma: Please see the Systemic Pathology “Nervous System”.

Q. Short note: Rhabdomyosarcoma.

Ans.

Rhabdomyosarcoma: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor with skeletal muscle
differentiation.

Classification / histologic type: Four subtypes are recognized:
1. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (20%)
2. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (50%)
3. Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma (20%)
4. Spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (10%).

Age of incidence:

« Alveolar and embryonal subtypes are the most common soft tissue sarcoms a of childhood and
adolescence, usually appearing before 20 years of age.
Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma occurs in adults.

= Spindle cell/sclerosing type affects all ages.

Location: They may arise in any anatomic location, but most often arise in the sinuses, head and neck, and
genitourinary tract.

Diagnosis: By biopsy followed by histopathology and immunohistochemistry.

Treatment: Surgical resection followed by chemotherapy, with or without radiation therapy.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1212)

Environmental Diseases

Q. Define environmental diseases.

Ans.
Environmental diseases: Environmental diseases are conditions caused by exposure to chemical or physical

agents in the ambient, workplace, and personal environments.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/410)

Q. Short note: Environmental pollution. (DU-13Ju)

Ans.
Environmental pollution: Environmental pollution is the introduction of contaminants into the natural
environment that causes adverse change.

1. Air pollution:
* Outdoor air pollution: The commonest pollutants are sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone,
nitrogen dioxide, lead, and particulate matter.

* Indoor air pollution: The commonest pollutant is tobacco smoke, but additional offenders are CO,
nitrogen dioxide, asbestos, volatile substances containing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
generated by cooking oils and coal burning, wood smoke, bioaerosols, radon, formaldehyde etc.

Water pollution: By different wastes and metals.

Soil contamination: Occurs when chemicals are released by spill or underground leakage.

Noise pollution: e.g. roadway noise, aircraft noise, industrial noise as well as high-intensity sonar.
Light pollution: Includes light trespass, over-illumination and astronomical interference.

Metals as environmental pollutants: Lead, mercury, arsenic, and cadmium are the heavy metals
most commonly associated with harmful effects in human.

Effects of Alcohol

Q. What are the diseases associated with ethanol abuse?
Q. What are the adverse effects of ethanol?

Ans

Diseases associated with ethanol abuse/ adverse effects of ethanol:

Acute alcoholism:
= Hepatic changes: Fatty change or hepatic steatosis.

= Gastric changes: Acute gastritis and ulceration.

= CNS changes: Alcohol acts as CNS depressant. Consequently there is stimulation and disordered
cortical, motor, and intellectual behaviour. Respiratory arrest may follow.

Chronic alcoholism: Chronic alcoholism virtually affects all organs and tissues, but principally

affects the following:

* Liver: Fatty change, alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, increased risk of
hepatocellular carcinoma.

= Gastrointestinal tract: Massive bleeding from gastritis, gastric ulcer, esophageal varices.

* Thiamine (Vitamin B,) deficiency: Peripheral neuropathies, Wemicke-Korsakoff syndrome,
cerebral atrophy, cerebellar degeneration, optic neuropathy.

= Cardiovascular: Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy (dilated congestive cardiomyopathy), hypertension,
decreased level of HDL, Increased risk of coronary heart disease.

= Pancreas: Acute and chronic pancreatitis.

= During pregnancy: Fetal alcohol syndrome (Microcephaly, growth retardation, facial
abnormalities in the new born, reduction in mental functions of the child as the child grows older)

Acute Radiation Syndrome

Q. What are the clinical features of acute radiation syndrome?
Ans

Clinical features of acute radiation syndrome:

1. Subclinical = Mild nausea and vomiting

= Lymphocytes < 1500/pL

2. Hematopoietic = Intermittent nausea and vomiting

= Petechiae, hemorrhage

= Maximum neutrophil and platelet depression in 2 wk
= Lymphocytes < 1000/pL

3. Gastrointestinal = Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea

= Hemorrhage and infection in 1-3 wk

= Severe neutrophil and platelet depression
= Lymphocytes < 500/yL

4. Central nervous system = Intractable nausea and vomiting

= Confusion, somnolence, convulsions

= Coma in 15 min - 3 hr

= Lymphocytes absent

(Ref: Robbins/10"/431 + 8/423 +7"/438)

Q. Short note: Kwashiorkor. (DU-10Ja)
Ans.

Kwashiorkor: Kwashiorkor occurs when protein deprivation is relatively greater than the reduction in total
calories.

Kwashiorkor occurs in children who have been weaned (often too early) and are subsequently fed an
exclusively CHO diet.

Symptoms:
1. Generalized or dependent edema

2. Weight loss (60-80% of normal)
3. Characteristic skin lesions “flaky paint” appearance

Q Shert note: Beriberi. (DU-13Ja,10Ju)
ARs.

Beriberi: Beriberi is a severe thiamine deficiency syndrome seen in population consuming refined grain.
This syndrome found in areas where polished rice is the major component of the diet.

Types: Adult beriberi is divided into two types-
a. Polyneuropathy (dry beriberi)
b. Beriberi heart disease (wet beriberi)
Wet beriberi:
1. Beriberi heart disease (wet beriberi) is associated with peripheral vasodilation, leading to-
= More rapid arterio-venous shunting of blood
= High-output cardiac failure, and
= Eventually peripheral edema.

2. The heart may be normal, have subtle changes, or be markedly enlarged and globular (owing to four
chamber dilation), with pale flabby myocardium.

3. The dilation thins the ventricular walls.

4. Mural thrombi are often present, particularly in the dilated atria.

Dry beriberi:
1. It takes the form of a non-specific peripheral neuropathy with myelin degeneration and disruption of
axons involving motor, sensory and reflex arcs.

2. It usually first appears in the legs, but it may also extends to the arms, so classically these patients
present with toe drop, foot drop and wrist drop.
3. This progressive sensory loss is accompanied by muscle weakness and hyporeflexia or areflexia.

(Ref: Robbins/10/443 + 8'"/1328)

chostochondral joint)

Pigeon chest deformity

Deformed pelvis

Lumbar lordosis

Bowing of the legs.

Q. Short note: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS).

Ans.

Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS): The National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
defines SIDS as-

“The sudden death of an infant under 1 year of age which remains unexplained after a through case

investigation, including performance of a complete autopsy examination of the death scene, and review of the
clinical history.”

Because these infants usually die while asleep its other names are crib death or cot death.

Blood

Blood: Blood is a specialized fluid form of connective tissue, which is composed of intercellular substance

(plasma) and suspended formed elements (RBC, WBC, platelets) which circulate within a close circuit of
cardio-vascular system.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. What is haemopoiesis? Mention the sites of haemopoiesis. (BUP-22M)

Q. Define haemopoiesis / haematopoiesis. (RU-16/14Ju)
Ans.

Haemopoiesis: Haemopoiesis means formation of cellular elements of blood. It encompasses proliferation,
differentiation and functional maturation of stem cells to terminally differentiated blood cells. It consists of-

1. Erythropoiesis: Formation of RBC.
2. Granulopoiesis: Formation of granulocytes (neutrophil, eosinophil & basophil).
3. Thrombopoiesis/ Megakaryopoiesis: Formation of platelets.
4. Lymphopoiesis: Formation of lymphocytes.
a. Thymic lymphopoiesis - formation of T (thymic) lymphocytes.

Q. What do you mean by extramedullary hemopoiesis? Mention sites and causes of
extramedullary hemopoiesis. (Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Extramedullary hemopoiesis (EMH): It is defined as haemopoiesis occurring in organs outside of the bone
marrow. It may be physiological or pathological.

1. Physiological: For example, during fetal development, before formation of mature marrow, EMH
occurs in the yolk sac, fetal liver and spleen.

2. Pathological: It is more frequently associated with pathologic processes in a response to
erythropoiesis failure in bone marrow. Examples are-

* Haemoglobinopathies (e.g. sickle cell disease)
* Thalassaemia

Q. What is stem cell? Mention the characteristics of pluripotent stem cells. (Very Important

for FCPS Part-I Exam.)

Ans.

Stem cell: Stem cells may be defined as the cells which maintain their numbers by self-replication and also
give rise to precursors of one or other of the various blood cell series (differentiation).

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/1)
Or,
It is defined as a cell with the ability to renew itself as well as to produce progeny destined to differentiate or
mature functional cells.

There are approximately 1 to 4 haemopoietic stem cells per 100,000 nucleated cells in haematopoietic tissue.
(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/2)

Characteristics of pluripotent stem cells: All blood cells are derived from pluripotent stem cells.

= Few in numbers (0.01% of the total marrow cells)
Has self-renewal capacity

= Can give rise to all types of blood cells
= Upon appropriate stimuli stem cells can be converted into any type of cells e.g. hepatocytes (this
property is called stem cell plasticity).

(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/2; Davidson’s/21"/988)

Sites and time of erythropoiesis:

From yolk sac (mesoblastic erythropoiesis): Starts at 2" week and completed at 6" week.
From liver (hepatic erythropoiesis): Starts at 6" week and continue up to birth.

From bone marrow (myeloid erythropoiesis): Starts at 16" week of intrauterine life and gradually
increase and taking the main sites of formation of cellular elements after birth.

Q. What is reticulocyte? (DU-09Ja)

Q. What are the dyes used in reticulocyte counting?
Q. Short note: Reticulocyte. (CU-03Ja)

Ans.

Reticulocyte: Reticulocytes are young red cells and derived from orthochromatic normoblasts by extrusion of
their nuclei. After the formation, they stay in the bone marrow for 24 hours, and then enter into the circulation.
During next | to 2 days in the circulation, they gradually loss their membrane and volume; thus mature into
edult red cells.

into capillaries

+ Reticulocyte

Fig: Reticulocyte.

Properties of reticulocytes:
Larger than mature RBC

No nucleus

Has some ribosome materials

Bluish tint in supra-vital staining

The clustering of the ribosomes forms a reticular network giving the name, reticulocyte

These cells can carry oxygen and enter the blood stream and are found in low concentrations in

normal blood. (for VIVA)

They appear in Romanowshy stained blood film as large polychromatic red cells without central pallor.

A oS iy

Normal count: 0.2 - 2 % of red cells (in a healthy individual). (Must be asked in VIVA)
Method of reticulocyte count: Rapid method of Schiling.

Stain used in reticulocyte counting: Supravital staining. (Must be asked in VIVA)

= Supravital staining with new methylene blue
= Supravital staining with brilliant cresyl blue.

Uses of reticulocyte count:
* Reticulocyte count denotes the rate of erythropoiesis in the bone marrow

* Increased number of reticulocyte in the peripheral blood indicates the response to treatment. It is

helpful in diagnosis and assessment of treatment.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/4,28,103; Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/4; Lecture DMC)

Q. Short note: Basophil.
Ans

Basophil: It is one type of granulocyte. The name is due to its basophilic (blue) granules in cytoplasm.
Criteria:

* Basophils are the rarest (<1 %) of the circulating leukocytes.
= Compact irregular dense nucleus.

---

#### 📄 Page 307

HAEMATOLOGY | 307

* Distinctive, large variable sized, dark-blue or purple granules of the cytoplasm often obscure the
nucleus.

Fyactions: Basophils are rich in histamine, serotonin, and heparin substances. These mediators cause
vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability & contraction of the smooth muscles.

Hematological significance:

* Basophils are present in increased numbers in myeloproliferative disorders, and are specially

prominent in chronic granulocytic leukaemia.
* When basophils are more than 10% of the differential leukocyte count, this is a sign of impending

accelerated phase or blast crisis.
(Ref: Dacie & Lewis/10"/107)

## Arif's Pathology & Haematology — Bone Marrow Examination

> **Source:** `Arif Pathology guide 2025(1).pdf` · **Pages 310–320** (11 extracted) · **UNIT-II : HAEMATOLOGY**

arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

3ONE MARROW
EXAMINATION

Q. What is bone marrow? Mention the normal composition of bone marrow.
Ans.

Bone marrow: Bone marrow is a spongy organ that fills the centre of various bones, where stem cells produce
RBC, WBC, and platelets.

Bone marrow is usually the primary site of hemopoiesis in adult. It replaces 1% of the body’s RBC daily,
creating more than 220 million RBC/day.

Normal composition of bone marrow: Bone marrow consists of-
= Specialized connective tissue cells

Reticulin fibrils

Adventitial reticular cells

Vascular sinusoid

Blood vessels

Fat cells

Nerve fibers

Macrophages

Cells of the lymphoid and haematopoietic series.

(Ref: Davidson’s/21"/988; de Gruchy/6*/1!)

Q. Classify bone marrow. (RU-18Ja)
Ans.
Classification of bone marrow:

1) Red bone marrow: In newbom, the entire skeleton is occupied by the red bone marrow. By the age of
20, red bone marrow is found only in the diploe of skull bones, in the ribs, sternum, vertebrae, in the
cancellous part of some of the short bones and, at the ends of long bones. It consists of an interlacing
network of reticular fibers into which reticular cells are attached.

2) Yellow bone marrow: At the age of 20, most of the bone marrow changes into the yellow variety
which consists mainly of adipose cells with an admixture of macrophages, undifferentiated
mesenchymal cells & reticular cells.

(Ref: A.K. Datta General Anatomy/8"/79)

Q. Define bone marrow aspiration.
Ans.

Bone marrow aspiration: Bone marrow aspiration means aspiration of particles of bone marrow by suction
via a wide-bore needle inserted into the bone marrow cavity.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/11)

Q. What are the sites of bone marrow aspiration? (RMU-23M, 18Nv, 16/15Ja,13/10Ju,09Ja)

Ans.

Sites of bone marrow puncture: (Very Important for VIVA)
a. Body of sternum- opposite 2™ or 3™ intercostal space (adults).
b. Tliac crest (adults and older children).
c. Medial aspect of the proximal part of the tibia (children under the age of 1 year).
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/11)

Q. What are the methods of bone marrow study? (For VIVA)
Ans.
Methods of bone marrow study:
1. Needle aspiration
2. Trephine biopsy
3. Surgical biopsy.
(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/139; Lecture SSMC)

Q. What are the parts of a bone marrow aspiration needle? (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Bone marrow aspiration needle: There are three parts of a bone marrow aspiration needle. They are-
1. Trocer (Stilette) with knob
2. Cnnula
3. Adjustable guard.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. What are the various stages of bone marrow examination?
Ans.
Various stages of bone marrow examination:

Methods:
1. Aspiration or needle biopsy
2. Trephine biopsy

Site of bone marrow puncture: Please see above.
Stages of bone marrow examination (Aspiration biopsy):

(a) The patient lies on his back.
(b) Clean the skin over sternum or other site with 70% alcohol (e.g. ethanol) or 0.5% chlorhexidine.
(c) Anaesthesize the area upto periosteum with local anaesthetic.
(d) A strong, wide-bore, short beveled needle fitted with a stilette and an adjustable guard should be used.
(e) After piercing the skin and subcutaneous tissues, when the needle point reaches the periosteum, adjust
the guard on the needle to allow it to penetrate about 5 mm further.
(f) Push the needle with a boring motion into the cavity of the bone.
(g) Remove the stilette.
(h) Draw about 0.2 ml of liquid marrow with a syringe.
(i) Make films on glass slides from the liquid marrow sample for microscopy.
(j) Fix the film with methyl alcohol for 2 minutes.
(k) Stain by the usual Romanowsky technique.
(1) Then assess / examine-
* The detail of the developing cells (e.g. normoblastic or megaloblastic)
The proportion of the different cell lines (myeloid : erythroid ratio)
The presence of cell foreign to the marrow (e.g. secondary carcinoma)
The cellularity of the marrow
The amount of iron stores present in macrophages or in developing erythroblasts.
(Ref: Dacie & Lewis/10"/116,117; de Gruchy/6"/11)

fe aine haps: Trephine is used to obtain a biopsy specimen in any case where aspiration gives a ‘dry’ tap
or ‘blood’ tap. Posterior iliac spine is the usual site. The trephine specimen is obtained by inserting the
biopsy needle into the bone and using a to-and-fro rotation to obtain a core of tissue and is examined as a

histological specimen after fixation in formalin, decalcification and sectioning.
(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/28,31; Dacie & Lewis/10"/124)

Q. What is dry tap? (DU-19M,18Nv/Ja, CU-19M) What are the causes of dry tap? (DU-1 lJa, RU-1 1Ja)
Q. Mention 4 conditions where dry tap is frequent. (DU-09Ja)

Q. Write short note on: Dry tap. (DU-06Ja, CU-16Ju, SU-10Ja)

Ans.

Dry tap: Failure to aspirate any material at all is referred to as a dry tap.

Causes of dry tap: (Very Important for VIVA)

1. Technical factors: Such as failure to site the tip of the needle in the bone marrow or to apply
sufficient suction.

2. Pathological factors: Pathological processes that interfere with aspiration include increased
connective tissue in the bone marrow, which occurs in-

a) Myelofibrosis

b) Hairy cell leukaemia

c) Leukaemia

d) Other myeloproliferative disorders

e) Metastatic carcinoma

f) Lymphoma

g) Multiple myeloma

h) Hodgkin's disease

i) Tuberculosis (involving the bone marrow)

j) Densely hypercellular bone marrow.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/13; Lecture SSMC & DMC)

Q. What is blood tap? (DU-18Nv/Ja)
Q. What are the causes of blood tap? (RU-1 1 Ja)

---

#### 📄 Page 317

HAEMATOLOGY 317

SSS —
Q. Short note: Blood tap. (CU-16Ju)
Ans.
Blood tap: Aspiration of blood without bone marrow particles is referred to as a blood tap.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/13)

Or,
It means small amount of blood comes by marrow aspiration.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Causes of blood tap: (Very Important for VIVA)
1. Faulty technique
2. Hypoplastic / aplastic marrow
3. (Also all the causes of dry tap).
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. Why there is dry tap in metastatic carcinoma, leukaemia, lymphoma or tuberculosis?
Ans.
In these conditions, needle tip goes to the diseased cells (neoplastic tissue) instead of marrow particles.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/13)

Q. What is trephine biopsy? (DU-11/09Ja)
Q. Short note: Trephine biopsy. (DU-19Nv,16Ju)
Ans.
Trephine biopsy: Trephine biopsy is a form of aspirating bone marrow which is performed by rotating a
specialized biopsy needle under pressure, usually into the iliac crest, to obtain a core extending from the
periosteum into the interstices of the bone marrow cavity.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/13; Dacie & Lewis/10"/124)

Procedure: Posterior iliac spine is the usual site for trephine biopsy. The trephine specimen is obtained by
inserting the biopsy needle into the bone and using a to-and-fro rotation to obtain a solid core of bone
including marrow and is examined as a histological specimen after fixation in formalin, decalcification and
sectioning.

(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/28; Dace & Lewis/10"/124)

Indications of trephine biopsy:
» Suspicion of leukaemia

= Myeloproliferative disorders

* Myelodysplasia

« Aplastic anemia

* Malignant lymphoma

=# Myeloma

* Amyloidosis

= Secondary carcinoma

= Causes of splenomegaly

* Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO)

» Any cause where aspiration gives a ‘dry’ or ‘blood’ tap.

Significance of trephine biopsy: It provides a panoramic view of the marrow from which overall marrow
architecture, cellularity & presence of fibrosis or abnormal infiltrates can be reliably determined.
(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/28,31; de Gruchy/6"/13)

Q. Mention the advantages and disadvantages of trephine biopsy.
Ans.

Advantages of trephine biopsy:
1. Trephine biopsy is more suited than aspiration for detection of foci of certain types of neoplastic cells

---

#### 📄 Page 318

318

arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

2. Foci of lymphoma can be detected by trephine biopsy in the absence of clinical & radiological
abnormality of bone
3. It provides a panoramic view of the marrow from which overall marrow architecture, cellularity &
presence of fibrosis or abnormal infiltrates can be reliably determined.

Disadvantages of trephine biopsy:

1. Itis less valuable than aspiration when individual cells detail is to be examined
2. Neoplastic cell foci and even significant region of hypoplasia may be unevenly distributed & thus may
not be revealed by a single trephine biopsy.

Q. How will you prepare and stain a peripheral blood film?
Q. Name the stains used for blood film study. (RU-16/14Ju)

Ans.

Preparation of blood film:
Requirements:

= Glass slide

= Spreader slide (specially designed glass slide with a smooth edge)

* A disposable blood lancet

= Sterile gauze / cotton swabs

= 70% alcohol / spirit.

Procedure:

1. A drop of blood by finger prick is taken on a grease-free clear slide. The drop should be on the right
hand side.

2. The slide is fixed with the left hand by holding the left side between thumb and fore finger.

3. Another slide having smooth, even edge is taken as a spreader.

4. The spreader should be held with the right hand and placed on the slide in front of the blood drop at an
angle of 45° on the right.

5. The spreader is spread towards the blood till it touches the drop and the blood drop is allowed to run
along the spreader.

6. A film is drawn before the blood has reached the ends by light, quick and smooth gliding movement of
the spreader (head of film) towards the other end making the tail of the film.

7. Then dried the blood film in the air.

taini blood film:

Commonly used stains:

* Romanowsky stains
* Leishman’s stain
* Giemsa stain

Procedure:
Place air dried blood film on the staining rack.

Cover the blood film with Leishman’s stain.

Wait for 1 minute. (The cells are fixed by methyl alcohol present in the stain)
Add distilled water double amount of the stain.

Mix the stain and distilled water by gentle blowing by mouth.

Wait for 7 minutes.

Wash the stain with water until the film is pink.

Place the slide in a slanting position till the film is dry.

Q. Define ESR. (DU-10Ju, RU-16/15Ja) Name the methods of ESR estimation.

Q. State the clinical importance of ESR estimation.

Q. State the causes of raised ESR. (RU-19/18Nv, 16/1 5Ja,13Ju, 1 1/10/09Ja)

Q. Short note: Raised ESR. (RU-08Ja)

Q. Short note: ESR. (DU-21Oct/M,17/16/14Ja, SU-22/21Nv,19M,15Ja, 10Ju, RU-20Nv,18M,17/13/
07Ja, CU-16Ju)

Ans.

ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate): When a volume of blood is mixed with a specific amount of
suitable anticoagulant and is allowed to stand in a vertical position in a narrow tube, the blood cells (/ formed

elements) settle down leaving the clear plasma above. The sedimentation of red cells that takes place in first
hour is called ESR.

(N.B: Anticoagulant used: Trisodium citrate)

Methods of ESR estimation:
1. Westergren method
2. Wintrobe method

Normal value of ESR:
1. Westergren method 0 - 10 mm in first hour 0 - 20 mm in first hour
2. Wintrobe method 0 - 8 mm in first hour 0 - 10 mm in first hour

Clinical importance of ESR:
1. It is a measure of biochemical changes of blood. It has no specific diagnostic value. Thus, ESR is
non-specific, but it is useful as a screening test
2. Although high ESR always indicates presence of active disease but normal ESR does not exclude the
active disease
3. It also monitors the prognosis of disease process.

Conditions with high ESR: (Very Important for VIVA)

A) Physiological conditions:
1. Old age (over the age of 60 years, ESR of 30 mm in first hour may be normal)
2. Pregnancy
3. Vaccination
4. High altitude

B) Pathological conditions:
Multiple myeloma (t /g)

TB (t fibrinogen)

SLE (tlg & fibrinogen)

Rheumatoid arthritis (t/g & fibrinogen)
Advanced malignancy (f fibrinogen)
Aplastic anemia (| PCV)

Rheumatic fever (f /g & C-reactive protein)
Kala-azar (t globulin).

ANAS LS

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/28)

Q. Mention the major physiological factors affecting ESR. (DU-08Ja)
Q. Mention the factors that influence ESR determination.

Ans

Factors modifying ESR:
1. Red cell factors:

Weight of cells: ESR © weight of cells

Surface area: ESR 0 ——_—___—
Surface area

Roleaux formation: Roleaux sediment more rapidly than single cell as the weight of the cell
increases in roleaux & surface area decreases.

Number of RBC: Increased number of red cell reduces ESR and decreased number increases it.
Erythrocyte / Plasma ratio: Ratio increased (tPCV) = | ESR & vice versa.

Anemia: In anemia, ESR increases because change in erythrocyte / plasma ratio favours roleaux
formation. Microcytes sediment slower than macrocytes as macrocytes have decreased surface
area-volume ratio.

Shape: Red cells with an abnormal shape such as sickle cells or spherocytes hinder rouleaux
formation and thus lower ESR.

2. Plasma factors:

ESR is increased by elevated level of fibrimogen and to a lesser extent by elevated level of
globulin (a2, B, y globulin). These proteins favour roleaux formation by decreasing negative
charge of erythrocytes that tends to keep them apart.

ESR increased with increased acute phase protein, such as C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A
(SAA) protein etc.

Albumin and lecithin reduces ESR & cholesterol increases ESR

---

#### 📄 Page 330

330

arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Technical factors:
* Vertical position of tube: Its inclination produces high ESR, three degree angling accelerate 30%
ESR.
= Quantity of anticoagulant: | K*-oxalate / Na’-citrate: T ESR.
= Delay in test: tf ESR.
* Temperature: High temperature increases ESR.
* Vibration: More vibration more ESR.
« Length & diameter of tube: Estimation in long tube increases ESR than in short tube.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC; Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/133)

Q. How the changes in the blood component influence the value of ESR? (DU-10Ju)

Ans.

ESR will be raised in the following changes in blood component: (Very Important for VIVA)*

Number of RBC: Increased number of red cell reduces ESR and decreased number increases it.
Erythrocyte / Plasma ratio: Ratio increased (PCV) = | ESR & vice versa.

Anemia: In anemia, ESR increases because change in erythrocyte / plasma ratio favours roleaux
formation.

*Plasma fibrinogen: ESR is increased by elevated level of fibrinogen.
*Plasma globulin level: ESR is increased to a lesser extent by elevated level of globulin (a2, B, 7
globulin).
Acute phase protein: ESR increased with increased acute phase protein, such as C-reactive
protein, serum amyloid A (SAA) protein etc.
*Plasma albumin level: Albumin reduces ESR.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC; Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/133)

Q. Write the technical procedure of ESR done in laboratory (Westergreen method). (SU-04Ja)

Ans.

Procedure of ESR estimation (Westergreen method):
Materials required:

NAWSYWNS

Westergren tube (It is calibrated in mm from 0 — 200. Both ends of the tube are open)
Westergren tube rack (It is a special type of tube rack)

Test tube

Reagent: 3.8% sodium citrate (anticoagulant)

A sterile needle

Cotton

Spint.

Procedure:

Neer Y MS

Take 0.4 ml reagent in a test tube
Draw venous blood and add 1.6 ml of blood in the test tube and mix thoroughly
Draw the blood from the test tube in the Westergren tube by sucking by the mouth up to the mark ‘0’
Place the tube in the rack in the vertical position with the ‘0’ - mark above
Take the reading after 1 hour by noting down the level end of the clean plasma
Results can be given as ESR = mm in 1* hour.
(Ref: Lecture DMC; Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/132)

(N.B: In Wintrobe haematocrit method EDTA is used as anticoagulant).

Q What is the cut off point of anemia? (Very Important for VIVA)
ABS.
Qut off point of anemia: Anemia is said to be present if the hemoglobin level in the blood is below the cut off
point for the age and sex of the individual that is given below-
* Male: < 13 gn/dl

* Pregnancy: < 10.5 gm/dl.

Q. Give the basic structure of Hb in short.
Ans.
Basic structure of Hb:
* 4sub-units
* Each sub-unit consists of a globin chain and a haem moiety
* Total 4 globin chain (polypeptide chain) - 2 a chains and 2 f chains, and 4 ferrous iron.

Each globin chain combines with a heam group whose central iron atom is the site at which oxygen attaches to Hb.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC & ShSMC)

Q. Short note: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF). (RU-08Ju)

Ans.

Fetal hemoglobin (HbF): HbF or fetal Hb is normally present in the blood of the human fetus. It is normally
replaced by adult Hb (HbA) soon after birth. In certain individuals, it fails to disappear and persists throughout
life.

Structure: It consists of 2a chains and 2y chains (272).

Importance: HbF has a greater affinity for O2 than HbA because it dose not bind with 2,3 DPG (Dihydroxy
phosphoglycerate). This facilitates fetal RBCs to pick up O) at lower Po? available in the placenta. Moreover, it
is more resistant to alkali than HbA.

(N.B: 2,3 DPG only bind with B chain).
(Ref: Ganong/22""/534,535)

Conditions in which Hb-F is elevated:
Thalassaemia

Sideroblastic anemia
Haemoglobinopathies
Megaloblastic anemia

Aplastic anemia

Leukaemia

Early pregnancy.

* Oxyhaemoglobin method

Q. Which is the best method of haemoglobin estimation & Why? (Very Important for
PRACTICAL VIVA)
Ans.

Best method of haemoglobin estimation: Cyanmethaemoglobin method is the best method of haemoglobin
estimation, because-

The result is accurate (almost 99%)

Availability of a stable and reliable standard

Production of colour is permanent and persists for prolong period

All forms of haemoglobin, except HbS, can be converted into cyanmethaemoglobin

Reaction is rapid

Colour is measured by photoelectric method that minimizes visual errors

Large number of samples can be tested at a time.

(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/131; Lecture DMC)
