Q What are the disadvantages of acid haematin method?
Ans.
Disadvantages of Acid haematin method:
* Acid haematin is unstable. The colour fades away immediately after reaching the peak concentration.
The colour intensity has to be matched with the brown colour of comparator box visually.
* There is no international standard for this brown colour comparator.
* There is more chance of personal error as it is a visual method.
* Not all type of Hb is converted to acid haematin e.g. sulphhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin.
(Ref: Lecture DMC)

Q. Define PCV. (DU-10Ju, CMU-22Nv) Mention indication and methods of PCV estimation.
(RU-09Ju)

Q. How you are going to measure PCV? (RU-07Ja)

Q. Mention the importance of estimation of PCV. (RU-13Ju)

Q. Short note on: Packed cell volume (PCV) (RU-17/12Ju) / Haematocrit. (RU-11/08Ja)
Ans.

Packed cell volume (PCV): Packed cell volume or haematocrit is the volume of red blood corpuscles in
relation to that of whole blood.

Or,
It is the proportion of volume of red cell to the total volume of blood.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

It is expressed as the volume of RBC per litre of whole blood. It is also expressed as percentage. Such as, 45%,
i.e. 45 ml RBC is present in 100 ml of blood or, 0.45 L of RBC is present in | L of blood.

Normal level:
1. Male: 0.40 - 0.54 L/ L (40% - 54%)
2. Female: 0.37 - 0.47 L/L (37% - 47%)

Uses of PCV:
1. Determination of red cell indices
2. Assessment of anemia by the relationship 1 mm of PCV = 0.34 gm of Hb per 100 ml of blood
3. Assessment of polycythemia
4. Number of white cells can also be assessed by assuming the following relationship i.e. | mm of buffy
coat = 10000 WBC /mm’ of blood

---

#### 📄 Page 337

HAEMATOLOGY [ 337

5. Facilitate to find out nucleated red cells and immature white cells when these are very scanty in the
blood by examination of film made from buffy coat.

pCV is increased in:
1. Polycythemia vera
2. Secondary polycythemia due to chronic heart disease and COPD
3. Dehydration & haemo-concentration due to acute gastroenteritis, cholera, severe vomiting.

PCV is diminished in:
1. Anaemia
2. Haemodilution or overhydration

Q. Define anemia. (DU-07Ju,06M, RMU-22/21/20/19Nv,18M,17M/Ja,15/12Ja, BUP-22Nv,18M,
SU-20M, LONv, 16/1 1Ja, O7Ju/Ja, CU-14Ju,09/05Ja)

Ans.
Anemia: Anemia is defined as a clinical condition when the hemoglobin level in the blood is below the lower
extreme of the normal range for the age and sex of the individual.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/21)
Or,
Anemia may be defined as a state in which there is reduction of blood hemoglobin (Hb) level below the normal

range for the age and sex of the patient.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

A) Morphological classification: (On the basis of MCV, MCH & MCHC)

i) Iron deficiency anemia (most common cause)
ii) Thalassaemia
iii) Anemia of chronic disease
iv) Sideroblastic anemia

2. Normocytic normochromic anemia: (MCV 76-96 fL, MCH 27-32 pg & MCHC 31-35 g/dL, i.e. all
are normal, but RBC count low)
i) Acute blood loss

i) Megaloblastic macrocytic anemia

» Liver disease

B) Aetiological classification: According to the cause of anemia-

1. Haemorrhagic anemia:
i) Acute haemorrhage: Accidental trauma, surgical operation.
ii) Chronic haemorrhage:

« GIT lesion e.g. bleeding peptic ulcer, hookworm infestation, bleeding piles.
= Gynaecological disturbance e.g. Menorthagia.

2. Haemolytic anemia: (Due to excess RBC destruction)

i) Intra-corpuscular defect (hereditary) e.g. thalassaemia, sickle cell anemia.

ii) Extra-corpuscular defect (acquired) e.g. haemolytic disease of newborn, incompatible blood
transfusion.

3. Dyshaemopoietic anemia:
i) Due to deficiency of essential elements of erythropoiesis:
* Iron deficiency anemia
= Megaloblastic anemia (due to deficiency of vitamin B12 & folic acid)
= Nutritional anemia in PEM (protein-energy malnutrition)
* Anemia with scurvy (due to deficiency of vitamin C)

ii) Due to bone marrow disturbance:
» Aplastic anemia
= Sideroblastic anemia
* Anemia with renal failure (due to reduced erythropoietin secretion)
= Anemia with endocrine disorders.

C) Clinical classification:
1. Mild anemia: When Hb = 12 to 9 gm % (+)
2. Moderate anemia: When Hb = 9 to 6 gm % (++)
3. Severe anemia: When Hb = Less than 6 gm % (+++).

Q. What do you mean by morphological classification of anemia? (RU-1 lJu)
Ans.

Morphological classification of anemia: Morphological classification of anemia means the classification of
anemia based on the size of RBC and amount of hemoglobin present inside them (On the basis of MCV, MCH
& MCHC). Morphologically anemia is of the following types-

i) Microcytic hypochromic anemia: (MCV <76 fL, MCH <27 pg & MCHC <31 g/dl.)

ii) Normocytic normochromic anemia: (MCV 76-96 fL, MCH 27-32 pg & MCHC 31-35 g/dL, ice. all
are normal, but RBC count low)

iii) Macrocytic anemia: (MCV >96 fL, MCHC normal).
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/24; Hoffbrand/6"/27)

Total body iron: 3 - 5 gm, depending on the sex and weight of the individual. It is grater in males than in

b. Tissue iron:

- Essential (non-available) iron (myoglobin and enzymes of cellular respiration): 0.5 gm.
- Plasma (transport) iron: 3 - 4 mg.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/34,35)
Plasma (transport) iron:
Total iron in plasma: 3 - 4 mg
Bound to a specific protein, transferrin, a B-globulin, which is synthesized in liver
Each molecule of transferrin binds with one or two atoms of ferric iron.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/34,35)

Absorption of iron:

Daily intake: 10 - 20 mg iron

Chief dietary sources: Meats, especially liver and kidney, egg yolk, green vegetables & fruits (c.g. beet
root, kachu shak, dates, beans etc.) (V.V.I for VIVA)

Main site of absorption: Duodenum and proximal jejunum. (V.V.1 for VIVA)

Daily absorption: | - 2 mg, in duodenum and proximal jejunum. The amount of iron absorption is more or
less fixed. If a person intakes large amount of iron, a fixed amount will be absorbed and the rest will be
excreted. This is regulated by plasma apotransferrin level.

Absorption of iron depends on:
- The size of the iron stores

- The rate of erythropoiesis

- Dietary constituents.

Iron excretion:

- Capacity to excrete iron is extremely limited
- Daily iron loss from body is only 0.5 - 1.0 mg
- Tron losses mainly by the stool:
Shedding of intestinal cells
Iron-laden macrophages
- Less than 0.1 mg iron is lost through urine daily
- Iron loss also occurs in nails, hair, desquamated skin cells.

Iron balance: Under normal circumstances, iron absorption slightly exceeds iron excretion.
- Basal losses: 0.5 - 1.0 mg / day.

- Loss due to menstruation: 15 - 28 mg monthly, i.e. 0.5 - 1.0 mg /day.
- Requirement for growth: 0.6 mg/day.

Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA)

Q. What is iron deficiency anemia?
Ans.
fron deficiency anaemia: [ron deficiency is the state in which the content of iron in the body is less than
normal. It is the most common form of anemia in both developing and developed countries.
(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/12)

Q. Write the pathogenesis of iron deficiency anemia.

Ans.

Pathogenesis of iron deficiency anaemia: Iron deficiency anemia develops when the supply of iron is
sufficient for the requirements of haemoglobin synthesis. There are three major factors in the pathogenesis
of iron deficiency anemia:

1. An increased physiological demand for iron:
i) Children during the period of growth.
ii) Women during reproductive period of life:
= Menstruation: average monthly loss 15-28 iron
* Pregnancy: 300 mg iron is transferred to the fetus in each pregnancy
* Parturition
= Lactation.

Pathological blood loss: 60-70% of the total iron content of the body is contained in the Hb of RBC.
So, loss of blood to any extent causes lowering of the total body iron. Pathological blood loss may be due to-

i) Peptic ulcer

ii) Hemorrhoids (piles)

iii) Hiatus hernia

iv) Carcinoma of the stomach

v) Carcinoma of the colon

vi) Chronic aspirin/NSAID ingestion

vii) Oesophageal varices

viii) Ulcerative colitis

ix) Hookworm infestation

x) Menorrhagia (a loss of 80 mL or more of blood at each cycle) in female
xi) Post-menopausal uterine bleeding (due to carcinoma of the uterus)
xii) Rarely haematuria, repeated epistaxis, and haemoptysis.

Inadequate iron intake:
i) Nutritional deficiency due to-
= Inadequate diet or poor diet (in infants, young children or during pregnancy)
= Adult with poor economic status, dietary dislikes
= Anorexia (especially in pregnancy), and
* Poor bio-availability of dietary non-haem iron.

ii) Impaired absorption due to-
= Gastrectomy or gastro-enterostomy
= Tropical sprue
= Coeliac disease.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/39; Hoffbrand/6"/40)

Q. What are the causes of iron deficiency in children?
Q. Why iron deficiency is the most common type of anemia in infancy and childhood? (DU-07Ja)
Ans.
Causes of iron deficiency in children:
1. Inadequate intake of iron in the diet, which fails to meet the increased demands of growth.
2. Diminished iron stores at birth (due to maternal iron deficiency and multiple pregnancy).
3. Hookworm infestation.
4. Less common factors are blood loss, impaired absorption as in coeliac disease, and congenital
abnormalities of the gastrointestinal tract.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/41)

Q. What are the clinical features of iron deficiency anemia?
Ans.
Qinical features of iron deficiency anaemia:
i) Features of anaemia: Pallor of the skin and mucous membrane, lassitude, weakness, fatigue,
dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, angina & congestive cardiac failure (especially in older patients).

ii) Epithelial tissue changes (results from effect of chronic iron deficiency on epithelial tissues):
Angular stomatitis

Painless atrophic glossitis

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails)

Dysphagia as a result of pharyngeal webs (Paterson-Kelly or Plummer-vinson syndrome)

Rarely, leukoplakia of the tongue or mouth

In case of children, irritability, poor cognitive function and a decline in psychomotor development.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/42; Hoffbrand/6"/39)

(NB: The triad of anemia, koilonychia and dysphagia is known as Plummer-vinson syndrome or Paterson-
Kelly syndrome.)

Q. What are the clinical features of iron deficiency anaemia in infant and children?
Ans,

Clinical features of iron deficiency anaemia in infant and children:
Pallor

Irritability

Listlessness (feeling of having no energy)

Anorexia, and

Cardiac enlargement (uncommon, may occur in severe anaemia).

Abnormal haemoglobins are inherited as autosomal co-dominants
One normal and one abnormal gene —>Heterozygote
Two identical abnormal genes + Homozygote

Thalassaemia (hereditary hemolytic anaemia): The thalassaemias are a heterogenous group of disorders
sh a genetically determined reduction in the rate of synthesis of one or more types of normal haemoglobin
plypeptide chain.

Types of thalassaemia:
1. B-thalassaemia

2. a-thalassaemia

Hhalassaemia: In B-thalassaemia, the inadequate production of B-chains leads to a reduction in the amount of
iA in the red cell, and a microcytic hypochromic anaemia results.

Trpes of B-thalassaemia: (V.V./ for VIVA)
A) On the basis of the extent of reduction of B-chain synthesis:

1. B* thalassaemia: There is incomplete suppression of B-chain synthesis
2. B° thalassaemia: There is complete absence of B-chain synthesis.

B) Clinical classification:
1. B-thalassaemia major (Cooley’s anaemia): Severe illness characterized by major or total
suppression of B-chain synthesis and is the homozygous form of the disease.
* *-thalassaemia (Hb-A is present in small amount)
* °-thalassaemia (Hb-A is completely absent)

2. B-thalassaemia minor: Suppression of B-chain synthesis is much less severe. It is heterozygous
state and is a mild or asymptomatic condition.

3. Thalassaemia intermedia: Severity of those diseases lies between that of the major and minor forms.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/134)

tthalassaemia: The a thalassaemias are disorders in which there is defective synthesis of a chains with
rsalting depression of production of the haemoglobins that contain a chains, i.e. Hb-A, Hb-A; & Hb-F. The
éficiency of a chains leads to an excess of y chains in the fetus, and of B chains in the adults which aggregate

form Hb-H (B,) or Hb Bart’s (y,).

Iwes of a-thalassaemia:

1, Silent carrier: 1 gene is deleted.
2. a-thalassaemia trait: 2 genes are deleted.
3. Hb-H disease: 3 genes are deleted.

4. Hb-Bart’s hydrops fetalis: All 4 genes are deleted. Affected infants either died in utero or shortly

after birth.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/134,141)

Q. Write the genetic basis of B-thalassaemia major. (DU-19M)
Ans.

Etiopathogenesis (genetic basis) of thalassaemia:

* [tis an inherited impairment of hemoglobin production, in which there is partial or complete failure to
synthesize a specific type of globin chain.

* Itis a congenital / hereditary hemolytic anemia.

* It is an autosomal recessive disorder, so heterozygous subjects are generally healthy.

* -thalassaemia major (Cooley’s anaemia) is the severe form of the illness characterized by major or
total suppression of B-chain synthesis and is the homozygous form of the disease.

= Parents to offspring transmission (i.e. vertical transmission)

* Both males and females can be equally affected.

Q. What is the difference between thalassaemia and hemoblobinopathies?
Ans

Difference between: thalassaemia and hemoblobinopathies: Thalassaemia»is a quantitative disorder
{ where globin chain is normal but rate of production is reduced, On the other hand, hemoblobinopathies is a

{ qualitative disorder which is characterized by the production of structurally defective haemoglobin due to
‘ abnormalities in the formation of the globin moiety.

Q. Give the clinical findings of a patient with B-thalassaemia major.
Ans.
Clinical findings of B-thalassaemia major:
i) Symptoms:
* Features of anaemia (progressive pallor, fatigue & weakness, lassitude, tiredness)
* Jaundice (mild to moderate)
« Features of hypersplenism (bleeding manifestations & infection)
ii) Signs:
* Clinical triad of-
- Anemia
- Jaundice
- Splenomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly) - Enlargement of the liver and spleen, abdominal swelling
& discomfort.
« Bony changes - Expansion of the marrow in the malar bones leads to a thalassaemic facies
(mongoloid facies)
* Growth retardation

#### 📄 Page 357

HAEMATOLOGY | 357

* Complications
a. Infections- Pneumococcal, Haemophilus, Mningococcal infection, Yersinia enterocolitica,
Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV.
b. Iron overload-

» Iron overload caused by repeated transfusions damages the liver (causing cirrhosis) and
the endocrine organs with failure of growth, delayed or absent puberty, diabetes mellitus,
hypothyroidism and hypoparathyroidism.

>» Iron damages the heart and death occurs from congestive heart failure and cardiac
arrythmias. Severe anaemia usually results in cardiac dilatation. Pericarditis occurs in about half
of the patients.

c. The child fails to thrive, and anorexia, diarrhea, loss of body fat, and recurrent fever occur.
d. Osteoporosis.

iii) Thinning of the cortex of many bones leads to pathological fractures and bossing of the skull (c.g.
frontal bossing) with a ‘hair-on-end’ appearance on X-ray skull (please see the picture below) and
bone pain may occur.

iv) Other occasional clinical features include epistaxis, skin pigmentation, leg ulcers and gall-stones.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/137; Hoffbrand/6"/92; Lecture SSMC)

Q. What are the causes of death in thalassaemia?

Ans.
Cause of death in thalassaemia: (V.V./ for VIVA)
* Ifuntreated, death occurs from severe anemia or infection before the age of five years
* If regularly transfused, patients die in second or third decade from congestive heart failure,
cirrhosis, or diabetes.

Q. What is the confirmatory test of thalassaemia? (V.V./ for VIVA)
Ans.

Confirmatory test of thalassaemia: Hemoglobin electrophoresis. From this test carrier state can also be
detected.

Q. Sign symptoms of thalassaemia when appear? (V.V./ for VIVA)

Ans.
At the age of 6 months (when the Hb-F is replaced by Hb-A).

Q. Mention the principal of treatment of thalassaemia.
Ans.
Principal of treatment of thalassaemia:
i) Regular blood transfusion
ii) General management
= Avoid iron containing food
= Folic acid supplementation (5 mg daily to prevent folate deficiency)
= Zinc supplementation (to prevent growth failure)
ili) Splenectomy
ivy) Bone marrow transplantation
v) Induction of y-chain synthesis
vi) Gene therapy.
(Ref: Medicine Lecture SSMC)

Q. Short note: Hemoglobin electrophoresis.
Ans.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis: It is a blood test that can detect different types of hemoglobin.

It uses the principles of gel electrophoresis to separate out the various types of hemoglobin and is a type of
native gel electrophoresis.

Usefulness:
« The test can detect abnormal levels of Hb-S, the form associated with sickle-cell disease, as well as
other abnormal hemoglobin-related blood disorders, such as hemoglobin C.
* It can also be used to determine whether there is a deficiency of any normal form of hemoglobin, as in
the group of diseases known as thalassaemias.
= The hemoglobin electrophoresis is also known to be thalassaemia screening, this also can be helpful
for the patient who is frequently need of fresh blood transfusion.

Method: Different hemoglobins have different charges, and according to those charges and the amount,
hemoglobins move at different speeds in the gel whether in alkaline gel or acid gel. Electrophoresis is done by
the use of cellulose acetate.

(Ref: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemoglobin_electrophoresis)

Hb-Bart's hydrops fetalis: The most severe manifestation of the a thalassaemia gene is Hb-Bart’s hydrops
fetalis in which there is almost total suppression of a-chain synthesis with a gross excess of y-chains.

Clinical picture:
1. Affected infants are either born dead or die within a few hours of birth.
2. They are underweight, pale, mildly jaundiced, grossly oedematous, and have hepatosplenomegaly and

ascites

Laboratory diagnosis:

Blood picture:
* Hb% — Reduced (around 6 gm/dl).

* Peripheral blood film:

- RBC: Anisocytosis & poikilocytosis, hypochromia, target cells, basophilic — stippling,
polychromasia, and large numbers of nucleated red cells.
Reticulocytes: Increased.

Biochemical findings:
* Serum bilirubin: Increased.

Hemoglobin electrophoresis: 80-90 % Hb-Bart’s, with a small amount of Hb-H and a third ‘fast’ component,
Hb-Portland. There is usually no Hb-A, Hb-A, or Hb-F.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/142)

Q. What is Hb-S? (RMU-23M)
Q. Short note: Sickle cell anaemia. (CU-15Ja, RU-12Ja, SU-03S)
Q. Short note: Hb-S. (CU-17Ja)

Ans.
Sickle cell anaemia: It is a group of hereditary disorders which is characterized by the production of an

abnormal haemoglobin called haemoglobin-S (sickle haemoglobin).

They include the heterozygous (sickle-cell trait) and the homozygous (SS disease) states for Hb-S, and
conditions in which Hb-S is combined with other haemoglobin structural variants or thalassaemia.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/124)
Sickled

Structure of Hb-S: In Hb-S, the haemoglobin structure is a2}2. But, in number-6 position of B-chain, glutamic
acid is replaced by valine.

Clinical features:

1. Severe haemolytic anaemia
2. Sickle cell crisis:

* Vaso-occlusive crisis

= Aplastic crisis

* Haemolytic crisis (rare)
3. Splenic sequestration syndrome
4. Hand-foot syndrome
5. Splenomegaly
6. Bacterial infection
7. Ulcers of the lower leg
8. Pulmonary hypertension
9. Pigment (bilirubin) gallstones
10. Infarction of the renal medulla with papillary necrosis and haematuria
11. Osteomyelitis
12. Conjunctival icterus
13. Chronic leg ulcers
14. Hearing loss, finger clubbing and priapism.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/126; Hoffbrand/6"/99)

* MCV, MCH and MCHC all are normal.

* Peripheral blood film:
RBC: Normocytic, normochromic with anisocytosis & poikilocytosis. Sickle cells, target cells
and Howell-Jolly bodies are present

Reticulocytes: Increased (10-20%)

Q. What are three types of crisis in sickle cell anaemia?
Q. Short note: Sickle cell crisis.
Ans.
Sickle cell crisis: They are the sudden changes which may be life threatening. These may be-
1. Vaso-occlusive crisis: Consists of sudden attack of bone pain, usually in the limbs, joints, back and
chest, or of abdominal pain.

2. Aplastic crisis: Occurs when there is sudden cessation of marrow erythropoiesis related, in most
cases, to infection with human parvovirus.

3, Haemolytic crisis: Rarely.
(Ref: de Gruchy/5"/146)

Q. Why there is anaemia in sickle haemoglobinopathies?
Ans

The sickle cells are destroyed prematurely by mononuclear phagocyte system leading to anaemia.

Q. Short note: Sideroblastic anemia.
Ans.
Sideroblastic anemia: The sideroblastic anaemias are a group of disorders of varying etiology in which the
marrow shows marked dyserythropoiesis and an abnormal intramitochondrial accumulation of iron in erythroid
precursors.
Types:
1. Hareditary
2. Acquired
* Primary
* Secondary

Q. Short note: Sideroblasts.
Ans.
Sideroblasts: Sideroblasts are erythroblasts with Prussian blue positive iron granules in their cytoplasm.
Types:

a) 1” type: Seen in normal bone marrow and represents iron that has not been utilized for haemoglobin
synthesis. The granules are few in number, small, difficult to see, scattered through the cytoplasm, and
not localized in the perinuclear zone. 30 - 50% of erythroblasts in normal marrow are sideroblasts of
this type. They are not seen when iron deficiency is present.

b) 2" type: It is abnormal, found in dyserythropoiesis or haemolysis (percent saturation of transferrin is
increased). Large, numerous granules and are scattered diffusely through the cytoplasm.

c) 3™ type: Found in conditions in which haem synthesis is disturbed, e.g. sideroblastic anaemias. The
granules are more numerous and commonly large. They frequently form a complete or partial ring
around the nucleus called “ring sideroblasts”. Less commonly, the abnormal granules are diffusely
scattered through the cytoplasm.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/52)

Q. Which vitamin deficiencies are responsible for macrocytic anaemia? (RMU-24M)

Ans.
Vitamin deficiencies responsible for macrocytic anaemia:
1. vit-B)2
2. Folic acid.

Q. Which one is more common, vit-Bi2 or folic acid deficiency? Why? (V.V./ for VIVA)
Q. Why vit-B12 deficiency takes a longer time to develop?
Ans.
Folic acid deficiency is more common than vit-B12 deficiency, because-
* Loss of folic acid by heating during cooking is more (60 - 90%) than that of vit-B12 (10-30%).
* The minimal adult daily requirements of folic acid is more (100-200 1g) than that of vit-B12 (24 yg).
* Vit-Br can be stored in liver for longer time: Body stores of vit-Bi2 is 2-5 mg which is sufficient for 2-
4 years; whereas the body stores of folic acid is 5-20 mg but which is sufficient only for 4 months

(because daily requirement of folic acid is more).
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/58; Hoffbrand/6"/59)

(N.B: Although body stores of folic acid is more; deficiency of folic acid is also more common than vit-B12).

Q. Write down the clinical manifestations of vit-Bi2 and folic acid deficiency.
Ans.
Clinical manifestations of vit-B12 deficiency: There are three cardinal clinical manifestations of vit-B12
deficiency of whatever cause:

1. Macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia

2. Glossitis

3. Peripheral neuropathy and sub-acute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/63)

Clinical manifestations of folic acid deficiency: There are two cardinal clinical manifestations of folate
deficiency:

1. Macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, and

2. Glossitis.

Deficiency of folate, in contrast to that of vitamin B12, does not produce sub-acute combined degeneration of

the spinal cord, but peripheral neuropathy is occasionally seen.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/66)

Q. Why neurological deficiency occurs in vit-Bi2 deficiency? (For JTEM)
Ans

Cause of neurological deficiency in vit-B,, deficiency: Other than the reaction of conversion of methyl
tetrahydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate; another reaction is dependent on vit-B,. — isomerization of methyl

malonyl co-enzyme A to succinyl co-enzyme A.
A deficiency of vit-B,2 thus leads to increased plasma and urine levels of methyl malonic acid.

Interruption of succinyl pathway and consequent build up of methyl malonate and propionate could lead to the
formation and incorporation of abnormal fatty acid into neuronal lipids.

This biochemical abnormality predisposes to myelin break down and thereby produces neurologic
complication of vitamin B,2 deficiency.
(Ref: Robbins/8""/657)

Sources of vitamin Biz: Mainly animal protein origin; kidney, liver and heart are the richest sources, but
lesser amounts occur in other foods including muscle meats, fish, shellfish, eggs, cheese and milk. Vegetables
contain practically no vit-B12, in contrast to their high content of folate.

Sources of folic acid: The richest sources are liver, kidney, yeast and fresh green vegetables, especially leafy
vegetables such as spinach and cabbage. Lesser amounts are present in other food stuffs including muscle
meat, some fruit, nuts and cereals. Milk has a moderately low folate content.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/61)

Q. Why it is dangerous to administer folic acid in vit-B,2 deficiency? (For VIVA)

Ans.

Dangers of administration of folic acid in vit-B,. deficiency: If folic acid supplementation is given in
megaloblastic anemia due to vit-B,2 deficiency, anemia may undergo significant improvement, but nervous
system manifestation is not relieved, rather can accelerate the progress of neurologic damage. Because, extra
amount of vitamin B,2 is necessary to convert the supplemented folate into tetra-hydrofolate. Therefore vit-B,;
deficiency exacerbated. So, it is dangerous.

(Ref: de Gruchy/5""/69)

Q. Why a megaloblast if formed? Mention the morphology of a megaloblast. (RU-20M,09Ju)
Q.Short note: Megaloblast. (RU-18/08Ja)

Ans.

Megaloblast: Megaloblasts are abnormal nucleated red cell precursors which occur in the bone marrow of
persons with either vit-B12 or folate deficiency, which are abnormal both in appearance and function.

Their abnormal appearance is due to disturbance of cell growth and maturation, resulting from interference
with DNA synthesis, usually due to deficiency of vit-B12 or folate.

Fig: Megaloblasts in PBF.

* Nucleus: Stippled appearance chromatin network.

that of the cytoplasm.

* Mitosis: Mitoses are more common, and are sometimes abnormal in appearance.
* Maturation: Maturation is arrested.

Q. What is Schilling test? Give its indications and interpretations of results.

Q. How Schilling test is performed?

Q. Short note: Schilling test. (DU-1 1Ja, SU-11/10Ja)

Ans.

Schilling test: It is the measurement of urinary excretion of radiolabelled oral Bi2 with and without
administration of intrinsic factor (IF).

Indication: Investigation of absorption of vit-B12 in patients who are vit-B2 deficient i.e. whether the capacity
to absorb the vitamin is normal.

Principle: The capacity to absorb B12 normally is measured by administering a dose of B,2 labelled by a
radioisotope of cobalt and measuring the percentage that is excreted in the urine. “Co and *’Co are suitable isotopes.

Procedure & interpretations:

= — | yg radioactive vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) is administered orally to a fasting subject.

* 2 hours later 1000 pg unlabelled vit-B12 is administered parenterally (IM).

* Injection flushes out about 1/3™ of the absorbed radioactive vit-B12 into urine in next 24 hours.

= Normal subjects excrete 10% or more of the | pg dose in their urine.

= Patients with pernicious anaemia or vit-B12 deficiency associated with intestinal malabsorption excrete
< 5% (but occasionally upto 7%) of the dose.

= Borderline results of up to 10% (8-10%) may occur in atrophic gastritis.

* If absorption is subnormal, a second parenteral injection of unlabelled Bi2 is given 24 hours later,
followed by a further test dose of radioactive vit-B12 with intrinsic factor.

= If absorption returns to normal, diagnosis is pernicious anaemia.

= If absorption is again subnormal, a lesion of the small intestine is likely.
(Ref: Dacie & Lewis/10"/167,168,179,180; de Gruchy/5"/68)

feraicious anaemia: Pernicious anaemia is a chronic disorder in which the basic pathological lesion is gastric

Q. Give the pathogenesis of pernicious anaemia. (RMU-21M, CU-10Ja)

Ans.

Pathogenesis of pernicious anaemia: The fundamental defect in pernicious anaemia is a failure of secretion
of intrinsic factor (IF) by the stomach due to permanent atrophy of the gastric mucus membrane. In the
absence of intrinsic factor, the vit-B12 of food is not absorbed, resulting in vit-B12 deficiency.

The pathogenesis of the gastric atrophy of pernicious anaemia is uncertain. Current evidence suggests that it is
the end-result of a complex interaction between genetic and autoimmune factors.

Genetic factors:

* About 10% of patients more than one family member, of either the same or a different generation, is
affected.

* Blood group A is more common among patients and their relatives than in the general population.

* It occurs most frequently in people of northern European ancestry, and less frequently in people of
southern European stock and in Asians.

* Fair skin and blue eyes, are common in patients with pernicious anaemia.

Asielnunune factors: (For VIVA)

Parietal cell antibody (antibodies against gastric parietal cell) have been found in the serum (85%) or
gastric juice of most patients with pernicious anaemia.

* Intrinsic factor antibodies: Two types are found in the sera and gastric juice (50-70%) of patients
with pernicious anaemia.

Q. A male of 52 years underwent gastrectomy operation a few years back. He subsequently

Ans.

Laboratory diagnosis of pernicious anaemia:
A. Blood picture:

Hb% — Reduced (3 g/dl or even less)

MCV increased (110-140 fl), MCH increased (33-38 pg), but MCHC normal

Peripheral blood film:

RBC: Macrocytosis (presence of many oval macrocytes) with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis.

Normocytes and microcytes are also present. Cells containing Howell-Jolly bodies and
megaloblasts may be present.

WBC: Moderate neutropenia with hypersegmented neutrophils.
Platelets: Moderate thrombocytopenia.

B. Bone marrow examination:

Cellularity: Increased (/ Hypercellular)

MIE ratio: Decreased

Erythropoiesis: Intensely active and predominantly megaloblastic.

Granulopoiesis: Active, giant metamyelocyte may be found.

Megakaryopoiesis: Normal or slightly increased, occasionally decreased.

Bone marrow iron stain: Increased iron granules in erythroid precursors and in reticular cells.

C. Biochemical findings:

a.
b.

d.
é:

Serum iron and ferritin are increased

Serum bilirubin may be slightly increased

Plasma lactate dehydrogenase is invariably increased

Serum haptoglobin level is reduced

Serum folate is usually normal, but red cell folate is almost always reduced.

D. Special tests:

Serum vit-B12 assay - low
Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies - present in most cases
Radioactive vit-B12 absorption test (Schilling test) — abnormal (diagnostic)
Serum gastrin level — 80% patients have elevated serum gastrin level
Antibody against gastric parietal cell (in serum and gastric juice).
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/73)

Q. Is there bone marrow aplasia in aplastic anaemia? (For VIVA)

Ans.

No, there is no bone marrow aplasia in aplastic anaemia. There is hypoplasia of bone marrow. If total bone
marrow aplasia occurs, there will be no blood cells at all in the blood.

Q. Is there any organomegally in aplastic anaemia? (For VIVA)
Ans.
No, there is no organomegally in aplastic anaemia (i.e. no hepatomegally, no splenomegally & no
lymphadenopathy). Even there is no bony tenderness.
(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/292)

Q. Why ESR is so high in aplastic anaemia?
Ans.
ESR is so high in aplastic anaemia: The fundamental pathological pathological feature is a reduction in the
amount of haemopoietic tissue, causing an inability to produce normal numbers of mature cells for discharge
into the blood stream. So, RBC count becomes very low, and subsequently ESR becomes so high.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/111)

2. Supportive therapy:
* Prevention and treatment of infection;
* Prevention and treatment of hemorrhage;
= Red cell transfusion for anaemia.

3. Measures to accelerate recovery from pancyropenia:
= Bone marrow transplantation;
* Anti-thymocyte globulin;
» Anabolic agent administration:
* Corticosteroid administration.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/112)

Q. State 5 causes of haemolytic anaemia.
Ans.
Haemolytic anaemia: Anaemia due to excess RBC destruction caused by shortened life span of RBC.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/146)
Or,
Haemolytic anaemias are defined as those anaemias that result from an increase in the rate of red cell
destruction.
Or,
Haemolytic anaemias can be defined as those resulting from a reduction in the red cell survival to below the
normal of 120 days.
(Ref: Lecture DMC)

The life span of the normal red cell is 100-120 days; in the haemolytic anaemias it is shortened by varying
degrees, and in very severe cases may be only a few days. Haemolytic anaemia may not be seen until the
lifespan is less than 30 days.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/146; Hoffbrand/6"/75)

Etiological classification:
A) Haemolvtic anaemias due to intracorpuscular (intrinsic) mechanisms:

= Membrane defects:

- Hereditary xerocytosis & hydrocytosis

= Haemoglobin defects:

(a) Haemoglobinopathies:
- Sickle cell anaemia
- Other homozygous disorders (Hb-C, Hb-E, Hb-D, etc.)
- Unstable hamoglobin disease

(b) Thalassaemia:
- -thalassaemia major
- Hb-H disease

(c) Double heterozygous disorders:
- Sickle-cell B-thalassaemia, etc.

* Enzyme defects:
(a) Non-spherocytic congenital haemolytic anaemia:
- Pyruvate kinase deficiency
- Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
(b) Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia and favism.

2. Acquired: Paroxysmal nocturmal haemoglobinuria.

Q. What is classical haemolytic uraemic syndrome?

Clasical_haemolytic_uraemic_ syndrome: The triad of acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and
haemolytic anaemia in infants and young children is referred to as classical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

Clinical features:

Diarrhoea, vomiting, and pyrexia (most cases)

Pallor and slight jaundice (develops within 5-14 days), and the child becomes oliguric

In occasional cases there is evidence of nervous system involvement

Q. Explain why G6PD deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia?
Ans

G6PD deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) functions to
reduce nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate. It is the
only source of NADP in red cells and as NADP is needed for the production of reduced glutathione a
deficiency renders the red cells susceptible to oxidant stress. Haemoglobin and red blood cell (RBC) are
usually protected from oxidant stress by reduced glutathione (GSH). In G6PD deficiency, NADPH and GSH
synthesis is impaired.

(Ref: Hoffbrand/6""/79)

Q. What are the clinical features in G6PD deficiency?
Ans

Clinical features in G6PD deficiency: G6PD deficiency is usually asymptpmatic. Although G6PD is present
in all cells, the main syndromes that occur are as follows:

1. Acute haemolytic anaemia in response to oxidant stress, e.g. drugs, fava beans or infections.
2. Neonatal jaundice.

3. Rarely, a congenital non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia.
(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/79)

Q. What is paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)?
Ans.

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH): This is an uncommon disorder characterized by chronic
haemolytic anaemia with intermittent haemoglobinuria.

The fundamental abnormality is an acquired defect of the red cell membrane—possibly a deficiency of
decay accelerating factor, a complement regulatory protein—which renders it unusually sensitive to lysis by
the complement of normal serum.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/199)

Q. What is march haemoglobinuria?

Ans.

March (exertional) haemoglobinuria: It is a rare disorder in which haemoglobinaemia and
haemoglobinuria follow exercise, classically in the upright position, notably on walking, marching, and
running.

The majority of patients are healthy, young, adult males, often soldiers or athletes who complain of the passing
of red urine after marching or running, respectively. It may also occur in squash players.

Haemoglobinuria usually lasts for several hours after the exertion, but in rare cases it persists for several days.
it is often the only symptom but sometimes is accompanied by mild constitutional symptoms, e.g. nausea,
abdominal cramps, aching in the back or legs, especially the thighs, or a burning feeling in the soles of the feet;
these symptoms are usually relatively mild. The degree of haemolysis is seldom sufficient to cause anaemia.

Q. Short note: Spherocytes.

Ans.

Spherocytes: Spherocytes are the cells that are more spheroidal (i.e. less disk-like) than normal red cells but
maintain a regular outline. Their diameter is less and their thickness is greater than normal.

Fig: Spherocytes.

Diagnosis: Spherocytes can be recognized by their appearance in the blood film, and their increased osmotic
fragility in hypotonic saline solutions. In blood films, spherocytes appear as small, round, deeply staining cells
in which the normal area of central pallor is lost.

(N.B: Cardinal feature of spherocyte: No area of central pallor.) (Must to Know)
(N.B: Cardinal feature of normal RBC: Central V3" pallor.)

Types & where found: The spherocytes that occur in haemolytic anaemia are of two types:

1. Congenital spherocyte (of HS): Here the spherocytosis is due to an intrinsic defect of the cell
membrane, and found in hereditary spherocytosis.

2. Acquired spherocyte: They are produced by the action of some abnormal extrinsic factor on a
previously normal cell. Acquired spherocyte may occur in auto-immune acquired haemolytic
anaemia, septicemia and in haemolytic disease of the newborn.

(Ref: Dacie & Lewis/10"/87; de Gruchy/6"/152)

Q. What is schistocyte? (RU-18/17Nv)

Q. Short note: Schistocytes.

Ans.

Schistocytes: Schistocytes or fragmented red cells that are the products of premature red cell destruction.

They are found in many blood diseases. They are smaller than normal red cells and of varying shape.
Sometimes they have sharp angles or spines (spurs), and sometimes they are round in contour, usually
staining deeply but occasionally palely as the result of loss of haemoglobin at the time of fragmentation. They
may take the forms of crescent, triangles, helmets and microspherocytes.

Fig: Schistocytes.

They occur in following situations:
=  Thalassaemia
= Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
= Cardiac haemolytic anaemia
= Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
= Disseminated intra-vascular coagulation (DIC)
= As the result of direct thermal injury as in severe burns.

(Ref: Dacie & Lewis/10"/91,92)

Q. Short note: Coomb’s test. (DU-23Nv,21Ja,20Nv/M, 19M, 12Ja,07Ju,05M, BUP-19M, CU-1 1Ja)
Q. Short note: Direct Coomb’s test. (DU-08Ja)
Ans.

Coomb’s test: (V.V./ for VIVA)

Principle: The antiglobulin (Coombs’) test is a fundamental and widely used test in both blood group
serology and general immunology. Antihuman globulin (AHG) is produced in animals following the injection
of human globulin, purified complement or specific immunoglobulin (e.g. IgG, IgA, or IgM). When AHG is
added to human red cells coated with immunoglobulin or complement components, agglutination of the red
cells indicates a positive test.

Antiglobulin

Antibody (196, IgA or igM)
or complement (C3)

Fig: The antiglobulin test for antibody or complement on the surface of red blood cells (RBC). The
antihuman globulin (Coombs’) reagent may be broad spectrum or specifi c for immunoglobulin G
(IgG), IgM, IgA or complement (C3).

Types: The antiglobulin test may be cither direct or indirect.

Direct antiglobulin (Coombs’) test: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is used for detecting the presence of

antibody bound to the red cell surface. A positive test occurs in:

* Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

* Haemolytic disease of newborn (HDN)

* Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia

= Haemolytic transfusion reaction.
Indirect antiglobulin (Coombs’) test: The indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) is used to detect antibodies in the
plasma, e.g.

= Antibody screening in pre-transfusion testing.

* Screening in pregnancy for antibodies that may cause haemolytic disease of the newborn.

(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/404; Dacie & Lewis/10'"/246)

Ans.
Important indications of Coomb’s test:

1. Haemolytic disease of the newborn

2. Autoimmune or drug-induced immune haemolytic anaemia
3. Haemolytic transfusion reaction

4. Cold haemagglutinin disease

5. Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria

6. Organ transplant and bone marrow transplantation.

Q. Write down the functions of WBC.
Ans.
Functions of WBC:
1. Neutrophils: Neutrophils are migratory phagocytic cells. They locate, ingest and kill microbes. They
are the most important cells involved in the body’s defences against microorganisms, and lack of
adequate numbers of neutrophils predisposes to infection, particularly by bacteria.

2. Eosinophils: Allergic reaction, killing of parasites.
3. Monocytes and macrophages: Phagocytosis and catabolism of necrotic material.

4. Lymphocytes: Humoral and cell-mediated immunity.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/187)

2. Immunocytes: The /ymphocytes, their precursor cells and plasma cells make up the immunocyte ;

Q. What are the causes of neutrophilic leukocytosis (neutrophilia)? (CMU-23M,22/18Nv)
Q. What are the causes of leukocytosis?

Q. Short note: Neutrophilia. (SU-14Ju, RU-16/14/07Ja)

Ans.

Leukocytosis: Leukocytosis is the increase in the total number of WBC above 11,000 / mm’.

Neutrophilia: Neutrophilia is the increase in the total number of neutrophil above 7,500 / mm’.
Causes of neutrophilic leukocytosis (neutrophilia) / leukocytosis:

Physiological causes:

Exercise

Newbom

Pregnancy and parturition

Ingestion of food

Emotional stress

Diurnal variation - slight increase in the afternoon.

ANWPYNH

Pathological causes:

1. Bacterial infection, particularly acute pyogenic bacterial infection associated with inflammation
(most commonly by S. aureus, S. pyogens, S. pneumoniae, E. coli, Proteus species, Pseudomonas, N.
meningitides etc.). Infection is the most common cause of neutrophilia, e.g. abscess, acute appendicitis,
tonsillitis, bacterial pneumonia, pyelonephritis etc.

2. Non-infectious inflammatory disorders such as rheumatic fever, certain collagen disorders, gout,
acute glomerulonephritis

Tissue injury due to infarction (e.g. myocardial infarction), burns, surgery
Haemorrhage

Stress such as labour, severe colic, convulsions

Metabolic disorders such as diabetic ketoacidosis

Malignant neoplasm

Corticosteroid administration in high doses

. Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)

10. Polycythaemia.

Q. Write short note on: Leukopenia. (DU-07Ju)
Q. Write short note on: Neutropenia. (DU-09Ja)
Ans.

Leukopenia: A reduction in the total count of WBC below 4,000 / mm’.

#### 📄 Page 399

a
Neutropenia: It refers to decreased number of neutrophils below its lower limit of absolute count 1500 cells /

mm of circulatory blood.

HAEMATOLOGY | 399

(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/69)
Causes of leukopenia / neutropenia:

1. Viral infections, e.g. viral hepatitis, dengue, influenza, measles, atypical pneumonia

2. Bacterial infections, e.g. typhoid and paratyphoid fever (may be normal count)

3. Protozoal infections, e.g. chronic malaria, kala-azar

4. Aplastic anaemia

5. Megaloblastic anaemia

6. Hypersplenism (splenic sequestration)

7. Systemic lupus erythematosus

8. Drugs, e.g. certain analgesics, anti-inflammatory agents, antibiotics, anti-malarial, cytotoxic and many
others

9. Excessive irradiation

10. Miscellaneous.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/193; Hoffbrand/6"/118)

Q. Short note: Agranulocytosis.

Ans.

Agranulocytosis: Literally, it means absence of granulocytes from the peripheral blood. It is a clinical
syndrome characterized by complete or ‘almost complete’ absence of neutrophils in the peripheral blood, with
severe constitutional symptoms and marked necrotic ulceration, especially of the mouth.

Causes of agranulocytosis: Drug idiosyncrasy-
= Antipyretic and NSAIDs e.g. aminopyrine, amidopyrine and noramidopyrine etc.
* Tranquillizers e.g. chlorpromazine, promazine, and other phenothiazines.
= Antithyroid drugs e.g. propylthiouracil, carbimazole and methimazole.
= Antibiotics and antimalarials e.g. sulphonamides, dapsone etc.

Clinical features:

History of exposure of offending agents e.g. drugs.

Sudden onset of high grade fever.

Severe sore throat and prostration.

Ulcerating necrotizing lesions on the gingiva, floor of the mouth, buccal mucosa, pharynx, or
anywhere within the oral cavity are characteristic features of agranulocytosis.

* WBC: Marked leukopenia and absence of neutrophils
* Platelets: Normal, decreased or increased

Or,

Loeffler’s syndrome and other forms of pulmonary infiltration

Neoplastic conditions (like AML, CML, lymphoproliferative disorders, particularly Hodgkin's

disease, rarely carcinoma)

7. Certain vasculitic and collagen disorders (such as polyarteritis nodosa)

8. Recovery from acute infection

9. Post-splenectomy

10. Hypereosinophilic syndrome

11. Familial

13. Miscellaneous.

Q. Define leukaemia. (DU-23M,22Nv,21Ja,20Nv/M, 19/18M,08Ju, RMU-24M,23/22/2 1M,20Nv, 19M,
18Ja, 1 7Nv/Ja, 14Ju/Ja, 12/1 1/10Ju,07Ja, CMU-23NvM, | 6Ju, 1 4Ju/Ja, 13/12/10/07Ja, 1 IJu, SMU-
23M,22Nv/M,21Nv,20/19M, BUP-22Nv)
Ans.
Leukaemia: Leukaemia is a neoplastic disorder characterized by abnormal proliferation of haemopoietic cells
causes progressively increasing infiltration of the bone marrow, and in most cases liver, spleen, lymph node
and other lymphatic tissues.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/206)
Or,
Leukaemia is the malignant neoplasm of haemopoietic stem cells characterized by diffuse replacement of bone
marrow by neoplastic cells which in most cases appear in the blood and my infiltrate the liver, spleen, lymph
nodes and other tissues including brain.
(Ref: Lecture DMC)
Or,
Leukemias are a heterogeneous group of malignant neoplastic disorders of uncommitted or partially committed
haemopoietic stem cell characterized by diffuse infiltration and replacement of normal hemopoietic tissues by
neoplastic cells in the bone marrow and usually the presence of leukemic cells in the peripheral blood.
(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/77)

Neoplastic cells are immature haemopoietic cells. Neoplastic cells (leukaemic cells) are most commonly of
myeloid or lymphoid series, but rarely of erythroid or megakaryocyte series.

Q. Define haematological malignancies.

Ans.

Haematological malignancies: Haematological malignancies are a diverse group of malignant conditions
arising from cells of the blood forming organs.

(Ref: Lecture DMC)

Acute Leukaemia

Q. What is acute leukaemia? (SU-03M)
Ans.
Acute leukaemia: Acute leukaemias are malignant disorders characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of
immature haemopoietic cells i.e. blast cells, either myeloblast or lymphoblast. It is rapidly fatal if untreated,
but potentially curable with appropriate treatment.
Or,

This is a malignancy in which the marrow precursor cells are blocked at any early step of differentiation.
Primitive blasts accumulate in the bone marrow, spill over into the peripheral blood and may infiltrate tissue. It
is defined as presence of over 30% blast cell in the bone marrow at clinical presentation.

(Ref: Lecture DMC)

Nice to Know: (Very Important to Know)
= Acute leukaemia may occur at any age. In children, especially young children, it is usually |
lymphoblastic in type, while in adults it is usually myeloid.

= In acute leukaemia more than 30% of the bone marrow consists of blast cells. Blast cells less |
than 30% but more than 5% (usually 20%) indicates myelodysplastic suyndrome. ;

= Inchronic leukaemias, b/ast cells are present in smaller proportions, and the course of the disease |
is less aggressive than acute leukaemias but are Jess responsive to therapeutic intervention. These '
conditions are more commonly seen in middle aged and elderly patients.

= The chronic leukaemias are distinguished from acute leukaemias by their slower progression. '
Paradoxically, they are also more difficult to cure. So, acute leukaemia is worst than chronic |
leukaemia.

= Without therapeutic intervention, acute leukemia follows a short and precipitous course, marked |
by anemia, infection, and hemorrhage, and death occurs within 6 to 12 months. '
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/210,212; Hoffbrand/S°/157,174; BRS Pathology/S*/172) |

Ans.

Chronic granulocytic leukaemia (CGL) / Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML): Chronic granulocytic
leukaemia is characterized by malignant proliferation of well differentiated granulocytes in the bone marrow
and in peripheral blood with markedly increased granulocyte count.

Or,
It is a neoplasm of pleuripotent hemopoietic stem cells leading to preferential proliferation of granulocytic
progenitors.

(Ref: Lecture DMC)
Or,
Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a clonal disorder of pluripotent stem cell and are distinguished from
acute ones by their slow progression.
(Ref: Lecture MuMC)

Q. What is Philadelphia chromosome? (DU-21Ja,20Nv/M, 18M, SUST-21 Nv, CU-17M)
Q. Short note: Philadelphia chromosome. (DU-05Ja, RMU-24M, SMU-23M, RU-17M,16/15/14/
12Ju, CU-12Ju,08Ja)

Ans.
Philadelphia chromosome: It is an abnormal chromosome 22.

Mechanism of formation:
1. Here reciprocal translocation between chromosome 22 and 9 occurs.
2. The C-abl (abelson cellular proto-oncogene) on part of chromosome 9 is transferred to the BCR (break
point cluster region) of chromosome 22.
3. At the same time, part of long arm of chromosome 22 is transferred to long arm of chromosome 9.
4. It appears that segments of C-abl DNA are joined to DNA sequence in chromosome 22 results in
oncogene production and altered structure and function.

Pathogenesis: It is related to CML, but cause is unknown.

Importance: Prognosis.
(Ref: de Gruchy/5"/237)

Q. What do you mean by blastic crisis? (DU-24Nv,13Ju, RU-12Ja)

Q. What is ‘blast crisis’ or blastic transformation? (DU-17M, CMU-23Nv, RU-10Ja)

Q. Short note: Blastic crisis. (DU-22M,17/16/15Ja, RU-18/17Ja) (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Blastic_crisis: It means the disease is transformed to acute leukaemia. It may be myeloid (70%) or
lymphatic type (30%); and it occurs at a rate of 10%/year, relatively refractory to treatment and is the cause
of death in majority of cases. Prognosis is poor in myeloid type.

Clinical presentation:

* Symptoms: Malaise, fatigue, anorexia, night sweats, bone pain, splenic discomfort.
* Signs: Weight loss, pallor, pyrexia, sternal tenderness, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy (which is
typically absent in the chronic phase of the disease).

1. Hb % - Decreased
2. Increase in number of blast cells:
- Myeloblast (70 - 80%)
- Lymphoblast (20 - 30%)
3. Increasing basophil
4. Thrombocytopenia.

Bone marrow: Increased proportion of blast cells (80% or more).

Others: Development of new chromosome abnormalities is also diagnostic.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/240)

Q. Short note: Juvenile CGL.

Ans.

Juvenile CGL: Juvenile CGL is a rare disorder in children (usually under 3 yrs) that bears certain
resemblances to CGL but tends to involve-

1) Greater lymph node enlargement.
2) Less marked splenomegally.
3) More frequent infections.
4) Facial rash.
5) More haemorrhagic manifestations.
6) Thrombocytopenia.
7) Philadelphia chromosome negative.
8) Relatively shorter course.
9) Prognosis is worse than classical CGL.
(Ref: de Gruchy/5""/260,261)

Q. What is chloroma? (Very Important for VIVA)
Q. Short note: Chloroma. (RU-17Ju,12Ja)
Ans.
Chloroma: Chloroma is a term used to describe the occurrence of localized sub-periosteal leukaemic tumour
masses.
Or,
Achloroma (myeloid sarcoma / granulocytic sarcoma / extramedullary myeloid tumor) is a solid
collection of leukemic cells occurring outside of the bone marrow.

Chloromas develop both in AML and CML/CGL during the onset of blastic transformation.

Location: Chloromas may occur in virtually any organ or tissue. They are found most frequently in the skull,
but they also occur in other bones, particularly the sternum, ribs, vertebrae, and sacrum. Other organs or tissues
which can be involved include skin (also known as /eukemia cutis) and the gums, lymph nodes, the small
intestine, the mediastinum, the lung, epidural sites, the uterus, the ovaries, and the orbit of the eye.

Symptoms: Symptoms of chloroma are related to their anatomic location; although they may also
be asymptomatic.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/240 + 5'"/263; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myeloid_sarcoma)

Leukaemoid reaction: The term leukaemoid reaction is used to describe the occurrence of a peripheral blood
picture resembling that of leukaemia in a subject who does not have leukaemia.

The blood picture may suggest the presence of leukaemia because of marked elevation of the total white cell
count, or the presence of immature white cells, or both. Leukaemoid reactions may be either myeloid or
lymphoid.

(Ref: de Gruchy/5""/272)

Types of leukaemoid reactions with causes:
1. Myeloid leukaemoid reaction: Here the blood picture resembling to that of myeloid leukaemia.

Causes:

* Infection: Pneumonia, meningitis, septicaemia, military tuberculosis.
* Secondary to non-haematological malignancy

= Acute haemolysis

2. Lymphatic leukaemoid reaction: Here the blood picture resembles to that of lymphoblastic leukaemia.

Causes:

Infectious mononucleosis
Cytomegalovirus infection
Pertussis

Measles

Chicken pox

Carcinoma

Miliary tuberculosis.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/252)

## Arif's Pathology & Haematology — Myeloproliferative Disorders, Lymphoproliferative Disorders, and Lymphoma

> **Source:** `Arif Pathology guide 2025(1).pdf` · **Pages 424–428** (5 extracted) · **UNIT-II : HAEMATOLOGY**
#### 📄 Page 424

424 | aris representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

“MYELOPROLIFERATIVE
DISORDERS,
LYMPHOPROLIFERATIVE
DISORDERS, AND
LYMPHOMA

Myeloproliferative Disorders
(V.V.I for VIVA)

Q. Define and classify myeloproliferative disorders. (DU-05Ja, SU-22Nv,20M, BUP-21Nv/M,
CU-19M)

Q. What are the myeloproliferative disorders? (CU-16Ju,09Ja)

Q. Short note: Myeloproliferative disorder.

Ans.

Myeloproliferative disorder: Myeloproliferative disorders are proliferative neoplastic disorders due to
uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal progenitor cells which are capable of producing erythroid, myeloid, and
megakaryocytic series.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/311)

Or,
Myeloproliferative disorders are a group of conditions arising from marrow stem cells and characterized by
clonal proliferation of one or more haemopoietic components in the bone marrow and, in many cases, the liver

and spleen.
(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/201)

Classification: Four disorders are included in this classification-
1. Polycythaemia rubra vera (proliferation predominantly involves erythropoiesis)
2. Essential thrombocythaemia (proliferation predominantly involves megakaryopoiesis)
3. Myelofibrosis with myeloid metaplasia (idiopathic / primary myelofibrosis)
4. Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML).
(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/90; de Gruchy/6"/311)

(Note: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), which used to be classified as a myeloproliferative disorder but is
now recognized as a separate entity.)
(Ref: Hoffbrand/S"/232)

---

#### 📄 Page 425

as —

NS —
Myelofibrosis

HAEMATOLOGY | 425

Q Define and classify myclofibrosis with clinical features.

Q Short note: Myclofibrosis.
Ans.
Myclofibrosis: The term myelofibrosis is used to describe fibrosis and collagen formation in the marrow.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/311)
Or,
Myelofibrosis is a disorder charactererized by progressive generalized reactive fibrosis of the bone marrow in
association with the development of haemopoiesis in the spleen and liver (known as myeloid metaplasia).
(Ref: Hoffbrand/5"/238)
Or,
Myelofibrosis is a disorder of unknown etiology characterized by bone marrow fibrosis, extramedullary
haemopoiesis and leucoerythroblastic blood picture.
(Ref: Short Case in Clinical Medicine/5"/252)

Synonyms:
® Idiopathic myelofibrosis
* Myelosclerosis
= Agnogenic myeloid metaplasia
s

Myelofibrosis with myeloid metaplasia (MMM).
(Ref: Hoffbrand/5"/238)
Types:
1. Primary myelofibrosis: Myelofibrosis developing in polycythaemia vera.
2. Secondary myelofibrosis: Tuberculosis, secondary carcinoma, Hodgkin’s disease, leukaemia, and a
variety of other haematological disorders.

1. It is a disease of adult life, occurring most commonly between the ages of 40 and 70 years.
2. Symptoms of anaemia- weakness, lassitude, fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitation, and signs of
CCF (in severe case).
3. Massive splenomegaly (main physical sign) and hepatomegaly.
Weight loss, anorexia, fever, night sweats are common.
5. Bleeding problems, bone pain, gout, acute abdominal pain, leg cramps, or jaundice are presenting
manifestations.
6. Radiological bone changes occur in about 30% of cases.

>

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/311)

Q. Give the laboratory diagnosis of myelofibrosis.

Q. Highlights the peripheral blood film of myelofibrosis.
Ans

Laboratory diagnosis of myelofibrosis:
A) Blood picture:
1. Hb% - Reduced (normal or increased in some patients).

2. Peripheral blood film:
RBC: Normocytic, normochromic with marked anisocytosis and poikilocytosis. Characteristic
‘tear-drop’ cells and also oval or elliptical cells are common. Polychromasia and
basophilia are often prominent. Numerous normoblasts and nucleated red cells are present.

WBC: Normal, reduced or raised.
Platelet: Normal, reduced or raised.

Reticulocytes: Moderately raised.

B) Bone marrow: Fibrotic hypercellular marrow.
C) Spleen: Markedly enlarged, shows myeloid metaplasia.
D) Liver: Enlarged with foci of extramedullary hemopoiesis.
E) Serum urate and LDH level: High.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/313)

Polycythaemia
(V.V.1. for VIVA & MCQ)

Q. Define polycythaemia. (CMU-22Nv) What are the causes of polycythaemia? (DU-13Ju, CU-
16/12Ju,10Ja)

Q. Short note: Polycythaemia. (SMU-23M, CU-15/11Ju, RU-09Ju)
Ans.

Polycythaemia: Polycythaemia means elevated levels of all cellular components of blood.

It is usually used when there is elevation of red cell count alone, or in combination with elevation of
granulocyte or platelet numbers.

An increase in red cell count is typically accompanied by an increase in the haemoglobin concentration and
haematocnit (PCV).

(Ref: de Gruchy/5""/318)
Or,

Polycythaemia is defined as an increase in the haemoglobin concentration above the upper limit of normal for
the patient’s age and sex.

(Ref: Hoffbrand/6""/203)
Causes / types of polycythaemia:

A. True polycythaemia: Increase in the total number of red cells in the body (due to alteration of
erythropoietin).

1. Primary polycythaemia / Polycythaemia rubra vera: Idiopathic (decreased erythropoietin).
2. Secondary polycythaemia (erythrocytosis): Increased erythropoietin.

a. Secondary to tissue hypoxia (appropriate cause):
High altitude

Congenital heart disease

Chronic pulmonary disease (e.g. COPD)

Hypoventilation syndromes (obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea)
Smoking

Renal transplantation

b. Secondary to inappropriately increased erythropoietin production:
= Non-neoplastic kidney disease — cysts, hydronephrosis
= Tumours of kidney and liver — renal cell cancer (RCC), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
= Cerebellar haemangioblastoma, phaeochromocytoma, adrenal adenoma etc.

3. Benign familial polycythaemia.

B. Relative polycythaemia: A reduction in plasma volume relative to the volume of red cells
(erythropoietin is normal).

a. Dehydration

b. Bums

c. Reduced fluid intake

d. Redistribution of body fluids

e. Spurious polycythaemia (polycytheaemia of stress).

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/295; Hoffbrand/6"/204)

---

#### 📄 Page 427

HAEMATOLOGY 427

Q. Write the blood picture of polycythaemia rubra vera. (CU-10Ja)
Q. Short note on: Polycythacmia vera / Polycythaemia rubra vera. (DU-06M, CU-12/1 1Ja,06S)

Ans.
Polycythaemia vera: It is a chronic, progressive, and ultimately fatal disease, in which the fundamental
abnormality is an excess production of the formed elements of the blood by a hyperplastic bone marrow.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/295)

Clinical features:
Common:

1. Cerebral symptoms, especially headache and dizzines

2. Cardiovascular symptoms

3. Development of red face or bloodshot eyes

4. Weakness, lassitude, and tiredness

5. Gastrointestinal symptoms, especially dyspepsia

6. Visual disturbances

7. Pruritus

8. Thrombotic complications

9. Haemorrhagic manifestations

10. Peripheral vascular disease

11. Accidental discovery on routine examination.
Occasional:

1. Splenomegaly

2. Gout

3. Incidental discovery in investigation of other medical problems

4. Psychiatric manifestations.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/297)

Laboratory diagnosis:

A. Blood picture:
= Hb% - Increased (18 - 24 gm /dl, my be higher)

PCV - Raised (60-70%, and sometimes higher)
ESR - Decreased (1 mm/hour)
MCV, MCH & MCHC - Reduced.

Peripheral blood film:

= RBC count - Increased

= WBC - Leukocytosis

= Platelet - Thrombocytosis

= Reticulocytes - /.5% or above.

B. Bone marrow examination: Trephine biopsy my be needed.
= Cellularity - Increased

MEE ratio - Normal or reduced

Erythropoiesis - Increased

Granulopoiesis - Increased

Megakaryopoiesis - Increased.

C. Others:
a. Serum uric acid level - Increased
b. Serum lactate dehydrogenase level - Increased.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/299)

(N.B: The JAK2 mutation is present in the bone marrow and peripheral blood granulocytes in over 95% of

patients.)
(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/295)

Lymphoproliferative disorders: These are heterogenous disorders of neoplastic proliferation of mature
lymphoid cells.

Or,
Lymphoproliferative disorders (LPDs) refer to several conditions in which lymphocytes are produced in
excessive quantities. They typically occur in patients who have compromised immune systems.

ivmphoeytes (hairy cells). The disease is marked by pancytopenia & splenomegaly

Q. What is immunoproliferative disorder? (RU-11Ju)

Ans.

Immunoproliferative disorders: Immunoproliferative disorders (also known as “immunoproliferative
diseases” or “immunoproliferative neoplasms”) are disorders of the immune system that are characterized by
the abnormal proliferation of the primary cells of the immune system, which includes B cells, T cells and
Natural killer (NK) cells, or by the excessive production of immunoglobulins (also known as antibodies).

These disorders are subdivided into three main classes, which are-

1. Lymphoproliferative disorders
2. Hypergammaglobulinemia, and
3. Paraproteinemia.

(Ref: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunoproliferative_disorder)

Q. Short note: Paraprotein. (CU-13Ja)

Ans.

Paraprotein: Paraprotein is one type of immunoglobulin molecule or one type of heavy chain or one type of
light chain (monoclonal protein). It is produced under neoplastic proliferations of monoclonal cells of the
lymphoid series.

Paraproteinaemia: These are the disorders characterized by abnormal proliferation of immunoglobulin-
producing cells with an increase in serum level of a single homogenous immunoglobulin or its fragments.

Or,
Paraproteinemia is the presence of excessive amounts of a single monoclonal gammaglobulin (called a
paraprotein) in the blood.

Or,
The term paraproteinaemia refers to the presence of a monoclonal immunoglobulin band in serum and reflects
the synthesis of immunoglobulin from a single clone of plasma cells.

(Ref: Hoffbrand/6"/273,286)

Synonym: Monoclonal gammopathy, plasma cell dyscrasia.

Causes / Disorders associated with paraproteinaemia: (V.V./ for VIVA)
Multiple myeloma

Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinaemia

Chronic lymphatic leukaemia

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

Benign monoclonal gammopathy

Heavy chain disease

Primary amyloidosis.

: Multiple myeloma is a chronic, progressive, and fatal malignant condition in which the

Q. What is solitary myeloma?
Ans.

Solitary myeloma (Plasmacytoma): It is a single neoplastic lesion of plasma cell origin. About 3 - 5% of
plasma cell neoplasms present as a solitary lesion of either bone or soft tissue. The bony lesions tend to occur

in the same locations as in multiple myeloma. Extraosseous lesions are often located in the lungs, oropharynx,

or nasal sinuses.
(Ref: Robbin’s/10"/607 + 7'/681)

Q. What is Bence-Zones proteinuria?

Q. How Bence-Jones protein is detected in urine? (SU-10Ja)

Q. Short note on: Bence-Jones protein. (DU-05S, RU-15Ja, CU-10Ja)

Ans.

Bence-Jones protein: It is an immunoglobulin light chain either « (kappa) or A (lambda).

Bence-Zones proteinuria: When urine contains Bence-Zones proteins which is an free monoclonal k or A-
light chain of immunoglobulin is called Bence-Zones proteinuria.

It is found in various pathological conditions like-

1. Multiple myeloma

2. Macroglobulinaemia
3. Amyloidosis

4. Lymphoma

5. Leukaemia.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/287)
Detection of Bence-Jones protein in urine:

1. Heat test: Bence-Jones proteins have unique behavior in heating. Urine containing Bence-Jones
proteins flocculates when heated slowly to 50-60°C. The flocculated proteins on boiling, and reappears
on cooling below 60°C.

---

2 Electrophoretic method: The most reliable means for the detection of Bence-Jones proteins is
electrophoresis of a concentrated urine specimen on cellulose acetate. The monoclonal light chains
usually migrate as a marrow band in the globulin region,

Q. What are the causes of hyperviscosity syndrome?
Ans.
Causes of hyperviscosity syndrome:
1. Polycythemia (most common)
2. Myeloma
3. Acute or chronic leukaemias
4. Rarely haemophilia, treated with massive dose of cryoprecipitate.

Q. What are the effects of hyperviscosity syndrome?

Ans.
Effects of hyperviscosity syndrome: Hyperviscosity syndrome is characterized by the following:

« Visual impairment associated with venous congestion, which is reflected by striking tortuosity and
distention of retinal veins; retinal hemorrhages and exudates can also contribute to the visual problems.

« Neurologic problems such as headaches, dizziness, deafness, and stupor, all stemming from sluggish
blood flow and sludging.

« Bleeding related to the formation of complexes between macroglobulins and clotting factors as well as
interference with platelet functions.

* Cryoglobulinemia resulting from the precipitation of macroglobulins at low temperatures, which
produces symptoms such as Raynaud phenomenon and cold urticaria.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/611)

## Arif's Pathology & Haematology — Bleeding Disorders

> **Source:** `Arif Pathology guide 2025(1).pdf` · **Pages 436–458** (23 extracted) · **UNIT-II : HAEMATOLOGY**
#### 📄 Page 436

V6 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

CHAPTEF

LEEDING DISORDERS

Basic Physiology of Haemostasis
(Ref: Pathoma Lecture Notes)
(This part will make your conception clear and concrete and will help to correlate the later)

Primary Hemostasis

Primary hemostasis - make a platelet plug.

Secondary hemostasis - make fibrin mesh by coagulation cascade to stabilize platelet plug.

Q. What are steps of primary hemostasis?
Ans.

1. Vasoconstriction

2. Platelet adhesion

3. Platelet activation

4. Platelet aggregation.

Q. What causes vasoconstriction?

Ans.

Vasoconstriction - mediated neurally and chemically. When endothelium is disrupted, endothelial cells secrete
endothelin for vasoconstriction. NO and prostacyclin production goes down (they vasodialate).

* Endothelin - powerful vasoconstrictor
* NOand prostacyclin (prostaglandin I) - vasodialator.

Q. What happens in platelet adhesion?

Ans.

Platelet adhesion - VWF (von willieband factor) is a glue that binds to exposed collagen in damaged tissue. It
then binds to glycoprotein VIII, and then glycoprotein IB (integrin IB) on platelet. VWF mainly comes from
endothelial cells, but are also found in alpha granules platelets.

---

#### 📄 Page 437

——————EEE =e —s
Q. What happens in platelet activation?
Ans.
Platelet changes shape after adhesion and is activated. It sceretes-
® Thromboxane A; {very powerful degranulator made by cyclooxygenase (COX)}
« Alpha granules (contain fibrinogen and VWF) = AVF
® Delta granules (contain SAC - serotonin for vasoconstriction, ADP which is necessary for expression
of GP IIB/IIIA receptor by platelet and stimulates degranulation, and calcium that helps in secondary
hemostasis).

Q. What happens in platelet aggregation?

Ans. ,
A single fibrinogen is linked to multiple platelets via their glycoprotein IIB/IIIA. This creates platelet plug.
Platelet plug is weak and needs secondary hemostasis (coagulation cascade) for stabilization.

Q. What are 2 classification of platelet disorders?

Ans.
Qualitative disorders - bad platelet.

Quantitative disorders - good platelet but too few in numbers {petechiae (spots in skin due to bleeding) seen
in thrombocytopenia and not usually in qualitative disorder}.

Q. What are common features of patient with problem in primary hemostasis?

Ans.

Key sign is mucosal and skin bleeding; intracranial bleeding with severe thrombocytopenia (low platelet) (can
kill you).

= Mucosal bleeding - epistaxis (nose bleeding), hemoptysis (coughing blood), GI bleeding, hematuria,
and menorrhagia (heavy menses)

« Skin bleeding - petechiae (bleeding spots on skin), purpura (>3mm bleeding spots), ecchymoses
(>1cm), easy bruising,

Secondary Hemostasis

Q. What does secondary hemostasis do?

Ans.
« Itcreates fibrin mesh via coagulation cascade to stabilize platelet plug.

= It creates thrombin (factor Ila). Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin (factor Ia). Fibrin is then cross
linked.

Q. What causes disorders of secondary hemostasis?
Ans.
They occur due to factor abnormalities.

Q. What is clinical presentation of disorders of secondary hemostasis?
Ans.
= Deep bleeding in muscles and joints (recall that disorders of primary hemostasis has bleeding in skin
and mucosal surface).
= Rebleeding after surgical procedures.

Q. How do extrinsic and intrinsic pathway of coagulation cascade start? What lab tests
measures intrinsic and extrinsic pathways?
Ans.

---

#### 📄 Page 438

438 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Intrinsic pathway - Starts with factor 12 which is activated by subendothelial collagen (SEC). Measured by
APTT lab test.

Extrinsic pathway - starts with factor 7 which is activated by tissue thromboplastin/tissue factor. Measured by
PT lab test.

Bleeding Disorders

Q. Define haemorrhagic disorder with example. (DU-24Nv, BUP-22Nv, RMU-22M,18Nv/Ja,
17Nv,14/08Ju, SU-20M, CU-11/09/08Ja)
Q. Short note: Haemorrhagic disorder / bleeding disorder.
Ans.
Hemorrhagic disorder: The haemorrhagic disorders are a group of disorders of widely differing etiology,
which have in common an abnormal tendency to bleed due to a defect in the mechanism of haemostasis.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/338)

Clinical features of bleeding disorders:

(a) Spontaneous bleeding into the skin, mucous membranes and internal tissues.

(b) Excessive or prolonged bleeding following trauma or surgery.

(c) Bleeding from more than one site.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/338)

Pathogenesis of bleeding disorder: Three major components of the normal haemostatic mechanism- the
vascular, platelet, and coagulation components act together in a co-ordinated fashion to arrest bleeding. A
breakdown in the normal haemostatic mechanism i.e. a defect in any one of these three components causes an
abnormal tendency to bleed.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/338)

Q. Write in brief about idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). (RMU-21Nv/M,19M)
Q. Short note: ITP. (DU-13/09/08Ja, RU-09Ju)
Q. Short note: ITP including PBF and bone marrow finding. (RU-15Ju)
ABS.
ITP: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an autoimmune disease characterized by
thrombocytopenia in almost all cases due to antibody formation.

(Ref: de Gruchy/6""/351)

Synonyms of ITP:
1. Primary and essential thrombocytopenic purpura

2. Purpura hemorrhagica
3. Wealhot’s disease
4. Auto-immune thrombocytopenia.
(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/106)

Types: Two clinical types are recognized-

1. Acute self-limiting type: Occurs most commonly in children aged 2 -6 years.
2. Chronic type: Occurs most commonly in young to middle aged females.
(Ref: de Gruchy/5"/378,379)

Clinical features:
1, Spontaneous bleeding (occur usually from skin and mucus membrane as petechiae or ecchymoses, or both)

2. Petechial bleeding (pin-point to pin-head sized) are seen especially on the arms and legs, the neck,
and the upper part of the chest

3. Gastrointestinal bleeding e.g. hematemesis and malena
4. Hematuria, menorrhagia, metrorrhegia, epistaxis, hemoptysis and gum bleeding may be present

---

#### 📄 Page 446

446 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

5. Hemorrhage into the peritoneal or pleural cavities (rarely)

6. Cerebral haemorrhage (most common cause of death in severe thrombocytopenia)
7. Subconjunctival and retinal haemorrhage are relatively common

8. Usually no anaemia, but if there is history of menorrhagia, anaemia may occur

9. Splenomegaly in less than 10% of cases.

(Ref: de Gruchy/5"/378)

Fig: Clinical presentation of ITP.

Laboratory diagnosis of ITP:
1) Routine blood test:
(a) Hb% - usually reduced
(b) ESR - normal

2) Peripheral blood film (PBF):

(a) RBC - Nommocytic, normochromic
(b) WBC - Normal or moderately increased
(c) Platelet count - Reduced, may be large, small or atypical

3) Screening tests:
(a) BT - Prolonged, up to 30 min or more

(b) CT — Normal
(c) Platelet count - Reduced (< 1 lak /mm’)
(d) Torniquet test - Positive in most cases

4) Bone marrow examination:
(a) Cellularity - Hypercellular
(b) M/E ratio - Increased
(c) Erythropoiesis - Normal
(d) Granulopoiesis - Active, maturing to segmented form

(e) Megakaryopoiesis - Increased and some immature and dysplastic (abnormal size and shape) cells
are found

5) Other tests: Anti-platelet antibody detection - Present in 70% cases.
(Ref: de Gruchy/5"/379; Hoffbrand/6"/336)

Q. Mention the confirmatory tests of ITP. (V/VA DMC)
Ans.
Confirmatory tests of ITP:
* Bone marrow examination: Increased megakaryopoiesis.
=  Anti-platelet antibody.

Q. Give the pathogenesis of chronic ITP. (RU-1 7Ju,14Ja)

Ans.

Pathogenesis of chronic ITP: It is an autoimmune disorder caused by the formation of autoantibodies
against platelet antigen. Membrane glycoprotein usually glycoprotein Ib/IIla or Ib-IX acts as platelet antigen.
The antiplatelet-antibody is class-IgG and known as platelet-associated immunoglobin (PLA-IgG). Opsonized

platelets (platelets bound with antiplatciet antibodies) are susceptible to phagocytosis by mononuclear
phagocytic cells mainly in the spleen. It is more common in female of reproductive age groups and aggravated
during pregnancy, because estrogen helps to express the Fe receptors, on phagocytic cells and increase the
platelet destruction. New born babies of pregnant women with chronic ITP is also be affected by the passive
transfer of PLA-IgG formed in mother and show consequent destruction of platelets and thrombocytopenia.

Formation of autoantibodies (IgG) against platelet antigen
(Membrane glycoprotein usually glycoprotein IIb/IIIa or Ib-1X)

mononuclear phagocytic cells mainly in the spleen.

(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/106)

Q. Short note: von-Willebrand factor.

Ans.
von-Willebrand factor: von-Willebrand factor is a plasma protein coagulation factor synthesized by

endothelial cells and megakaryocytes.

Function of von-Willebrand factor: It has two roles-
1. It promotes platelet adhesion to subendothelium at sites of vascular injury.

2. vWF is a carrier protein for factor VIII (the antihemophilic factor), and the two proteins circulate
together as a complex, thus preventing more rapid removal of the coagulation protein from the plasma.
(Ref: de Gruchy/5"/361,407,433; BRS Pathology/5"/196)

Q. Short note: von-Willebrand disease. (DU-10Ju)

Ans.
von-Willebrand disease: von Willebrand disease is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder. This
autosomal disorder is marked by deficiency of vWF, a large multimeric protein synthesized by endothelial

cells and megakaryocytes.
Classification of von-Willebrand disease:

a. Type I: Mild quantitative defect
b. Type II: Qualitative defects of intermediate severity
c. Type III: Extremely severe with virtually no vWF.

Inheritance: Most cases show autosomal dominant inheritance; however, type III and some cases of type II
are autosomal recessive.

---

#### 📄 Page 450

450 | arif's representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Characteristics:
= Impaired platelet adhesion
= Prolonged bleeding time
* Functional deficiency of factor VIII.

Hemostatic defects: Dual hemostatic defects-
a) Deficiency of vWF leads to a failure of platelet adhesion, resulting in deficient platelet plug
formation manifestation clinically by primary hemostatic bleeding and prolonged bleeding time

b) A functional deficiency of factor VIII occurs as a consequence of the deficit of vWF, its carrier
protein. Deficiency is manifest by secondary hemostatic bleeding and prolonged APTT.

Laboratory screening tests:
* Bleeding time: Prolonged

=» APTT: Prolonged
* Clotting time: Prolonged
= Platelet count: Normal
* PT: Normal
=» Thrombin time (TT): Normal
= Confirmatory tests: vWF assay.
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5""/195,196; Hoffbrand/6'"/352)

Constitutional disturbances like fever
Chronic haemophilic arthritis (permanent joint damage due to repeated hemorrhage into a joint)
Pressure effects and sequelae of haematomas (e.g. Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture)
Infections e.g. Hepatitis A, B, C, D and HIV (due to repeated blood transfusion).
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/391,392; Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/113)

Q. Why Haemophilia is called X-linked recessive disorder? (DU-19Nv)

Ans.

Haemophilia is called X-linked recessive disorder: Hemophilia is the classic example of an X-linked
recessive disorder, because:

Defective gene is located on X chromosome.

Males are affected; females are carrier.
Affected male will not transmit the disorder to his son (no male to male transmission), because his Y

chromosome cannot carry the hemophilic gene. However, all (100%) of his daughters will be carrier
of hemophilia because they inherit his X chromosome containing hemophilic gene. Most of these
carrier women will be unaffected clinically because of presence of a normal allele from mother.

Female carrier will transmit the disorder to half of her sons and cartier state to half of her daughters

(50% sons will be affected, and 50% daughters will be carrier).
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/390; Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/113)

CU-08Ja)

of DIC: The key event underlying DIC is increased activity of thrombin in the circulation that

wansfusion reaction and some snake bites.

In addition to its role in the deposition of fibrin in the microcirculation, intravascular thrombin formation
produces large amounts of circulating fibrin monomers which form complexes with fibrinogen and interfere
with fibrin polymerization, thus contributing to the coagulation defect. Intense fibrinolysis is stimulated by
thrombi on vascular walls and the release of split products interferes with fibrin polymerization, thus
contnbuting to the coagulation defect. The combined action of thrombin and plasmin causes depletion of
fibrinogen and all coagulation factors. Intravascular thrombin also causes widespread platelet aggregation
in the vessels. The bleeding problems which may be a feature of DIC are compounded by thrombocytopenia
caused by consumption of platelets.

Very Important for VIVA
