Blood Grouping & Cross Matching

Q. Classify blood group systems. (CU-12Ja)
Q. Short note: Blood group. (CU-09Ju)
Ans.

Blood group: Classification of blood according to presence of different antigens on the plasma membrane to
RBC is called blood group.

Major/ Principal blood groups: The chief blood groups are-
1. ABO blood groups: Based on the presence or absence of group specific antigen in the RBC membrane.
2. Rh blood groups: Based on the presence or absence of Rh antigen in the RBC membrane.
3. M&N blood groups: Used to determine patemity.
(Ref: S. Wright/13"/46)

1. Lutheran blood group system
2. Lewis blood group system

3. Kell blood group system

4. Kidd blood group system

5. Duffy blood group system

6. Diego blood group system

7. Dombrock blood group system
8

Colton blood group system.
(Ref: de Gruchy/6"/432)

Importance of blood group:
i) To avoid the hazards of mismatched blood transfusion

ii) To identify certain blood diseases e.g. immune haemolytic anaemia
iii) Paternity test

iv) Medico legal cases (to identify criminals)

v) Various experimental studies in hematological laboratories.

Q. Short note: ABO blood group. (CU-08Ju)

Ans.

ABO blood group: The ABO blood group system consists of four main groups - AB, A, B, and O which are
determined by the presence or absence of the A & B antigens on the surface of RBC.

Q. What is cross matching? Write down the aim and necessity of cross matching. (DU-08Ja)
Ans.
Cross matching: It is the antigenic matching of donor’s and recipient’s blood group antigens (RBC) and
antibodies (plasma).
Or,

The only sure safeguard against transfusion complications is to match the serum of the recipient directly
against the cells of the donor. This is called cross matching.

(Ref: S. Wright’s/13*/49)

Once the ABO & Rh blood groups of donor and recipient are known it is necessary to proceed with cross
matching before transfusion can be performed.

Necessity of cross matching:
1. There may be error in sample identification
2. The recipient’s serum may contain antibodies other than Anti-A, Anti-B & Anti-D. About 1% of
hospital patients possess antibodies outside the ABO and Rh system
3. Non cross matched O group blood is not free of risk
4. Non cross matched Rh -ve blood to Rh +ve recipient is not entirely innocuous.

Aim: To detect antibody in the recipient serum against the Donor’s red cells.
(Ref: Lecture DMC)

test:
Take one drop of 2% saline suspension of donor’s cells

Kept at room temperature for one hour

antiglobulin test:
Take two drop of 2% suspension of donor’s cells
Add six drop of patient’s serum
Incubate at 37°C for 30-60 minutes
Wash the cells three times in large volume of saline and drain
Add one drop of antiglobulin serum to the final cell button
Centrifuge the mixture lightly
Look for agglutination.

Interpretation: Agglutination of red blood cells is a positive result and indicates the presence of antibody
against the antigen in the serum.

Q. Define complete antibody and incomplete antibody.

Q. Compare and contrast between complete antibody and incomplete antibody.
Ans.
Complete antibody: An antibody that can directly agglutinate saline-suspended red blood cells.

Incomplete antibody: An antibody that cannot directly agglutinate saline-suspended red blood cells, it needs
an additive to complete the agglutination.

Q. What are the tests for selection of appropriate blood?
Ans.
Tests for selection of appropriate blood:
1. Determination of blood group: ABO system & Rh D for both recipient and donor.
2. Screening of recipient serum for irregular atypical antibodies (non ABO antibodies).
3. Cross matching.
(Ref: Basic Hematolegy, Dr. Maineddin’121)

Q. Why cross matching is essential for blood transfusion? (DU-O08Ja)

Ans.

Cress matching is essential for blood transfusion: Beside ABO & Rh typing, there are several other coups.
So, matching of ABO & Rh system only does not indicate that donor’s & recipient's blood are the same, and &
does not exclude the possibility of mismatched reaction.

For this reason, cross matching is important pnor to blood transfusion.

Febrile reaction: Common in patients receiving repeated transfusions e.g. persons with aplastic anaemia.

Allergic reaction: Skin rash, hypotension, tachycardia, respiratory distress & rarely anaphylactic shock.

oP

Circulatory overload: May cause pulmonary congestion and acute heart failure and is the most

Haemolytic reaction: Due to mismatched blood transfusion.

Q. Mention the immediate and delayed complications of blood transfusion.
Q. Name the immediate blood transfusion reactions. (DU-14Ju)
Q. Write the delayed complications of blood transfusion. (CU-16Ja,13Ju)
Q. Mention the diseases that can be transmitted by blood transfusion. (DU-18M)
Ans.
Immediate and delayed complications of blood transfusion:
A. Immediate complications:
1. Pyrogenic reaction (immediate simple febrile reaction): These reactions occur either during or
shortly after a transfusion and cause chills and fever in the recipient
2. Allergic reactions (occur in about 1% of all transfusion) e.g. skin rash, hypotension, tachycardia,
respiratory distress & rarely anaphylactic shock
Hemolytic transfusion reaction
Circulatory overload (most common cause of death following transfusion)
Bacterial contamination of blood
Biochemical upsets following massive blood transfusion:
Hyperkalemia
Citrate toxicity
Metabolic acidosis/alkalosis

Q. What are the features of a haemolytic transfusion reaction? How will you establish the
diagnosis?

Q. Short note: Transfusion reaction. (CU-10Ju)

Ans.

Haemolytic transfusion reaction: The antibodies capable of reacting with red cell antigens may lead to red
cell destruction (a/most always donor red cells).

Types: It is two types-

1. Immediate hemolytic transfusion reaction (intravascular): This type of transfusion reaction is
associated with ABO incompatibility.
Clinical features: Within less than | hour of the start of the transfusion, the patient complains of-

Heat in the vein

Throbbing in the head

Flushing of the face

Chest tightness

Nausea

Lumbar pain

Tachycardia

Hypotension

Rigor and pyrexia usually follow.

Laboratory test:

= Routine hematological tests: Hb conc., ESR, TC & DC of WBC, platelet count, and blood film
Serum bilirubin- increased
Schumm’s test for hemoglobinemia- positive
Coagulation study: APTT, PT, TT- prolonged; fibrinogen titer- decreased; FDP- increased
Renal function test: Serum urea & creatinine- increased
Repetition of blood grouping of recipient and donor blood, cross matching and Ab screening test

=» Measurement first 24 hours urine and test for hemoglobinuria, may be detected if intravascular
hemolysis occurred.

2. Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction: It is occurred in individual who is previously sensitized to red
cell antigens by transfusion or pregnancy.

Clinical features:

= Fever

» Jaundice

=» Anemia
Laboratory findings:

= No antibody is detected in routine pre-transfusion testing but the transfusion of blood containing
Ag to which the recipient has previously been sensitized provokes a brisk anamnestic response.
(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/123; de Gruchy/6"/438)

Q. Enumerate in brief the Rh-incompatibility. (SU-17M)
Q. Short note: Rh-incompatibility. (DU-13/11Ju, CU-15Ja,12Ju,09/07Ja,08Ju)
Ans.

Rh-incompatibility: It is a condition occurs when there is anti-Rh antibody in the serum of Rh (+ve) person
followed by antigen-antibody reaction.

Occurrence: Rh-incompatibility may develop in one of the following conditions-

1. When an Rh (-ve) person is transfused with Rh (+ve) blood, he/she will develop anti-D antibody. After
subsequent transfusion with Rh (+ve) blood, he/she suffers from hemolytic transfusion reaction, in
which anti-D antibody binds with Rh-antigen on the RBC membrane causing destruction of the RBC
(hemolysis).

2. In case of a Rh (-ve) mother pregnant with a Rh (+ve) fetus may develop erythroblastosis fetalis
usually from second to third pregnancy.

Explanation: When an Rh (-ve) mother carries an Rh (+) fetus, some fetal red blood cells enter the maternal
circulation at the time of delivery. Fetal RBC stimulates anti-D antibody production in the mother. During the
next pregnancies, anti-D antibody from mother crosses the placenta to the Rh (+ve) fetus & causes hemolytic
transfusion reaction in the fetus. Rh-incompatibility in a Rh (+ve) fetus growing in an Rh (-ve) mother results
in two clinical syndromes-

= Hydrops fetalis
= Hemolytic disease of newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis).

Prevention:
1. Administration of anti-Rh (anti-D) globulin after child birth or abortion within 72 hours or earlier
2. Prevent or minimize foeto-maternal bleeding during manual removal of placenta
3. No prophylactic ergometrine
4. Avoid Rh (+ve) blood transfusion to Rh (-ve) person.

Treatment: Replacement of the newborn infant’s blood with Rh (-ve) blood. Approximately 400 ml of Rh
(-ve) blood is infused over a period of 1.5 or more hours while the baby’s own Rh (+ve) blood is being
removed after a regular interval during first few weeks of life.

(Ref: Hoffbrand/5"/356-357; de Gruchy/5"/477)

Q. What do you mean by hemolytic disease of newborn (HDN)? (DU-18M)

Q. Short note: Hemolytic disease of newborn (HDN). (BUP-22Nv)

Ans.

Hemolytic disease of newborn (HDN): If Rh-ve mother carries Rh+ve fetus, small amounts of fetal blood
enter into maternal circulation during delivery and produce agglutinins against the Rh+ve blood. During next
pregnancy the agglutinin crosses the placenta and if the second fetus having Rh+ve blood then they cause

---

hemolysis and various forms of hemolytic disease of the newborn (Erythroblastosis fetalis). If the hemolysis in
the fetus is severe, the infant may die in utero or may develop anaemia, jaundice or oedema (Hydrops fetalis).

Q. What do you mean by massive blood transfusion? What are the complications of massive
blood transfusion? (DU-18Ja)

Ans.

Massive blood transfusion: Massive blood transfusion is usually defined as the replacement of total blood
volume within 24 hours period e.g. in adult receiving (5 liter) blood transfusion within 24 hours.

(Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/124)

Complications of massive blood transfusion:
* Hypothermia

= Coagulation defect

= Thrombocytopenia

= Iso-sensitization

Q. Short note on: Anticoagulants. (DU-13/07Ja, RU-16Ja,13/11/10Ju)
Ans.

Anticoagulants: Anticoagulants are the drugs which are used to prevent unwanted coagulation.
Classification:
1. Acting in vitro (outside the body): Citrate, oxalate, EDTA, heparin, dextran sulphate etc.
2. Acting in vive (within the body): Dicoumarol, warfarin, phenindione.
3. Both in vitro and in vivo: Heparin, dextran sulphate, ancord.

Q. What is the advantage of double oxalate?

Q. What is the advantage of mixture of ammonium oxalate & potassium oxalate?

Ans.

Advantage of double oxalate: Ammonium salt causes swelling of RBC & potassium salt causes shrinkage of

RBC. Thus to prevent swelling, thereby bursting of RBC and also shrinkage of RBC, so double oxalate is used.
(Ref: Lecture DMC)

Q What is the disadvantage of sodium citrate?
Ans.
Disadvantage of sodium citrate: Sodium citrate is always used in solution which will alter the concentration

of blood & thus actual PCV, Hb%, TC, DC will not be obtained.
(Ref: Lecture DMC)

Q. Why EDTA is called an ideal anticoagulant?

EDTA is called an ideal anticoagulant because it-

= Platelet can be counted more accurately by preventing platelet clumping

Q. What do you mean by hypersplenism? What are the causes of hypersplenism?

Ans.
Hypersplenism: Hypersplenism is a syndrome which is characterized by the triad of-

1. Splenomegaly
2. Anaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or any combination of these, in association with hyperplasia

of the marrow precursors of the deficient cell types

3. Correction of the blood cytopenia(s) by splenectomy.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/629)

Common causes of hypersplenism:

1. Kala-azar and malaria
2. Chronic hemolytic anemia

3. CLL, CML, myelofibrosis and lymphoma.
‘ (Ref: Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/32)

#### 📄 Page 5

Preface

“Bismitlahin Rakmanin Raho” “ss

First of all, I am revealing my gratefulness to almighty Allah for his endless compassion & mercy
to complete and publish the completely new (15"") edition-2025 of this book in meantime.

This New Edition 2025 is an exclusive one which is unique compared to the previous editions. It
contains the solutions of all the Prof. questions of different Universities (DU, CU, CMU, RU, RMU,
SUST, BSFMMU’S & BUP) up to Prof. November 2024 as well as assessment questions of different
Medical Colleges of recent batches.

Recently Robbins & Cotran PATHOLOGIC BASIS OF DISEASE 10” (New) edition has
become available in Bangladesh which is hugely different from the previous (9") edition. Systemic and
General Pathology part has been totally re-written using that new (10") edition Robbins Pathology
and the South Asia (11") edition as well, that has made the book unique and totally updated.

Use of “BRS Pathology”-5" Edition, “Hoffbrand, Moss & Pettit”-6" Edition and “Dacie &
Lewis”-10" Edition along with “de Gruchy”-6" Edition has made the Hematology portion peerless.
Moreover use of “UNDERGRADUATE BASIC HEMATOLOGY by Dr. Mainuddin Ahmed” has
made this book special for Rajshahi Medical College (RMC) and other medical colleges under
Rajshahi University (RU). Clinical Pathology portion is totally written from “Davidson’s Medicine” —
24" & 23" Edition that is always preferable by the teachers. Systemic and General Pathology are totally
written from “Robbins Pathology”-10" Edition, “BRS Pathology”-5" Edition, “Harsh Mohan”-7"
Edition, “Pathoma Lecture Notes”-New Edition & “Davidson’s Medicine” — 24" & 23" Edition
with the help of the lectures of different Medical colleges of Bangladesh.

In fact, no pains have been spared to make the book as attractive & appealing to the students as
possible & I hope that I have been able to provide a complete guide to the students which will not only
be of help in their class work, but will also give them a better understanding of the subject. The content
of this book is enriched with huge amount of information that will help the post graduate entrance
examinees also (MD/MS/M.Phil/Diploma/FCPS Part-I). It is also equally effective for the BDS students.

I have tried to make this book so complete that the readers need not to travel here and there to
search this and that during examination, because everything is here that you are searching for. This will
save both your time and money. MCQ (updated up to Prof. November 2024) has also been added that
has made this book more effective.

I would like to thank our honorable Teachers for their proper guidance to perform best so far. I
would also like to thank my dear MBBS classmates of batch SS-34, SSMC, my present & past
colleagues, seniors & juniors, my friends, my students of arif’s Medical Academy especially the
students of “Pathology course” & also the students of different Medical Colleges in Bangladesh & all of
my well-wishers. It is requested that the discrepancies, if any noticed may please be intimated to me, so
that it may be taken care of in the next edition.

Frank opinions, critical comments & constructive suggestions for further improvement of the
book will be thankfully acknowledged.

Dhaka Dr. Md. Arif Hossain
24" February, 2025 Sir Salimullah Medical College

Vascular Structure and Function

‘ Diseases of blood vessels: Two principal mechanisms underlie vascular disease:

(1) Narrowing (stenosis) or complete obstruction of vessel lumens, either progressively (e.g. by
atherosclerosis) or precipitously (e.g. by thrombosis or embolism)

(Ref: Robbins/10"/485,518)

All vessels except capillaries share a three-layered architecture consisting of an endothelium lined intima, a
surrounding smooth muscle media, and supportive adventitia, admixed with extracellular matrix.

---

#### 📄 Page 24

24 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

The intima normally consists of a single layer of endothelial cells sitting on a basement membrane which is
demarcated from the media by the internal elastic lamina.

The adventitia lics external to the media and in many arteries is separated from the media by a well-defined

external elastic lamina.
Capillaries are approximately the diameter of a red cell (7 to 8 ym); they have an endothelial cell lining but

no media, although variable numbers of pericytes, cells that resemble smooth muscle cells, typically lie just
deep to the the endothelium.

Arteries are divided into three types based on their size and structural features:
(1) Large or elastic arteries, including the aorta, the major branches of the aorta (the innominate,
subclavian, common carotid, and iliac arteries), and the pulmonary arteries;
(2) Medium sized or muscular arteries, comprising smaller branches of the aorta (e.g., the coronary and
renal arteries); and
(3) Small arteries (<2 mm in diameter) and arterioles (20 to 100 um in diameter), within tissues and
organs.

Lymphatics are thin-walled channels lined by specialized endothelium; they provide conduits to return

interstitial tissue fluid and inflammatory cells to the bloodstream.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/485)

Congenital anomalies of blood vessel:

---

#### 📄 Page 25

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY 25

1. Developmental or berry ancurysms occur in cerebral vessels; when ruptured, these can cause fatal
intracerebral hemorrhage.

2. Arterio-venous fistulas are direct connections (usually small) between arteries and veins that bypass
capillaries.

3. Fibromascular dysplasia is a focal irregular thickening in medium and large muscular arteries
including renal, carotid, splanchnic, and vertebral vessels.

4. Anomalous coronary artery origin occurs from a developmental anomaly in which both coronary
arteries arise over the same coronary cusp of the aortic valve.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/487)

Arteriovenous fistulas: Arteriovenous fistulas are are direct connections (usually small) between arteries and
veins that bypass capillaries.

Cause / etiology:

= Developmental defects

Rupture of an arterial aneurysm into the adjacent vein
Penetrating injuries that pierce arteries and veins
Inflammatory necrosis of adjacent vessels

Surgically generated arteriovenous fistulas (for hemodialysis)

Clinical importance:
= Rupture, leading to intracerebral hemorrhage

= Large or multiple arteriovenous fistulas become clinically significant by shunting blood from the
arterial to the venous circulations, forcing the heart to pump additional volume and leading to high-
output cardiac failure.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/487)

Q. Define malignant hypertension. (Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Malignant hypertension: Accelerated or malignant hypertension is a clinical syndrome characterized by
severe pressure elevations (i.e. systolic pressure more than 200 mm Hg, diastolic pressure more than 120 mm
Hg), renal failure, and retinal hemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilledema (swelling of the
optic nerve that reflects increased intracranial pressures).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/490)

It can develop in previously normotensive persons but more often is superimposed on preexisting “benign”
hypertension.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/490)

Q. What are the complications of hypertension?
Ans.
Complications of hypertension:
* Increasing risk of atherosclerosis
Cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure (hypertensive heart disease)
Myocardial infarction (heart attack)
Multi-infarct dementia
Aortic dissection
Renal failure
Cerebral hemorthage (stroke)
Hypertensive retinopathy
Hypertensive encephalopathy.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/490)

Arteriosclerosis & Atherosclerosis

Q. Define and classify arteriosclerosis. (SU-14Ju) (Very Important for VIVA)

Q. Short note: Arteriosclerosis. (DU-07Ja)

Ans.

Arteriosclerosis: Arteriosclerosis (literally means “hardening of the arteries”) is a generic term for arterial

wall thickening and loss of elasticity.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/493)

Or,
Arteriosclerosis is a general term used to include all conditions with thickening and hardening of the arterial

walls.
(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/371)

Classification: There are four general patterns, with different clinical and pathologic consequences.

1. Arteriolosclerosis: Affects small arteries and arterioles, and may cause downstream ischemic injury.
The two anatomic variants are-

*  Hyaline arteriolosclerosis (characterized by hyaline thickening of arteriolar walls)

" Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (characterized by concentric, laminated, “‘onionskin’”’ thickening of
arteriolar walls)

2. Ménckeberg medial calcific sclerosis: Characterized by calcifications of the medial walls of
muscular arteries, typically starting along the internal elastic membrane. Adults older than age 50 are
most commonly affected.

3. Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia: It occurs in muscular arteries larger than arterioles. It is driven
by inflammation (as in a healed arteritis or transplant-associated arteriopathy) or by mechanical injury
(e.g. associated with stents or balloon angioplasty) and can be considered as a healing response.

4. Atherosclerosis: It is the most frequent and clinically important pattern characterized by intimal
lesions called fibrous plaques, or atheromas, occur within the intima of arteries, most frequently the
coronary arteries, cerebral arteries, large vessels of the lower extremities, and the renal and mesenteric arteries.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/493; BRS Pathology/5""/123)

Atherosclerosis is an thickening and hardening of large and medium-sized muscular arteries, primarily due
to involvement of tunica intima and is characterised by fibrofatty plaques or atheromas.

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/373)
Atheroma / atherosclerotic plaque: A fully developed atherosclerotic lesion is called atheromatous
plaque, also called fibrous plaque, fibrofatty plaque or atheroma.

a

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/378)

Common sites of formation of atheroma / atherosclerotic plaque: The blood vessels which are most
extensively involved by atherosclerosis (in descending order) are:

Lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries
Coronary arteries

Popliteal arteries

Internal carotid arteries

Vessels of the circle of Willis.

Ww o

(Ref: Robbins/10"/501; BRS Pathology/5"/123)

Morphology of an atherosclerotic plaque: The key processes in atherosclerosis are intimal thickening and
lipid accumulation, which together form plaques.

A) Macroscopic:
= Colour: Yellow-tan and are raised above the surrounding vessel wall; any superimposed thrombus

over ulcerated plaques will be red-brown.
= Size: Plaques vary in size but can coalesce to form larger masses.

» Shape: Atherosclerotic lesions are patchy and rarely circumferential, usually involving only a
portion of any given arterial wall; on cross-section, the lesions therefore appear eccentric.

= Cut section: The plaques have a central (necrotic) core covered by a subendothelial fibrous cap:
1. Superficial fibrous cap: Composed of smooth muscle cells and relatively dense collagen.

2. Necrotic core: Deep to the fibrous cap is a necrotic core containing lipid (primarily cholesterol
and cholesterol esters), debris from dead cells, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages and lipid-laden
SMCs), fibrin, thrombus in varying degrees of organization, and other plasma proteins.

= Periphery of the lesions: Neovascularization (proliferating small blood vessels) present.

B) Microscopic: Atherosclerotic plaques have four principal components:
1. Cells including variable numbers of SMCs, macrophages, and T lymphocytes
2. Extracellular matrix (ECM) including collagen, elastic fibers, and proteoglycans
3. Intracellular and extracellular lipids (mostly cholesterol & cholesterol ester)
4. Calcifications (in later stage plaques).

Most atheromas contain abundant lipid, but some plaques (“fibrous plaques”) are composed almost
exclusively of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and fibrous tissue, which can be heavily calcified.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/499-502; BRS Pathology/5°/123; Harsh Mohan/7°/378)

Complications of atheromatous plaque:
1. Mechanical obstruction of blood flow.

2. Rupture of atherosclerotic plaques leading to catastrophic obstructive vascular thrombosis.
3. Atherosclerotic plaques can increase the diffusion distance from the lumen to the media, leading to
ischemic injury and weakening of the vessel wall that can result in aneurysm formation.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/494)

Q. Mention the types of atherosclerotic plaque.

Types of atherosclerotic plaque:

Q. What is the difference between arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis? (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Difference between arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis: Arteriosclerosis (literally means “hardening of
the arteries”) is a generic term for arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity. On the other hand,
atherosclerosis is the most frequent and clinically important variety of arteriosclerosis which is characterized
by formation of intimal lesions called atheromas (also called atheromatous or atherosclerotic plaques)
that protrude into and obstruct vascular lumen and weaken the underlying tunica media.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/493)

Q. What is foam cell? (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Foam cell: Foam cells are lipid-laden macrophages and lipid-laden smooth muscle cells.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/501; BRS Pathology/5"/123)

Q. What is ‘fatty streak’? Mention its significance.
Ans.

---

#### 📄 Page 31

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 31

a ea =
Fatty streaks: Fatty streaks are lesions composed primarily of lipid-filled foamy macrophages. Beginning as
small flat yellow macules, these can eventually coalesce into elongated streaks 1 cm long or longer.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/499)

Or,
Fatty streaks are lesions lying under the endothelium and are composed of closely-packed foam cells, lipid-
containing elongated smooth muscle cells and a few lymphoid cells. Small amount of extracellular lipid,
collagen and proteoglycans are also present.

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/377)

They are especially prominent in the aorta and other major arteries, more often on the posterior wall than
the anterior wall.

Significance:
= The lesions are not particularly raised and do not cause any significant flow disturbance.
* Fatty streaks on the intima by themselves are harmless but may be the precursor lesions of
atheromatous plaques.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/499; BRS Pathology/5"/124; Harsh Mohan/7"/378)

BSFMMU’S-23Nv, SMU-23M,22Nv/M,21Nv,19/18/17M,15Ju,12/11Ja, BUP-22M, RU-20/19Nv,

Q. Mention four important risk factors of atherosclerosis. (DU-07Ju)

Q. Mention four preventable risk factors for atherosclerosis. (SU-12Ju)
Ans.

Risk factors for atherosclerosis: (Very Importanf€ for VIVA)

Major risk factors:
Non-modifiable (constitutional):
1. Genetic abnormalities
2. Family history
3. Increasing age
4. Male gender

Modifiable (potentially controllable):
1. Hyperlipidaemia (more specifically hypercholesterolemia)
2. Hypertension
3. Cigarette smoking
4. Diabetes

Additional risk factors:
Inflammation & evevated C-reactive protein (CRP)
Hyperhomocystinemia
Metabolic syndrome
Lipoprotein a [Lp(a)]
Factors affecting hemostasis (Prothrombotic factors and elevated fibrinogen levels)
Other factors
= Obesity
* Lack of exercise / physical inactivity
= High carbohydrate intake

Description of some of the important risk factors:

4.

Genetics: Family history is the most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis.
Certain. Mendelian disorders are strongly associated with atherosclerosis (e.g. familial
hypercholesterolemia), but these account for only a small percentage of cases.

Age: Atherosclerosis is an age-related disease. Its incidence increases with age. Fully-developed
atheromatous plaques usually become clinically manifested in middle age or later (40 - 60 years).

Gender: Atherosclerosis is more common in men in all age groups, although the incidence
increases in postmenopausal women.

Hyperlipidemia:

= Hyperlipidemia and more specifically hypercholesterolemia-is a major risk factor for
atherosclerosis; even in the absence of other risk factors, hypercholesterolemia is sufficient to
initiate lesion development.

* Atherosclerosis is directly proportional to increase LDL, also known as “bad cholesterol”
and decrease HDL, also known as “good cholesterol”.

Hypertension: It is a major risk factor, and is associated with, premature atherosclerosis. It
increases the risk of IHD by approximately 60%.

Diabetes mellitus:

* It induces hypercholesterolemia and markedly increases the risk of atherosclerosis.

* Atherosclerotic peripheral vascular occlusive disease, often leading to gangrene of the
lower extremities, is common in diabetic patients.

* The incidence of myocardial infarction (MI) is twice as high in diabetics as in non-diabetics.

Metabolic syndrome: It is characterized by insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia
(elevated LDL and depressed HDL), hypercoagulability, and a proinflammatory state.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/494; Harsh Mohan/7"/373)

Q. Give the etio-pathogenesis of atherosclerosis. (CU-14Ju) (Very Important for VIVA)

21Nv,19M,14/12/11Ju, SU-12Ju,06M)

22M, CU-16Ju/Ja, 1 3Ju,12Ja)

Q. How atheroma is formed? (CU-18Nv)

Ans.

Pathogenesis of atherosclerosis: Atherosclerosis progresses in the following sequence:
1.

Endothelial injury and dysfunction, causing (among other things) increased vascular permeability,
leukocyte adhesion, and thrombosis

Accumulation of lipoproteins (mainly LDL and its oxidized forms) in the vessel wall

Monocyte adhesion to the endothelium, followed by migration into the intima and transformation
into macrophages and foam cells

Platelet adhesion

Factor release from activated platelets, macrophages, and vascular wall cells, including smooth
muscle cell recruitment, either from the media or from circulating precursors

Smooth muscle cell proliferation, extracellular matrix production, and recruitment of T-cells
Lipid accumulation both extracellularly and within cells (macrophages and smooth muscle cells)
Calcification of ECM and necrotic debris late in the pathogenesis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/497)

Role of lipids in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis: Hyperlipidemia may initiate endothelial injury,
promote foam cell formation, act as a chemotactic factor for monocytes, inhibit macrophage motility, or injure
smooth muscle cells.

The mechanisms by which hyperlipidemia contributes to atherogenesis include the following:

A. Impaired endothelial cell (EC) function: Chronic hyperlipidemia (particularly hypercholesterolemia) can
directly impair endothelial cell function by increasing local reactive oxygen species production; besides
causing membrane and mitochondrial damage, oxygen free radicals accelerate NO decay, dampening its
vasodilator activity.

B. Modified LDL:

With chronic hyperlipidemia, lipoproteins accumulate within the intima, where they may aggregate
or become oxidized by free radicals produced by inflammatory cells.
These modified lipoproteins (oxidized LDLs) are ingested by macrophages and smooth muscle
cells but cannot be completely degraded; chronic ingestion leads to the formation of lipid-laden
macrophages called foam cells. The early lesions containing lipid-filled macrophages are called fatty
streaks.
Modified lipoproteins (oxidized LDLs) are toxic to endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and
macrophages, and can induce endothelial cell dysfunction.
Modified lipoproteins (oxidized LDLs) also stimulate the release of growth factors, cytokines, and
chemokines that create a vicious inflammatory cycle of monocyte recruitment and activation.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/498; BRS Pathology/5"/125)

Q. Mention the complications of atherosclerosis. (DU-17M,06S,05Ja, RU-03Ja)
Q. Discuss briefly the complications of atherosclerosis. (DU-07Ju)

Q. Mention the effects of atherosclerosis. (Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.
Effects / complications of atherosclerosis: Atherosclerotic plaques are susceptible to following clinically
important changes-
1. Rupture, ulceration, or erosion of the surface of atheromatous plaques exposes highly thrombogenic
substances and leads to thrombosis, which can partially or completely occlude the vessel lumen.
2. Ischemia: Thrombosis can partially or completely occlude the vessel lumen resulting in acute tissue
infarction (e.g. myocardial or cerebral infarction).
Hemorrhage into a plaque.
Atheroembolism: Plaque rupture can discharge atherosclerotic debris into the bloodstream, producing
microemboli.
5. Aneurysm formation: Atherosclerosis-induced pressure or ischemic atrophy of the underlying media,
with loss of elastic tissue, causes weakness and potential rupture.
Calcification: Atheromas often undergo calcification.
Infarction: Ischemia induced infarction results in various organs due to atherosclerotic plaque-
* Heart: Myocardial infarction (Heart attack).
* Brain: Cerebral infarction (stroke).
* Aorta: Aortic aneurysms.
® Small intestine: Ischaemic bowel disease, infarction.
* Peripheral vessels: Peripheral vascular disease (gangrene of the legs).
8. Complication due to atherosclerotic stenosis (Gradual occlusion of vessel lumen):

* Mesenteric occlusion & bowel ischemia
* Sudden cardiac death
* Chronic ischemic heart disease (IHD)

Q. What is spider telangiectasia? Where it commonly seen? (For VIVA)

Ans.

Spider telangiectasia: Spider telangiectasias are non-neoplastic vascular malformations grossly resembling
a spider. These manifest as radial, often pulsatile lesions composed of dilated subcutaneous arteries or

arterioles (resembling spider legs) about a central core (resembling a spider’s body) that blanch with
pressure.

Location: These commonly occur on the face, neck, or upper chest and are most frequently associated with
hyperestrogenic states (e.g. in pregnant women or patients with cirrhosis).
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/519)

Aneurysms and Dissections
(Important for VIVA)

* Aneurysm: An aneurysm is a localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or the heart that may be
congenital or acquired. When it involves the aorta, it is called aortic aneurysm.

True aneurysm: When an aneurysm involves all the layers of an intact (but attenuated) arterial wall or the
thinned ventricular wall of the heart, it is called a true aneurysm.

Atherosclerotic and congenital vascular aneurysms and ventricular aneurysms that follow transmural
myocardial infarctions are of this type.

False_aneurysm: A false aneurysm (also called a pseudoaneurysm) is a defect in the vascular wall
leading to an extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space (‘‘pulsating hematoma’’).

Examples include a ventricular rupture after myocardial infarction that is contained by a pericardial
adhesion or a leak at the sutured junction of a vascular graft with a natural artery.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/504)

Classification of aneurysm: Aneurysms are classified by macroscopic shape and size-

1. Saccular aneurysms are essentially spherical outpouchings (involving only a portion of the vessel wall).
2. Fusiform aneurysms involve diffuse, circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/505)

(Ref: Robbins/10"/506)

Arterial dissection: An arterial dissection arises when blood enters a defect in the arterial wall and tunnels

through medial or medial-adventitial planes. Dissections are often, but not always, aneurismal.

Both true and false aneurysms as well as dissections can rupture, often with catastrophic consequences.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/505)

Aortic dissection: Aortic dissection occurs when blood separates the laminar planes of the media to form
a blood-filled channel within the aortic wall.

Aortic dissection is generally associated with aortic dilation; it can be disastrous if the dissection then
ruptures through the adventitia and hemorrhages into adjacent spaces.

Aortic dissection occurs principally in two groups of patients:

(1) Men aged 40 to 60 years, with antecedent hypertension (more than 90% of cases)

(2) Younger patients with syndromic diseases affecting the aorta (e.g. Marfan syndrome).

Hypertension is the major risk factor for aortic dissection.

Clinical features: The classic clinical symptoms of aortic dissection are the sudden onset of excruciating
pain, usually beginning in the anterior chest, radiating to the back between the scapulae, and moving
downward as the dissection progresses; the pain can be confused with that of myocardial infarction.

The most common cause of death is rupture of the dissection and bleeding into the pericardial, pleural, or
peritoneal cavities.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/507)

Vasculitis
(Important for VIVA)

Vasculitis: Vasculitis is a general term for vessel wall inflammation with protean manifestations depending
on the vascular bed affected (e.g. central nervous system vs. heart vs. small bowel).

Clinical_manifestations: Clinical manifestations typically include constitutional signs and symptoms
associated with systemic inflammation, such as fever, myalgias, arthralgias, and malaise.

Affected vessels: Vessels of any type (large, medium & small) in virtually any organ can be affected; most

vasculitides affect small vessels ranging from arterioles to capillaries to venules.

Pathogenesis: The two pathogenic mechanisms of vasculitis are-

1. Infectious vasculitis: Direct invasion of vascular walls by infectious pathogens.
2. Non-infectious vasculitis (immune-mediated inflammation): The main immunologic mechanisms
underlying noninfectious vasculitis are-
= Immune complex deposition
* Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs)
=  Anti-EC antibodies

#### 📄 Page 42

42 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Some Important Topics for VIVA

Giant cell (temporal) arteritis: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis is a chronic, classically granulomatous
inflammation of large- to small-sized arteries.

Temporal arteritis is the most common form of vasculitis among elderly adults. It is rare before age 50.

It principally affects arteries in the head. Vertebral and ophthalmic arteries, as well as the aorta (giant cell
aortifis), also can be involved. Ophthalmic artery involvement can lead to sudden and permanent blindness,
(Ref: Robbins/10"/511)

Takavasu_arteritis: Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium and larger arteries
characterized principally by ocular disturbances and marked weakening of the pulses in the upper extremities
(hence the name pulseless disease).

Takayasu artentis classically involves the aortic arch. In a third of patients, it also affects the remainder of
the aorta and its branches, with pulmonary artery involvement in half of cases; coronary and renal arteries
may be similarly affected.

Takayasu aortitis shares many attributes with giant cell aortitis, including clinical features and histology;
indeed, the distinction is typically made based on the age of the patient. Those over 50 years of age are
designated as giant cell aortitis, while those under 50 are designated as Takayasu aortitis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/512)

Fig: Takayasu arteritis.
{Aortic arch angiogram showing narrowing of brachiocephalic, carotid, and subclavian arteries (arrows)}

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): PAN is a systemic vasculitis of small- or medium-sized muscular arteries
that typically affects renal and visceral vessels but spares the pulmonary circulation.

Vessels of the kidneys, heart, liver, and gastrointestinal tract are involved in descending order of frequency.

The cause remains unknown in the majority of cases. PAN is primarily a disease of young adults but can
occur in all age groups.

Clinical manifestations result from ischemia and infarction of affected tissues and organs. Typical
presentation involves some combination of rapidly accelerating hypertension due to renal artery
involvement; abdominal pain and bloody stools caused by vascular gastrointestinal lesions; diffuse
myalgias; and peripheral neuritis, predominantly affecting motor nerves. Renal involvement is often a major
cause of mortality. Untreated, PAN is typically fatal; however, immunosuppression can yield remissions or

cure in 90% of cases.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/513)

Kawasaki disease: It is an acute, febrile, usually self-limited illness of infancy and childhood associated
with large- to medium-sized vessel arteritis (80% of the patients are younger than 4 years of age).
In genctically susceptible persons, a variety of infectious agents (mostly viral) have been posited to trigger the disease.

Its clinical significance stems from the involvement of coronary arteries. Coronary arteritis can result in
aneurysms that rupture or thrombose, causing myocardial infarction.
(Ref: Robbins/10°/513)

---

#### 📄 Page 43

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 43
Granulomatosis_ with polyangiitis (Previously called Wegener granulomatosis): It is a necrotizing

vasculitis characterized by the triad of-
* Acute necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract (ear, nose, sinuses, throat) or the lower
respiratory tract (lung) or both.

* Necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels (e.g. capillaries,
venules, arterioles, and arteries), most prominent in the lungs and upper airways but affecting other
sites as well.

* Focal necrotizing, often crescentic, glomerulonephritis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/514)

Churg-strauss syndrome: Churg-Strauss syndrome (also called allergic granulomatosis and angiitis) is a
small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis classically associated with asthma, allergic rhinitis, lung infiltrates,
peripheral eosinophilia, extravascular necrotizing granulomas, and a striking eosinophilic infiltration of vessels
and tissues.

Cutaneous involvement (with palpable purpura), gastrointestinal bleeding, and renal disease (primarily as
focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis) are the major associations. Cytotoxicity produced by the myocardial
eosinophilic infiltrates often leads to cardiomyopathy; cardiac involvement is seen in 60% of patients and is a
major cause of morbidity and death.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/515)

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease): Thromboangiitis obliterans is characterized by segmental,

thrombosing, acute and chronic inflammation of medium and small-sized arteries, especially the tibial and
radial arteries, that often leads to vascular insufficiency, typically of the extremities.

It occurs almost exclusively in heavy cigarette smokers, usually before the age of 35.

Clinical features:
= Raynaud phenomenon
Instep foot pain induced by exercise (instep claudication)
Superficial nodular phlebitis (venous inflammation)
Severe pain—even at rest (due to the neural involvement)
Chronic extremity ulcerations, progressing over time to frank gangrene.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/515)

Raynaud Phenomenon

Raynaud phenomenon: Raynaud phenomenon results from exaggerated vasoconstriction of arteries and
arterioles in responses to cold or emotion. It most commonly affects the extremities, particularly the fingers
and toes, but also occasionally the nose, earlobes, or lips.

The involved digits classically show “red, white, and blue” color changes from most proximal to most distal,
correlating with proximal vasodilation, central vasoconstriction, and more distal cyanosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/516)

Fig: Raynaud phenomenon.

Types: Raynaud phenomenon can be a primary entity or secondary to other disorders.

---

#### 📄 Page 44

44 | arif's representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

1. Primary Raynaud phenomenon (previously called Raynaud disease): Caused in response to cold or
emotional stresses.

2. Secondary Raynaud phenomenon: Caused by other diseases like SLE, scleroderma, Buerger disease,
or even atherosclerosis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/516)

Varicose Veins
(Important for VIVA)

Varicose veins: Varicose veins are abnormally dilated, tortuous veins produced by prolonged, increased
intraluminal pressure with vessel dilation and incompetence of the venous valves.

The superficial veins of the upper and lower leg are commonly involved because venous pressures in these
sites can be markedly elevated (up to 10 times normal) by prolonged dependent posture. Varicosities in two
other sites also deserve special mention: esophageal varices & hemorrhoids.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/517)

|

Fig: Varicose veins of the leg (arrow).

Congenital Heart Disease

Q. Short note: Congenital heart disease (CHD).
Ans.

Congenital heart disease: Congenital heart disease (CHD) refers to abnormalities of the heart or great vessels
that are present at birth.

Most CHD anises from faulty embryogenesis during gestational weeks 3 to 8, when major cardiovascular
structures form and begin to function.

Incidence: 5% of live births.

Clinical features: Most of the various structural anomalies in CHD can be organized into three major
categories according to the major functional abnormalities they cause:

= Left-to-right shunt

® Right-to-left shunt

* Obstruction

{N.B: A shunt is an abnormal communication between chambers or blood vessels. Abnormal channels permit
blood flow down pressure gradients from the left (systemic) side to the right (pulmonary) side of the
circulation or vice versa. }

1. Right to left shunt (cyanotic congenital heart disease): (Very Important for VIVA)

Clinical features:

=" Hypoxemia and cyanosis (a dusky blueness of the skin and mucous membranes)
Paradoxical embolism

Clubbing of the tips of the fingers and toes (hypertrophic osteoarthropathy)
Polycythemia

Clubbing of the tips of the fingers and toes

Examples:

* Tetralogy of Fallot

Transposition of the great arteries

Persistent truncus arteriosus

Tricuspid atresia

Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection

2. Left-to-right shunts (acyanotic congenital heart disease): (Very Important for VIVA)
Clinical features:

* Not initially associated with cyanosis, but may be cyanotic (late cyanotic congenital heart discase, or
Eisenmenger syndrome).

= Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

or blood vessels.

Examples:

Q. Short note: Fallot’s tetralogy / the tetralogy of Fallot. (RU-17Nv, CU-13Ju)
Ans.
Fallot’s tetralogy: The four cardinal features of the tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) are- (V.V./ for VIVA)

1) Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

2) Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonary stenosis)
3) An aorta that overrides the VSD

4) Right ventricular hypertrophy.

The first three features result embryologically from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum,
and the right ventricular hypertrophy is a secondary consequence of the pressure overload.

Clinical features:
1, Even untreated, TOF can be tolerated into adulthood
2. As the child grows, the heart increases in size.
3. Most infants with TOF are cyanotic from birth or soon thereafter (classic TOF); some may not show
cyanosis (so-called “pink tetralogy”).

Morphology: The heart is typically enlarged and is classically “boot-shaped” due to marked right ventricular
hypertrophy.

Treatment: Complete surgical repair is possible for classic TOF but is more complicated for persons with
pulmonary atresia and dilated bronchial arteries.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/538)

Heart Failure

Q. What is heart failure?
Ans.
Heart failure: Heart failure is defined as the condition in which a heart cannot pump blood to adequately meet
the metabolic demands of peripheral tissues, or can do so only at elevated filling pressures.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/530)

2. Liver and portal system:

« The liver is usually increased in size and weight (congestive hepatomegaly) due to prominent
passive congestion.

" Congestion is most prominent around central veins which is reflected as congested red-brown
pericentral zones, with relatively normal-colored tan periportal regions, producing the
characteristic “nutmeg liver” appearance

* With long-standing severe cases, the central areas can become fibrotic, eventually culminating in

= Portal venous hypertension also causes enlargement of the spleen with platelet sequestration
(congestive splenomegaly), and can also contribute to chronic congestion and edema of the bowel
wall.

3. Pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal spaces: Systemic venous congestion can lead to fluid
accumulation (effusions) in the pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal spaces (a peritoneal effusion is also

called ascites).

4. Subcutaneous tissues:
= Edema of the peripheral and dependent portions of the body, especially foot/ankle (pedal) and

pretibial edema, is a hallmark of right-sided heart failure.
* In chronically bedridden patients, presacral edema may predominate.

= Generalized massive edema (anasarca) can also occur.

Q. Classify various types of ischaemic heart disease. (CMU-23Nv, SU-20M, CU-19M)
Q. Mention the conditions of IHD. (SU-06Ja,0SM/Ja)
Ans.
Ischemic heart disease (IHD): It represents a group of related entities resulting from myocardial ischemia—
an imbalance between myocardial supply (perfusion) and cardiac demand for oxygenated blood.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/542)

Types_/ syndromes of IHD: IHD can declare itself through one or more of the following clinical
presentations:
1. Angina pectoris (literally “chest pain”) - in which ischemia is not severe enough to cause infarction
® Stable (typical) angina (pain precipitated by exertion)
* Unstable or crescendo angina (prolonged or recurrent pain at rest)
= Prinzmetal angina (intermittent chest pain at rest caused by vasospasm)
2. Myocardial infarction (MI) - in which ischemia causes frank cardiac necrosis
Chronic IHD with heart failure
4. Sudden cardiac death (SCD).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/542,543; BRS Pathology/5'"/137)

Q. Why IHD is often called coronary artery disease? (Important for VIVA)
Ans.

---

#### 📄 Page 53

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 53

IHD is often called coronary artery disease: In more than 90% of cases, myocardial ischemia results from
reduced blood flow due to obstructive atherosclerotic lesions in the epicardial coronary arteries;
consequently, [HD is frequently referred to as coronary artery disease (CAD).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/542)

(**N.B: In most cases there is a long period (up to decades) of silent, slow progression of coronary lesions
before the sudden onset of symptoms. Thus, LHD is often the late manifestation of coronary atherosclerosis
that began during childhood or adolescence.)

(Ref: Robbins/¥"/538)

Nice to Know:

Atherosclerotic lesions in coronary arteries are distributed in one or more of the three major coronary
arterial trunks, the highest incidence being in the anterior descending branch of the left coronary
(LAD), followed in decreasing frequency, by the right coronary artery (RCA) and still less in
circumflex branch of the left coronary (CXA). About one-third of.cases have single-vessel disease, most

often left anterior descending arterial involvement; another one-third have two-vessel disease, and the
remainder has three major vessel disease.

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/407)

Q. Discuss the pathogenesis of IHD. (RU-17Nv)

Ans,
Pathogenesis of IHD: The dominant cause of the [HD is partial or complete interruption of arterial blood
flow to the myocardium resulting insufficient coronary perfusion relative to myocardial demand.

It is convenient to consider the etiology of IHD under three broad headings:

i) Coronary atherosclerosis: Chronic, progressive atherosclerotic narrowing of the epicardial coronary
arteries.

ii) Variable degrees of superimposed acute plaque change: Rupture, superficial erosion, ulceration,
fissuring, or deep haemorrhage etc.

iii) Non-atherosclerotic causes:
Vasospasm
Stenosis of coronary ostia
Coronary arteries
Thrombotic diseases (e.g. polycythaemia vera, sickle cell anaemia)
Embolism
Trauma to coronary arteries
Aneurysms
Compression of a coronary from outside.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/542; BRS Pathology/5"/137; Harsh Mohan/7"/408)

Q. Mention the consequences of myocardial ischemia. (For VIVA)

Ans.
Consequences of myocardial ischemia (IHD): Depending upon the suddenness of onset, duration, degree,
location and extent of the area affected by myocardial ischaemia, the consequences may be:

Stable angina

Unstable angina
Myocardial infarction (MI)
Sudden cardiac death.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/543; Harsh Mohan/7"/408)

Q. What is acute coronary syndrome? (Important for VIVA)
Ans

Acute coronary syndrome: The triad of unstable angina, acute myocardial infarction (MI), and sudden
cardiac death are sometimes referred to as acute coronary syndrome.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/543; Harsh Mohan/7"/408)

Angina Pectoris
(Important for VIVA)

Q. Define angina pectoris. What are the types of it?
Q. Short note: Angina pectoris. (DU-21Oct/M, RU-19M, CU-18Nv)
Ans.
Angina pectoris: Angina pectoris (literally “chest pain”) is characterized by paroxysmal and usually
recurrent attacks of substernal or precordial chest discomfort caused by transient (15 seconds to 15
minutes) myocardial ischemia that is insufficient to induce myocyte necrosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/543)
Or,

Angina pectoris is the episodic chest pain caused by inadequate oxygenation of the myocardium.

(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/137)

---

#### 📄 Page 55

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY [ss

Types of angina:

1. Stable (typical) angina: It is the most common form of angina. It is classically described as a
crushing or squeezing substernal sensation that can radiate down the left arm or to the left jaw
(referred pain). The pain is precipitated by exertion (i.c. physical activity, emotional excitement or
psychological stress) and is relieved by rest (decreasing demand) or administering vasodilators,
such as nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers (thereby increasing perfusion).

It is caused by an imbalance in coronary perfusion (due to chronic stenosing coronary
atherosclerosis) relative to myocardial demand.

2. Unstable or crescendo angina: It is a pattern of increasingly frequent, prolonged (>20 min), or
severe angina, precipitated by progressively lower levels of physical activity or even occurring at
rest.

It is generally caused by disruption of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed thrombosis. It can
also be caused by distal embolization of the thrombus, and/or vasospasm.

Unstable angina serves as a warning for MI, that’s why it is referred to as ‘pre-infarction angina’ or
‘acute coronary insufficiency’.

3. Prinzmetal variant angina: It is an uncommon form of episodic myocardial ischemia caused by
coronary artery spasm.

(Ref: Robbins/10""/543; BRS Pathology/5"/137; Harsh Mohan/7"/409)

(N.B: Myocardial infarction differs from unstable angina, since there is evidence of myocardial necrosis.)
(Ref: Davidson’s/23"/493)

(N.B: In angina, there is no elevation of enzymes in the blood as there is no irreversible myocardial injury.)
(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/409)

Myocardial Infarction (MI)

Q. What is myocardial infarction (MI)? What are the types of MI?
Ans.

Myocardial infarction (MI): MI, also commonly referred to as “heart attack,” is the death of cardiac
muscle due to prolonged ischemia.

It is the most important and feared consequence of coronary artery disease.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/543; Harsh Mohan/7"/409)

Patterns of MI: There are two distinct patterns of myocardial ischemic necrosis:

1. Transmural (ful thickness) infarction: Ischemic necrosis involves the full or nearly full thickness
of the ventricular wall (from the endocardium to the epicardium) in the distribution of the affected
coronary artery.

2. Subendocardial (non-transmural) infarction: Ischemic necrosis involves the inner third of the
ventricular wall. It occurs as a result of a plaque disruption followed by a coronary thrombus that
becomes lysed (therapeutically or spontaneously) before myocardial necrosis extends across the full
thickness of the wall.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/546; BRS Pathology/5"/138; Harsh Mohan/7"/410)

Multifocal microinfarction is another pattern of myocardial ischemic necrosis which is seen when there is
pathology involving only smaller intramural vessels.
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/547)

Q. Discuss in brief the epidemiology of MI. (RU-08Ju)
Ans.
Incidence and risk factors / epidemiology of MI:
« Myocardial infarction is the most important cause of morbidity from IHD and is one of the leading
causes of death in the Western world.
* Roughly 1.5 million individuals in the United States suffer an MI each year.
* It can occur at virtually any age, but the frequency rises progressively with increasing age. Nearly 10%
occur in people under age 40, and 45% occur in people under age 65.
« Blacks & whites are equally affected.
= Men are at significantly greater risk of MI than women.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/543; BRS Pathology/5"/137)

Q. Discuss in brief about the pathogenesis of MI (myocardial infarction). (DU-21Ja,20NvM,
19Nv, CMU-22Nv, RMU-21M,08Ju, SU-15Ja)
Ans.
Pathogenesis of MI:
A) Coronary arterial occlusion:
a) Thrombotic occlusion of coronary artery: The following sequence of events likely underlies most MIs-
* An atheromatous plaque is eroded or suddenly disrupted by endothelial injury, intraplaque
hemorthage, or mechanical forces, exposing subendothelial collagen and necrotic plaque
contents to the blood.
* Platelets adhere, aggregate, and are activated, releasing thromboxane Az, adenosine
diphosphate (ADP), and serotonin—causing further platelet aggregation and vasospasm.
« Activation of coagulation by tissue factor and other mechanisms adds to the growing
thrombus.

---

#### 📄 Page 57

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 57

* Within minutes, the thrombus can evolve to completely occlude the coronary artery lumen.

b) Non-thrombotic occlusion of coronary artery: The mechanisms include-
1. Vasospasm with or without coronary atherosclerosis, perhaps in association with platelet
aggregation or due to drug ingestion (e.g. cocaine or ephedrine).

2. Emboli from the left atrium in association with atrial fibrillation, a left-sided mural thrombus,
vegetations of infective endocarditis, intracardiac prosthetic material; or paradoxical emboli
from the right side of the heart or the peripheral veins, traversing a patent foramen ovale and
into the coronary arteries.

3. Uncommon causes of MI without atherothrombosis include disorders of small intramural
coronary vessels (e.g. vasculitis), hematologic abnormalities (e.g. sickle cell disease), amyloid
deposition in vascular walls, vascular dissection, marked hypertrophy (e.g. due to aortic
stenosis), lowered systemic blood pressure (e.g. shock), or inadequate myocardial “protection”
during cardiac surgery.

B) Myocardial response: Coronary arterial obstruction diminishes blood flow to a region of
myocardium, causing ischemia, rapid myocardial dysfunction, and eventually—with prolonged
vascular compromise—myocyte death. The anatomic region supplied by that artery is referred to as
the area at risk. The outcome depends predominantly on the severity and duration of flow

deprivation.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/544)

(N.B: Myocardial ischemia leads to loss of function within 1 to 2 minutes but causes necrosis only after 20 to

30 minutes.)

(Ref: Robbins/10'/553)

Q. What types of necrosis occurs in myocardial infarction? (Very Important for VIVA)

Q. Mention the clinical features of myocardial infarction (MI). (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Clinical features of myocardial infarction (MI):

* Prolonged (more than 30 minutes) central chest pain described as crushing, stabbing, or Squeezing
Anxiety and fear of impending death
Nausea and vomiting
Hypotension
Rapid, weak pulse
Profuse sweating (diaphoresis)
Breathlessness
Collapse/syncope
Painless or ‘silent’? MI (asymptomatic): Older patients or those with diabetes mellitus.

Nice to Know:
Painless or ‘silent’? MI: In as many as 25% of patients the onset of MI is entirely asymptomatic (e.g. in

the setting of diabetic neuropathy), and the disease is discovered only by electrocardiographic changes
or laboratory tests that show evidence of myocardial damage.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/550)

Q. Mention the biochemical changes in MI. (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Biochemical changes in MI:
1. Cessation of aerobic glycolysis within seconds (due to myocardial ischemia).
2. Inadequate production of high-energy phosphate (e.g. Creatine phosphate and ATP) due to onset of
anerobic glycolysis.
3. Accumulation of potentially noxious breakdown metabolites (such as lactic acid).
4. Induction of enzymatic change, such as-
=" CK-MB — Rises within 4-6 hours after MI
* AST — Rises in 12 hours after MI
=» LDH — Rises in 12 hours after MI
5. Release of myoglobin, troponin-I and troponin-T by the injured cardiac myocytes.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/550; Davidson’s/22"/590)

Q. Mention the treatment of myocardial infarction (MI).
Q. Mention the therapeutic interventions of MI with their rationale.
Ans

Therapeutic interventions / treatment of MI:

Urgent hospitalization, preferably in dedicated cardiac unit (CCU)
Oxygen supplementation to improve blood oxygen saturation
Morphine (to relieve pain and improve dyspneic symptoms)
Nitrates (to induce vasodilation and reverse vasospasm)
Antiplatelet agents (such as aspirin, ADP receptor inhibitors, and GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors)
Anticoagulant therapy with unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, direct thrombin
inhibitors, and/or factor Xa inhibitors to prevent coronary artery thrombus propagation
Beta blockers (to decrease myocardial oxygen demand and to reduce risk of arrhythmias, unless
contraindicated such as in heart failure)
Prompt reperfusion to salvage myocardium, by either fibrinolytic medications or transcatheter
interventions
Improve myocardial oxygen supply versus demand by management of other factors, such as
anxiety, ischemic pain, abnormal hemodynamics, anemia, and respiratory disorders
Early arrhythmia monitoring and management.

(Ref: Robbins/10""/550; Davidson’s/23"/498)

Q. What are the complications of acute myocardial infarction (MI)? (DU-12Ja,09Ju, RU-
1 7Nv/Ja, 16/1 5Ja,10/09/08/07Ju)

Q. What are the consequences and complications of myocardial infarction? (DU-22Nv, |3Ja)

Q. Enumerate the complications of myocardial infarction (MI). (DU-19Nv, BUP-22Nv, RMU-
22/21/19/18Nv, SU-20M)

Q. Short note: Complications of MI. (DU-14Ja) (Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Complications of MI: Nearly three-fourths of patients experience one or more of the following complications
after an acute MI:

1. Contractile dysfunction:
= Left ventricular failure with hypotension
* Pulmonary edema
= Respiratory impairment
= Severe “pump failure” (cardiogenic shock)

2. Papillary muscle dysfunction leading to postinfarct mitral regurgitation.
3. Right ventricular infarction leading to right-sided heart failure.
Myocardial rupture: Rupture complicates only 1% to 5% of MIs, but is frequently fatal when it

occurs. It occurs most commonly within 3 to 7 days after infarction.

= Left ventricular free wall rupture (most common) - usually resulting in rapidly fatal
hemopericardium and cardiac tamponade.

= Ventricular septal rupture - creates a VSD with left-to-right shunting.

= Papillary muscle rupture - leads to severe mitral regurgitation.

5. Arrhythmias: It is the most common cause of sudden death in the first hour following MI. MI-
associated arrhythmias include-

= Heart block of variable degree (including asystole)
Bradycardia

Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias

Ventricular premature contractions or ventricular tachycardia,
Ventricular fibrillation.

6. Pericarditis: Pericarditis typically appears 2 to 3 days after infarction and then gradually resolves over
the next few days. Rarely patients can develop an intense pericarditis weeks after MI (Dressler
syndrome).

7. Chamber dilation: Because of the weakening of necrotic muscle, there may be disproportionate
stretching, thinning, and dilation of the infarcted region (especially with anteroseptal infarcts).

8. Mural thrombosis, potentially leading to left-sided thromboembolism.
9. Ventricular aneurysm

10. Progressive heart failure (chronic IHD).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/551; BRS Pathology/5"/138,139)

(N.B: One-third of patients who are unfortunate enough to suffer a STEMI at home will die, usually of an
arrhythmia within 1 hour of symptom onset and before they can receive medical attention.)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/551)

Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is defined as unexpected death due to cardiac disease with no symptom or
death <1 hr after symptom arise.
(Ref: Pathoma Lecture Notes)

The mechanism of SCD is most often a lethal arrhythmia (e.g. asystole or ventricular fibrillation).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/551)

Causes of sudden cardiac death (SCD): Ventricular arrhythmia due to-
1. Coronary artery disease / severe atherosclerosis (80% to 90% of cases)

2. Non-atherosclerotic causes (younger victims):

Cardiac conduction abnormalities, hereditary or acquired

Dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Congenital coronary arterial abnormalities

Myocarditis

Mitral valve prolapse

Pulmonary hypertension

Other miscellaneous causes, such as pericardial tamponade, pulmonary embolism, systemic
metabolic and hemodynamic alterations, catecholamines, and drugs of abuse, particularly cocaine
and methamphetamine.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/555)

Ans.

Vegetative heart diseases: (Important for VIVA)
1. Rheumatic fever & rheumatic heart disease
2. Infective endocarditis (IE)
3. Non-infected (sterile) vegetations
= Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)
* Endocarditis of systemic lupus erythematosus (Libman-Sacks disease).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/561)

Comparison of the four major forms of vegetative endocarditis:

1. Rheumatic fever phase of rheumatic heart disease is marked by a small, warty vegetations along
the lines of closure of the valve leaflets.

2. Infective endocarditis is characterized by large, irregular masses in the valve cusps that can extend
into the chordae.

3. Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) typically exhibit small, bland vegetations, usually
attached at the line of closure. One or many may be present.

4. Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) has small or medium-sized vegetations on either or both sides of
the valve leaflets.

Rheumatic fever: Rheumatic fever (RF) is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem

Rheumatic fever (RF) is a systemic, post-streptococcal, non-suppurative inflammatory disease, principally
affecting the heart, joints, central nervous system, skin and subcutaneous tissues.

Sia

Or,
Rheumatic fever is a multisystem inflammatory disorder with major cardiac manifestations and sequelae,
most often affecting children between 5 and 15 years of age.

It usually occurs 1 to 4 weeks after an episode of pharyngitis caused by group A B-hemolytic streptococci.
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/139)

Rheumatic heart disease (RHD): Acute rheumatic carditis is a common manifestation of active rheumatic
fever (RF) and may progress over time to chronic rheumatic heart disease (RHD), which is characterized
principally by deforming fibrotic valvular disease, particularly involving the mitral valve.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/560)
Or,
The chronic stage of RF involves all the layers of the heart (pancarditis) causing major cardiac sequelae
referred to as rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/418)

Valves involved in RHD:
= Mitral valve (65%-70% cases)
= Aortic valve (25% cases).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/560)

Q. Write down the diagnostic criteria of rheumatic fever. (BUP-22M)

Q. What are the criteria for diagnosis of rheumatic fever? (DU-18Ja,12Ju, SU-17M)

Q, Enumerate the major criteria of rheumatic fever. (CU-19Ny)

Q. Short note: Jones criteria. (DU-23M, CU-15/13Ja) (Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Diagnosis of rheumatic fever: The diagnosis of rheumatic fever is done by the so-called revised Jones

criteria, based on two or more major manifestations, or one major and two or more minor
manifestations, along with evidence of preceding streptococcal infection.

Major manifestations:
1. Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints
2. Pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis, or endocarditis)
3. Subcutaneous nodules (typically on extensor surfaces of extremities)
4. Erythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash
5. Sydenham chorea, a neurologic disorder with involuntary rapid movements

Minor manifestations: Nonspecific signs and symptoms that include-
Fever

Arthralgia

Raised ESR or C-reactive protein (CRP)

Previous rheumatic fever

Leukocytosis

First-degree AV block {Prolonged P-R interval in ECG}

Supporting evidence of preceding streptococcal infection:

1. Recent scarlet fever
2. Raised anti-streptolysin O (ASO) or other streptococcal antibody titer
3. Positive throat culture.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/562; Davidson’s/23"/515; BRS Pathology/5"/140)

Q. Write down the pathology / morphology of rheumatic heart disease. (CU-03S, SU-03S/Ja)

Ans.

Pathology / morphology of rheumatic heart disease: (4mportant for VIVA)
A) ! Morphology of acute rheumatic heart disease:

During acute rheumatic fever, focal inflammatory lesions are found in various tissues. They are
most distinctive within the heart, where they are called Aschoff nodules or Aschoff bodies.
Aschoff bodies consist of fragmented collagen and fibrinoid material, foci of lymphocytes
(primarily T-cells), occasional plasma cells, plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow
cells (pathognomonic for RF), and occasional multinucleated giant cells called Aschoff cells or
Aschoff giant cells.

Diffuse inflammation and Aschoff bodies may be found in any of the three layers of the heart,
causing percarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis (pancarditis).

Inflammation of the endocardium and the left-sided valves typically results in fibrinoid necrosis
within the cusps or along the tendinous cords. Overlying these necrotic foci are small (1-2 mm)
vegetations (fibrin & platelet — sterile vegetations), called verrucae, along the lines of closure.

Fig: Acute rheumatic heart disease. Small vegetations (verrucae) are visible along
the line of closure of the mitral valve leaflet (arrows).

B) Morphology of chronic rheumatic heart disease:

Macroscopic:

Leaflet thickening
Commissural fusion and shortening
Thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords

Fibrous bridging across the valvular commissures and calcification create “fish mouth” or
“buttonhole” stenosis.
Dilatation of left atrium.

= Right ventricular hypertrophy due to long-standing lung changes.

Microscopic:
= Diffuse fibrosis and ncovascularization in the valvular Icaflets.

= Aschoff bodies are replaced by fibrous scar.

(Ref: Robbins/10"'/561)

Q. Write down the cardiac lesions of rheumatic fever. (CMU-21/20Nv)

Ans.

Cardiac lesions of rheumatic fever: Cardiac lesions of RF are in the form of pancarditis which is the focal
inflammatory involvement of the interstitial tissue of all the three layers of the heart (endocardium,
myocardium and pericardium). The pathognomonic feature of pancarditis in RF is the presence of distinctive
Aschoff nodules or Aschoff bodies.

1. RHEUMATIC ENDOCARDITIS: Endocardial lesions of RF may involve the valvular and mural
endocardium, causing rheumatic valvulitis and mural endocarditis, respectively. Rheumatic valvulitis
is chiefly responsible for the major cardiac manifestations in chronic RHD.

2. RHEUMATIC MYOCARDITIS: The most characteristic feature of rheumatic myocarditis is the
presence of distinctive Aschoff bodies. These diagnostic nodules are scattered throughout the
interstitial tissue of the myocardium and are most frequent in the interventricular septum, left ventricle
and left atrium.

3. RHEUMATIC PERICARDITIS: Inflammatory involvement of the pericardium commonly
accompanies RHD. It may manifest as breathlessness or chest pain.
(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/420-422; Davidson’s/23"/515)

Q. Classify endocarditis. (SU-13Ju) (For VIVA)

Ans.
Endocarditis: Endocarditis is an inflammation of the inner layer (endocardium) of the heart. It usually
involves the heart valves, and is characterized by a prototypic lesion, the vegetation.

Classification of endocarditis: Based on ctiology-

1. Infective endocarditis: Microorganisms is the source of inflammation.

2. Non-infective endocarditis:
* Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) - most commonly found in previously damaged valves.
* Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) - occurs more often in patients with SLE.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/563,564)

Q. Classify infective endocarditis. (DU-19M)

Q. Short note: Infective endocarditis. (CU-04S) (Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Infective endocarditis: Infective endocarditis (IE) is a microbial infection of the heart valves or the mural
endocardium that leads to the formation of vegetations composed of thrombotic debris and organisms, often

associated with destruction of the underlying cardiac tissues.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/563)

Types:
1. Acute infective endocarditis {here the organisms are highly virulent (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus

(50% of cases)}.
2. Sub-acute infective endocarditis {hcre the organisms are of low virulence, e.g. viridans streptococci

(more than 50% of cases)}.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/563; BRS Pathology/5"/141)

Causative agents: Although fungi and other classes of microorganisms can be responsible, most nfections are
bacterial (bacterial endocarditis).

Streptococcus viridans (50-60% cases)
* Staphylococcus aureus (20-30% cases)

Q. What is acute infective endocarditis? (For VIVA)

Ans.

Acute infective endocarditis (ABE): Acute infective endocarditis is typically caused by infection of a
previously normal heart valve by a highly virulent organism (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus) that rapidly
produces destructive lesions.

These infections may be difficult to cure with antibiotics alone, and often require surgery.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/563)

Q. What is sub-acute infective endocarditis? (DU-11Ju) (For VIVA)

Ans.

Sub-acute infective endocarditis (SABE): Subacute infective endocarditis is typically caused by infection of
a previously damaged or otherwise abnormal valve by an organism with lower virulence (c.g. viridans
streptococci) with overall less destruction.

In such cases the disease may pursue a protracted course of weeks to months, and cures can often be achieved
with antibiotics alone.

(Ref: Robbins/10'/563; Harsh Mohan/7"/425)

Q. Mention the distinguishing features of acute and subacute bacterial endocarditis.
Ans.

Distinguishing features of acute and subacute bacterial endocarditis: (For VIVA)

1. Duration <6 weeks > 6 weeks
2. Most common organism | Staph. aureus Streptococcus viridans
3. Virulence of organisms | Highly virulent Less virulent
4. Previous condition of | Usually previously normal Usually previously damaged

Q. Discuss the etiopathogenesis of infective endocarditis. (DU-19M)
Ans.
Etiopathogenesis of infective endocarditis:
A. Etiology:
1. Infective agents:

* Staphylococcus aureus (most common causative organisms in ABE)
Streptococcus viridans (most common causative organisms in SABE)
The so-called HACEK group (Haemophilus, Astinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella)
Streptococcus bovis
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Staphylococcus epidermidis

arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Gram-negative enteric bacilli
* Fungi.

2. Predisposing factors:

b. Bacteraemia, septicacmia and pyaemia: Some of the common examples are-

* Periodontal infections such as trauma from vigorous brushing of teeth, hard chewiny tooth

extraction and other dental procedures.
Infections of the bowel, biliary tract and genitourinary tracts
Surgery of the bowel, biliary tract and genitourinary tracts
Skin infections such as boils, carbuncles and abscesses.
Upper and lower respiratory tract infections including bacterial pneumonias
Intravenous drug abuse

c. Underlying heart disease
* Chronic rheumatic valvular disease (in about 50% cases)
= Congenital heart diseases (e.g. VSD, subaortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, bicuspid aortic
valve, coarctation of the aorta, and PDA)
* Other causes are syphilitic aortic valve disease, atherosclerotic valvular disease, floppy mitral
valve, and prosthetic heart valves.

d. Impaired host defenses

Neutropenia

Immunodeficiency

Malignancy

Therapeutic immunosuppression
Diabetes mellitus

Alcohol or intravenous drug abuse.

B. Pathogenesis: Organisms causing infective endocarditis on entering the blood stream from any of the

above-mentioned routes are implanted on the cardiac valves or mural endocardium because they have
surface adhesion molecules which mediate their adherence to injured endocardium.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/563; Harsh Mohan/7'"/425)

Q. What are the complications of infective endocarditis? (DU-19M)
Ans.
Complications of infective endocarditis: (Very Important for VIVA)
A. Cardiac complications:
* Valvular stenosis or insufficiency
Perforation, rupture, and aneurysm of valve leaflets
Abscesses in the valve ring (ring abscess)
Myocardial abscesses
Suppurative pericarditis
Cardiac failure from one or more of the foregoing complications.

B. Extracardiac complications:
* Systemic emboli may cause infarcts & abscess in the brain, kidneys, spleen & lung.
= Petechiae may be seen in the skin and conjunctiva.

« Osler’s nodes in SABE (painful, tender nodules on the finger tips of hands and feet) & Janeway’s
spots in ABE (painless, non-tender subcutaneous maculopapular lesions on the pulp of the fingers)

* Glomerulonephritis (due to deposition of antigen-antibody complex in the glomerulus).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/564; Harsh Mohan/7"/428)

(N.B: The causes of death are cardiac failure, persistent infection, embolism to vital organs, renal failure and

rupture of mycotic aneurysm of cerebral arteries.)

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/428)

Q. Define cardiomyopathy. Mention its type. (CU-04S)
Ans.

Cardiomyopathies: The term cardiomyopathy (literally, heart muscle disease) is used to describe any
cardiac dysfunction resulting from a myocardial abnormality.

Types: There are two major groups of cardiomyopathies:
1. Primary cardiomyopathies involve predominantly the heart. They may be genetic or acquired (e.g.
viral myocarditis, anthracycline cardiotoxic).

2. Secondary cardiomyopathies have myocardial involvement as a component of a systemic or
multiorgan disorder (e.g. hemochromatosis, amyloidosis).

According to anatomic abnormalities, cardiomyopathies can be classified into three distinct pathologic
patterns:
1. Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) (including arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy) — most common (90% of cases)
2. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
3. Restrictive cardiomyopathy.
(Ref: Robbins/10°/567)

Q. Define and classify pericarditis. (SU-05Ja)

Pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium is called pericarditis.

ft may occur secondary to a variety of cardiac, thoracic, or systemic disorders, metastases from remote
neoplasms, or cardiac surgical procedures.

A) Acute pericarditis:
2. Fibrinous & serofibrinous pericarditis (most frequent type)

B) Chronic or healed pericarditis:
1. Adhesive mediastino-pericarditis: The pericardial sac is obliterated, and adherence of the external
aspect of the parictal layer to surrounding structures produces a great strain on cardiac function.
2. Constrictive pericarditis: The heart may be encased in a dense, fibrous or fibrocalcific scar that lms

Q. Give an account of constrictive pericarditis. (SU-05Ja)
Ans.

Constrictive pericarditis: The heart may be encased in a dense, fibrous or fibrocalcific scar that limits
diastolic expansion and seriously restricts cardiac output, resembling restrictive cardiomyopathy.

A well-defined history of a previous pericarditis may or may not be present.

In constrictive pericarditis, the pericardial space is obliterated, and the heart is surrounded by a dense, adherent
layer of scar with or without calcification, often 0.5 - 1.0 cm thick, that can resemble a plaster mold in extreme
cases (concretio cordis).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/578)

= Malignant:
- Sarcoma (angiosarcoma).

2. Secondary or metastatic neoplasms (most frequently from lung and breast carcinomas, melanomas,
leukemias, and lymphomas).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/527-580)
