Ans.

Hodgkin lymphoma: Malignant neoplasm of lymph node characterized by the presence of neoplastic giant
cells called Reed-Sternberg cells (RS cells) and pleomorphic infiltration by \ymphocyte, cosinophil,
macrophage, plasma cell, neutrophil and follicular dendritic cells.

Criteria:
* Characteristically affects young adults (20-40 age groups).
* Males are affected twice as commonly as female.
* Arises in a single node or group of nodes and spreads first to anatomically contiguous lymphoid
tissues.
* Histological hallmark is presence of RS (Reed-Sternberg) cells.

Clinical features:
= May be asymptomatic.
* May present with painless peripheral lymphadenopathy (usually rubbery and discrete, but may
become matted)
Hepatosplenomegally
Systemic features (“B’ symptoms): Fever (Pel-Ebstein fever), night sweats, weight loss, pruritus.

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL): Malignant neoplasms of lymphoid cells or other cells native to lymphoid

Criteria:

* May arise at any age (peak incidence is 65-70 years).

* Males are affected nvice as commonly as female.

* Usual presentation is localized or generalized peripheral lymphadenopathy, which are discrete,
painless and firm.

* Spreads rapidly to non-contiguous areas.

* Involvement of mesenteric, oropharyngeal lymphoid structures (Waldeyer’s ring) and epitrochlear
lymph nodes is very much common.

*  Extranodal involvement is also common e.g. bone marrow, GIT, stomach, lung, thyroid, skin, testis,
CNS ete.

« Systemic features are gencrally less common.

* Histological hallmark is absence of RS (Reed-Sternberg) giant cells.

Etiology:
* Unknown in majority of cases.
= Infectious agents, e.g. virus (HTLV-1, EBV, HHV-8, HIV-1, HCV), bacteria (H. pylori — causes
gastric lymphoma), protozoa (malaria — causes Burkitt lymphoma).

Classification of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma: There are various classifications in the field of NHL:
1. REAL classification (please see below)
2. Working classification

Working classification: In this classification, NHL is divided into three major prognostic subgroups
(depending on the rate at which the cells are dividing)-
1. Low grade:
* Low cell proliferation rate.
* Asymptomatic for many years.
* Slow indolent course.
*  Incurable, but the patient survives for long time.

2. High grade:
* High cell proliferation rate.
= Early symptoms are common.
= Fatal, if untreated.

* Responds better to treatment (potentially curable disease).

3. Intermediate grade.

Investigations: Please see below.
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/611; Basic Hematology, Dr. Mainuddin/74; de Gruchy/5"/283; Hoffbrand
Haematology/6""/254)

Atelectasis (Collapse)

Q. Define and describe atelectasis (collapse).
Ans

Atelectasis (collapse): Atelectasis refers either to incomplete expansion of the lungs (neonatal atelectasis) or
to the collapse of previously inflated lung, producing areas of relatively airless pulmonary parenchyma.

Types:
1. Resorption (or obstruction) atelectasis: It is the consequence of complete obstruction of an airway,

which in time leads to resorption of air trapped in the distal alveoli, without impairment of blood flow
through the affected alveolar walls.

Here, airway obstruction is most often caused by excessive secretions (e.g. mucus plugs) or exudates
within smaller bronchi, as may occur in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, and
postoperative states. Aspiration of foreign bodies and intrabronchial tumors: may also lead to airway
obstruction and atelectasis.

2. Compression atelectasis: It results whenever significant volumes of fluid (transudate, exudate, or
blood), tumor, or air (pneumothorax) accumulate within the pleural cavity.

3. Contraction atelectasis: Occurs when focal or generalized pulmonary or pleural fibrosis prevents
full lung expansion.

Significant atelectasis reduces oxygenation and predisposes to infection.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/675)

Pulmonary Edema

Q. Define and classify pulmonary edema. What are the causes of pulmonary edema?

Ans.

Pulmonary edema: Pulmonary edema is the accumulation of excessive interstitial fluid in the alveoli, which
can result from hemodynamic disturbances (cardiogenic pulmonary edema) or increased capillary
permeability due to microvascular injury (non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/675; BRS Pathology/5"/211)

Classification and causes of pulmonary edema:
1. Haemodynamic edema:

i) Increased hydrostatic pressure (increased pulmonary venous pressure):
= Left-sided heart failure (common)
= Volume overload

* Pulmonary vein obstruction

ii) Decreased oncotic pressure (less common):
« Hypoalbuminaemia
« Nephrotic syndrome
« Liver disease
* Protein-losing enteropathies

iii) Lymphatic obstruction (rare)

2. Edema due to alveolar wall injury (Microvascular or epithelial injury):
i) Direct injury
* Infections: bacterial pneumonia
Inhaled gases: high concentration oxygen, smoke
Liquid aspiration: gastric contents, near-drowning
Radiation
Lung trauma

Acute Lung Injury (ALI) & Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

Q. Define acute lung injury (ALI) & acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
Q. Short note: ARDS. (BUP-22Nv,20Nv/M, 16Ju) (Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Acute lung injury (ALT): Acute lung injury (ALI) is characterized by the abrupt onset of hypoxemia and
bilateral pulmonary edema in the absence of cardiac failure (non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/676)

ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a manifestation of severe ALI.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/676)
Or,
ARDS is a clinical syndrome of progressive respiratory insufficiency caused by diffuse alveolar damage in
the setting of sepsis, severe trauma, or diffuse pulmonary infection.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/678)

(N.B: Both ARDS and ALI are associated with inflammation-associated increases in pulmonary vascular
permeability, edema, and epithelial cell death. The histologic manifestation of these diseases is diffuse
alveolar damage.)

66

Synonyms: “Shock lung”, “diffuse alveolar damage”, “acute alveolar injury”, and “acute lung injury”.

Conditions associated with development of ARDS:
1. Infection: Sepsis, diffuse pulmonary infections (Viral, Mycoplasma, and Pneumocystis pneumonia;
miliary tuberculosis), gastric aspiration.

2. Physical/injury: Mechanical trauma including head injuries, pulmonary contusions, near-drowning,
fractures with fat embolism, burns, ionizing radiation.

3. Inhaled irritants: Oxygen toxicity, smoke, irritant gases and chemicals.
4. Chemical injury: Heroin or methadone overdose, acetylsalicylic acid, barbiturate overdose, paraquat.
5. Haematological conditions: Transfusion associated lung injury (TRALI), disseminated intravascular

coagulation (DIC).
6. Others: Pancreatitis, uraemia, cardiopulmonary bypass, hypersensitivity reactions (organic solvents,
drugs).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/676)
Clinical features:

1. Profound dyspnea and tachypnea
2. Cyanosis and hypoxemia
3. Respiratory failure
4. Appearance of diffuse bilateral infiltrates on radiographic examination.
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/678)

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)

Q. What do you mean by chronic obstructive lung diseases? (DU-18M)
Q. Define COPD. (CMU-24M, CU-20Nv, 18/17M,09/07Ja)

Q. Write briefly on COPD. (RMU-21M)

Q. Short note: COPD. (CU-13Ju) (Important for VIVA)

Ans.
COPD (Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease): COPD is defined by the World Health Organization
(WHO) as “a common, preventable and treatable disease that is characterized by persistent respiratory

symptoms and airflow limitation that is due to airway and/or alveolar abnormalities caused by exposure
to noxious particles or gases.”

It is currently the fourth leading cause of death in the world.

Characteristics include a marked decrease in the FEV, and an increased or normal forced vital capacity (FVC),
resulting in a decreased FEV, : FVC ratio.

Clinicopathologic manifestations: COPD has two major clinicopathologic manifestations-

1. Emphysema
2. Chronic bronchitis.

i) PD:
1. Cigarette smoking
2. Poor lung development early in life
3. Exposure to environmental and occupational pollutants
4. Airway hyperresponsiveness

(Note: Emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma, and bronchiectasis all are obstructive airway disease).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/675; BRS Pathology/5"/202)

Emphysema

Necessary Lung Anatomy:

Pulmonary acinus: The part of the lung tissue distal to a terminal bronchiole is called an acinus.
(N.B: Lobule is a cluster of acini.)

Parts of an acinus: An acinus consists of 3 parts:

Respiratory bronchioles originate from a terminal bronchiole.
Each respiratory bronchiole divides into several alveolar ducts.

Each alveolar duct opens into many alveolar sacs (alveoli) which are blind ends of the respiratory
passages.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/680; Harsh Mohan/7'"/442)

Q. Define (DU-24Nv) and classify emphysema. (BSFMMU’S-23Nv, CMU-23M,2INv)
(Important for VIVA)
Q. Write the types of emphysema. (DU-24Nv,I8M)
Q. Discuss in brief the various types of emphysema. (SU-20M)
Ans.
Emphysema: Emphysema is a chronic obstructive airway disease characterized by irreversible
enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole, accompanied by destruction of their walls
without obvious fibrosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/675)
Or,

Emphysema is dilation of air spaces with destruction of alveolar walls and lack of elastic recoil.

(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/204)

Types of emphysema: Emphysema is classified into four major types: (1) centriacinar, (2) panacinar, (3)
paraseptal, and (4) irregular.

i) Centriacinar (centrilobular) emphysema (95% of cases): The central or proximal parts of the acini,
formed by respiratory bronchioles are affected, whereas distal alveoli are spared. It occurs
predominantly in heavy smokers, often in association with chronic bronchitis (smoking associated
emphysema).

ii) Panacinar (panlobular) emphysema: In this type the acini are uniformly enlarged from the level of
the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli. This type of emphysema is associated with a,-
antitrypsin deficiency and is exacerbated by smoking.

iii) Distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema: In this type, the proximal portion of the acinus is normal, but
the distal part is predominantly involved. This type of emphysema probably underlies many of the
cases of spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.

iv) Irregular emphysema (airspace enlargement with fibrosis): In this type, the acinus is irregularly
involved, is almost invariably associated with scarring.

Q. Give the etiopathogenesis of pulmonary emphysema. (DU-18M, CU-18M)

Q. Write down the pathogenesis of emphysema. (DU-24Nv)

Ans.

Etiopathogenesis of emphysema: Clinically significant emphysema is largely confined to smokers and to
patients with a,-antitrypsin deficiency. Mechanisms relating to these factors that contribute to the
development of emphysema include the following:

1. Toxic injury and inflammation: Inhaled cigarette smoke and other noxious particles damage
respiratory epithelium and cause inflammation, which results in variable degrees of parenchymal
destruction. A wide variety of inflammatory mediators (including leukotriene B4, interleukin [IL]-8,
TNF, and others) are released by resident epithelial cells and macrophages and variously attract
inflammatory cells from the circulation (chemotactic factors), thus amplify the inflammatory process
(proinflammatory cytokines), and induce structural changes (growth factors).

2. Protease-antiprotease imbalance: Several proteases are released from the inflammatory cells and
epithelial cells that break down connective tissue components. In patients who develop emphysema,
there is a relative deficiency of protective antiproteases (congenital a,-antitrypsin deficiency).

3. Oxidative stress: Substances in tobacco smoke, alveolar damage, and inflammatory cells all produce
oxidants, which may beget tissue damage, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation.

4. Infection: Although infection is not thought to play an initiating role in the tissue destruction,
bacterial and/or viral infections may acutely exacerbate existing disease.

Asthma

Q. Define and classify asthma.
Q. What are non-allergic causes of asthma?

Q. Short note: Bronchial asthma. (Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Asthma: Asthma is a heterogeneous disease, usually characterized by chronic airway inflammation and
variable expiratory airflow obstruction that produces symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath,
chest tightness, and cough, which vary over time and in intensity.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/683)

Or,

Asthma is characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction caused by airway hyper-responsiveness to a
variety of stimuli.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/687)

Clinical features:
= Recurrent episodes of wheezing (in response to allergen exposure)
* Cough (particularly at night and/or in the early morning)
* Breathlessness
* Chest tightness.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/686)

Classification of asthma:

1. Extrinsic (allergic / atopic) asthma (evidence of allergen sensitization and immune activation): This
commonest type of asthma is a classic example of IgE-mediated (type-I) hypersensitivity reaction.
Disease begins in childhood, usually in patients with a family history of allergy.

2. Intrinsic (non-atopic) asthma (no evidence of allergen sensitization): It usually begins in adult life
and is not associated with a history of allergy. It is several subtypes. In all types, episodes of
bronchospasm may have diverse triggers, such as-

* Respiratory infections (especially viral infections, e.g. rhinovirus, parainfluenza virus and
respiratory syncytial virus etc.)
= — [rritants (e.g. smoke, fumes)

* Cold air
=» Stress
= Exercise

= Drugs (e.g. aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/683; BRS Pathology/5'/203; Harsh Mohan/7'"/464; Pathoma Lecture Notes)

Q. Mention the pathogenesis of bronchial asthma. (CU-19M)

Q. Short note: Atopic asthma. (For VIVA)

Ans.

Atopic asthma: This is the most common type of asthma and is a classic example of IgE-mediated (type-I)
hypersensitivity reaction. The disease usually begins in childhood and is triggered by environmental
allergens, such as dusts, pollens, cockroach or animal dander (excreta), and foods etc.

Most patients of this type have a positive family history of asthma and/or preceding allergic diseases such
as rhinitis, urticaria or infantile eczema etc.

Pathogenesis: Atopic asthma is caused by IgE-mediated (type-I) hypersensitivity reaction to environmental
allergens in genetically predisposed individuals which includes an early-phase (immediate hypersensitivity)
reaction and the late-phase reaction.

Initial sensitization to inhaled antigens
(e.g. house dust, pollens, animal danders, moulds etc.)

Stimulate induction of Ty2 cells that release cytokines such as IL-4 & IL-5

1

eosinophil (IL-5)

Q Mention the histologic findings of asthma.
Q What is airway remodeling?
Ans.

Histologic findings of asthma:
lt. Occlusion of bronchi and bronchioles by thick, tenacious mucus plugs, which often contain shed

epithelium.

2. Curschmann spirals, which may result from extrusion of mucus plugs from subepithelial mucous
gland ducts or bronchioles.

3. Charcot-Leyden crystals composed of the eosinophil-derived protein galectin-10

4. Other characteristic histologic findings of asthma, collectively called “airway remodeling”, include:
* Thickening of airway wall

Sub-basement membrane fibrosis (due to deposition of type-I and type-III collagens)

Increased vascularity

Increase in the size of the submucosal glands and number of airway goblet cells

Hypertrophy and/or hyperplasia of the bronchial wall muscle with increased extracellular matrix.

(Ref: Robbins/10'/686)

Bronchiectasis

Q. Define bronchiectasis. Enumerate the causes of bronchiectasis. (Important for VIVA)
Q. Write briefly the aetio-pathology of bronchiectasis. (DU-05M)
Ans.
Bronchiectasis: Bronchiectasis is a disorder in which destruction of smooth muscle and elastic tissue by
inflammation stemming from persistent or severe infections leads to permanent dilation of bronchi and
bronchioles.
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/687)
Or,

Bronchiectasis is defined as abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchi and bronchioles caused by
chronic infection, with inflammation and necrosis of the bronchial wall.

(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/205; Harsh Mohan/7"/465; Davidson’ s/23"'/578)

Causes / etiology of bronchiectasis:
A) Congenital or hereditary conditions that predispose to chronic infections:
1. Cystic fibrosis (CF)
2. Intralobar sequestration of the lung
3. Immunodeficiency states
4. Ciliary dysfunction syndromes
* Primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile cilia syndrome)
* Kartagener’s syndromes (bronchiectasis, situs inversus and sinusitis)

B) Acquired:

1. Post-infectious conditions: Severe necrotizing pneumonia caused by bacteria (M. tuberculosis,
S. aureus, H. influenzae, Pseudomonas) viruses (adenovirus, influenza virus, HIV), and fungi
(Aspergillus species) may develop bronchiectasis as a complication.

2. Bronchial obstruction: Due to tumours, enlarged lymph nodes, foreign bodies, or mucus
impaction.

3. Immune disorders: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and post-
transplantation (chronic rejection after lung transplant and chronic graft-versus-host disease after
hematopoietic stem cell transplantation).

4. Idiopathic (up to 50% of cases).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/687)

Pathogenesis: Loss of muco-ciliary clearance system is the main problem. Mucus accumulation followed by
bacterial overgrowth leads to pus filled infection and permanent dilation of airways.

Bronchial obstruction (e.g. by mucus impaction, tumours, or foreign bodies)
Normal clearing mechanisms are impaired

Pooling of secretions distal to the obstruction

{

Infections
Inflammation of the airway associated with necrosis & fibrosis

Eventual permanent dilatation of the airways.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/687; Davidson’s/23"/578; Harsh Mohan/7"/465; Pathoma Lecture Notes)

Nice to Know:

Relation of bronchiectasis with cystic fibrosis (CF): In cystic fibrosis, the viscid mucous secretions from all
the exocrine glands of the body, including the sub mucosal glands of the respiratory tract cause obstruction,
dilatation and infection of the airways.

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/631)

Q. What is Kartagener’s syndrome? (For VIVA)
Ans.

Kartagener’s syndrome: Kartagener’s syndrome is a ciliary dysfunction syndrome manifested by sinusitis,
bronchiectasis, and situs inversus (sometimes with hearing loss and male sterility).

Cause: It is caused by a defect in the motility of respiratory, auditory, and sperm cilia that is referred to as
primary ciliary dyskinesia, an uncommon autosomal recessive syndrome. In this condition, there is a
structural defect in dynein arms of cilia.

Pathogenesis: Impaired ciliary activity predisposes to infection in the sinuses and bronchi and disturbs
embryogenesis, sometimes resulting in situs inversus. Male infertility is an important manifestation of ciliary
dyskinesia.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/687; Davidson’s/23"/550,578; BRS Pathology/5""/205; Pathoma Lecture Notes)

Q. What is presentation and complication of bronchiectasis? (For VIVA)
Ans.
Presentation of bronchiectasis:
= Severe, persistent cough
Expectoration of foul smelling, sometimes bloody sputum
Dyspnea and orthopnea (in severe cases)
Pleuritic chest pain
Hemoptysis (which may be massive)
Recurrent pneumonia

Complication of bronchiectasis:
* Development of clubbing of the fingers

* Metastatic brain abscess
* Amyloidosis
* Corpulmonale.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/688; Davidson’s/23"/578; BRS Pathology/5"/205; Pathoma Lecture Notes)

Merphologic features: Bronchiectasis usually affects the lower lobes bilaterally, particularly distal bronchi

and bronchioles beyond the segmental bronchi. The airways are dilated, sometimes up to four times normal
Size.

Gressly, the lungs may be involved diffusely or segmentally (locally). Bilateral involvement of lower lobes
occurs most frequently.

The dilated airways, depending upon their gross or broncho-graphic appearance, have been subclassified into
the following different types:

1. Cplindrical: The most common type characterised by tube-like bronchial dilatation.
2. Fusiform: Having spindle-shaped bronchial dilatation.

3. Saccular: Having rounded sac-like bronchial distension.

4. Varicose: Having irregular bronchial enlargements.

Cut surface of the affected lobes, generally the lower zones, shows characteristic honey-combed appearance.

Fig: (Left) Types of bronchial dilatations in bronchiectasis; (Right) Sectioned surface shows honey-
combed appearance of the bronchiectatic lung in the lower lobe.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/687; Harsh Mohan/7"/465)

Restrictive Lung Diseases

Q. What do you mean by restrictive lung disease? (DU-18M) Give example.
Ags.

Restrictive lung disease: Restrictive lung diseases are a group of disorders characterized by reduced
expansion of lung parenchyma and decreased total lung capacity.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/678; BRS Pathology/5"/203)

In restrictive lung disease, both total lung capacity and FEV1 decrease proportionately, resulting in a normal
FEV; /FVC ratio.
Restrictive defects occur in two broad kinds of conditions:
1. Chest wall disorders (e.g. severe obesity, pleural diseases, kyphoscoliosis and neuromuscular
diseases such as poliomyelitis)
2. Chronic interstitial and infiltrative diseases, such as pneumoconioses and interstitial fibrosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/678; BRS Pathology/5"/203)

Interstitial Lung Diseases

Interstitial lung diseases: Chronic interstitial pulmonary diseases are a heterogeneous group of disorders
characterized predominantly by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium associated with
pulmonary function studies indicative of restrictive lung disease.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/688)
Or,
Interstitial lung disease is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by interstitial accumulations of
cells or noncellular material within the alveolar walls that restrict expansion and often interfere with gaseous

exchange.
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5'"/205)

Major categories of chronic interstitial lung diseases:

Pneumoconiosis: (Very Important for VIVA) The term pneumoconiosis describes the non-neoplastic
lung reaction to inhalation of mineral dusts encountered in the workplace, including disease induced by

chemical fumes and vapors.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/691)

Or,
Pneumoconioses encompass a group of chronic fibrosing diseases of the lung resulting from exposure to

organic and inorganic particulates, most commonly mineral dust.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/695)

Pulmonary Embolism and Infarction

It is the major cause of sudden death in hospitalized (bedridden) patients. Occlusion of the pulmonary
artery is nearly embolic and main source is thrombi in the deep veins of the leg (e.g. politeal vein) in more than

95% of cases.

Morphology:

Macroscopic: The pulmonary infarct is classically hemorrhagic and appears as a raised, red-blue area in the

early stages.

Histologically: The diagnostic feature of acute pulmonary infarction is the ischemic necrosis of the lung
substance within the area of hemorrhage, affecting the alveolar walls, bronchioles, and vessels.

Clinical features:

* Large pulmonary embolus impacted in the main pulmonary artery causing instantaneous death.
* Small emboli induce only transient chest pain, cough, and pulmonary hemorrhage.

Laboratory diagnosis:

Serum D-dimer measurement

Ventilation perfusion (V/Q) scanning
Chest x-ray: May be normal; or a wedge-shaped pulmonary infiltrate (usually after 12 to 36 hours)
CT pulmonary angiography (definitive diagnosis)

Q. What is lobar pneumonia (SU-04S,03Ja) and bronchopneumonia?
Q. Discuss the etiology (DU-14Ja, RU-17M) & pathogenesis of lobar (DU-06Ja,CU-05Ja)
pneumonia.
Q. Discuss the pathogenesis of bacterial pneumonia.
Ans.
Bacterial pneumonia: It has two pattems of anatomic distribution: /obar pneumonia and
bronchopneumonia.
1. Lobar pneumonia: It is an acute bacterial infection resulting in fibrino-suppurative consolidation of
a large portion of a lobe or of an entire lobe. The /ower lobes are affected most commonly.

2. Bronchopneumonia: It is an acute bacterial infection characterized by patchy consolidation of the
lung (34 cm. in diameter, more often multilobar, often bilateral & basal).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/704)

Pathogenesis / predisposing factors of bacterial pneumonia: Pneumonia can result whenever the Jocal

defense mechanisms are impaired or the systemic resistance of the host is lowered.

A) Factors altering the defense mechanisms of lung:
1. Altered consciousness: Oropharyngeal contents may be aspirated in states causing

unconsciousness e.g. in coma, cranial trauma, seizures, stroke, drug overdose, alcoholism etc.

2. Loss or suppression of cough reflex: \t may allow aspiration of gastric contents, as a result of
coma, anaesthesia, neuromuscular disorders, drugs, or chest pain.

3. Dysfunction of the mucociliary apparatus: Passage of bacteria into the lung parenchyma is
favoured by either impairment of ciliary function or destruction of ciliated epithelium, owing to
cigarette smoking, viral respiratory infections, inhalation of hot or corrosive gases, old age, or
genetic defects of ciliary function (e.g. immotile cilia syndrome).

4. Accumulation of secretions in conditions such as cystic fibrosis and bronchial obstruction.

Interference with the phagocytic and bactericidal activities of alveolar macrophages by alcohol,
tobacco smoke, anoxia, or oxygen intoxication.

6. Pulmonary congestion and edema.

B) Factors lowering the resistance of the host:

1. Chronic diseases
2. Immunologic deficiency
3. Treatment with immunosuppressive agents
4. Leukopenia.
(Ref: Robbins/10°/705; Harsh Mohan/7"/448)

Nice to Know:
Bronchopneumonia is particularly frequent at the extremes of life (i.e. in infancy and old age), as a terminal
event in chronic debilitating diseases and as a secondary infection following viral respiratory infections such

as influenza, measles etc.
(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/452)

Q. Short note: Lung abscess. (DU-19Nv)
Ans.
Lung abscess: [t is the localized area of suppuration within the lung parenchyma that leads to
parenchymal destruction & manifested radiologically as cavity with air-fluid level.
Or,
The term pulmonary abscess describes a local suppurative process that produces necrosis of lung tissue.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/711)

Causes:

1. Aspiration of infective material (the most frequent cause): Risk factors include-
» Suppressed cough reflexes (e.g. acute alcohol intoxication, opioid abuse, coma, anesthesia, seizure
disorders)
* Severe dysphagia (e.g. neurologic deficits, esophageal disease)
* Protracted vomiting
* Poor dental hygiene.

Aspiration first causes pneumonia, which progresses to tissue necrosis and formation of lung abscess.

2. Antecedent primary lung infection: Postpneumonic abscess formation (usually associated with S.
aureus, K, pneumoniae, and pneumococcus).

3. Septic embolism: Infected emboli may arise from thrombophlebitis of the systemic venous circulation
or from the vegetations of infective bacterial endocarditis on the right side of the heart.

4. Bronchial obstruction: By bronchogenic carcinoma, adenoma, foreign body (postobstructive
pneumonia).

5. Local spread: Direct extension of suppurative infections from the esophagus, spine, pleural avity,
liver abscess, subphrenic abscess.

6. Haematogenous spread from other sites of infection as pelvic abscess, pyemia, or septicaemia.
7, Miscellaneous: Traumatic penetrations of the lungs.

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY

115
es

Causative organisms: Under appropriate circumstances any bacterial pathogen can produce an abscess; but
the most common organisms include- (For VIVA)

1. Aerobic and anaerobic streptococci
2. Staphylococcus aureus

3. Pseudomonas

4. Klebsiella

5. Proteus

6.

Anaerobic organisms normally found in the oral cavity (e.g. Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, and
Peptococcus etc.)

Morphology:
= Abscesses vary in diameter from a few millimeters to large cavities of 5 to 6 cm.
= They may affect any part of the lung and may be single or multiple.

* Cardinal histologic change in all abscesses is suppurative destruction of the lung parenchyma
within the central area of cavitation.

Continued infection leads to large, poorly demarcated, fetid, green-black, multilocular cavities
designated gangrene of the lung.

* Inchronic cases considerable fibroblastic proliferation produces a fibrous wall.
Clinical features:

Cough with copious amounts of foul-smelling purulent or sanguineous sputum
Fever, chest pain, and weight loss

Occassional haemoptysis

Clubbing of the fingers and toes

Radiographic evidence of a fluid-filled cavity.

Complication: (For VIVA)
Extension of the infection into the pleural cavity
Hemorrhage
Development of brain abscesses or meningitis from septic emboli
Secondary amyloidosis (in chronic long-standing cases).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/711; Harsh Mohan/7"/457; BRS Pathology/5"/213; Lecture SSMC)

Primary tuberculosis: Primary tuberculosis is the form of disease that develops in a previously unexposed
and therefore unsensitized person.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/369)

Primary tuberculosis occurs after initial infection (first exposure) with Mycobacterium tuberculosis or
Mycobacterium bovis. About 5% of newly infected people develop clinically significant disease. Rest 90-95%
cases of primary TB remain asymptomatic (fever, malaise). Source of organism is exogenous here in primary TB.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/369)

2. Intestine
3. Skin
4. Oropharyngeal &

Ghon’s focus.
ii) Lymphangitis
iii) Hilar lymphadenitis (inflammation of the lymph nodes of the hillum of the lungs).

Q. What is secondary tuberculosis?

Ans.

Secondary tuberculosis: Secondary tuberculosis is the form of the disease that develops in a previously
sensitized host.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/370)

It may follow shortly after primary TB, but more commonly it arises from reactivation of dormant primary
lesion months to years after the initial infection, particularly when host resistance is weakened. It may also
result from exogenous re-infection because of waning of protection afforded by primary diseases or because
of a large inoculum of virulent bacilli.

Reactivation is more common in low-prevalence areas, and reinfection plays an important role in regions of
high contagion.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/370; Lecture SSMC)

Q. Define miliary tuberculosis. (DU-09Ja) (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Military tuberculosis: In some cases, bacilli within the macrophage spread to regional lymph node in the
hilum of the lung and thence to the blood stream, which in tum distributes the organisms to almost all
parts of the body. It is called miliary tuberculosis.

(Ref: Microbiology Lecture, SSMC)

Miliary tuberculosis is most prominent in the liver, bone marrow, spleen, adrenals, meninges, kidneys,
fallopian tubes & epididymis, but can involve any organ. It occurs when the body immunity fails to control the
primary infection.

(Ref: Robbins/10""/373)

Q. Write down the pathology / morphology of pulmonary tuberculosis.
Q. Discuss the pathological characteristics of secondary pulmonary tuberculosis. (DU-09Ja)
Ans.
Pathology / morphology of pulmonary tuberculosis:
Primary pulmonary tuberculosis:
i) There is a focal lesion in the lung called Ghon’s focus
ii) Lymphangitis and enlargement of hilar lymph nodes
iii) Ghon’s focus, together with nodal involvement (lymphangitis and lymphadenitis) is called the Ghon’s
complex
iv) The Ghon’s focus gradually gets healed up and calcified (Ghon’s body)

v) If the infection is not contained, the organisms may reach the blood stream causing systemic
tuberculosis affecting various organs (milliary tuberculosis).

Secondary pulmonary tuberculosis:
Gross:
1. Lesion is located in the apex of one or both lungs
2. It begins as a small focus of consolidation, usually <3 cm
3. Initial lesion may be located in the other region of the lung
4. Inalmost every cases of re-infection, the regional nodes develop foci of similar tubercular lesion

Microscopic:
1. Accumulation of large number of activated macrophage at the site of primary lesion and the formation
of tubercle

2. The tubercle comprises an organized aggregation of activated macrophages; because they resemble
epithelial cells, they are called epithelioid cells

3. Epithelioid cells have a pale, pink, granular cytoplasm

---

#### 📄 Page 120

120 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

5.

Epithelioid cells fuse to form giant cells
These giant cells may attain diameters of 40-50 1m. They comprise a large mass of cytoplasm
containing 20 or more small nuclei arranged either peripherally (Langhans-type giant cell) or
haphazardly (Foreign-body type giant cell)
A peripheral collar of fibroblast, lymphocyte, and macrophage surrounds the granuloma
Sometimes the central part of the granuloma undergoes characteristic caseous necrosis to produce a
soft tubercle, the characteristic hallmark of TB.

(Ref: Microbiology Lecture, SSMC; Robbins/10'/100,371)

Q. Mention the common clinical features of pulmonary TB. (For VIVA)

Ans.

Clinical features of pulmonary TB:

Systemic symptoms include malaise, anorexia, weight loss, and fever.

Fever is low grade and remittent (appearing late each afternoon and then subsiding)

Night sweats

Persistant cough for 3 weeks or more with sputum production (at first mucoid and later purulent)

Some degree of hemoptysis is present in about one-half of all cases

Pleuritic chest pain may be present

Extrapulmonary manifestations of tuberculosis are legion and depend on the organ system involved.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/370)

Q. How you can diagnose a case of pulmonary TB? (For VIVA)
Q. How will you investigate pulmonary tuberculosis? (BUP-22Nv)
Ans

Diagnosis of pulmonary TB:

1. History and physical examination

2. Radiologic findings of consolidation or cavitation in the apices of lung

3. Sputum for AFB staining and culture - gold standard (culture on solid agar media shows growth at 3
to 6 weeks, but culture in /iquid media can provide an answer within 2 weeks)

4. ESR- High

5. PCR amplification of M. tuberculosis DNA - GeneXpert {can detect as few as 10 organisms in
clinical specimens, e.g. pleural, ascitic, pericardial, joint fluid & CSF compared to >10,000
organisms required for smear positivity (AFB)}

6. FNAC and biopsy of lymph node (if present)

7. Antibiotic susceptibility test (C/S) (as multi-drug resistance is common now)

8. MT test / tuberculin skin test (not diagnostic).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/371; Lecture SSMC)

Why early morning sample: Secretions build up in the airway overnight. So this sample is likely to contain
more bacilli.

Q. Which one is confirmatory test? (V.V.1. for VIVA)
Ans.
GeneXpert to see the bacterial DNA.

Ans.
Sputum for AFB staining: Ziehl-Neelsen (Z-N) staining.
Sputum for culture: Lowenstein-Jensen media.

Q. Short note: Mantaux / tuberculin test. (DU-07Ju) (For VIVA)

Ans.

Mantoux / tuberculin test: Infection with M. tuberculosis typically leads to development of delayed
hypersensitivity to M. tuberculosis antigen which can be detected by this test.

This test has no diagnostic value and only indicates the occurrence of past and recent infection when the
reaction is positive. The test becomes positive about 2-4 weeks after infection.

Reagent: Punfied protein derivatives (PPD). WHO recommended tuberculin is ‘‘PPD-RT-23 with Tween 80”.
Dose: 5 tuberculin units (TU) — 0.1 ml.

Technique of injection: 0.1 ml PPD is slowly injected on the flexor aspect of the forearm intradermally.
Reaction: Visible & palpable induration, that peaks in 48-72 hours.
Reading: Reading is taken after 72 hours (3™ days). Induration is measured in mm.

Interpretation:

1. Positive reaction: Induration exceeding 10 mm. (it indicates that, the person is infected with M.

tuberculosis; it dose not prove that the person is suffering from the disease, i.e. a positive tuberculin
test does not differentiate between infection and active disease).

Negative reaction: Induration less than 6 mm.

3. Doubtful reaction: Induration between 6 and 9 mm. (Here the reaction may be due to M.
tuberculosis or atypical mycobacteria).

False positive reaction:
* Prior BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) vaccination
* Atypical mycobacterium infection

False negative reaction:
* Viral infections (e.g. HIV, measles, chicken pox)
* Sarcoidosis
* Malnutrition
* Malignancy
* Hodgkin lymphoma
* Immunosuppression
= Overwhelming active tuberculosis
* Incorrect injection of PPD.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/371; Park/25"/197; Lecture SSMC)

Q. A diabetic 50 years old male presented with chronic cough and haemoptysis. Chest x-ray
shows apical opacity and transbronchial biopsy reveals granuloma. What is the most likely

diagnosis? Is their any chance of widespread dissemination in this patient? (DU-07Ja)
Ans
Most likely diagnosis: Pulmonary tuberculosis (secondary).

Chance of wide spread dissemination: Normally secondary tuberculosis spreads locally, not by lymphatic
or haematogenous route. But if there is inadequate treatment or impaired host defense (that may occur to
this patient, as he 1s diabetic) organisms may seed into lymphatics or pulmonary venous system. In first
case organisms reach via lymphatic system to the right heart and cause miliary pulmonary disease. In later
case, organisms reach the right ventricle and cause systemic miliary tuberculosis

Q. What do you mean by bronchogenic carcinoma? (DU-08Ja) Give the aetiopathogenesis of
bronchogenic carcinoma. (SMU-23M, CMU-22Nv, RU-12Ju)

Q. Write the risk factors of bronchogenic carcinoma. (SU-14Ja)

Q. Give the aetiology (CU-05Ja, SU-05Ja) & pathogenesis of bronchogenic carcinoma.

Q. Write briefly the etiopathological factors responsible for bronchogenic carcinoma. (SU-08Ju)
Ans.

Bronchogenic carcinoma: Bronchogenic carcinoma refers to the malignant neoplasm of the lung arising
from the bronchial epithelium or mucous glands.

Or,
The term bronchogenic carcinoma is commonly used for cancer of the lungs which includes carcinomas
arising from the respiratory epithelium lining the bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli.

It is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in the world and the most common cause of cancer mortality
worldwide; occurs most often between ages 40 and 70 years, with the peak incidence in the 50s or 60s.
(Ref: Davidson’s/23"/599; BRS Pathology/5"/215,216; Robbins/10"/715)

Aetio-pathogenesis / risk factors of bronchogenic carcinoma:
1. Tobacco smoking (most important cause): 85% to 90% of lung cancers arise in smokers, and the most
common tumors in smokers are small cell and squamous cell carcinomas. Risk directly linked to
duration and amount of smoking (pack years).

2. Air pollution: Indoor air pollution, especially by radon (2™ most common cause).
Radiation exposure: High-dose ionizing radiation, especially in radium and uranium workers.

4. Asbestos: Increased incidence of lung cancer with asbestos and greater increase with combination of
asbestos and cigarette smoking.

5. Industrial hazards: Such as nickel, chromium, beryllium, arsenic, vinyl chloride and mustard gas etc.

6. Molecular genetics: Dominant oncogenes that are frequently involved in lung cancer include c-MYC,
K-RAS, EGFR and HER-2/neu.

Q. Write down the morphology of bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma. (CU-1! 1Ju,06M)

Q. Short note: Bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma, (SU-15Ja, RU-08Ja)

Ans.

Bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma: Bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly found
in men and is strongly associated with smoking. It is the most common lung cancer in male smokers.

These tumours usually arise in a large bronchus and are prone to massive necrosis and cavitation.

Pathogenesis: Chronic smoking — Chronic irritation in the columnar ciliated lining epithelium of the
respiratory tract + Squamous metaplasia (columnar cells are replaced by stratified squamous epithelium) —
Dysplasia — Carcinoma in situ — Invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

Morphology:
Macroscopic:

* Location: Central (most often around the hilum of lung).

* Types: Three types of growth pattern - fungating, infiltrative & cauliflower-like.

= Colour: Gray-white.

= Large lesions may undergo central necrosis, giving rise to cavitation.
Microscopic:

* Presence of keratinization (keratin pearls) and/or intercellular bridges.

moderately-differentiated and poorly-differentiated.

Q. Write about small cell carcinoma. (CU-04S)
Ans.
Small cell carcinoma: (formerly known as “oat cell” carcinomas)

Characteristics:
1. About 15% of all bronchogenic carcinoma

2. Shows the strongest association with smoking (99% of small cell carcinoma patients are smokers)
3. Arise from neuroendocrine cells (Kulchitsky cells)
4. Highly malignant, rapidly growing tumour (there is no known preinvasive phase)
5. Early metastasis and inoperable at presentation
6. Usually responds to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, less likely to be cured by surgery
7. Overall prognosis is poor. Survival is short (3 months to | year).
Morphology:
Macroscopic:
= Location: Central/hilar (by the time of diagnosis, most will have metastasized to hilar and
mediastinal lymph nodes).
* Colour: Pale-gray.
Microscopic:

1. Relatively small (or oat-like) tumor cells (round, oval, or spindle shaped) consisting:
Scant cytoplasm

Ill-defined borders

Finely granular nuclear chromatin (‘‘salt and pepper” appearance)

Absent or inconspicuous nucleoli

Frequent nuclear molding

A high mitotic count.

Q. Why small cell carcinoma is most dangerous? (For VIVA)

Small cell carcinoma is most dangerous: Because:

1. Most aggressive lung tumor

2. Early wide-spread metastasis (mostly at the time of diagnosis)

3. Poor prognosis

4. Virtually incurable by surgical means (chemotherapy and radiotherapy is needed)
5. Almost invariably fatal.

Q. Short note: Pancoast tumour. (RU-13Ja)

Ans.

Pancoast tumour: A Pancoast tumor, also called a pulmonary sulcus tumor or superior sulcus tumor, is a
tumor of the pulmonary apex. It is a type of lung cancer defined primarily by its location situated at the top end
of either the right or left lung.

It typically spreads to nearby tissues such as the ribs and vertebrae. Most Pancoast tumors are non-small cell
cancers.

The growing tumor can cause compression of a brachiocephalic vein, subclavian artery, phrenic nerve,
recurrent laryngeal nerve, vagus nerve, or, characteristically, compression of a sympathetic ganglion resulting
in a range of symptoms known as Horner’s syndrome.

Symptoms:
1. Due to compression of cervical sympathetic plexus / sympathetic ganglion: Horner’s syndrome

(ipsilateral partial ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and enophthalmos).
2. Due to compression of brachial plexus (in progressive cases): Thoracic outlet syndrome (pain and
weakness in the muscles of the arm and hand)

3. Due to compression of recurrent laryngeal nerve: Hoarseness of voice and bovine cough.
(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/540 + 10°/721)

The Pleura

Q. Define pleural effusion. Mention its causes.

Q. Short note: Pleural effusion.

Ans.

Pleura effusion: Abnormal accumulation of fluid within pleural space is called pleural effusion.

Pleural fluid normally present: 5 to 15 mL which is serous, relatively acellular, clear fluid.

It is a common manifestation of both primary and secondary pleural diseases, which may be inflammatory or
non-inflammatory.

disease, and Behcet disease.

* The lesions appear as single or multiple, shallow, hyperemic, mucosal ulceration covered by a thin
exudate and nmmed by a narrow zone of erythema.

* Lesions typically resolve spontaneously in 7 to 10 days but sometimes persist for weeks,
particularly in immunocompromised patients.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/732)

Q. What are the tumours and precancerous lesions of oral cavity?
Ans.

Tumours and precancerous lesions of oral cavity: (For VIVA)
1. Leukoplakia

2. Erythroplakia
3. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/731,734)

Q. What is leukoplakia? (CU-19/18Nv) State its common sites and its pathology.
Q. Short note: Leukoplakia. (DU-03M) (For VIVA)

Ans.
Leukoplakia: Leukoplakia is defined by the WHO as “a white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off and

cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease.”

Until proven otherwise by means of histologic evaluation, all leukoplakias must be considered precancerous.

Age at incidence: Adults at any age, but they are usually found in persons 40 to 70 years of age, with a2: 1
male preponderance.

Cause: Multifactorial origin, but most important cause is the use of tobacco (cigarettes, pipes, cigars and
certain forms of smokeless tobacco).

Sites: May occur anywhere in the oral cavity. But the favoured sites are-

* Buccal mucosa
* Floor of the mouth
* Ventral surface of tongue, palate and gingiva.

Fig: Leukoplakia.

is0_| arif's representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY
Morphology:

Macroscopic:
* — Solitary or multiple white patches or plaques.
* Sharply demarcated borders.
* They may be slightly thickened and smooth or wrinkled and fissured, or they may appear as raised,
sometimes corrugated, verrucous plaques.

Microscopic: Spectrum of epithelial changes ranging from-
* Hyperkeratosis overlying a thickened, acanthotic but orderly mucosal epithelium to
* Lesions with markedly dysplastic changes sometimes merging into carcinoma in situ.

Clinical importance: It is a precancerous state. So, it may tum into malignancy {squamous cell carcinoma
(SCC)}.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/734)

Q. What is erythroplakia? (CU-18Nv)
Q. Short note: Erythroplakia. (For VIVA)
Ans.

Erythroplakia: Erythroplakia is a red, velvety, possibly eroded area within the oral cavity that usually remains
level with or may be slightly depressed in relation to the surrounding mucosa.

The epithelium in such lesions tends to be markedly atypical, incurring a much higher risk of malignant
transformation (pre-malignant).

Age at incidence: Adults at any age, but they are usually found in persons 40 to 70 years of age, with a2: |
male preponderance.

Cause: Multifactorial origin, but most important cause is the use of tobacco (cigarettes, pipes, cigars and
certain forms of smokeless tobacco).

Histology of erythroplakia:

* Severe dysplasia / carcinoma in situ / minimally invasive carcinoma (approx. 90% cases)
* An intense subepithelial inflammatory reaction with vascular dilatation accounts for the reddish
clinical appearance of the lesion.

Clinical importance: It is a precancerous state. Risk of malignant transformation (SCC) is much higher
than is leukoplakia.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/734)

(N.B: Intermediate forms that have the characteristics of both leukoplakia and erythroplakia are termed
speckled leukoerythroplakia.)
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/735)

Salivary Gland

Q. Define xerostomia and sialadenitis. (For VIVA)

Ans.

Xerostomia: Xerostomia is defined as a dry mouth resulting from a decrease in the production of saliva.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/747)

Sialadenitis: Sialadenitis refers to the inflammation of the salivary gland which may be of traumatic, viral,
bacterial, or autoimmune origin.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/747,751)

particularly the parotids, and frequently involves other glandular organs such as the pancreas and testes).

Q. What is Sjogren syndrome?

Ans.

Sjigren syndrome: Sjégren syndrome is a chronic disease characterized by dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis
sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) resulting from immunologically mediated destruction of the lacrimal
and salivary glands.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/229)

(N.B: It occurs as an isolated disorder (primary form), also known as the sicca syndrome, or more often in
association with another autoimmune disease (secondary form). Among the associated disorders, rheumatoid
arthritis is the most common, but some patients have SLE, polymyositis, scleroderma, vasculitis, mixed
connective tissue disease, or thyroiditis.)

(Ref: Robbins/10"/229)

Tumors of salivary glands: The majority of the salivary gland tumours occur in the parotid gland (65% to

ee —< SS
Pleomorphic adenoma (mixed tumour): Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign, slow-growing neoplasm

composed of a heterogenous mixture of epithelial and mesenchymal cells.

(Ref: Robbins/10'/751)

Pleomorphic adenomas are the most common salivary gland neoplasms. They represent about 60% of
tumors in the parotid, are less common in the submandibular glands, and are relatively rare in the minor
salivary glands.

Cause: Is little known, but radiation exposure increase the risk.

Characteristics:
* Pleomorphic adenomas are benign tumors that consist of a mixture of ductal (epithelial),
myoepithelial, and mesenchymal cells, which explains why they are also termed mixed tumors.
* Malignant transformation is rare. When they appear, these cancers are among the most aggressive
of all salivary gland neoplasms, with mortality rates of 30% to 50% at 5 years
* Cancers are usually adenocarcinomas or undifferentiated carcinomas.

Clinical features:
1. Painless, slow growing, mobile, discrete masses within the parotid or submendibular areas or in
the buccal cavity.

2. Often, the tumour is difficult to remove completely because of its proximity to the facial nerve,
and it is likely to recur after resection.

3. The rate of recurrence following parotidectomy is about 4%.

Fig: Pleomorphic adenoma.

Morphology:
Macroscopic:
* Rounded, well demarcated masses that rarely exceed 6 cm in greatest dimension.
* They are encapsulated with some exceptions e.g. in palate, where the capsule is not fully developed.
* Cut surface is gray-white with myxoid and blue translucent areas of chondroid (cartilage-like)
stroma.

Microscopic / Histologic:
= Great heterogeneity.
* The epithelial elements resembling ductal cells or myoepithelial cells are arranged as ducts, acini,
irregular tubules, strands, or sheets of cells.
= These elements are typically dispersed within a background of loose myxoid and hyaline tissue
containing island of cartilage and, rarely, foci of bone.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/748; BRS Pathology/5"/226)

Q. Why it is called pleomorphic adenoma? (RU-18M)

Ans.

Naming of pleomorphic adenoma: Pleomorphism is a term used in histology and cytopathology to describe
variability in the size, shape and staining of cells and/or their nuclei. An adenoma is a benign tumor
originating in glandular tissue.

---

#### 📄 Page 143

a PT ———
Pleomorphic adenoma consists of a mixture of ductal (epithelial), myoepithelial and mesenchymal cells,
and therefore it shows both epithelial and mesenchymal {myxoid & chondroid (cartilage-like) elements}
differentiation. Because of this remarkable histologic diversity, this adenoma is called “Pleomorphic
adenoma”.

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 143

(Ref: Robbins/10""/748; BRS Pathology/5"/226; Lecture DMC)

Q. Give the morphologic features of adenoid cystic carcinoma. (RU-03Ja)
Ans.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma: It is a relatively uncommon tumor, which in approximately 50% of cases is
found in the minor salivary glands (in particular the palatine glands). Among the major salivary glands, the
parotid and submandibular glands are the most common locations.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/751)

Morphologic features of adenoid cystic carcinoma:

Gross appearance:
1. They are generally small, poorly encapsulated, infiltrative, gray-pink lesions.

Microscopic:
1. They are composed of small cells having dark, compact nuclei and scant cytoplasm.
2. The tumor cells are organized in a cribriform growth pattern that resembles swiss cheese.
3. The spaces between the tumor cells are often filled with hyaline material thought to represent
excess basement membrane.
4. Less common histologic patterns are tubular and solid.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/751)

Nose & Nasopharynx

Olfactory neuroblastoma (Esthesioneuroblastoma)
NUT midline carcinoma
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (associated with EBV infection).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/741)

Q. Short note: Achalasia. (Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Achalasia: Disordered esophageal motility with inability to relax the lower esophageal sphincter (LES).
Or,
Achalasia is persistent contraction of the lower esophageal sphincter and absence of esophageal pcristalsis,
leading to dilation of the esophagus.
Or,
It is a neuromuscular dysfunction of the oesophagus due to which the cardiac sphincter fails to relax during
swallowing and results in progressive dysphagia and dilatation of the oesophagus (mega-oesophagus).

Achalasia is characterized by the triad of-
* Incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation
= Increased lower esophageal sphincter tone
=  Aperistalsis of the esophagus.

Types & causes of achalasia:

1. Primary achalasia: It is rare and results from degeneration of nitric oxide—producing neurons that
normally induce lower esophageal sphincter relaxation. Degenerative changes in the extraesophageal
vagus nerve or the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus may also occur.

2. Secondary achalasia: It may arise in Chagas disease, in which Trypanosoma cruzi infection causes
destruction of the myenteric plexus, failure of peristalsis, and esophageal dilation.

Clinical features:

Dysphagia (difficulty in swallowing) for solids and liquids
Putrid breath

High LES pressure on esophageal manometry

‘Bird-beak’ sign on barium swallow study

Increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma

eS SS =

Treatment: Treatments for both primary and secondary achalasia aim to overcome the obstruction and include-
* Laparoscopic myotomy
Pneumatic balloon dilatation
* Botulinum neurotixin (Botox) injection (to inhibit contraction-promoting cholinergic neurons).
(Ref: Robbins/10°/757; BRS Pathology/5"/228; Pathoma/2014/102; Harsh Mohan/7"/521)

Q. What is oesophagitis? Give some examples.
Ans.

Oesophagitis: Inflammation of the oesophageal mucosa is known as oesophagitis.

Examples:
a. Lacerations (Mallory-Weiss tear)

b. Chemical and infectious oesophagitis (e.g. by alcohol, corrosive acids or alkalis, excessive hot fluids,
heavy smoking, radiation therapy etc.)
c. Reflux oesophagitis / gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
d. Eosinophilic oesophagitis (atopic)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/758)

Q. What is Malloy-Weiss syndrome? (Important for VIVA)

#### 📄 Page 147

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 147

TT
Malloy-Weiss syndrome: Longitudinal mucosal tears near the gastroesophageal junction are termed
Mallory-Weiss tears, and are most often associated with severe retching or vomiting secondary to acute
alcohol intoxication.

The patient presents with painful hematemesis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/758)

Q. Short note: Reflux oesophagitis /GERD. (Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Reflux esophagitis: Reflux of gastric acid into the lower esophagus duc to reduced lower esophageal
sphincter tone is termed as gastro-esophageal reflux disease (GERD).
Or,
GERD is the reflux of gastric contents into the lower esophagus.

{N.B: It is the opposite of achalasia, where LES (lower esophageal sphincter) tone is increased}.

Causes: Conditions that decrease LES tone or increase abdominal pressure contribute to GERD:
1. Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation (mediated via vagal pathways)
2. Abrupt increases in intra-abdominal pressure (c.g. after coughing, straining, or bending)
3. Other conditions that are associated with GERD include:

Alcohol and tobacco use

Obesity

Fat-rich diet

Caffeine

Centralnervous system depressants

Pregnancy

Hiatal hernia

Delayed gastric emptying

Increased gastric volume.

Clinical features of GERD: Typical symptoms include-
1, Heartburn (mimics cardiac chest pain, which may be mistaken for ischemic heart disease)
2. Dysphagia
3. Regurgitation of sour-tasting gastric contents (most often postprandially)
4. Asthma (adult-onset) and cough
5. Damage to enamel of teeth.

Treatment: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).

Complications:
1, Esophagitis
2. Esophageal ulceration with stricture
3. Barrett esophagus (columnar metaplasia of esophageal squamous epithelium).

tology:

1. Mild GERD: Simple hyperemia, evidenced by redness.

2. More significant gastric reflux is associated with erosions and influx of eosinophils into the
squamous mucosa. Basal zone hyperplasia and elongation of lamina propria papillae are also
common. Neutrophil infiltration is less frequent and is generally associated with bacterial or fungal

infection or chemical damage.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/759; BRS Pathology/5"/228; Pathoma/2014/102)

Q. Short note: Hiatal hernia.
Ans.

Hiatal hernia: Hiatus hemia is the herniation or protrusion of part of the stomach through the oesophageal
hiatus of the diaphragm.

It may cause lower esophageal sphincter incompetence and symptoms that are similar to GERD but it is
symptomatic in fewer than 10% of adults.

Anatomical types: There are 3 patterns in hiatus hernia-
1. Sliding or oesophago-gastric hernia (most common, occurring in 85% of cases): The herniated part
of the stomach appears as supra-diaphragmatic bell due to sliding up on both sides of the oesophagus

2. Rolling or para-oesophageal hernia (10% of cases): This is a true hernia in which cardiac end of the
stomach rolls up para-oesophageally, producing an intrathoracic sac.

3. Mixed or transitional hernia constitutes the remaining 5% cases in which there is combination of
sliding and rolling hiatus hernia.

Fig: Patterns of hiatus hernia.

« Heartbum (retrosternal burning sensation)
= Regurgitation of gastric juice into the mouth.

Both of above features are worsened due to heavy work, lifting weights and excessive bending

= Ulceration

* Bleeding
* Perforation
= Reflux esophagitis (more associated with sliding hernias).

(Ref: Robbins/10°/760; Harsh Mohan/7*/521)

Q. What is Barrett esophagus? (CU-19M) Mention its clinical importance. (DU-08Ju)

Q. Explain Barrett’s esophagus. (CU-18Nv)

Q. Short note: Barrett esophagus. (DU-06S/Ja, CMU-21Nv,20M) (Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Barrett esophagus: Barrett esophagus is a long-standing complication of chronic gastro-esophageal reflux
disease (GERD) that is characterized by intestinal metaplasia within the esophageal squamous mucosa and
is associated with an increased risk of cancer.

It is the single most important risk factors for esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Incidence: It is estimated to occur in as many as 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Peak age is
40-60 years of age.

Pathogenesis: In Barrett esophagus, the distal squamous epithelium is replaced by metastatic columner
epithelium as a response to prolonged injury.

Barrett’s oesophagus is a premalignant condition evolving sequentially-from Barrett’s epithelium
(columnar metaplasia with goblet cells) to dysplasia to carcinoma in situ and finally to oesophageal
adenocarcinoma.

Fig: Barret’s esophagus.

---

#### 📄 Page 150

150 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Morphology /pathologv:
Macroscopic features:
* A red, velvety mucosa located between smooth, pale pink esophageal squamous mucosa and light.
brown gastric mucosa
= It may exist as tongues or patches (islands).

Microscopic features:
* The most common finding is the replacement of squamous epithelium by metaplastic columnar
cells, along with goblet cells (definitive diagnosis)
* Intestinal metaplasia may be accompanied by dysplastic changes of the columnar cpithelium or
glands (ranging from low to high grade)
= Inflammatory changes, acute or chronic, are commonly accompanied.

Diagnosis: 2 criteria are required for diagnosis of Barret esophagus-
= Endoscopic evidence of metaplastic columnar mucosa above the gastroesophageal junction

* Histologic evidence of intestinal-type metaplasia in biopsy specimen showing replacement of the
squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells.

Reatment options:
= Surgical resection

* Esophagectomy
Newer modalities such as photodynamic therapy, laser ablation, and endoscopic mucosectomy
* Follow-up with endoscopy and biopsy at regular intervals.

Complications:
1. Local ulceration with bleeding and stricture.

2. Esophageal adenocarcinoma.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/761; Harsh Mohan/7"/523)

Q. Mention the diagnostic criteria of Barrett esophagus.
Ans.
Diagnostic criteria of Barrett esophagus: Two criteria are required for the diagnosis of Barrett esophagus-

1. Endoscopic evidence of metaplastic columnar mucosa above the gastroesophageal junction

2. Histologic evidence of intestinal-type metaplasia in biopsy specimen showing replacement of the
squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells.

(N.B: Goblet cells are diagnostic of Barrett esophagus and have distinct mucous vacuoles that stain pale
blue and impart the shape of a wine goblet to the remaining cytoplasm).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/761)

Q. Mention the risk factors of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Q. Write down the etiopathogenesis of squamous cell carcinoma of esophagus.

Ans.

Risk factors of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma occurs in adults
older than age 45 and affects males four times more frequently than females. Risk factors include-

1. Dietary:

= Deficiency of vitamins (A, C, B2, thiamin, Be)
Deficiency of trace elements (Zn, Mo)
Deficiency of fruits or vegetables
High content of nitrites / nitrosamines
Betel chewing

2. Tite style:

Poverty

Frequent consumption of very hot beverages
Fungus-contaminated foods

Alcohol consumption

Tobacco use

3. Esophageal disorder:

Caustic esophageal injury
Achalasia

Tylosis

Hiatus hernia

Diverticula
Plummer-Vinson syndrome

4. Genetic predisposition:
= Long standing coeliac disease
= Ectodermal dysplasia
= Epidermolysis bullosa
= Racial disposition (more common in African American)

5. Previous radiation to the mediastinum (5 to 10 or more years after exposure).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/763,764; Lecture SSMC)

Q. Mention the sites of esophageal cancer. (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Sites of esophageal cancer:
= Squamous cell carcinoma arises most frequently in the upper and middle thirds of the esophagus.

= Adenocarcinoma arises most frequently in the lower third of the esophagus.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/762,763; BRS Pathology/5"/229; Pathoma/2014/103)

Q. Write down the morphologic patterns of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Ans.

Morphologic patterns of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: Three morphologic patterns are described-

1. Protruded (60%): A polypoid, or exophytic lesion that protrudes into and obstruct the lumen.

2. Flat (15%): An ulcerated or diffusely infiltrative lesion spread within the wall of the esophagus,
causing thickening, rigidity, and luminal narrowing.

3. Excavated (25%): Tumors may invade surrounding structures including the respiratory tree
(causing pneumonia), the aorta (causing catastrophic exsanguination), or the mediastinum and
pericardium.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/764)

NORMAL STRUCTURE:

The stomach is ‘gland with cavity’, extending from its junction with lower end of the oesophagus (cardia) to
its junction with the duodenum (pylorus). The lesser curvature is inner concavity on the right, while the
greater curvature is the outer convexity on the left side of the stomach.

The stomach has 5 anatomical regions:

1.

gr Se bs

Cardia is the oesophagogastric junction and lacks the sphincter.

Fundus is the portion above the horizontal line drawn across the oesophagogastric junction.
Body is the middle portion of the stomach between the fundus and the pyloric antrum.
Pyloric antrum is the distal third of the stomach.

Pylorus is the junction of distal end of the stomach with the duodenum. It has powerful sphincter
muscle.

Fig: Anatomical subdivisions of the stomach.

Q. Define gastritis. Mention its types and causes.
Q. Define chronic gastritis. (SU-10Ju) Write down the pathogenesis and clinical features of

gastritis. (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Gastritis: Gastritis is simply defined as inflammation of the gastric mucosa.

Types of gastritis:

1. Acute gastritis: Acidic damage to the stomach mucosa due to imbalance between mucosal defenses
and acidic environment. Acid damage results in superficial inflammation, mucosal erosion (loss of
superficial epithelium), or ulcer (loss of mucosal layer).

Causes / risk factors: Acute gastritis is frequently associated with-
= Heavy use of NSAIDs, particularly aspirin
® Excessive alcohol consumption
» Ingestion of harsh chemicals, particularly acids or bases, either accidentally or as a suicide
attempt
Heavy smoking
Radiation therapy
Chemotherapy
Stress-related mucosal diseases
- Stress ulcers — in the setting of shock, sepsis, or severe trauma
- Curling ulcer — in the context of severe bums or trauma
- Cushing ulcer — in association with intracranial disease / brain injury
Systemic bacterial or viral infections (e.g. salmonellosis, CMV infection)
Mechanical trauma (e.g. nasogastric intubation)
Distal gastrectomy
Decreased oxygen delivery at high altitude.

---

#### 📄 Page 156

Clinical features:

May be asymptomatic

Epigastric pain

Nausea

Vomiting

Mucosal erosion

Ulceration

Hemorthage

Hematemesis

Malena

Rarely massive blood loss.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/765; BRS Pathology/5"/230; Pathoma/2014/104)

2. Chronic gastritis: Chronic gastritis is characterized by chronic mucosal inflammation and atrophy
of the mucosal glands.

In contrast to acute gastritis, the symptoms associated with chronic gastritis are typically less severe
but more persistent.

Causes / risk factors: Chronic gastritis is frequently associated with-

b.

H. pylori infection

Autoimmune gastritis

Radiation injury

Chronic bile reflux

Mechanical injury (e.g. an indwelling nasogastric tube)

Systemic diseases, such as Crohn disease, amyloidosis, or graft-versus-host disease.

: Divided into two types based on underlying etiology-

H. pylori gastritis: It is due to H. pylori induced acute and chronic inflammation. It is the
most common form of gastritis (90%). The antrum is the most commonly infected site for
H. pylori gastritis.

Clinical features: Epigastric abdominal pain.

Sequelae:
= Peptic ulcer disease (PUD)
* Gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type)
= MALT lymphoma (MALToma)

Treatment: Triple therapy (combinations of antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors).

Autoimmune atrophic gastritis: It is due to autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal
cells, which are located in the stomach body and fundus. It is associated with the presence of
antibodies to gastric parietal cells and/or intrinsic factor, followed by vitamin By,
deficiency and defective gastric acid secretion (achlorhydria).

Median age at diagnosis is 60 (slightly more women than men are affected).

Clinical features: Clinical features are mainly related to vitamin B,2 deficiency, including-
* Pemicious anemia (a form of megaloblastic anemia)

Atrophic glossitis (in which the tongue becomes smooth and beefy red)

Epithelial megaloblastosis

Malabsorptive diarrhea

CNS features of vitamin B,2 deficiency (e.g. subacute combined degeneration of spinal

cord

*  Itis often associated with other autoimmune diseases including Hashimoto thyroiditis,
type | diabetes mellitus, Addison disease etc.

Q. What is the role of H. pylori in the pathogenesis of peptic ulcer? (CU-12Ja, SU-
13Ju,11/Ja,08Ju)

Q. H. pylori does not invade the tissue, but it can cause peptic ulcer. Explain. (DU-08Ju)

Ans

Role of H. pylori in the pathogenesis of peptic ulcer: (Important for VIVA)

1. Although H. pylori do not invade the tissues, it induces an intense inflammatory and immune
response and liberates proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, IL-8 and tumour necrosis factor-
a (TNF-a).

2. It secretes urease enzyme that breaks down urea to form toxin compounds such as ammonium chloride
and monochloramine.

3. Bacterial proteases and phospholipases breakdown the glycoprotein-lipid complexes in the gastric
mucus, thus weakening the first line mucosal defense.

4. It enhances gastric acid secretion and impairs duodenal bicarbonate production.

---

#### 📄 Page 162

162 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

5. Thrombotic occlusion of surface capillaries is promoted by bacterial platelet activating factor.
6. Bacterial antigens (including lipopolysaccharide) recruit inflammatory cells to the mucosa.

(N.B: H. pylori infection most often presents as a predominantly antral gastritis with normal or increased
acid production.)

Fig: Damaging effects of H. Pylori in stomach.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/767)

Ans.
Clinical features of peptic ulcer disease: Peptic ulcers are remitting and relapsing lesions.
1. Periodic epigastric pain - burning or aching pain {in gastric ulcer, pain occurs immediately or within
1 to 3 hours after food during the day and never occurs at night. In duodenal ulcer, pain is severe,
occurs at late night (usually between 11 p.m. and 2 a.m.) (‘hunger pain’), and is usually relieved by
alkali or food}.

2. Nausea, vomiting, bloating, belching, heart-burn (retrosternal pain) and ‘water brash’ (burning
fluid into the mouth)

Anorexia and early satiety after meals

Weight loss in gastric ulcer patients & weight gain in duodenal ulcer patients
Haematemesis and melaena

Iron deficiency anemia

7. Acute perforation.

Awe &

Q. Short note: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). (DU-21Ja,20Nv/M)
Ans.
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST): Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) are mesenchyma|

tumors derived from the interstitial cells of Cajal, or pacemaker cells of the gastrointestinal muscularis
propria.

It is the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen, with annual incidences between 11 and 20 per
million people.

Age of incidence: GISTs are diagnosed at a peak age of 60 years, with fewer than 10% occurring before 4)
years of age.

Site of occurrence: More than half of these tumors occur in the stomach.They can also occur in the small
intestine, large intestine, and extragastrointestinal sites.

Behaviour: Their behaviour is generally benign but may be recurrent, aggressive or even metastasis may
occur.

Genetic mutation:

= c-kit oncogene (CD117) - detected by immunohistochemistry from Cajal cells
* Platelet-derived growth factor receptor-a (PDGFRA)

Morphology:
Gross:
= Primary gastric GISTs can reach 30 cm in diameter.
= They usually form a solitary, well-circumscribed, fleshy mass.
* The overlying mucosa is frequently ulcerated, and the cut tumor surface has a whorled appearance.

Microscopic:
= GISTs composed of thin elongated cells are classified as spindle cell type, while GISTs dominated by

plumper, epithelial-appearing cells are termed epithelioid type; mixtures of the two patterns are
common.

Symptoms:

* Mass effects
* Mucosal ulceration causing blood loss leading to anemia or related symptoms.

Diagnosis: GISTs may be discovered incidentally during radiologic imaging, endoscopy, or abdominal surgery
performed for other reasons.

Treatment:

* Complete surgical resection (primary treatment for localized GIST)
Targeted therapy / tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib) - which inhibits the tyrosine kinase activity of c-
kit and PDGFRA.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/779; BRS Pathology/5"/232; Harsh Mohan/7"/538)

Morphology of gastric carcinoma:

Gross / macroscopic: The three macroscopic growth patterns of gastric carcinoma, which may be evident at
both the early and advanced stages, are-

1. Exophytic: Protrusion of tumor mass into the lumen.
2. Flat or depressed: No obvious tumor mass is visible within the mucosa.
3. Excavated: Shallow or deep ulcer present in the wall of the stomach.

When there are large areas of infiltration, diffuse rugal flattening and a rigid, thickened wall may impart a
“leather bottle” appearance termed linitis plastica.

Microscopic:
a. Intestinal type: More common.
- Expanding growth pattern
- Bulky tumors, composed of columnar, gland-forming cells
- Abundant mucin may be present in gland lumens

b. Diffuse type:
- Infiltrative growth pattern
- Composed of signet-ring cells (that diffusely infiltrate the gastric mucosa)
- Excessive mucin production.

Fig: Morphology of gastric carcinoma.
(Note: A. Early gastric carcinoma; B. Advanced gastric carcinoma)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/775)

Linitis plastica: When there are large areas of infiltration, diffuse rugal flattening and a rigid, thickened wall
may impart a “leather bottle” appearance termed linitis plastica.
Or,
Linitis plastica is an extreme form of flat or depressed advanced gastric carcinoma.

Meckel Diverticulum

Meckel diverticulum: It is the blind outpouching of all three layers of the bowel wall (true diverticulum)
arises due to incomplete obliteration of vitellointestinal duct.

The most common congenital anomaly of the GI tract is Meckel diverticulum, which occurs in the ileum.

Characteristics: The “rule of 2s” is often used to help remember characteristics of Meckel diverticula, which:

* Occur in approximately 2% of the population

Are generally present within 2 feet (60 cm) of the ileocecal valve

Are approximately 2 inches (5 cm) long

Are twice as common in males

Are most often symptomatic by age 2 (only approximately 4% are ever symptomatic).

gastric mucosa and ectopic pancreatic tissue.

Complications: The common complications of Meckel’s diverticulum are perforation, haemorrhage and
diverticulitis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/755; Pathoma/2014/106; Harsh Mohan/7"/544)

Disorder of Intestinal Motility (Megacolon)

Q. What is megacolon? (CMU-22Nv)

Q. Short note: Megacolon.

Ans.

Megacolon: The term ‘megacolon’ is used for any form of marked dilatation of the entire colon or its
segment.

Types & causes:
1. Congenital:

a) Hirschsprung’s disease (common): Characterised by congenital absence of ganglion cells in the
bowel wall (enteric neurons) is called Hirschsprung’s disease. As a result, the aganglionic segment
remains contracted.

b) Myopathies, neuropathies (rare).

2. Acquired:
a) Obstructive: e.g. due to tumour, post-inflammatory strictures.

b) Endocrine: e.g. in myxoedema, cretinism.
c) CNS disorders: e.g. spina bifida, paraplegia, Parkinsonism etc.
d) Psychogenic: e.g. emotional disturbances, psychiatric disorders etc.
e) Connective tissue disease: e.g. Scleroderma.
f) Chagas’ disease: It is (by Trypanosoma cruzi) the only example resulting in acquired loss of
ganglion cells. In all other acquired causes listed above, the bowel innervation is normal.
(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/563, 564)

Hirschsprung Disease / Congenital Aganglionic Megacolon

Q. Short note: Hirschsprung disease. (DU-12Ju, CU-15Ja) (For VIVA)

Ans.

Hirschsprung disease / congenital aganglionic megacolon: It is a congenital disease caused by absence of
ganglion cells in the nerve plexus (Meissner’s & Auerbach’s plexus) usually of the distal hind gut with hypertrophy
of nerve fiber.

---

#### 📄 Page 175

SS —= — -——==
Hirschsprung disease causes functional obstruction of the colon. It occurs in pproximately | in 5000 live
births.

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 175

Pathogenesis: Hirschsprung disease results when the migration of neural crest cells from cecum to rectum
is arrested prematurely or when the ganglion cells undergo premature death. This produces a distal
intestinal segment that lacks both the Meissner submucosal plexus and the Auerbach myenteric plexus,
termed aganglionosis. Coordinated peristaltic contractions are absent, and functional obstruction occurs,
resulting in dilation proximal to the affected segment.

Sites:
~~ © Inabout 2/3" cases, rectum and sigmoid colon are involved
* Ano-rectal junction
* Recto-sigmoid junction
* Whole colon
s

Very rarely, portion of terminal ileum.

Fig: Hirschsprung disease showing constricted rectum and dilation of the sigmoid colon.

Clinical features: Clinical features vary from acute intestinal obstruction in neonate to chronic constipation in
later life.
1. In neonate:
* Failure to pass meconium
= Abdominal distension
* Bilious vomiting

2. In chronic presentation (in 1° few weeks of life):
= Chronic intermittent constipation
* Gradual abdominal distension
* Failure to thrive

3. In adult:
* Severe constipation.

Investigations:
s Plain x-ray abdomen

Barium enema x-ray
Rectal suction biopsy (reveals lack of ganglion cells)
Anorectal manometry.

(N.B: Diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease requires histologic confirmation that ganglion cells are absent
within the affected segment.)

Treatment: Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment and anastomosis of the normal proximal colon to
the rectum.

Enterocolitis

Intestinal obstruction

Fluid and electrolyte disturbances
Growth retardation

Malabsorption & Diarrhoea

Q. What is malabsorption syndrome? List five causes of malabsorption syndrome. (DU-
16Ja,14Ju)

Q. Short note: Malabsorption syndrome. (For VIVA)

Ans.

Malabsorption syndrome: Malabsorption is characterized by defective absorption of fats, fat- and water-
soluble vitamins, proteins, carbohydrates, electrolytes and minerals, and water,

A hallmark of malabsorption is steatorrhea, characterized by excessive fecal fat and bulky, frothy, greasy,
yellow or clay-colored stools.

Five important causes of malabsorption syndrome:

Pancreatic insufficiency

Celiac disease

Tropical sprue

Crohn disease

Cystic fibrosis

Primary bile acid malabsorption

Autoimmune enteropathy

Disaccharidase deficiency

Intestinal graft-versus-host disease (after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation).

VeWawsS Sve

Symptoms:
1. General symptoms:
* Diarthea, flatus, abdominal pain, weight loss, and muscle wasting
* Anorexia, abdominal distention, and borborygmi

2. Symptoms due to inadequate absorption of vitamins and minerals:
* Anemia and mucositis (due to pyridoxine, folate, or vitamin B,2 deficiency)
Bleeding (due to vitamin K deficiency)
Osteopenia and tetany (due to calcium, magnesium, or vitamin D deficiencies)
Peripheral neuropathy (due to vitamin A or B,2 deficiencies)
Endocrine and skin disturbances e.g. goiter and vitiligo (due to nutrient, micronutrient, and
vitamin deficiencies).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/783)

Q. Define and classify diarrhoea.

Ans.
Diarrhoea: Diarrhoea is defined as an increase in stool mass, frequency, or fluidity, typically greater than
200 gm per day. In severe cases stool volume can exceed 14 L per day and, without fluid resuscitation, result

in death.
(N.B: Painful, bloody, small-volume diarrhea is known as dysentery.)
Both nutrient malabsorption and increased secretion of fluid by the intestine may contribute to diarrhea.

Classification of diarrhoea: Diarrhoea can be classified into four major categories-
1. Secretory diarrhoea is characterized by isotonic stool and persists during fasting.

---

#### 📄 Page 177

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY 177

2 Osmotic diarrhoea, such as occurs with lactase deficiency, is due to the excessive osmotic forces
exerted by unabsorbed luminal solutes. The diarrhoea fluid is more than 50 mOsm more concentrated
than plasma, and diarrhea abates with fasting.

X Malabsorptive diarrhoea follows generalized failure of nutrient absorption, is associated with
steatorrhea, and is relieved by fasting.

4 Exudative diarrhoea duc to inflammatory disease is characterized by purulent, often bloody stools
that continue during fasting.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/784)

Q What is celiac disease?

Ans.

Celiac disease: Celiac disease (also known as celiac sprue or glutensensitive enteropathy) is an immune-
mediated disorder triggered by the ingestion of gluten-containing foods, such as wheat, rye, or barley, in

genetically predisposed individuals.

The malabsorptive diarrhea in celiac disease is due to loss of brush border surface area, including villous
atrophy, and, possibly, deficient enterocyte maturation as a result of immune-mediated epithelial damage.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/784,787)
