Infectious Enterocolitis

Q. Write about pseudomembranous colitis.

Ans.

Pseudomembranous colitis: Pseudomembranous colitis is generally caused by Clostridioides (formerly
Clostridium) difficile and is also referred to as antibiotic-associated colitis or antibiotic-associated
Giarrhea.

(N.B: While other organisms such as Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens type A, or Staphylococcus aureus
may also produce diarrhea in the context of antibiotic therapy, only C. difficile causes pseudomembranous

This condition is morphologically distinguished by superficial grayish mucosal exudates consisting of
necrotic, loosely adherent mucosal debris (pseudomembrane).

Cause: Overgrowth of exotoxin-producing Clostridium difficile.

Risk factors: Risk factors for C. difficile-associated colitis include-
* Antibiotic treatment

---

178 arif’s re resentation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

» Advanced age
« Hospitalization
* Immunosuppression.

Clinical features: Individuals with C. difficile-associated colitis present with-
= Fever

Leukocytosis

Abdominal pain

Cramps

Watery diarrhea

Dehydration.

Diagnosis: The diagnosis is usually made by detection of C. difficile toxin, rather than by culture, and js
supported by the characteristic histopathology.

Morphology: Mucopurulent exudate that characteristically erupts from damaged crypts to form “volcano”
lesions and coalesces to form pseudomembranes.

Treatment: Metronidazole and vancomycin.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/793; BRS Pathology/5""/237)

Q. Write about Whipple Disease.

Ans.

Whipple Disease: It is a rare, multi-visceral chronic disease characterized by macrophages loaded with
Tropheryma whippelii organisms.

Clinical presentation: The clinical presentation of Whipple disease is usually a triad of diarrhea, weight loss,
and arthralgia. Extraintestinal symptoms may precede malabsorption by months or years and include arthritis;
arthralgia; fever; lymphadenopathy; and neurologic, cardiac, or pulmonary disease.

Morphologic features: Distinctive PAS-positive macrophages in intestinal mucosa; Tropheryma whippelii
bacilli visualized by electron microscopy.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/794; Pathoma/2014/108; BRS Pathology/5""/234)

(N.B: Clinical symptoms occur because bacteria-laden macrophages accumulate within the small intestinal
lamina propria and mesenteric lymph nodes, causing lymphatic obstruction. Thus, the malabsorptive

diarrhea of Whipple disease is due to impaired lymph drainage.)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/794)

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)

Q. What do you mean by IBS? (SU-17M)

Ans.

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Imitable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder
characterized by chronic, relapsing abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits.

The peak prevalence of IBS is between 20 and 40 years of age, and there is a significant female
predominance.

Types: It should be recognized that IBS is a syndrome and that multiple illnesses may be represented under
this global descriptor. IBS is currently divided (as defined by successive revisions of the Rome criteria) into:

1. Diarrhea-predominant IBS

2. Constipation-predominant IBS

3. Mixed subtypes.

---

#### 📄 Page 179

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 179

Diagnosis: Despite very real symptoms, the endoscopic and microscopic evaluations arc normal in [BS
panents. Thus, the diagnosis depends on clinical symptoms and functional testing.

IBS is presently diagnosed using clinical criteria that require the occurrence of abdominal pain or
discomfort at least 3 days per month over 3 months with improvement following defecation and a change in
stool frequency or form.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/798)

Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)

Q. What is inflammatory bowel disease? (DU-11Ju) Describe the pathogenesis of inflammatory
bowel disease.
Q. Name the inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). (DU-24Nv,23M, RU-20M, 1 2Ja)
Q. Short note: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). (RU-17M,09Ja)
Ans.
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic condition resulting from
complex interactions between intestinal microbiota and host immunity in genetically predisposed
individuals that leads to inappropriate mucosal immune activation.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/798)

The two disorders that comprise IBD are ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease.

Ulcerative colitis involves only the colon and rectum and is generally limited to the mucosa and
submucosa. In contrast, Crohn disease, which has also been referred to as regional enteritis (because of
frequent ileal involvement) may involve any area of the GI tract and is typically transmural.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/799)

Etiology and pathogenesis: IBD results from a combination of abnormalities in immune regulation, host-
microbe interactions, and epithelial barrier functions in genetically susceptible individuals.

The genetic and environmental elements that contribute to disease:

1. Mucosal immunity: A plethora of immune signaling and regulatory genes including those encoding
HLA molecules and cytokines have been associated with IBD.

2. Autophagy and cellular stress responses: Genetic associations and molecular analyses indicate that
defects in autophagy and cellular stress responses contribute to IBD pathogenesis.

3. Host-microbial interactions: The gut microbiome (composed of bacteria, fungi, and viruses) can
modulate mucosal immunity. Conversely, the immune system can markedly alter the microbiome by
mechanisms that include luminal secretion of antimicrobial peptides and antibacterial IgA. This

interplay between microbes and the immune system may contribute to IBD pathogenesis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/799)

N ow:

Autophagy: Autophagy is a normal homeostatic mechanism that clears damaged organelles and is
upregulated in response to cellular stress including nutrient deprivation and endoplasmic reticulum stress.

Autophagy is also a means of clearing sources of reactive oxygen species and intracellular pathogens.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/800)

Q. Why Crohn’s disease & ulcerative colitis are considered idiopathic disease?

Ans.

Crohn’s disease & ulcerative colitis are considered idiopathic disease: The basis of the abnormalities
involved in the pathogenesis of IBD is still not established, that is why both ulcerative colitis & Crohn’s
disease are considered idiopathic disease.

Q. Write down morphology of Crohn’s disease.
Q. Mention three important features of Crohn’s disease. (DU-17Ja)
Q. Shot note: Crohn’s disease. (SU-20M,09Ja)

Ans.

Crohn’s disease: Crohn’s disease is a form of inflammatory bowel disease, which has also been referred to as
regional enteritis, commonly affects the terminal ileum, ileocecal valve, and cecum but may occur in any
area of the GI tract from the mouth to anus and is typically transmural.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/799,800)

Pathogenesis: The prime culprits appear to be T cells particularly CD4+ T cells and their products. Crohn's
disease appears to be the results of delayed type hypersensitivity reaction induced by IFN-y & TNF-a produced
by Ty cells.

Clinical features:

A. Intestinal manifestations:

Non-bloody diarrhoea, fever, abdominal pain
Weight loss

Iron deficiency anemia

Fibrosing strictures

Fistulae

Perforations

Peritoneal abscesses.

B. ee manifestations:

Migratory polyarthnitis
Uveitis

Sarcoiliitis

Ankylosing spondylitis
Erythema nodosum
Cutaneous granulomas
Clubbing of the fingertips
Pericholangitis

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Morphology:
Macroscopic:

Site of involvement: Any portion of the GI tract (from mouth to anus), but the most common sites
are terminal ilium and colon.

Distribution: Multiple, separate, sharply delineated areas (skip lesion).

Wall: Inflammation occurs in all layers, down to the serosa. This predisposes to strictures,
fistulas and adhesions.

Lumen: The lumen is narrowed which appears on X-ray as ‘string sign’. The mucosa shows
‘serpiginous ulcers’, while intervening surviving mucosa is swollen giving ‘cobblestone
appearance’.

Mesenteric fat: Frequently extends around the serosal surface (creeping fat).

Microscopic:

Non-caseating granulomas (a hallmark of Crohn disease)

Transmural infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells and
macrophages)

Distortion of mucosal architecture with loss of crypt epithelium

Patchy ulceration (which may take the form of deep fissures)

Epithelial metaplasia.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/800; Lecture SSMC)

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 181

Serpaginous vicers
Cobbiestone-like mucosa

Fig: Crohn’s disease of the terminal ileum.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/801; Harsh Mohan/7"/548; Lecture SSMC)

Q. Shot note: Ulcerative colitis.
Ans.
Ulcerative colitis: Ulcerative colitis is a severe ulcerating inflammatory bowel disease that is limited to the
colon and rectum (most common site) and is generally limited to the mucosa and submucosa.
(Ref: Robbins/10°/799,801)

Clinical features:
A. Intestinal manifestations:
* Bloody diarrhoea with stringy mucoid material
= Urgency
* Tenesmus
= Lower abdominal pain and cramps that are temporarily relieved by defecation.

B. Extra-intestinal manifestations:

Migratory polyarthritis

Uveitis

Sarcoiliitis

Ankylosing spondylitis

Skin lesions (e.g. pyoderma gangrenosum)
Pericholangitis

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.

(N.B: Arthritis is the most common extra-intestinal feature in both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.)

Morphology:
Macroscopic:
= Continuous involvement of rectum and colon without any uninvolved skip areas
Red, raw colonic mucosa that bleeds easily
Mucosa shows linear and superficial ulcers, with preservation of adjacent mucosa which has the
appearance of polyps (‘pseudopolyps’), and the tips of these polyps may fuse to create mucosal
bridges
* Chronic disease may lead to mucosal atrophy with a smooth mucosal surface that lacks normal folds
Unlike Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis is not transmural, as a result-

- Colonic wall is not thickened
- Serosal surface is normal
- Strictures do not occur

Microscopic:
* Diffuse inflammation limited to the mucosa and superficial submucosa
* Inflammatory infiltrates in lamina propria
* Crypt abscesses
* Crypt distortion

= Depletion of goblet cells and mucin from gland epithelium

= Granulomas are not present.
(Ref: Robbins/10'°/801-803; Harsh Mohan/7"/548; Lecture DMC, MMC)

Q. Short note: Carcinoid tumour. (DU-03Ja, SU-14Ju) (For VIVA)

Ans.
Carcinoid tumor: The term carcinoid is named as the tumor resembles a carcinoma-like lesion, but with a
much more indolent clinical course.

It is the malignant proliferation of neuroendocrine cells. Although characteristically slow growing, these
tumors are of low-grade malignancy and may metastasize.

When metastatic to the liver, neuroendocrine tumors can lead to carcinoid syndrome which is caused by the
elaboration of vasoactive peptides and amines, especially serotonin.

1. Appendix
2. Terminal ileum f (enos anit
3. Rectum
4. Colon

* Small, polypoid or plateau-like elevations rarely more than 3 cm in diameter.

Q. Short note: Carcinoid syndrome. (CU-09Ja) (For VIVA)

Ans.

Carcinoid syndrome: The term ‘carcinoid syndrome’ refers to the systemic symptoms produced when
vasoactive substances (serotonin) enters into systemic circulation from the carcinoid tumour.

Mechanism: Metastasis of carcinoid tumour to the liver allows serotonin to bypass liver metabolism.
Serotonin is released into the hepatic vein and leaks into systemic circulation via hepato-systemic shunts,
resulting in carcinoid syndrome.

Clinical features:

(a) Cutaneous flushing

(b) Watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps

(c) Bronchospasm

(d) Valvular lesions of the right side of the heart.

Symptoms can be triggered by alcohol or emotional stress, which stimulate serotonin release from the
tumour.

(Ref: Robbins/7"/868; Pathoma/2014/109; BRS Pathology/5"/235; Harsh Mohan/7"/560)

Q. Mention important predisposing factors for colorectal carcinoma.

Ans.

Colorectal carcinoma: Colorectal carcinoma (adenocarcinoma) is the most common malignancy of the GI
tract. This represent nearly 15% of all cancer related deaths, and is second only to lung cancer.

Predisposing factors for colorectal carcinoma:
1. Age: Incidence peaks at 60 to 70 years of age, and fewer than 20% of cases occur before age 50.
2. Sex: Males are affected slightly more often than female.
3. Dietary factors:
* Low intake of unabsorbable vegetable fiber
= High intake of refined carbohydrates and fat
4. Geographic variations
5. Obesity

Q. Mention role of diatery factors for causation of colon cancer. (RU-13Ju)
Ans.

Role of diatery factors for causation of colon cancer: The dietary factors most closely associated with

increased colorectal cancer rates are-

* Low intake of unabsorbable vegetable fiber and
* High intake of refined carbohydrates and fat.

---

#### 📄 Page 186

186 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Although these associations are clear, the mechanistic relationship between diet and risk remains poorly
understood. However, it is theorized that reduced fiber content leads to decreased stool bulk and altered
composition of the intestinal microbiota. This change may increase synthesis of potentially toxic oxidative by-
products of bacterial metabolism, which would be expected to remain in contact with the colonic mucosa for
longer periods of time as a result of reduced stool bulk.

Deficiencies of vitamins A, C, and E, which act as free-radical scavengers, may compound damage caused by
oxidants. High fat intake enhances the hepatic synthesis of cholesterol and bile acids, which can be converted
into carcinogens by intestinal bacteria.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/814)

Q. Write down the pathogenesis of colorectal carcinoma. (CMU-21M)

Ans.

Pathogenesis of colorectal carcinoma:

1. APC mutation/p-catenin mechanism:
= Loss of tumour suppressor APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene (80% cases of sporadic colon

cancer). Since the function of APC gene is linked to B-catenin, loss of APC gene results in
translocation of B-catenin to the nucleus where it activates transcription of other genes, mainly
MYC and cyclin D1, both of which stimulate cell proliferation.

= Point mutation in K-RAS gene follows loss of APC gene (seen in 10 to 50% cases of adenoma-
carcinoma).

= Deletion of DCC gene (60-70% cases of colon cancer).
= Loss of p53 tumour suppressor gene (70-80% cases of colon cancer).

2. Microsatellite instability (MSI) mechanism: This pathway accounts for 10-15% cases of colon
cancer. Basic mutation is loss of DNA repair gene. This results in a situation in which repetitive DNA
sequences (i.e. microsatellites) become unstable during replication cycle, termed microsatellite
instability (MSI), which is the hallmark of this pathway.

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7°/588)

2. Lymph node involvement
* Total number of lymph nodes examined
* Number of positive lymph nodes (important for staging)
* Presence of extranodal extension

3. Resection margins
* Proximal and distal margins (whether free of tumor)

Liver Failure

Q. Mention the clinical features and complications of liver failure.

Q. Short note: Liver failure.

Ans.

Liver failure: The most severe form of liver disease is liver failure, which may be acute (due to sudden and
massive hepatic destruction) or (more commonly) chronic, following years of insidious, progressive liver injury.

In some cases, individuals with chronic liver disease develop acute-on-chronic liver failure, in which an
unrelated acute injury is superimposed on late-stage chronic disease or there is a “flare” of the chronic
disease that leads to liver decompensation.

Whatever the sequence, 80% to 90% of functional capacity must be lost before hepatic failure appears.

5. Palmar erythema (a reflection of local vasodilatation)

6. Spider angiomas of the skin

7. In male - hypogonadism and gynecomastia.

Complications:
1. Coagulopathy

2. Hepatic encephalopathy

3. Portal hypertension

4. Bleeding esophageal varices
5. Hepatorenal syndrome

6. Portopulmonary hypertension.

(N.B: When the liver can no longer maintain homeostasis, liver transplantation offers the best hope for
survival; without transplantation, the mortality rate in persons with hepatic failure is about 80%.)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/826,831)

Q. Define acute liver failure. (CU-15Ju)
Q. Mention some causes of acute liver failure.
Ans.
Acute liver failure: Acute (‘fulminant’) liver failure is defined as an acute liver illness associated with
encephalopathy and coagulopathy that occurs within 26 weeks of the initial liver injury in the absence of pre-
existing liver disease.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/826)

Causes of acute liver failure: Mnemonic for causes of acute liver failure:
* A: Acetaminophen, hepatitis A, autoimmune hepatitis
B: Hepatitis B
C: Hepatitis C, cryptogenic
D: Drugs/toxins, hepatitis D
E: Hepatitis E, esoteric causes (Wilson disease, Budd-Chiari syndrome)
F: Fatty change of the microvesicular type (fatty liver of pregnancy, valproate, tetracycline, Reye
syndrome).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/831)

Rare causes of acute liver failure include abnormalities of blood flow, metabolic disorders, and
malignancies, most commonly leukemia or lymphoma (33%), followed by breast cancer (30%) and colon
cancer (7%). An etiology cannot be established in about 15% of adult and 50% of pediatric cases.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/826)

Ans.

Nausea, vomiting, and jaundice

Marked elevation of serum liver transaminases

Initial liver enlargement followed by shrinkage

Cholestasis — manifested by yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera (jaundice and icterus,
respectively)

Q. What do you mean by hepatic encephalopathy? (DU-18M,16Ju)
Q. Short note: Hepatic encephalopathy. (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Hepatic encephalopathy: Hepatic encephalopathy is a spectrum of disturbances in consciousness, ranging
from subtle behavioral abnormalities, to marked confusion and stupor, to deep coma and death.

It may progress over days, weeks, or months following acute hepatic injury.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/827)

Asustated fluctuating neurologic signs:
Rigidity and hyperreflexia.
*  Asterixis / flapping tremor (a particularly characteristic sign, which is manifested as nonrhythmic,
rapid extension-flexion movements of the head and extremities, best seen when the arms arc held in
extension with dorsiflexed wrists).

Fig: Asterixis / flapping tremor.

Pathogenesis: Hepatic encephalopathy is believed to be caused by elevated ammonia levels, which correlate
with impaired neuronal function and cerebral edema.

The principal source of the ammonia is the gastrointestinal tract, where it is produced by microorganisms
and also by enterocytes during glutamine metabolism. Normally, ammonia is transported in the portal vein to
the liver, where it is metabolized in the urea cycle; in severe liver disease, this detoxification mechanism fails.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/827)

Q. What do you mean by hepatorenal syndrome? (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Hepatorenal syndrome: It is a form of renal failure occurring in individuals with liver failure in whom there
is no intrinsic morphologic or functional cause for kidney dysfunction.

The syndrome’s onset is marked by a drop in urine output and increasing levels of urea and creatinine in the blood.

Sodium retention, impaired free-water excretion, and decreased renal perfusion and glomerular filtration rate
are the main renal functional abnormalities.

The decline in renal function is reversible if liver function is restored, for example, by liver transplantation.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/827)

Chronic Liver Disease (CLD) and Cirrhosis of Liver

Q. Define chronic liver disease. (CU-1|5Ja)
Ans.
Chronic liver disease (CLD): Chronic liver disease (CLD) or chronic hepatitis represents a scrics of liver
disorders of varying causes and severity in which hepatic inflammation and necrosis continue for at least 6
months.
Or,

Chronic liver disease (CLD) or chronic liver injury is defined as hepatic injury, inflammation and/or fibrosis
occurring in the liver for more than 6 months

(Ref: Davidson’s/23™/856)

Q. Define cirrhosis of liver. (DU-24Nv,22/17M, |3Ju,12Ja, BUP-22Nv,21Nv/M, RMU-22Nv,21/20/
19M,18/17Ja,15Ju, 14Ja,12/11Ju,10Ja, CU-19M,15Ju,05Ja, SU-06Ja) (V.V./ for VIVA)

Ans. ;

Cirrhosis of liver: Cirrhosis may be defined as the end-stage of chronic liver disease which is characterized by-

1. Bridging fibrous septae in the form of delicate bands or broad scars linking portal tracts with one
another and portal tracts with terminal hepatic veins

2. Parenchymal nodules containing proliferating hepatocytes encircled by fibrosis, with diameters
varying from very small ( <0.3 cm, micronodules) to large (several cm, macronodules)

3. Disruption of the architecture of the entire liver.
(Ref: Robbins/8"/837)
Or,
Cirrhosis (end-stage chronic liver disease) is a condition marked by diffuse remodeling of the liver into
parenchymal nodules (often regencrative) surrounded by fibrous bands and a variable degree of vascular
(often portosystemic) shunting.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/828)
Or,
Cirrhosis refers to the diffue transformation of the liver into regenerative parenchymal nodules surrounded
by fibrous bands.
(Ref: Robbins/11" (South Asia edition)/536)

Fig: Cirrhosis resulting from chronic viral hepatitis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/828)

sinusoidal endothelial cells

{

Eventual fibrosis
Remaining hepatocytes stimulated to regenerate

Proliferate as spherical nodules within the confines of fibrous septa

|

So, there is fibrosis, loss of architecture and formation of regenerative nodules

Q How ascites develop in cirrhosis & chronic liver disease? (DU-15Ju, RU-10Ja)

Ans.

Mechanism of ascites in liver cirrhosis:

1.

3.

5.

Splanchnic vasodilatation: Cirrhosis (fibrosis) of liver — Pronounced splanchnic vasodilatation >
Falling of systemic arterial pressure — Reduced renal blood flow — Activation of the renin—
angiotensin system with secondary hyperaldosteronism — ft Na* and H,0 retention by the kidney —
Plasma hydrostatic pressure — {Transudation of fluid into the peritoneal cavity — Ascites.

Percolation of hepatic lymph into the peritoneal cavity (lymph formation exceeds lymph return):
Cirthosis — Hepatic lymphatic flow (20 L/day in exchange of normal 800-1000 ml/day) exceeding
thoracic duct lymph return capacity — Percolation of excess amount of hepatic lymph (rich in
proteins) into the peritoneal cavity — Ascites.

Intestinal fluid leakage: Cirrhosis of liver — Portal hypertension — Increased perfusion pressure in
intestinal capillaries —- Movement of additional fluid out of intestinal capillaries into the abdomen — Ascites.

Secondary hyperaldosteronism: Cirrhosis of liver + Impaired hepatic metabolism of aldosterone >
t Aldosterone — Increased Na* and H,0 retention by the kidney —> Increased plasma hydrostatic
pressure — Increased transudation of fluid into the peritoneal cavity — Ascites.

Hypoalbuminaemia: Cirthosis of liver — Impaired function of liver — Decreased synthesis of
albumin — Hypoalbuminaemia — Decreased plasma oncotic pressure — Transudation of fluid into
the peritoneal cavity — Ascites.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/829; Davidson’s/23"/863)

Fig: Pathogenesis of ascites in cirrhosis.

Q. Why hypoproteinemic edema occurs in cirrhosis of liver? (RU-07Ja)
Ans.

Hypoproteinemic edema occurs in cirrhosis of liver: Liver is the principal site of protein (mainly albumin)

synthesis. In cirrhosis, the normal architecture of liver is altered. There is degeneration and intracellular
accumulation in the liver. The hepatocytes undergo necrosis and apoptosis. So, protein (albumin) synthesis is
decreased. Plasma oncotic pressure is decreased. As a result hypoproteinemic edema occurs.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/829; Davidson’s/23"/863)

Q. What are the causes of portal hypertension?
Ans.

Causes of portal hypertension: Increased resistance to portal blood flow may develop in a variety of
circumstances, which can be divided into prehepatic intrahepatic, and posthepatic:

1. Prehepatic causes:
* Obstructive thrombosis of portal vein

* Structural abnormalities such as narrowing of the portal vein before it ramifies in the liver

2. Intrahepatic causes:

Cirrhosis from any cause

Nodular regenerative hyperplasia

Primary biliary cirrhosis (even in the absence of cirrhosis)
Schistosomiasis

Massive fatty change

Diffuse, fibrosing granulomatous disease (e.g., sarcoid)

Q. What is fulminant hepatitis / fulminant liver failure? (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Fulminant hepatitis / fulminant liver failure: Very rapid onset acute liver failure is referred to as

“fulminant liver failure” and is typically the result of massive hepatic necrosis which is most often induced

Q. Give the clinicopathologic syndromes of viral hepatitis.
Ans.

Ciinicopathologic syndromes of viral hepatitis: Major features of the main clinicopathologic syndromes
associated with viral hepatitis are as follows-
(1) Acute asymptomatic infection with recovery.
(2) Acute symptomatic infection (anicteric or icteric) with recovery.
(3) Acute liver failure with massive to submassive hepatic necrosis (10% of cases).

Q. Mention the microscopic features in liver in acute viral hepatitis. (DU-17M)
Ans.

Morphology of liver in acute viral hepatitis:
Macroscopic:
= In mild acute viral hepatitis: Liver may be normal in size, or enlarged (due to inflammation).

= Acute viral hepatitis associated with acute liver failure and massive liver necrosis: Liver may
be shrunken.

Microscopic:

* Portal and lobular inflammatory infiltrate comprised predominantly of lymphocytes and
variably admixed with plasma cells and eosinophils.

= Hepatocyte injury may result in necrosis or apoptosis, often with pigmented macrophages
scavenging the dead cell debris.

* Necrosis of groups of hepatocytes (i.e. confluent necrosis) may be seen in severe cases and can
progress to necrosis of the entire lobule (ie. panlobular or panacinar necrosis) or connect
vascular structures (i.e. bridging necrosis).

* Liver failure can develop with massive hepatic necrosis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/837)

Q. What is carrier state of hepatitis?

Ans.

Carrier state of hepatitis: A “carrier” is an individual who harbors and can transmit an organism, but has no
symptoms.

For hepatotropic viruses, carrier state has been used to describe two separate scenarios:
(1) Individuals who harbor the virus but have no liver disease
(2) Individuals who harbor the virus and have asymptomatic nonprogressive liver damage.

In both cases, particularly the latter, affected individuals constitute reservoirs of infection.

For HBV infection, the term “healthy carrier” has been used for an individual with HBsAg and anti-HBe, but
without HBeAg. These patients have normal aminotransferases, low or undetectable serum HBV DNA, and
lack of significant inflammation or liver injury on biopsy.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/837)

Q. Give an outline of the spectrum of liver diseases associated with alcohol abuse. (DU-10Ju)

Q. Short note: Alcoholic liver disease.

Ans.

Alcoholic liver disease: Alcoholic liver disease is a chronic disorder that can give rise to steatosis, alcoholic

hepatitis, progressive steato-fibrosis, and marked derangement of vascular perfusion leading eventually to
cirrhosis.

Excessive alcohol (ethanol) consumption is a major cause of liver disease in most Western countrics.
Consumption of 80 g/day of alcohol is considered to be the threshold for development of alcoholic liver
disease, but may be lower in women.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/842)

Fig: Alcoholic liver disease. The interrelationships among hepatic steatosis, alcoholic hepatitis, and
alcoholic cirrhosis are shown, along with depictions of key morphologic features.

Spectrum of liver diseases associated with alcohol abuse: There are three distinctive, albeit overlapping,
forms of alcoholic liver injury- (Important for VIVA)

(1) Steatosis, or fatty change

(2) Alchoholic steato-hepatitis
(3) Fibrosis, which leads to cirrhosis.

(NB: Only 10% to 15% of alcoholics develop cirrhosis.)
Factors influencing the development of alcoholic liver disease:

1, Gender: Women are more susceptible than men, although the majority of patients are men.

2. Ethnic and genetic differences: Cirrhosis rates are higher for Africans Americans than for Caucasian
Americans, despite similar levels of alcohol consumption. Studies with twins suggest that there is a
genetic component in alcohol-induced liver disease (strong family association).

3. Co-morbid conditions: Iron overload, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and infection with HCV and
HBV synergize with alcohol to increase the severity of liver disease.

Laboratory findings: Laboratory findings reflect hepatic dysfunction and include-
= Elevated serum aminotransferases (ratio of serum AST and ALT level 2 : | or greater)

= Hyperbilirubinemia
= Variable elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
= Hypoproteinemia (globulins, albumin, and clotting factors)
= Anemia.
Morphology:
Macroscopically:

= The fatty liver of chronic alcoholism is enlarged (as heavy as 4 to 6 kg), soft, yellow, and greasy.
® Steatosis may be separated into microvesicular and macrovesicular forms.

Microscopically:
* Ballooned hepatocytes (these are injured, swollen hepatocytes with cleared-out cytoplasm and
cytoskeletal damage, which when extensive, results in formation of Mallory hyaline).
* Inflammation and necrosis.
®  Perivenular / pericellular fibrosis.

In advanced disease, common proximate causes of death:
1. Hepatic coma
2. Massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage
3. Inter-current infection (to which these patients are predisposed)
4. Hepatorenal syndrome (often following a bout of alcoholic hepatitis)
5. Hepatocellular carcinoma (in | to 6% of cases annually).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/842-845)

Haemochromatosis

Q. Short note: Haemochromatosis. (Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Haemochromatosis: Hemochromatosis is caused by excessive iron absorption, most of which is deposited in
the liver and pancreas, followed by the heart, joints, and endocrine organs.

When hemochromatosis results from an inherited disorder, it is referred to as hereditary hemochromatosis.
When accumulation occurs as a consequence of parenteral administration of iron, usually in the form of
transfusions, or other causes, it is called secondary hemochromatosis.

Important involved organs: Liver, pancreas, heart, joints, and endocrine organs.
Types & causes:

1. Primary / hereditary haemochromatosis
2. Secondary haemochromatosis (Hemosiderosis)
a. Parenteral iron overload due to red cell transfusions
= Severe chronic hemolytic anemias (e.g. sickle cell disease)

= Severe forms of thalassemia
= Bone marrow failure (e.g. aplastic anemia)

b. Conditions associated with increased iron uptake
= B-Thalassemia
= Myelodysplastic syndrome

c. Increased oral intake of iron
» African iron overload (Bantu siderosis)

Congenital atransferrinemia

e. Chronic liver disease
## Alcoholic liver disease
= Porphyria cutanea tarda

f. Neonatal hemochromatosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/848)

Wilson Disease

Free copper is normally taken up by hepatocytes and incorporated into apoceruloplasmin to form
ceruloplasmin, which is secreted into the blood. Ceruloplasmin accounts for 90% to 95% of plasma copper.
Excess copper within hepatocytes that is not incorporated into ceruloplasmin is sequestered in lysosomes and
transported into the bile, from which it is eventually excreted in the feces.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/850)

Q. Short note: Wilson disease. (Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Wilson disease (hepato-lenticular degeneration): It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation
of the ATP7B gene, resulting in impaired copper excretion into bile and a failure to incorporate copper into
ceruloplasmin. This disorder is marked by the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in many tissues and
organs, principally in the liver, brain, and eye.

Pathogenesis: In this disease, the initial steps of Cu absorption and transport to liver are normal. Deficiency of
ATP7B decreases copper transport into bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits
ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood. These defects lead to a decrease in circulating ceruloplasmin
accompanicd by the accumulation of copper in hepatocytes.

---

#### 📄 Page 215

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 215

—_—_—_—_—_—_—_——! aves =—====
Thus, excess hepatic copper causes toxic injury by following three mechanisms:

(1) Promoting the formation of free radicals by the Fenton reaction

(2) Binding to sulfhydryl groups of cellular proteins

(3) Displacing other metals from hepatic metalloenzymes.

Hepatocyte injury causes non-ceruloplasmin-bound copper to be spilled into the blood and accumulate in
certain tissues, particularly the basal ganglia of the brain and the cornea. Concomitantly, urinary excretion
ef copper markedly increases, but not to levels sufficient to prevent deposition of copper in tissues.

Qimical features:

* Age at onset ranges from 6 to 40 years of age (average age is 11.4 years).

* Neurologic involvement may lead to movement disorders (tremor, poor coordination, chorea or
choreoathetosis) or rigid dystonia (spastic dystonia, masklike facies, rigidity, and gait disturbances).

* Eye lesions called K-F rings (Kayser-Fleischer rings)

s

Psychiatric symptoms

* Hemolytic anemia (due to red cell membrane damage caused by oxidants produced by free copper).
Diagnostic tests:

« Decreased serum ceruloplasmin

* Increased hepatic copper content (the most sensitive and accurate test)

* Increased urinary excretion of copper (the most specific test)

= Sequencing of the A7P7B gene

= Demonstration of Kayser-Fleischer rings by slit examination.
Treatment:

* Early recognition and long-term copper chelation therapy (with D-penicillamine or trientine) or zinc-
based therapy (which blocks uptake of dietary copper in the gut) is effective.
* Individuals with hepatitis or unmanageable cirthosis require liver transplantation, which can be curative.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/850-851)

Q. What is K-F ring? (Important for VIVA)
Ans.
K-F ring (Kayser-Fleischer ring): Toxic brain injury primarily involves the basal ganglia, and nearly all
patients with neurologic involvement develop eye lesions called K-F rings (Kayser-Fleischer rings), green to
brown deposits of copper in Descemet membrane in the limbus of the cornea.

(Ref: Robbins/10°/850)

Hepatocellular Carcinoma

Q. Write down the etiology of hepatocellular carcinoma. (DU-07Ja)
Q. Give the morphology of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Q. Short note: Hepatocellular carcinoma.

Ans.

Hepatocellular_carcinoma: Most primary liver cancers arise from hepatocytes and are termed
hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (also known erroneously as hepatoma).

Incidence: It accounts for approximately 5.4% of all cancers worldwide and is one of the most common

cancers in geographic regions with high rates of hepatitis B infection. There is a pronounced male
predominance, as high as 8: 1.

Causes: Most HCCs occur in the setting of chronic liver disease with cirrhosis, while 15% to 20% arise in
noncirrhotic livers. The most common underlying diseases are-
= Chronic viral hepatitis (B and C)
Hereditary hemochromatosis
a,-antitrypsin deficiency
Alcoholic liver disease
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
Aflatoxin (a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus species)
Wilson disease
Chronic biliary diseases

Clinical features: The clinical manifestations of HCC are nonspecific and include-
* Abdominal pain

Malaise

Fatigue

Weight loss

Hepatomegaly

Features of underlying chronic liver disease.

Investigations:
* Elevated levels of serum a-fetoprotein

= Ultrasonography of whole abdomen

* CT scan and MRI with contrast studies

« Triphasic CT scan (early enhancement of the tumor due to contrast uptake in the arterial phase,
followed by rapid venous washout, is considered diagnostic of HCC)

= Biopsy followed by histopathology.

Morphology:
Gross:
= HCC may form a single mass or multiple discrete masses, or it may diffusely infiltrate the liver.
= They may be pale and yellow due to fatty change or green due to cholestasis.

* HCC ranges from well-differentiated to highly anaplastic undifferentiated lesions.

= Well and moderately differentiated HCC are composed of cells that resemble normal
hepatocytes, while poorly differentiated tumors show marked cytologic atypia.

« The tumor cells grow in thick plates or trabeculae, pseudoglandular structures with bile
plugs, or sheets.

---

#### 📄 Page 217

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 217

Fig: Hepatocellular carcinoma.

* Tumors larger than 2 cm are more likely to be associated with vascular invasion and intrahepatic
metastases.

= Hematogenous metastases, especially to the lung, tend to occur late in the disease.

= Lymph node metastases occur in <5% of cases.

Prognosis: The overall 5-year survival rate is 30% for tumor confined to the liver and only 5% to 10% for
cases with extrahepatic spread.

Cause of death in HCC:
* Cachexia
* Gastro-intestinal or esophageal variceal bleeding
* Liver failure with hepatic coma

* Rupture of the tumour with fatal haemorrhage (rarely).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/868)

Liver Abscess

Q. Short note: Liver abscess. (RU-08Ju)
Ans.
Liver abscess: It is a form of liver infection that is common in developing countries.

Cause: Liver abscesses are usually caused by echinococcal and amebic infections, and less commonly, by
other protozoal and helminthic organisms. Most abscesses are pyogenic, representing a complication of
bacterial infection elsewhere.

Portal of entry: The organisms reach the liver by-
= Portal vein
= Arterial supply
= Ascending infection in the biliary tract (ascending cholangitis)
* Direct invasion of the liver from a nearby source, or
= A penetrating injuty.

The majority of hepatic abscesses used to result from portal spread of intra-abdominal infections (e.g.
appendicitis, diverticulitis, colitis). With improved management of these conditions, spread now occurs
primarily through the biliary tree or the arterial supply in patients suffering from some form of immune
deficiency (e.g. old age with debilitating disease, immune-suppression or cancer chemotherapy with marrow
failure). In these settings abscesses may develop without a primary focus elsewhere.

Morphology:
= It may occur as solitary or multiple lesions, ranging in size from mm to massive lesions many cm in diameter
= Bacteremic spread tends to produce multiple small abscesses, whereas direct extension and trauma
usually cause solitary large abscesses

* Biliary abscesses, which are usually multiple, may contain purulent material from adjacent bile ducts
= The causative organism can occasionally be identified in the case of fungal or parasitic abscesses

= Rupture of subcapsular liver abscesses has also led to peritonitis or localized peritoneal abscesses

s

Echinococcal infection has a characteristic cystic structure; the wall is laminated and hooklets and
intact organisms can be identified
* Calcification in the cystic wall is common.

a. Fever
b. Right upper quadrant pain
c. Tender hepatomegaly
d. Jaundice.

Management:
a. Antibiotic therapy (for the smaller lesions)

b. Surgical drainage (for the larger lesions).

Prognosis: Mortality rate with large liver abscesses ranges from 30% to 90%. With early recognition and

management, up to 80% of patients can survive.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/839 + 8/854)

Cholesterol concentrations exceed the solubilizing capacity of bile (supersaturation), due to hepatocellular
hypersecretion of cholesterol & gall bladder hypomotility

Cholesterol can no longer remain dispersed and nucleates into solid cholesterol monohydrate crystals
Hypersecretion of mucus in the gall bladder traps the nucleated crystals

Stone formation

B) Pathogenesis of pigment stones: Pigment gall stones are complex mixtures of abnormal insoluble calcium
salts of unconjugated bilirubin along with inorganic calcium salts.

Infections.

Clinical features:
1. Progressive nght upper quadrant or epigastric pain (colicky / dull and constant) that lasts for more
than 6 hours.
2. Fever, anorexia, tachycardia, sweating, nausea, and vomiting.

Laboratory tests:
1. CBC: Leukocytosis.

2. Serum bilirubin level: Raised (suggests obstruction of the common bile duct)
3. Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level: Raised.

(N.B: A definitive diagnosis can only be made following USG / CT scan of whole abdomen with special
attention to hepatobiliary system.)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/875; BRS Pathology/5"/255)

Q. What is chronic cholecystitis?

---

#### 📄 Page 223

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY 223

Q. What are the morphological changes in chronic cholecystitis? (CMU-22M, RU-19Nv)

Ans,

Chronic cholecystitis: Chronic inflammation of the gallbladder due to chemical irritation from longstanding
cholelithiasis, with or without superimposed bouts of acute cholecystitis.

Morphological changes in chronic cholecystitis: The morphologic changes in chronic cholecystitis are
extremely variable and sometimes minimal.

Gross:

Gallbladder may be contracted, of normal size, or enlarged.

Thickening of the wall as a result of extensive fibrosis

Serosa is usually smooth and glistening.

Subserosa and submucosa are often thickened from fibrosis (mucosa itself is generally preserved)
Occassionally the lumen contains green-yellow, mucoid bile and usually stones.

On sectioning, the wall is variably thickened, and has an opaque gray-white appearance.

Microscopic:

= Degree of inflammation is variable.

= Gallbladder mucosa and subserosal fibrous tissue may be infiltrated by chronic inflammatory cells
(e.g. lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophage etc.).

* Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses (pseudodiverticula or pockets in the wall of the gallbladder / entrapped
epithelial crypts) may be found, which is characterized by outpouchings / herniation of gallbladder
mucosa into the muscular wall.

* Extensive dystrophic calcification within the wall may yield a porcelain gallbladder, which is
characterized by shrunken, hard gallbladder due to chronic inflammation & fibrosis.

= An atrophic, chronically obstructed, dilated gallbladder containing clear secretions (a condition known
as hydrops of the gallbladder) & xanthoma cells (lipid containing cells with foamy cytoplasm) may
be found in xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/876; BRS Pathology/5'/255)

Fig: Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses (pockets) i in the wall of the gall bladder.

Q. What are the potential complications of chronic cholecystitis?
Ans.
tial complications of chronic cholecystitis:
Bacterial superinfection with cholangitis or sepsis.
Gallbladder perforation and local abscess formation.
Gallbladder rupture with diffuse peritonitis.
Biliary enteric (cholecystenteric) fistula, with drainage of bile into adjacent organs, entry of air and
bacteria into the biliary tree, and potentially, gallstone-induced intestinal obstruction (ileus).
* Aggravation of preexisting medical illness, with cardiac, pulmonary, renal, or liver decompensation.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/876)

Q. What type of carcinoma occurs in gall bladder?
Ans.

Carcinoma of the gall bladder:

---

#### 📄 Page 224

224 arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

= Most carcinomas of the gall bladder are adenocarcinomas (as lined by columnar epithelium).
* About 5% are squamous cell carcinoma or have adenosquamous differentiation.
= Squamous cell carcinoma of the gall bladder may occur in long-standing gall stone, as gall stone
causes squamous metaplasia of gall bladder epithelium.
= A minority may show carcinoid or a variety of mesenchymal features (carcinosarcoma).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/876 + 9'"/880)

Q. Mention the morphology of carcinoma of gall bladder.
Ans.

Morphology of carcinoma of gall bladder: Carcinomas of the gall bladder show two patterns of growth-
infiltrating and exophytic.

= Infiltrating pattern: It is more common and appears diffuse thickening and induration of the
gallbladder wall. Deep ulceration can cause direct penetration of the gall bladder wall or fistula
formation to adjacent viscera into which the neoplasm has grown.

= Exophytic pattern: It grows into the lumen as an irregular, cauliflower mass. The luminal portion
may be necrotic, hemorrhagic, and ulcerated. The most common sites of involvement are the fundus

and the neck; about 20% involves the lateral walls.
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/877 + 9'"/880)

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 225

HISTOLOGY: The parenchyma of each kidney is composed of approximately one million microstructures
called nephrons. A nephron, in turn, consists of 5 major parts, each having a functional role in the formation
of urine: the glomerular capsule (glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule), the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT),
the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), and the collecting ducts.

Glomerulus Bowman's Proximal convoluted tubule Distal convoluted tubule

Renal artery

i. ee, ae

Collecting tubule

Fig: Structure of a nephron.

The major function of glomerulus is complex filtration from the capillaries to the urinary space. The barrier to
glomerular filtration consists of the following 3 components:
i. Fenestrated endothelial cells lining the capillary loops.

ii. Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) on which the endothelial cells rest.
iii. Filtration slit pores between the foot processes of the visceral epithelial cells (podocytes) external to

GBM.

Q. What are the different immune mechanisms involved in glomerular injury? Write down the
pathogenesis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. (DU-15Ju)

Ans.

Pathogenesis of AGN:

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis:

Causative agent: Group A B-hemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogen).

Past history: It usually appears | to 4 weeks after a sterptococcal infection of the pharynx (sore throat) or skin
(infected scabies / impetigo).

Pathogenesis: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immunologically mediated disease.

= Following streptococcal infection, formation of antibody against M-protein of streptococcal cell wall
— Formation of antigen-antibody complex in circulation — Deposition of Ag-Ab complex in
glomeruli.

= Streptococcal antigen is settled in glomeruli — Formation of antibody & reaction of Ab with the
settled streptococcal Ag in glomeruli.

* Release of enzyme (e.g. proteinase) from bacteria — enzyme causes alteration of glomerular basement
membrane — Formation of Ab against the altered glomerular basement membrane — Ag-Ab reaction.

Q. Write down the prognosis of AGN.
Ans.
Prognosis of AGN:
1. Children: More than 95% eventually recover totally with conservative therapy. A small minority of
children (<1%) become severely oliguric, and develop a rapidly progressive form of
glomerulonephritis, and a few may progress to chronic glomerulonephritis (chronic renal failure).

2. Adult: About 60% recover promptly, some develop rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and others
chronic glomerulonephritis.

Nice to Know:
* In children, primary glomerulonephritis is the cause in majority of cases of the nephrotic syndrome;
most frequent being minimal-change disease (lipoid nephrosis) (65%).
* In adults, on the other hand, systemic diseases (diabetes, amyloidosis and SLE) are more frequent

causes of nephritic syndrome. The most common primary glomerular disease in adults is membranous
glomerulonephritis (40%).

Q Write in short about lipoid nephrosis (RU-07Ja)/ minimal change disease. (RU- 18M)
Q Short note: Minimal change disease. (RU-17M,10Ja)

Ans.
Minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis): Minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis) is seen most often in

young children but can also occur in older children and adults. It is the prototype of the nephrotic syndrome.

h ws characterized by diffuse effacement of foot processes of epithelial cells (podocytes) in glomeruli that
appear Virtually normal by light microscopy.

The peak incidence is between 2 and 6 years of age. The most characteristic feature of this condition is the
dramatic response to corticosteroid therapy.

Etielogy & pathogenesis: It involves some immune dysfunction, eventually resulting in the elaboration of a
cytokine that damages visceral epithelial cells (podocytes) and cause proteinuria. The ultrastructural changes
pomt to a primary visceral epithelial cell injury, and loss of glomerular polyanions. Thus, defects in the
charge bamer may contribute to the proteinuria.

Morphology:
Macroscopic: Kidney tends to be pale or even yellowish in colour and slightly larger & heavier than normal.
Microscopic:

* No visible basement membrane changes;

* Fused foot processes of podocytes;

* Lipid accumulation in renal tubular cells.

Prognosis: Despite massive proteinuria, renal function remains good, and the long term prognosis is excellent
for children and adults.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/914; BRS Pathology/5"/265)

Q. Why minimal change disease is called lipoid nephrosis?

Ans.

Minimal change disease is called lipoid nephrosis: The cells of the proximal tubules are often laden with
lipid and protein, reflecting tubular reabsorption of lipoproteins passing through diseased glomeruli, thus the
historical term lipod nephrosis.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/914)

Q. What is membranous nephropathy / glomerulonephropathy?
Q. Write the morphology of membranous glomerulonephropathy. (SU-08Ja)
Ans.
Membranous nephropathy / glomerulonephropathy: Membranous nephropathy is a common cause of the
nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is characterized by diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall due to
the accumulation of deposits containing Ig along the subepithelial side of the basement membrane.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/912)

Morphology:
* Light microscopy: Uniform diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall.

* Electron microscopy: Basement membrane markedly thickened by intramembranous and
epimembranous (subepithelial) immune complex deposits appearing as irregular spikes protruding
from the GBM (“spike and dome” appearance).

* Immunofluorescence microscopy: Shows granular deposits of immunoglobulins and various amount

of complement along the GBM. a
(Ref: Robbins/10"/913; BRS Pathology/5"/265)

Q. Short note: Diabetic nephropathy. (SU-05M)
Ans

Diabetic nephropathy: The term diabetic nephropathy is applied to the conglomerate of lesions that often
occur concurrently in the diabetic kidney. It is one of the leading causes of chronic kidney failure.

Advanced or end stage kidney disease occurs in as many as 40% of both insulin dependent type | diabetes and
type 2 diabetes.

Glomerular syndromes occur in diabetic nephropathy: By far the most common lesions involve the
glomeruli and are associated clinically with three glomerular syndromes-

1. Non-nephrotic proteinuria

2. Nephrotic syndrome and

3. Chronic renal failure.

However, diabetes also affects the arterioles (causing hyalinizing arteriolar sclerosis), increases susceptibility
to the development of pyelonephritis and particularly papillary necrosis, and causes a variety of tubular lesions.

Lesions caused by diabetic nephropathy: Three lesions are encountered-
1. Glomerular lesions
2. Renal vascular lesions, principally arteriosclerosis;
3. Pyelonephntis, including necrotizing papillitis.

Morphology:
= Basement membrane markedly thickened;

* Diffuse or nodular mesangial accumulations of basement membrane-like material.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/923,1118; BRS Pathology/5""/265)

Q. Give the pathogenesis of acute tubular injury (ATI) / acute tubular necrosis (ATN).

Q. Short note: Acute tubular necrosis.

Ans.

Acute _tubular_injury (ATI) / acute tubular necrosis (ATN): Acute tubular injury (ATI) is a
climicopathologic entity characterized by damage to tubular epithelial cells and an acute decline in renal
fanction, often associated with shedding of granular casts and tubular cells into the urine.

It is the most common cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) and may produce oliguria (defined as urine output of
<400 mL/day).

(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/567,568)
Types and causes:

1. Ischaemic ATI (due to decreased or interrupted blood flow):
Hypotension and shock (hypovolemic shock)
Severe trauma
Acute pancreatitis
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
2. Nephrotoxic ATI (due to direct toxic injury to the tubules):
= Drugs (such as gentamycin and other antibiotics)
= Radiographic contrast agents
= Poisons including heavy metals (e.g. mercury)
= Organic solvents (e.g. carbon tetrachloride)

3. Combined ischaemic & nephrotoxic ATI:
= Haemoglobinuria (mismatched blood transfusion and other hemolytic crises)
= Myoglobinuria (due to severe skeletal muscle injuries).
(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/ 10/562)

Clinical features:
= Electrolyte abnormalities
* Acidosis
= Uremia
= Signs of fluid overload, often with oliguria.
(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/569)

1. Tubular injury &
2. Persistent and severe disturbances in blood flow.

Q. Short note: Pyelonephritis. (For VIVA)
Ans.

Pyelonephritis: Pyelonephritis is defined as inflammation affecting the tubules, interstitium, and renal
pelvis. It is one of the most common diseases of the kidney.

Types: It occurs in two forms-
1. Acute pyelonephritis - is generally caused by bacterial infection and is associated with urinary tract

infection (UTI).
2. Chronic pyelonephritis - is a more complex disorder; bacterial infection plays a dominant role, but
other factors (vesicoureteral reflux, obstruction) predispose to repeat episodes of acute pyelonephritis,

(Ref: Robbins/10"/927)

Proteus

Staphylococci
Polyoma virus
Cytomegalovirus

Adenovirus.

Routes of infection: There are two routes by which bacteria can reach the kidneys:
1. Through the bloodstream (haematogenous infection)
2. From the lower urinary tract (ascending infection) - most common.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/927)

Q Define acute pyelonephritis. What are the predisposing factors for acute pyelonephritis?

ABS.
Agate pyelonephritis: Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation of the kidney caused by bacterial
and sometimes viral (e.g. polyomavirus) infection, which can reach the kidney by hematogenous spread or,
more commonly, through the ureters in association with vesicoureteral reflux.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/928)

Predisposing factors for acute pyelonephritis: Acute pyelonephritis is often associated with the following:

1. Urinary tract obstruction, either congenital or acquired

2. Instrumentation of the urinary tract, most commonly catheterization

3. Vesicoureteral reflux

4. Pregnancy

5. Gender and age: Females are more affected. But with increasing age the incidence in males rises as a
result of prostatic hypertrophy and instrumentation

Pre-existing renal lesions

Diabetes mellitus

Immuno-suppression and immunodeficiency.

ID

Q. What are the complications of acute pyelonephritis? (DU-11Ja)
Ans.
Complications of acute pyelonephritis:
a) Papillary necrosis (mainly in diabetics, sickle cell disease, and in those with urinary tract obstruction)
b) Pyonephrosis (when there is total or almost complete obstruction, particularly when it is high in the
urinary tract)
c) Perinephric abscess.

Q. List the causes of acute renal failure. (DU-1 1 Ju)

Q. Short note: Acute renal failure / acute kidney injury.

Ans.

Acute renal failure (ARF) / acute kidney injury (AKI): It refers to a sudden and usually reversible loss of
renal function, which usually develops over days or weeks and usually accompanied by a reduction in urine volume.

(Ref: Davidson/21"/482)
Or,
Acute renal failure / acute kidney injury is characterized by rapid decline in GFR (within hours to days), with
concurrent dysregulation of fluid and electrolyte balance, and retention of metabolic waste products normally
excreted by the kidney including urea and creatinine.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/898)

Q. What is chronic renal failure (CRF) / chronic kidney disease (CKD)? What are the causes of
CRF/CKD?
Ans.
Chronic renal failure (CRF) / chronic kidney disease (CKD): It refers to an irreversible deterioration in
renal function which classically develops over a period of years.

Or,
Chronic kidney disease (previously called chronic renal failure) is defined as the presence of a diminished
GFR that is persistently less than 60 mL/minute/1.73 m’ for at least 3 months, from any cause, and/or
persistent albuminuria.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/898)

Causes of CRF/CKD:
1) Diabetes mellitus (20 - 40%)
2) Interstitial diseases (20 - 30%)
3) Glomerular diseases (10 - 20%) e.g. IgA nephropathy is most common
4) Hypertension (5 - 20%)
5) Systemic inflammatory diseases (5 - 10%) e.g. SLE, vasculitis
6) Congenital and inherited (5%) e.g. polycystic kidney disease, Alport’s syndrome
7) Renal artery stenosis (5%)
8) Unknown (5 - 20%).

(Ref: Davidson/21"/487)

Q. Write the morphology of renal cell carcinoma. (DU-10Ja)

Q. Write the microscopic findings of renal cell carcinoma.

Q. Short note: Renal cell carcinoma. (DU-07Ju,05S)

Ans.

Renal cell carcinoma (adenocarcinoma of the kidney): Renal cell carcinomas are derived from the renal
tubular epithelium (adenocarcinoma of the kidney), and represent 80% to 85% of all primary malignant
neoplasms of the kidney and 2% to 3% of all cancers in adults.

Classification: It is of 3 types - clear cell carcinoma, papillary renal cell carcinoma, chromophobe renal
carcinoma.

Morphology:
Macrescepic:

om

4.

The tumour may arise in any portion of the kidney, but more commonly affects the poles.

Clear cell carcinomas arise most likely from proximal tubular epithelium, and usually occur as
solitary unilateral lesions. They are spherical masses of varying size and composed of yellow to
orange to gray-white tissue, with prominent areas of cystic softening or of hemorrhage, either
fresh or old.

Papillary renal cell carcinomas arise from distal convoluted tubules, and have gross evidence of
necrosis, hemorrhage, and cystic degeneration. They tend to be bilateral and multiple.

Chromophobe-type renal cell carcinoma tends to be grossly tan-brown.

Microscopic:

1.

2.

Clear cell carcinoma (65%): Cells are rounded or polygonal shape. Abundant clear or granular
cytoplasm.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma (10-15%): Composed of cuboidal or low columnar cells arranged
in papilla formation with fibrovascular cores. The cells may have a clear or, more commonly,
pink cytoplasm.
Chromophobe renal carcinoma (5%): It is made up of cells having clear, flocculent cytoplasm
with very prominent, distinct cell membranes. The nuclei are surrounded by halos of clear
cytoplasm.

(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/578-580 + 10'/950)

Fig: Renal cell carcinoma.

Q Short note: Wilms tumour / nephroblastoma. (DU-06M,04Ja, CMU-23M, SU-05/03Ja)
Ans,
Wilms tumour: It is the most common primary renal tumour of childhood. It occurs usually between 2 to 5

years of age. Approximately 5-10% of Wilms tumor involve both kidneys, either simultaneously or one after
the other.

Pathogenesis:
« Wilms tumour associated gene is located at chromosome 11p13.
® = The risk of Wilms tumour is increased in association with three congenital malformations:
1. WAGR syndrome
2. Denys-Drash syndrome
3. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome

Morphology:
Gross:
« A large, solitary, well-circumscribed mass.
= 10% are either bilateral or multicentric at the time of diagnosis.
* On cut section, the tumour is soft, homogenous, and tan to grey with occasional foci of haemorthage,
cyst formation and necrosis.

Microscopic:
= Different stages of nephrogenesis.

* The classic triphasic combination of blastemal, stromal, and epithelial cell types is observed in the vast
majority of lesions.

* Epithelial differentiation is usually in the form of abortive tubules or glomeruli.

= Stromal cells are usually fibrotic or mixoid in nature, although skeletal muscle differentiation is not
uncommon.

* Rarely, other heterologous elements are identified, including squamous or mucinous epithelium,
smooth muscle, adipose tissue, cartilage, and osteoid and neurogenic tissue.

= Approximately 5 % of tumours reveal anaplasia.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/480)

Renal Stones

Q. Mention the types of renal stones. (Very Important for VIVA)
Q. What is staghorn calculi?

Ans.

Types of renal stone: There are four main types of renal calculi-

1. Calcium oxalate and phosphate stones: Most stones (about 70%) are calcium containing, composed
largely of calcium oxalate or calcium oxalate mixed with calcium phosphate.

2. Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones (triple stones or struvite stones) (about 15%): Formed
largely after infection by urea-splitting bacteria (e.g. proteus and some staphyllococci), which convert
urea to ammonia. The resultant alkaline urine causes the precipitation of magnesium ammonium
phosphate salts. These form some of the largest stones, as the amounts of urea excreted are normally
huge. Indeed, so-called staghorn calculi occupying large portions of the renal pelvis are almost
always a consequence of infection.

3. Uric acid stones (5% to 10%): Common in patients with hyperuricemia, such as gout.

4. Cystine stones (1% to 2%): Caused by genetic defect in the renal reabsorption of amino acids,
including cystine, leading to cystinuria.
(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10°/576 + 10/947)

Cryptorchidism: Cryptorchidism is a complete or partial failure of the intra-abdominal testes to descend into
the scrotal sac and is associated with testicular dysfunction and an increased risk of testicular cancer.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/966)
Or,

Cryptorchidism refers to incomplete descent of the testis from the abdomen to the scrotum and is present in

5%, it may be present at other sites along its descent from intra-abdominal location to the scrotal sac.

characterized by-

* Increase in interstitial stroma

« Leydig cells are relatively prominent

= It is the most common testicular germ cell tumor (50%)

Fig: Seminoma.

Pathology / morphology of seminoma:
Macroscopic:
= Seminomas produce bulky masses, sometimes 10 times the size of the normal testis.
* The typical seminoma has a homogeneous, gray-white, lobulated cut surface, usually devoid
of hemorrhage or necrosis.
* Generally the tunica albuginea is not penetrated, but occasionally extension to the epididymis,
spermatic cord, or scrotal sac occurs.

Microscopic:
* Seets of uniform cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by delicate fibrous septa
containing a lymphocytic infiltrate.
= Insome tumors, ill-defined granulomas also are present.
* The classic seminoma cell is round to polyhedral and has a distinct cell membrane; clear or
watery-appearing cytoplasm; and a large, central nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli.
= The cytoplasm contains varying amounts of glycogen.

Fig: Seminoma; cut surface (in the right).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/970; BRS Pathology/5'"/289)

(N.B: An identical tumor of seminoma arises in the ovary, where it is called dysgerminoma, and in the central
nervous system, usually in midline structures such as the pineal gland, where it is referred to as germinoma.)
(Ref: Robbins/10"/970)

Q. Write down the prognosis of a typical seminoma. (SUST-21Nv)
Ans.
Prognosis of a typical seminoma: The prognosis of classic seminoma is better than other germ cell tumours.
The tumour is highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive and most patients are cured by orchiectomy with or
without chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/973; Harsh Mohan/7""/715)

ether germ cell tumors.
Characteristics:

a. This tumor is analogous to choriocarcinoma of the ovary

b. Incidence peaks in the second to third decade

c. Histologic characteristics include cells that resemble placental syncytiotrophoblasts and
cytotrophoblasts

d. This tumor causes an increase in serum hCG

e. Highly chemosensitive.

Morphology:
Macroscopic:
* Often they cause no testicular enlargement and are detected only as a small palpable nodule.
= Typically, these tumous are small, rarely larger than 5 cm in diameter.
= Haemorthage and necrosis are extremely common.

Microscopic:
= The tumor is composed of two intimately juxtaposed cell types, syncytiotrophoblasts and
cytotrophoblasts.
* Syncytiotrophoblasts are large multinucleated cells with abundant eosinophilic vacuolated
cytoplasm containing hCG.

= Cytotrophoblasts are more regular and tend to be polygonal, with distinct borders and clear
cytoplasm; they grow in cords or sheets and have a single, fairly uniform nucleus.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/972; BRS Pathology/5"/291)

Q. Short note: Teratoma. (DU-17Nv,16/15/14Ja, BSFMMU’S-23Nv, RU-20Nv,19M,17Ju/M,16Ja, 10Ju)
Ans.

Teratoma: Teratoma refers to GCTs having various cellular or organoid components reminiscent of the
normal derivatives of more than one germ layer.

They may occur at any age from infancy to adulthood.
Malignant potential: It is most frequently malignant.

Classification: It can be classified as one of three subtypes:

(1) Mature teratoma: This teratoma is almost always malignant (whereas the corresponding ovarian
tumor is almost always benign)

(2) Immature teratoma: Primitive neural elements are often present, and behavior is malignant.

(3) Teratoma with malignant transformation: This teratoma contains malignant tissue, such as
squamous cell carcinoma.

Morphology:
Gross:
* Teratomas are usually large (5-10 cm in diameter).
* Gross appearance is heterogenous with solid, sometimes cartilaginous, and cystic areas.
* Haemorrhage and _ necrosis usually indicate admixture with embryonal carcinoma,
choriocarcinoma or both.

---

#### 📄 Page 256

256 arif’s re resentation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Microscopic:

* Teratomas are composed of collections of differentiated cells or organoid structures (such as neural
tissue, muscle bundles, islands of cartilage, squamous epithelium lining epidermal-like surfaces with
or without skin adnexal structures, structures reminiscent of thyroid gland, bronchial epithelium, and
bits of intestinal wall or brain substances ) embedded in a fibrous or myxoid stroma.

= Elements may be mature (resembling various adult tissues) or immature (sharing histologic features
with fetal or embryonic tissue).

«  Teratoma with somatic-type malignant transformation: There may be a focus of squamous cell
carcinoma, mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma, sarcoma, or other cancers.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/973; BRS Pathology/5"/290)

Q. Mention the mode of spread of testicular tumor.
Ans

Mode of spread of testicular tumor: Testicular tumours may spread by both /ymphatic and haematogenous routes:
1. Lymphatic spread: It is common to all forms. In general, retroperitoneal para-aortic nodes are the
first to be involved. Subsequent spread may occur to mediastinal and supraclavicular nodes.
2. Haematogenous spread: Primarily to the lungs, but liver, brain, and bones may also be involved.

Metastases from seminomas typically involve lymph nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs later in the course of
dissemination. Nonseminomatous GCTs tend to metastasize earlier and more frequently via a hematogenous
Toute.

(Ref: Robbins/10°/973; Harsh Mohan/7"/697)

Q. Short note: Nodular hyperplasia of prostate. (RU-20Nv, CU-20/16Ju)

Q. Short note: Benign prostatic hyperplasia. (DU-04M)
Ans.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia: BPH (also referred to as nodular hyperplasia) is the most common benign
prostatic disease in men older than age 50 years.

---

#### 📄 Page 259

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 259

It results from nodular hyperplasia of prostatic stromal and epithelial cells and often leads to urinary
obstruction. It is characterized by the formation of large, fairly discrete nodules in the periurethral region of the

prostate, which, when sufficiently large, compress and narrow the urethral canal to cause partial, or sometimes
virtually complete, obstruction of the urethra,

It is not a premalignant lesion.

Age of incidence: Over 50 years, most often between 60 & 70.

Morphology:
Gross:
« Prostate is enlarged, weight become 3 to 5 times normal (60 to 100 gm).
Nodules in lateral lobe may compress urethra to a slit-like orifice.
Cross section shows hyperplastic nodules of various size, colour and consistency.
Nodules that contain mostly glands are yellow-pink and soft and exude a milky white prostatic fluid.
Nodules composed primarily of fibromuscular stroma are pale gray and firm.
There is no true capsule.

Microscopic:

® Individual nodules contain small to large to cystically dilated glands that are separated by bland
spindle-shaped stromal cells.
The glands are lined by two layers of cells, an inner columnar secretory cell layer and an outer layer of
cuboidal or flattened basal epithelium, and infolding of the glands may produce a papillary architecture.
In markedly enlarged glands, compromise of the vascular supply may produce prostatic infarcts, which
may have adjacent areas of squamous metaplasia.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/976)

Fig: Well-defined nodules of BPH compress the urethra into a slitlike lumen.

Q. Give the pathogenesis of benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Ans.
Pathogenesis of benign prostatic hyperplasia: The main androgen in the prostate is dihydrotestosterone

(DHT), which is the ultimate mediator of prostatic growth. It is synthesized in the prostate from
testosterone through the action of type 2 5a-reductase.

DHT binds to and activates androgen receptors (ARs) found in both stromal and epithelial prostate cells.
Binding of DHT stimulates ARs to translocate from the cytoplasm to the nucleus and activate the
transcription of androgen-dependent genes, which encode several growth factors and their receptors.

---

#### 📄 Page 260

260 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & ~ HAEMATOLOGY

Although the ultimate cause of BPH is unknown, it is believed that DHT-induced growth factors act by
increasing the proliferation of stromal cells and decreasing the death of epithelial cells.

Fig: Pathogenesis of benign prostatic hyperplasia.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/976)

Q. Mention the effects of nodular hyperplasia of prostate.
Ans.
Effects of nodular hyperplasia of prostate:
= Prostatic enlargement and stromal smooth muscle—mediated contraction causes urinary obstruction
* Increased resistance to urinary outflow leads to bladder hypertrophy and distention, accompanied by
urine retention.

The inability to empty the bladder completely creates a reservoir of residual urine that is a common
source of infection.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/977)

Q. Mention the clinical features of nodular hyperplasia of prostate.
Ans.

Clinical features of nodular hyperplasia of prostate:
* Increased urinary frequency
Nocturia
Difficulty in starting and stopping the stream of urine
Overflow dribbling
Dysuria (painful micturition)
Increased risk of developing bacterial infections of the bladder and kidney
Sudden acute urinary retention (that requires emergency catheterization for relief).

(Ref: Robbins/10°/977)

Q. Give the difference between benign and malignant prostatic hyperplasia.
Ans.

Difference between benign and malignant prostatic hyperplasia:

Benign glands contain basal cells that are absent in cancer.

Prostatic cancers have extensive bony metastases, whereas benign enlargements have not.

Neoplastic glands are typically smaller than benign glands.

In contrast to benign glands, prostate cancer glands are more crowded, characteristically lacking
branching and papillary infolding.

5. Serum levels of PSA are elevated to a lesser extent in benign nodular hyperplasia, as compared to cancer.

Ans.
Prostatic carcinoma:
Primary tumors:
Adenocarcinoma of the prostate (most common)
=" Miscellaneous tomours and tumour-like conditions
- Ductal adenocarconoma
- Small cell carcinoma of prostate
Secondary tumors:

= Urothelial cancer.

Prostate cancer is the second cause of cancer-related death in men, surpassed only by lung cancer.

Incidence: Men over age 50.

Etiology:

Age

Race

Family history

Hormone levels (e.g. androgen)

Environmental influence

Precursor lesions {prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN)}.

Gross:
* In approximately 70% of cases, carcinoma of the prostate arises in the peripheral zone of the gland
* On cross-section of the prostate the neoplastic tissue is gritty and firm.

ae
Most adenocarcinomas consist of glands arranged in well-defined, easily recognized patterns.
* The glands are typically smaller than benign glands and are lined by a single uniform layer of
cuboidal or low columnar epithelium.
* In contrast to benign glands, malignant glands have tightly packed cells and characteristically lack
branching and papillary infoldings.

Aefey>

---

#### 📄 Page 262

262 | arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

» The outer basal cell layer typical of benign glands is absent.

= The cytoplasm of the tumor cells ranges from pale-clear to a distinctive amphophilic appearance.
* Nuclei are enlarged and often contain one or more large nucleoli.

= There is some variation in nuclear size and shape, but in general pleomorphism is not marked.

= Mitotic figures are uncommon.

Local extension: Local extension most commonly involves periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base
of the urinary bladder, which in advanced disease may result in ureteral obstruction.

Metastases:
= Lymphatic spread: Obturator nodes and eventually to the para-aortic nodes.
* Hematogenous spread: Occurs chiefly to the bones, particularly the axial skeleton. Bony metastases
are typically osteoblastic. The bones that are most commonly involved, in descending order of
frequency, are lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and nbs.

Fig: Metastatic osteoblastic prostatic carcinoma within vertebral bodies.

« Localized prostate cancer is asymptomatic, and is usually discovered by the detection of a
suspicious nodule on rectal examination or elevated serum PSA level.

* Patients with clinically advanced prostatic cancer may present with symptoms of urinary
obstruction, such as difficulty in starting or stopping the stream, dysuria, frequency, or hematuria.

= Some patient pesent with back pain caused by vertebral metastases and diagnosed by radionuclide
bone scanning.

* Digital rectal examination (DRE)

* Trans-rectal ultrasound

* Trans-rectal ultraso-guided needle biopsy
* Measurement of serum PSA levels.

Treatment:
1. Surgery (radical prostatectomy)
2. Radiation therapy
3. Androgen deprivation therapy
* Orchiectomy
= LHRH agonists.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/978-982)

Grade and stage are the most important prognostic factors in prostate cancer. Grading is performed using the
Gleason system.

(Ref: Robbins/10°/980)

Q. Describe the value of PSA in prostate cancer. (CU-17M)
= Short note: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA). (CU-18M)

= Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a product of prostatic epithelium and is normally secreted in the
semen. It is an androgen-regulated serine protease whose function is to cleave and liquefy the seminal
coagulum formed after ejaculation.

In normal men, only minute amounts of PSA circulate in the serum.

Normal value of PSA: 4 ng/ ml.

Causes of increased PSA: PSA is organ specific but not cancer specific. Serum levels of PSA are elevated in-
* Carcinoma of prostate
* Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
=  Prostatis
* Prostate gland infarction
= Instrumentation of prostate
* Ejaculation.

Clinical importance of PSA:
1. Measurement of PSA is the most important test used in the diagnosis and management of prostate

cancer.
20-40% of patients with a serum PSA > 4.0 ng/ml will have prostate cancer on biopsy.
High levels of serum PSA (> 100 ng/ml) almost always indicate distant bone metastases.
PSA is most useful for monitoring response to treatment and disease progression.
It is also a tumour marker of some breast cancers.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/981; Davidson’s/23"/439,1322,1324)

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
(Important for VIVA)

Q. What do you mean by pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)? Write down the etiology, pathogenesis
and complication of PID. (CU-10Ja)
Ans.
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID): Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection that begins in the vulva
or vagina and spreads upward to involve most of the structures in the female genital system, resulting in pelvic
pain, adnexal tenderness, fever, and vaginal discharge.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/988)

Etiology:
1. Gonococcus infection (most common cause)
2. Chlamydia infection
3. Staphylococci
4. Streptococci
5. Coliform bacteria
6. Clostridium perfringens.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/988)

Pathogenesis:
= Gonococcal PID: Inflammatory changes start to appear approximately 2 to 7 days after inoculation.
Endocervical mucosa is the most common site of initial involvement. Gonococcal infection may also
begin in the Bartholin gland and other vestibular, or periurethral glands. From these sites, the
organisms may spread upward to involve the fallopian tubes and tubo-ovarian region.

= Non-gonococcal PID: The non-gonococcal bacterial infections that follow induced abortion, dilation
and curettage of the uterus, and other surgical procedures are thought to spread upward from the uterus
through the lymphatics and venous channels rather than on the mucosal surfaces. Therefore, these
infections tend to produce more inflammation within the deeper layers of the organs than gonococcal
infections.

Complications:

1. Acute complications:
=  Peritonitis
* Bacteremia (which in tum may result in endocarditis, meningitis, and suppurative arthritis).

2. Remote complications / chronic sequelae:
* Infertility, and tubular obstruction
= Ectopic pregnancy
* Pelvic pain
* Intestinal obstruction (due to adhesions between the small bowel and the pelvic organs).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/989)

Q. What do you mean by CIN? (DU-19M,07Ju, RU-21/20Nv,10Ja, CU-18M) Mention its type.
(RU-20Nv, 19M, 1 0Ja)

Q. Mention the cytologic findings of high grade CIN. (SU-10Ju)

Q. Short note: Cervical intra-epithelial neoplasia (CIN). (DU-08Ja, CU-19Nv,07Ja, RU-20M,
18Ja)

Q. Short note: Carcinoma in situ, cervix. (RU-13Ja) (Important for VIVA)

Ans.
Cervical intra-epithelial neoplasia (CIN): CIN is a spectrum of precancerous changes in cervical
epithelium, and is graded on progressively severe degree of changes. It includes dysplasia and CIS (carcinoma

in situ).
Characteristics:
1. They represent a continuum of morphologic change with indistinct boundaries.
2. They do not invariably progress to cancer and may spontaneously regress, with the risk of persistence
or progression to cancer increasing with the severity of the precancerous change.
3. They are associated with human papillomavirus (HPV), and high-risk HPV (types 16, 18 & above) are
found in increasing frequency in high-grade CIN.
4. Progression to invasive carcinoma (when it occurs) may take place in a few months to more than a decade.

Classification: CIN have been classified in a variety of ways-
A. Cervical intra-epithelial neoplasia (CIN) system (depending on the extent of epithelial
involvement):
1. CIN-I: Mild dysplasia
2. CIN-II: Moderate dysplasia
3. CIN-III: Severe dysplasia (carcinoma in situ).

B. Dysplasia / carcinoma in situ system:
1. Mild dysplasia
2. Severe dysplasia (carcinoma in situ)

C. Squamous intra-epithelial lesion (SIL), current classification: The three-tier classification system
(CIN) has been recently simplified to a two-tiered system-
1. Low grade squamous intra-epithelial lesion (LSIL): CIN-I (mild dysplasia).
2. High grade squamous intra-epithelial lesion (HSIL): CIN-II & CIN-III (moderate & severe
dysplasia, carcinoma in situ).
