Q. Short note: Transformation zone. (RU-19Nv)

Ans.
Transformation zone: Anatomically, cervix is divided into the exocervix (visible on vaginal exam) and

endocervix.

=  Exocervix is lined by squamous epithelium.
= Endocervix is lined by columnar (mucus-secreting) epithelium.

The point where the squamous and columnar epithelium meets is referred to as the sguamocolumnar junction.

With the onset of puberty, the squamocolumnar junction undergoes eversion, causing the columnar epithelium
to become visible on the exocervix. The exposed columnar cells, however, eventually undergo squamous
metaplasia, forming a region called the transformation zone, where tumors most commonly arise.

So, the area of the cervix where the columnar epithelium abuts the squamous epithelium is termed the
“transformation zone.”

Or,
The region of the cervix where squamous metaplasia occurs is referred to as the “transformation zone’.

Importance: Most tumors of the cervix are of epithelial origin and are caused by oncogenic strains of HPV.
immature squamous metaplastic epithelial cells in the transformation zone are most susceptible to HPV
infection, and as a result this is where cervical precursor lesions and cancers develop.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/995; Pathoma 2011)

Q. Give the morphology of cervical carcinoma.
Q. Give the morphology of cervical squamous cell carcinoma. (CU-07Ja)
Ans.
= It is one of the most common neoplasms in women.
= Average age of patients is between 45 and 50 years.
= With the advent of widespread screening (by Pap test), many cervical carcinomas are detected at sub-
clinical stage, so death due to this has declined sharply.

Morphology of cervical carcinoma: Invasive cervical carcinoma may manifest as fungating (exophytic) or
infiltrative masses. On histologic examination-

= Squamous cell carcinomas: These are composed of nests and tongues of malignant squamous
epithelium, either keratinizing or non-keratinizing, invading the underlying cervical stroma.

= Adenocarcinomas: They are characterized by proliferation of glandular epithelium composed of
malignant endocervical cells with large, hyperchromatic nuclei and relatively mucin-depleted
cytoplasm, resulting in dark appearance of the glands, as compared with the normal endocervical
epithelium.

« Adenosquamous carcinomas: They are composed of inter-mixed malignant glandular and squamous
epithelium.

» Neuroendocrine carcinomas: They typically have an appearance similar to small-cell carcinoma of
the lung, but differ in being positive for high-risk HPVs.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/998,999)

Q. How cervical carcinoma spread?
Ans.
Spread of cervical carcinoma:
= Direct spread by local extension into other pelvic structures, including paracervical soft tissue,
urinary bladder, ureters (resulting in hydronephrosis), rectum, and vagina. Lymphovascular invasion
results in local and distant lymph nodes metastases.

= Distant (blood-borne) metastasis to the liver, lungs, bone or bone marrow.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/999; Manual of Clinical Oncology/7"/323)

= Ureteral obstruction
=  Pyelonephritis
=» Uremia.
2. Distant metastasis.

Q. How carcinoma cervix can be prevented? (CMU-24M, BUP-22Nv)
Q. Short note: Cervical cancer screening and prevention.
Ans.
Prevention of cervical cancer: (V.V.I. for VIVA)
1. Primary prevention:
= Avoidence of the precipitating and risk factors (e.g. early marriage, multiple sex partners,
smoking etc.)

® Counseling / health education: To reduce high risk sexual behavior & to encourage safe sexual
behavior (e.g. use of condom).

® Vaccination: Prophylactic HPV vaccine (against HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18) for all school girls
(12-18 years) and women (16-25 years) with dose schedule 0-2-6 months.

2. Secondary prevention:

* Screening & early detection: Premalignant / precancercous stages can be detected by some non-
invasive means (screening tests). Screening is recommended to begin at age 21 years. The most
common screening tests are:

- Pap’s smear / Pap’s test

- HPV DNA testing by PCR ra
- Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA)
- Colposcopy.

3. Treatment (for the pre-malignant lesions).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1000; DeVita/11"/2090)
(NB: Screening means systematic application of a test in asymptomatic person to identify pre-clinical lesions).

#### 📄 Page 274

274 | arif's representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Pap test: Pap tests are cytologic preparations of exfoliated cells from the cervical transformation zone that
are stained with the Papnicolaou method.
(Ref: Robbins/100'/1000)
Or,
\ Pap smear, also called a Pap test, is a screening procedure for cervical cancer. \t tests for the presence of
pre-cancerous or cancerous cells on the cervix.

Procedure:
1. Sample (cell) collection: Using a spatula or cytobrush, the transformation zone of the cervix is
circumfterentially scraped for sample (cell) collection.
Smearing: Collected specimen (cells) is smeared on clean glass slides.
Fixation: By 95% alcohol.

bw

Staining & examination under microscope: The stained slide is then examined under a
microscope by the cytotechnologist (a person specifically trained to identify cytologic abnormalities).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1001; Manual of Clinical Oncology/7""/323,324)

Schedule for Pap test: In general the first smear should be at 21 years of age or within 3 years of onset of
sexual activity, and thereafter every 3 years. After 30 years of age, women who have had normal cytology
results and are negative for HPV may be screened every 5 years. Women who have a normal cytology result
but test positive for high-risk HPV DNA should have cervical cytology repeated every 6 to 12 months.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1001)

Papanicolaou’s grading:
Class I : Normal.
Class II : Inflammatory atypia (infection).
Class III : Mild dysplasia (CIN-I), moderate dysplasia (CIN-II).
Class IV : Severe dysplasia / carcinoma in situ (CIN-III).
Class V ; Invasive squamous carcinoma.

(Ref: DeVita/11'"/2094)

Importance of Pap test:

1. It is the main screening tool for cervical diseases, especially carcinoma cervix.

2. It is also used to get advice about further investigations like colposcopy.

(N.B: False negative error rate of Pap test is around 10-20%).
(Ref: Manual of Clinical Oncology/7"/323,324)

Q. Short note: Anovulatory cycle. (RU-18Nv)

Ans.

Anovulatory cycle: Anovulation or an anovulatory cycle is a menstrual cycle with no ovulation (failure to
ovulate). It is the most frequent cause of dysfunctional uterine bleeding during menarche and menopause.

Failure of ovulation (anovulation) is the result of prolonged and excessive oestrogenic stimulation without the
development of progestational (luteal) phase.

Q. Short note: Endometriosis. (DU-23M,07/05Ja, RU-19/18Nv,17Nv/Ja,16/15/14/13/12Ja, CU-
12Ju, SU-06Ja)

Ans.

Endometriosis: Endometriosis is defined by the presence of “ectopic” endometrial tissue at a site outside of

the uterus.

The abnormal tissue most commonly includes both endometrial glands and stroma, but may consist only of
stroma in some cases.

Fig: Endometriosis.

f

: It occurs in the following sites, in descending order of frequency-
Ovaries

Uterine ligaments

Recto-vaginal septum

Cul de sac

Pelvic peritoneum

Large and small bowel and appendix

Mucosa of the cervix, vagina, and fallopian tubes

Laparotomy scars.

euaweunel

Age group: The disorder is principally a disease of women in active reproductive life, most often in 3" & 4"
decades, affecting approx. 6-10% of women.

Pathogenesis: The major theories for the development of endometriosis- (Important for VIVA)

1. Regurgitation theory: According to this, endometrial tissue is implanted at abnormal locations.
Retrograde menstruation through the fallopian tubes occurs regularly even in normal women and could
mediate spread of endometrial tissue to the peritoneal cavity.

2. Benign metastases theory: According to this, endometrial tissue from the uterus can “spread” to
distant sites (e.g., bone, lung, and brain) via blood vessels and lymphatic channels.

3. Metaplastic theory: Metaplastic theory suggests that ectopic endometrium develops in situ from local
tissues by metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium (mesothelium of pelvis or abdomen).

4. Extrauterine stem/progenitor cell theory: It is a recent idea that proposes that stem/progenitor cells
from the bone marrow differentiate into endometrial tissue.

Q. What is chocolate cyst? (CU-12Ja, RU-10Ju) (Important for VIVA)

Q. Explain chocolate cyst. (CU-18Nv)

Q. Short note: Chocolate cyst of ovary. (RU-17Nv,13Ju,07Ja, SU-13Ju)

Ans.

Chocolate cyst: Endometriotic lesions bleed periodically in response to both extrinsic cyclic (ovarian) and
minnsic hormonal stimulation. This bleeding produces nodules with a red-blue to yellow brown appearance on
or just beneath the serosal surfaces and organizing hemorrhage causes extensive fibrous adhesions between
tubes, ovaries, and other structures and obliterates the pouch of Douglas.

The ovaries may become markedly distorted by large cystic masses (3 to 5 cm in diameter) filled with brown
fluid resulting from previous hemorrhage; these are often referred to clinically as chocolate cysts or
endometriomas.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1006)

Q. Short note: Adenomyosis. (RU-19M,15Ju,07Ja)

Ans.

Adenomyosis: Adenomyosis is defined as the presence of endometrial tissue within the uterine wall
(myometrium). It occurs in up to 20% of uteri.

Fig: Adenomyosis.

Diagnosis: On microscopic examination, irregular nests of endometrial stroma, with or without glands, are
arranged within the myometrium, separated from the basalis by at least 2 to 3 mm.

Clinical features / complications:
= Menometrorthagia (irregular and heavy menses)

* Colicky dysmenorrhea

= Pelvic pain (particularly during the menstrual period).

Q. Write the pathology of endometrial hyperplasia.

Q. Short note: Endometrial hyperplasia.

Ans.

Endometrial hyperplasia: It is defined as an abnormal proliferation of the endometrial glands relative to
the stroma, resulting in an increased gland-to-stroma ratio when compared with norma! proliferative

endometrium.

Cause: Endometrial hyperplasia is associated with prolonged estrogenic stimulation of the endometrium,
which in turn may be caused by-

* Anovulatory cycles
* Obesity (peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens)

a
* Menopause
* Polycystic ovarian syndrome
* Functioning granulosa cell tumors of the ovary
* Excessive ovarian cortical function (cortical stromal hyperplasia)
* Prolonged administration of estrogenic substances (estrogen replacement therapy)

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY [ 281

Presentation: Classic presentation is postmenopausal uterine bleeding.

Types: The most current WHO classification divides endometrial hyperplasia into two major categories (based
on presence or absence or cellular atypia):

1. Non-atypical (typical) hyperplasia:
= There is no cellular atypia
= Cardinal feature is an increase in the gland-to-stroma ratio
= Glands show variation in size and shape and may be dilated
= Rarely progress to carcinoma i.e. low malignant potential (approximately 1% to 3%)

2. Atypical hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia or carcinoma in situ):

= Presence of ‘atypical cells’ in the hyperplastic epithelium

## The extent of cellular atypia may be mild, moderate or severe

= The cytologic features present in these cells include loss of polarity, large size, irregular and
hyperchromatic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and altered nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio

= The glands are commonly back-to-back and often have complex outlines due to branching structures.

= Jt is a precancerous condition and is associated with an increased risk of endometrial
adenocarcinoma (23% to 48%).

Major complication: It is a frequent precursor to the most common type of endometrial carcinoma (the risk
of carcinoma varies with the degree of cellular atypia).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1006; Harsh Mohan/7"/723; BRS Pathology/5""/302; Pathoma Lecture Notes)

Risk factors for endometrial carcinoma:

= Age—more than 40 years. Peak incidence in 55-65 years.

= Obesity

* Diabetes

= Hypertension

* Infertility

= Unopposed estrogen stimulation
=» Endometrial hyperplasia.

Nice to Know:

Endometrial carcinoma is the most common invasive cancer of the female genital tract. Although it may be
asymptomatic for a period of time, it usually produces irregular or postmenopausal vaginal bleeding with
excessive leukorrhea.

(Ref: Robbins/¥"/1014,1018)

Q. Write about leiomyoma. (RU-19M)

Q. Short note: Leiomyoma. (RU-14Ja)

Ans.

Leiomyoma (fibroid) of uterus: Uterine leiomyomas (commonly called fibroid) are the benign smooth
muscle neoplasms of the uterus and perhaps the most common tumours in women. These benign tumours
may be present in about 75% of females of reproductive age. It may occur singly, but more often are multiple.

Fig: Leiomyoma (fibroid) of uterus.

Pathology / morphology:
* Sharply circumscribed, discrete, round, firm, gray-white tumor of varying sizes from small, barely
visible nodules to massive tumors that fill the pelvis.
* Except in rare instances, they are found within the myometrium of the corpus.

® They can occur within the myometrium (intramural), just beneath the endometrium (submucosal), or
beneath the serosa (subserosal).

* Oncut section, they exhibit characteristic whorled pattern
* Large tumors may develop areas of yellow-brown to red softening (red degeneration).

Intramural Submucosal

Subserosal
Uterine fibroid

Fig: Different varieties of fibroid uterus.

Histologically:
* They are essentially composed of 2 tissue elements—whorled bundles of smooth muscle cells admixed
with variable amount of connective tissue.

® Individual smooth muscle cells are uniform in size and shape with abundant cytoplasm and central
oval nuclei
* Mitotic figures are scarce.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/1014)

{N.B: Leiomyomas are also found in arrector pili (pilar leiomyoma — very painful), nipples, scrotum, labia &
less frequently deep soft tissue and gut wall}.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Polycystic_ovarian_ syndrome (PCOS) (formerly called Stein Leventhal syndrome): It is\a complex

by testosterone but the level of LH is sufficient to cause luteinisation of ovarian theca and granulosa cells
which then secrete androgen inappropriately. and) produce an abnormal state of anovulation. A hereditary
basis for the syndrome has been suggested in some cases.

Q Classify ovarian teratoma, (SU-15Ju)

AA
Qvarian teratoma: Teratomas are tumours composed of different types of tissues derived from the three
germ cell layers-—ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, in varying combinations.

Types: Teratomas are divided into three types-

1. Mature (benign) teratomas: Most benign tcratomas are cystic and known as dermoid cysts.

2. Immature (malignant) teratomas: These are rare tumors found chiefly in pre-pubertal adolescents
and young women under 20 years of age. They grow rapidly, and frequently penetrate the capsule, and
spread cither locally or distantly. They are predominantly solid tumours that contain immature or
embryonal structures in contrast to the mature or adult structures of the benign teratomas.

3. Monodermal or highly specialized teratomas: These are rare group of tumors most common of

which are struma ovarii and carcinoid.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1023)

Q. What is struma ovarii? (RU-18M)

Ans.

Struma ovarii: A struma ovarii (literally: goitre of the ovary) is a rare form of specialized or monodermal
teratoma that contains mostly thyroid tissue, which may cause hyperthyroidism.

Thyroid tissue must comprise more than 50 percent of the overall tissue to be classified as a struma ovarii.

Struma ovarii accounts for approximately 5 percent of all ovarian teratomas. The vast majority of struma ovarii

are benign tumors; however, malignant tumors of this type is found in a small percentage of cases.
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5'"/306; Robbins/10"/1024; Harsh Mohan/7"/737)

Q. Short note: Dermoid cyst of ovary. (DU-22Nv,11Ju,10Ja, SMU-23M,19Nv,05Ja, RU-09/07Ja)
Q. Short note: Dermoid cyst. (DU-22M, RMU-23M)

Ans. (Important for VIVA)

Benign cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst): Benign cystic teratomas are often referred to as dermoid cysts,

because they are almost always lined by skin-like structures.

They account for approximately 20% of ovarian tumours and 90% of germ cell tumours. They are the most
frequent benign ovarian tumours, and are usually found in young women during their active reproductive life.

Morphology:
Macroscopic:
= They are bilateral in 10% to 15% of cases.
= They are unilocular cysts containing hair & cheesy sebaceous material.
= The cyst wall is thin and opaque grey-white, wrinkled, apparent epidermis.
= From this epidermis, hair shafts frequently protrude.
* Within the wall, tooth structures & areas of calcification are present.

Microscopic:
= The cyst wall is lined by skin, including hair follicles & other skin appendages.
= Structures from other germ layers can be identified, such as cartilage, bone, gastrointestinal,

neural, respiratory and thyroid gland tissues.

Q. Give the morphology of dysgerminoma. (RMU-23/21M,14Ja,12Ju, CU-18Nv,05Ja)

Q. Write about dysgerminoma. (RU-19Nv)

Q. Short note: Dysgerminoma of ovary. (RU-18Ja,17Nv,08Ju)

Ans.

Dysgerminoma: Dysgerminoma is a germ cell tumour of ovary, and is best considered as the ovarian
counterpart of the seminoma of the testis. It comprises about 2% of all ovarian cancers and about half of
malignant germ cell tumors.

About 10% of patients with dysgerminoma have elevated B-hCG level in the plasma. All dysgerminomas are
malignant and are extremely radiosensitive.

Age of incidence: They may occur in childhood, but 75% occur in the 2™ & 3™ decades.

Morphology:
Grossly:
* Usually unilateral (80 - 90%).
* They are solid tumors.
* They vary in size from barely visible nodules to masses that virtually fill the entire abdomen.
= Oncut surface, they have a yellow-white to gray-pink appearance and are often soft & fleshy with foci
of haemorrhage and necrosis.

Histologically:
* The tumour cells are arranged in diffuse sheets, islands and cords separated by scanty fibrous stroma.
* Fibrous stroma is infiltrated with mature lymphocytes & occasional granulomas.

* On occasion, small nodules of dysgerminoma are encountered in the wall of an otherwise benign

Q. Enumerate the gestational trophoblastic diseases. (RU-12Ju)
Q. What are the gestational trophoblastic tumors?

Q. Short note: Gestational trophoblastic disease. (RU-10Ja)
Ans.

Gestational trophoblastic tumors: Gestational trophoblastic disease encompasses a spectrum of tumors and
tumorlike conditions characterized by proliferation of placental tissue, either villous or trophoblastic

The major disorders of this type are:
Hydatidiform mole (complete and partial)
Invasive mole

Placental-site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT)
Choriocarcinoma (frankly malignant).

Q. Mention morphology of hydatidiform mole. (CU-12Ju)

Q. Short note: Hydatidiform mole. (SU-20Nv) (Very Important for VIVA)

Ans.

Hydatidiform mole: Hydatidiform mole is characterized by cystic swelling of the chorionic villi,

accompanied by variable trophoblastic proliferation. They are associated with an increased risk of persistent
trophoblastic disease (invasive mole) or choriocarcinoma.

They are usually diagnosed during early pregnancy (average 9 weeks) by pelvic sonography.

Age of incidence: Molar pregnancy can develop at any age, but the risk is higher at the two ends of
reproductive life, in teenagers and between 40 and SO years of age.

Clinical characteristics:
* Vaginal bleeding
* Spontaneous miscarriage
= Rapid increase in uterine size

---

#### 📄 Page 293

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY 293

se —-
\ hydatidiform mole can be mistaken for a normal pregnancy, but the uterus is often too large for the
supposed state of gestation. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels also greatly exceed those of a

sermal pregnancy of similar gestational age.

Qinical variants: It occurs in two variants:
(1) Complete hydatidiform mole: No embryo is present; 46,XX karyotype, of exclusively paternal
derivation (a phenomenon called androgenesis).

(2) Partial hydatidiform mole: Embryo is present; triploidy (c.g. 69,XXY) and rarely tetraploidy
(92,XXXY) occur, thought to be due to fertilization of the ovum by two or more spermatozoa. The
usual result is 69 chromosomes derived from two paternal and one maternal haploid set.

Morphology:

Macroscopic:
= Uterine cavity is filled with a delicate, friable mass of thin-walled, translucent, cystic, grape-like
structures consisting of swollen edematous (hydropic) villi.
= Fetal parts are frequently seen in partial moles.

Microscopic:
* Complete moles show abnormalities that involve all or most of the villous tissue. The chorionic
villi are enlarged, scalloped in shape with central cavitation (cisterns), and lack adequately
developed vessels.

* Partial moles show only a fraction of the villi are enlarged and edematous, and the trophoblastic
hyperplasia is focal and less marked than in complete moles.

Fig: Complete hydatidiform mole.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1033; BRS Pathology/5"/310)

Ans.

(Ref: Lecture DMC)

a. Macroscopic feature: A mass of grape like structures of varying sizes filling the uterus

b. Microscopic feature:

= Marked thinning of the stromal tissue due to accumulation of fluid

nm

Q. Mention morphology of invasive mole. (CU-12Ju)

Q. Short note: Invasive mole.

Ans.

Invasive mole: Invasive mole is an infiltrative lesion that penetrates or even perforates the uterine wall.

Morphology: There is invasion of the myometrium by hydropic chorionic villi, accompanied by proliferation
of both cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast. The tumor is locally destructive and may invade parametrial
tissue and blood vessels. Hydifopic villi may embolize to distant sites, such as lungs and brain, but do not grow
in these organs as true metastases, and even without chemotherapy they eventually regress.

Clinical features:
* Vaginal bleeding
* Irregular uterine enlargement
* Persistently elevated serum hCG.

Treatment: The tumor responds well to chemotherapy but may result in uterine rupture, necessitate
hysterectomy.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/1034)

Fig: Invasive mole presenting as a hemorrhagic mass adherent to the uterine wall.

Q. Short note: Choriocarcinoma.
Ans.
Choriocarcinoma: Gestational choriocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of trophoblastic cells derived

from a previously normal or abnormal pregnancy, such as an extrauterine ectopic pregnancy. It is rapidly
invasive and metastasizs widely, but once identified responds well to chemotherapy.

It may be preceded by several conditions:
* 50% arise in complete hydatidiform moles
* 25% in previous abortions
* Approximately 22% follow normal pregnancies with the remainder occurring in ectopic pregnancies.

---

#### 📄 Page 295

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 295

Fig: Choriocarcinoma presenting as a bulky hemorrhagic mass invading the uterine wall.

hology:
Macroscopic:
* Itisasoft, fleshy, yellow-white tumour that usually has large pale areas of necrosis and extensive
haemorrhage.

Microscopic:
= [t consists entirely of proliferating syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts.
® Chorionic villi are absent.
® Mitoses are abundant and sometimes abnormal.
* The tumour invades the underlying myometrium, frequently penetrates blood vessels, and in some
cases extends out onto the uterine serosa and into adjacent structures.

Ciinical features: Irregular vaginal spotting of a bloody, brown fluid.

Metastases: Widespread metastases are characteristic; the most common sites are the lungs (50%) and vagina
(30% to 40%), followed by, in descending order of frequency, the brain, liver, bone, and kidney.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1034)

Q. A 3 month pregnant woman, 40 yrs age come with vaginal bleeding. Ultrasonogram of
lower abdomen shows cystic changes in uterus and grape like clusters. What is your
provisional diagnosis and most serious complication? (Important for VIVA)

Provisional diagnosis: Hydatidiform mole.

Complication: Choriocarcinoma.

Q. What is psedocyesis? How can you differentiate urine of pregnant lady from urine of
trophoblastic tumor by examining urine? (RU-07Ju)

Ans.

Psedocyesis: A condition in which a patient has nearly all of the usual signs and symptoms of pregnancy such
2s enlargement of the abdomen, weight gain, cessation of menses and morning sickness, but the patient is not
pregnant. It is usually seen in women who cither are very desirous of having children or wishes to avoid
pregnancy. Treatment is usually donc by psychiatric means.

Differentiation of urine of pregnant lady from urine of trophoblastic tumor by examining urine: The
HCG level in pregnant women is below | lac unit but in trophoblastic tumor it is more than | lac and it may be
up to S lacs.

breast is erythematous and painful, and fever is often present.

= Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts: It is known by a variety of names, including
recurrent subareolar abscess, periductal mastitis, and Zuska disease. Women, and sometimes men,
present with a painful erythematous subareolar mass that mimics a bacterial abscess. More than
90% of afflicted individuals are smokers.

= Duct ectasia: It presents as a palpable periareolar mass that is often associated with thick, white
nipple secretions and occasionally with skin retraction. Pain and erythema are uncommon and not
associated with cigarette smoking.

present as a painless palpable mass, skin thickening or retraction, or mammographic densities or

or multiple hard’ palpable masses or mammographic densities. The masses are associated with
areas of densely collagenized stroma, a feature that may make it difficult to obtain lesional tissue
by needle biopsy. Within the stroma are atrophic ducts and lobules with thickened basement
membranes that are surrounded by a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate.

= Granulomatous Mastitis: Granulomatous-inflammation of the breast may be a manifestation of
systemic granulomatous diseases (e.g.,. granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis)

or of inflammatory or infectious disorders that are localized to the breast.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1040; Lecture SSMC)

Q. Mention the morphology of non-proliferative breast changes (fibrocystic changes). (CU-03Ja)
Ans.
Morphology of non-proliferative breast changes (fibrocystic changes): There are three principal

morphologic changes: a) cystic change, often with apocrine metaplasia; b) fibrosis; and c) adenosis.

1. Cysts: Cysts are lined either by a flattened atrophic epithelium or by metaplastic apocrine cells.
Metastatic cells have an abundant granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei, resembling the
normal apocrine epithelium of sweat glands. Calcifications are common.

2. Fibrosis: Cysts frequently rupture, with release of secretory material into the adjacent stroma. The
resulting chronic inflammation and fibrosis contribute to palpable nodularity of the breast.

3. Adenosis: It is defined as an increase in the number of acini per lobule. It is a normal feature of
pregnancy. In nonpregnant women, adenosis can occur as a focal change. The acini are lined by
columnar epithelial cells, and calcifications are occasionally present within the lumens.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/1042)

Q. Give the morphology of fibroadenoma of breast. (RMU-22Nv, CU-20Nv)
Q. State the microscopic featres of fibroadenoma. (CU-20Ju)
Q. Short note: Fibro-adenoma of breast. (SU-12Ja, CU-16Ja,13Ju)

Q. Short note: Fibro-adenoma. (RU-18Nv)
Ans.

Fibroadenoma (adenofibroma): Fibroadenoma is the most common benign tumor of the female breast.
= Age: Most patients are between 15 to 30 years of age.
* Number: Frequently multiple and bilateral.

---

#### 📄 Page 299

Clinical feature: Young women usually present with a palpable mass and older women with a
mammographic density or clustered calcifications. The lesion is firm, rubbery, painless, well-
circumscribed and freely mobile.

Fibroadenoma

Fig: Fibroadenoma of breast.
Morphology:
Grossly:

The tumors are well circumscribed, rubbery, and freely movable nodules usually in upper-outer
quadrant of breast.

They vary in size from less than 1 cm to large tumours that replace most of the breast.

Cut surface is firm, grayish white and often contain slit-like spaces (formed by compressed ducts)
lined by epithelium.

Fig: A well-circumscribed mass which is clearly demarcated from the surrounding yellow adipose tissue.
Histologically:
* The stroma is usually delicate, cellular and often myxoid, resembling normal intralobular stroma.

The arrangements between fibrous overgrowth and ducts may produce two types of patterns:

a. Intracanalicular pattern: Stroma compresses and distorts ducts into slit-like spaces.

b. Pericanalicular pattern: Encircling masses of fibrous stroma around the patent or dilated ducts.
In older women, the stroma typically becomes densely hyalinized and the epithelium atrophic.

Q. Short note: Paget’s disease of nipple. (DU-04S, CU-03S) (Important for VIVA)

Ans.
Paget’s disease of nipple: Paget disease of the nipple is a rare manifestation of breast cancer (1% to 4% of
cases) that presents as a unilateral erythematous eruption with a scale crust. Pruritus is common, and the

lesion may be mistaken for eczema.

The nipple bears a crusted, scaly and eczematoid lesion with a palpable subareolar mass in about 50-60%
of cases.

#### 📄 Page 301

a
tuis often associated with an invasive or non-invasive ductal carcinoma of the underlying breast. Most of the
patients with palpable mass are found to have invasive (infiltrating) duct carcinoma, while those with no
palpable breast lump are usually subsequently found to have intraductal carcinoma (DCIS).

Fig: Paget’s disease of nipple.

Pathogenesis: Malignant cells (Paget cells) extend from the underlying ductal carcinoma (DCIS) within the
ductal system via the lactiferous sinuses into nipple skin without crossing the basement membrane. The
malignant cells disrupt the normally tight squamous epithelial cell barrier, allowing extracellular fluid to seep
out onto the nipple surface and form an oozing scaly crust.

Fig: Paget disease of the nipple.

(Ductal carcinoma in situ arising within the ductal system of the breast can extend up the lactiferous ducts
and into the skin of the nipple without crossing the basement membrane)

Morphology:
Gross:
* The skin of the nipple and areola is crusted, fissured and ulcerated.
= Have oozing, hyperaemia and oedema.

Fig: Paget’s diseases of the breast. The region of nipple and areola is crusted and ulcerated.

Microscopic:
* Presence of Paget’s cells (malignant cells) singly or in small clusters in the epidermis.
* Paget’s cells are larger than the epidermal cells, anaplastic, hyperchromatic and usually surrounded by a
clear zone or halo.
Diagnosis:
* Nipple biopsy

Ciinical presentation of breast cancer (carcinoma of the breast):
(a) Presence of a painless hard lump.

Q. Write down the risk factors involved in breast cancer. (DU-08Ju, SU-20Nv, CU-20Nv)
(V.V.L for VIVA & MCQ)
Ans.

Risk factors for the development of breast cancer:
1. Gender: 99% of affected patients are female.

2. Age:
" Incidence increases with increasing age (peaking at the age of 70-80 years).

= Rarely found before the age of 25 years except in some familial cases.

3. Germline mutations: Inherited mutations in the p53, BRCA-1, or BRCA-2 tumor suppressor genes are
associated with increased risk.

4. First-degree relatives with breast cancer: First-degree relatives (mother, sister, daughter) of women
with breast cancer have 2 to 6-fold higher risk of development of breast cancer.

5. Geographic and racial factors: Incidence of breast cancer is about 4-6 times higher in developed
countries (North America, North Europe, Australia), and low in developing countries of Asia and
Africa.

6. Early menarche and late menopause (increases estrogen exposure): Menarche at ages younger
than 11 years increases risk by 20% compared to menarche at ages greater than 14. Late menopause
also increases risk.

Age at first pregnancy: Nulliparity & first pregnancy after 30 years of age increases the risk.

4. Benign breast disease: Proliferative fibrocystic disease with atypical epithelial hyperplasia increases
the risk of developing invasive carcinoma.

5. Estrogen exposure: Postmenopausal hormone replacement therapy (HRT) increases the risk of breast
cancer, particularly when estrogen and a progestin are given together for a period of years. Oral
contraceptives are unlikely to increase the risk of breast cancer.

6. High breast density: High breast density is potentially susceptible to neoplastic transformation. Dense
breast also make detection of cancer more difficult by mammography.

7. Radiation exposure: Radiation of the chest, whether due to cancer therapy, atomic bomb exposure, or
nuclear accidents, results in a higher rate of breast cancer.

---

#### 📄 Page 307

|

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 307

History of breast cancer in one breast: associated with increased incidence in the opposite breast.

Diet: Large amounts of animal fats, high calorie foods; cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption
increases the risk.

10. Obesity: Possibly due to production of estrogens by adipose tissue.
11. Exercise: There is a small protective effect for women who are physically active. -

12. Breast-feeding: The longer women breast-feed, the greater is the reduction in the risk.

13. Environmental toxins: Environmental contaminants such as organochlorine pesticides could have
estrogenic effects of humans.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1046; BRS Pathology/5"/312; Harsh Mohan/7"/750)

Q. Outline the prognostic factors involved in breast carcinoma. (DU-23/19Nv,16/14Ju, BUP-
19M, SU-08Ju)

Ans.

Prognostic factors of breast carcinoma:
A. Major prognostic factors:

1.

Invasive carcinoma versus in situ disease:

* In situ carcinoma is confined to the ductal system & cannot metastasize. So, great majority of
DICS will be cured with adequate treatment.

= In contrast, at least half of invasive carcinomas will have metastasized locally or distantly at

the time of diagnosis. Their prognosis is bad.
Distant metastases: Once distant metastases are present, cure is unlikely.
Lymph node metastases: Axillary lymph node status is the most important prognostic factor for
invasive carcinoma in the absence of distant metastasis. The less the lymph node metastasis, the
more the chance of good prognosis.
Tumor size: The size of the carcinoma is the second most important prognostic factor and is
independent from lymph node status. The more the size of the cancer, the prognosis is bad.
Locally advanced diseases: Carcinomas invading into skin or skeletal muscle are usually large
and may be difficult to treat surgically.
Inflammatory carcinoma: Breast cancer presenting with breast swelling and skin thickening due
to dermal lymphatic involvement have a particularly poor prognosis.
Lymphovascular invasion: Tumor cells are present within vascular spaces (either lymphatics or
small capillaries) in about half of all invasive carcinomas. This finding is strongly associated with

the presence of lymph node metastases. It is a poor prognostic factor for overall survival in women
without lymph node metastases and a risk factor for local recurrence.

B. Minor prognostic factors:

1.

Molecular subtype: The molecular subtype, determined by expression of ER and HER2 and
proliferation, is an important prognostic factor.

Special histologic types: The survival rate of women with some special types of invasive
carcinomas (tubular, mucinous, lobular, papillary, adenoid cystic) is greater than that of women
with cancers of no special type.

Histologic grade: All invasive carcinomas are graded using the Nottingham Histologic Score that
classifies invasive carcinomas into three groups (grade I, II, III) that are highly correlated with
disease free and overall survival.

Proliferative rate: Tumors with high proliferation rates have a poorer prognosis but may respond
better to chemotherapy.

---

#### 📄 Page 308

308 arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Estrogen and progesterone receptors (ER/PR): Oestrogen is known to promote the breast
cancer. Presence or absence of hormone receptors on the tumour cells can help in predicting the
response of breast cancer to endocrine therapy. Accordingly, patients with high levels of ER and
PR on breast tumour cells have a slightly better prognosis.

n

6. HER2/neu overexpression: HER2/neu overexpression is associated with poorer survival, but
its main importance is as a predictor of response to agents that target this receptor (targeted
therapy).

7. DNA content: Aneuploid tumors having abnormal DNA indices, have slightly worse prognosis.

8. Response to neoadjuvant therapy: The subgroups of patients who achieve a pathologic
complete response to neoadjuvant therapy have a greater than 95% long-term survival.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1058; Harsh Mohan/7"/755)

Q. Name the molecular subtypes of breast carcinoma. (CU-15Ju)
Q. Write down the molecular classification of breast cancer. (CU-20/19/18M)
Q. Discuss the molecular subtypes of invasive breast carcinoma. (CMU-21M,15Ju)
Ans.
Molecular classification of breast cancer: V.V.I for VIVA
1. Luminal A: Hormone-receptor (ER & PR) strongly positive; HER2 negative.
2. Luminal B: Hormone-receptor (ER & PR) low positive; HER2 negative.
3. HER2-enriched: HER2 positive; hormone-receptor (ER & PR) positive/negative.
4. Basal-like: Hormone-receptor (ER & PR) and HER? all are negative (‘Triple negative’).

Out of all these, basal-like type has worst prognosis while luminal type A responds well to endocrine
therapy and has good prognosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1060; BRS Pathology/5"/311; Harsh Mohan/7"/757)

Q. Discuss the role of ER, PR & HER2 in the prognosis of breast carcinoma. (DU-23Nv, CMU-
21M)
Q. Discuss the role of ER & HER2 in the prognosis of breast cancer. (CU-15Ju)
Ans.
Role of ER, PR & HER2 in the prognosis of breast cancer: V.V.I for VIVA
Tumours that express both ER & PR (or only ER or PR) is correlated with a better prognosis, because
they respond well to endocrine therapy.
* Presence of HER2/neu is associated with a poorer prognosis, because tumours that overexpress
HER2 tend to metastasize earlier.
(Ref: BRS Pathology/5"/312; Lecture DMC)

Q. Short note: Breast cancer. (CU-14Ja)

Ans.

Breast cancer: Carcinoma of the breast is the most common non-skin malignancy in women and is second
only to lung cancer as a cause of cancer deaths. A woman who lives to age 90 has a one in eight chance of
developing breast cancer.

= Site of involvement: Breast cancer occurs most frequently in the upper outer quadrant of the breast.
It occurs more often in left breast than the right and is bilateral in about 4% cases.

* Sites of metastasis: Mainly in the axillary lymph nodes, lung, liver, and bone.

Ans.

Gynaecomastia: Enlargement of the male breast is known as gynaecomastia.

It may be unilateral and bilateral and presents as a button-like subareolar enlargement. In advanced cases, the
swelling can simulate the adolescent female breast.

ay

Pathogenesis: Gynaecomastia may occur as a result of an imbalance between estrogens, which stimulates
breast tissue, and androgens, which counteract these effects.

Causes:
1. Pubertal gynaecomastia (young boys between 13 and 17 years of age)
2. Failure of the androgenic functions of the testis (in older males)
3. Cirrhosis of liver
4. Testicular tumours
5. Pituitary tumours
6. Carcinoma of the lung
7. Exogenous oestrogen therapy as in carcinoma of the prostate
8. Testicular atrophy in Klinefelter’s syndrome (secondary gynaecomastia)
9.

Drugs (such as alcohol, marijuana, heroin, antiretroviral therapy, anabolic steroids used by some
athletes and body builders, and some psychoactive agents)
10. Idiopathic gynaecomastia (without any obvious cause).

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1044; Harsh Mohan/7"/748)

7NDOCRINE SYSTEM

Thyroid Gland

Trachea

Histology: The thyroid gland is divided by thin fibrous septa into lobules composed of follicles (about 20-40)
which are the main functional units of the thyroid. The follicles are lined by cuboidal to low columner
epithelium with numerous fine microvilli extending into the follicular colloid that contains the glycoprotein,
thyroglobulin (which contains the thyroid hormones within its molecule). The thyroid gland follicles also
contain a population of parafollicular cells, or C cells, which synthesize and secrete the hormone calcitonin.
{Ref: Robbins/10"/1075; Harsh Mohan/7"/793}

Q. Define thyrotoxicosis & hyperthyroidism. Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism.
Ans.

Thyrotoxicosis & hyperthyroidism: Hyperthyroidism, also called thyrotoxicosis, is a hypermetabolic
clinical and biochemical state caused by excess production of thyroid hormones (T3 and T,).

Because it is caused most commonly by Ayperfunction of the thyroid gland, it is often referred to as
hyperthyroidism.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1075; Harsh Mohan/7"/793)

Causes of hyperthyroidism:

Primary:

Diffuse hyperplasia of the thyroid (Graves disease) - approximately 85% of cases
Hyperfunctioning (“toxic”) multinodular goiter

Hyperfunctioning (“toxic”) adenoma

Thyroiditis

Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism

6. Neonatal thyrotoxicosis associated with maternal Graves disease

{N.B: Strictly speaking, hyperthyroidism is only one (albeit the most common) cause of thyrotoxicosis, as in
certain conditions the oversupply of thyroid hormone is related to either excessive release of preformed
thyroid hormone (e.g. in thyroiditis) or to an extrathyroidal source (e.g. Struma ovarii, exogenous thyroxine
intake etc.) rather than hyperfunction of the gland.}

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1076 + 9°/1083)

Q. Define hypothyroidism. Enumerate the causes of hypothyroidism.
Ans.
Hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism is a hypometabolic clinical state resulting from inadequate production
of thyroid hormones for prolonged periods, or rarely, from resistance of the peripheral tissues to the effects of
thyroid hormones.

(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/793)

Or,
Hypothyroidism is a condition caused by a structural or functional derangement that interferes with the
production of thyroid hormone.
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/1077)

Causes of hypothyroidism:

Primary:
1. Genetic defects in thyroid development (rare)
2. Thyroid hormone resistance syndrome (rare)

Thyroiditis

Q. What are the inflammatory conditions of the thyroid gland?
Ans.

Inflammatory conditions of the thyroid gland (thyroiditis): Thyroiditis encompasses a diverse group of
disorders characterized by some form of thyroid inflammation. This discussion focuses on the three most
common and clinically significant subtypes:
= Hashimoto thyroiditis
= Granulomatous (de Quervain’s) thyroiditis (painful) - probably secondary to a viral infection
* Subacute lymphocytic (painless) thyroiditis (postpartum thyroiditis).
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1178)

Q. Describe briefly the pathogenesis of Hashimoto thyroiditis. (DU-06Ja)
Q. Short note: Hashimoto thyroiditis. (DU-11Ja) (Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Hashimoto thyroiditis: Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in destruction of the
thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure.

Epidemiology: It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in areas of the world where iodine levels are
sufficient. This disorder is most prevalent between 45 and 65 years of age and is more common in women
than in men, with a female predominance of 10:1 to 20:1.

Pathogenesis: Hashimoto thyroiditis is caused by a breakdown in self-tolerance to thyroid auto-antigens >
This results in progressive autoimmune destruction of thyroid cells by infiltrating cytotoxic T cells, locally
released cytokines, or by antibody-dependent cytotoxicity.

Induction of thyroid autoimmunity is accompanied by a progressive depletion of thyrocytes by apoptosis
and replacement of the thyroid parenchyma by mononuclear cell infiltration and fibrosis. Multiple
immunologic mechanisms may contribute to thyroid cell death, including-

= CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated cell death: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells may cause thyrocyte destruction.

= Cytokine mediated cell death: Excessive T-cell activation — Production of Ty! inflammatory
cytokines e.g. y-IFN — Recruitment and activation of macrophages — Damage to follicles.

* Binding of anti-thyroid antibodies (anti-thyroglobulin, and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies)
followed by antibody dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity.

Grave’s Disease

Q. Mention the expected laboratory findings in Grave’s disease.

Q. Short note: Grave’s disease. (BUP-22Nv,16Ja, DU-19M,15/14/10/08Ju) (Important for
VIVA)

Ans.

Grave’s disease: Grave’s disease is an autoimmune thyroid disorder which the most common cause of
endogenous hyperthyroidism and is characterized by a triad of clinical findings-

1. Hyperthyroidism associated with diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland
2. Infiltrative ophthalmopathy with resultant exophthalmos
3. Localized, infiltrative dermopathy (sometimes called pretibial myxedema).

Age: It has a peak incidence between 20 & 40 years of age. Women are affected as much as 10 times more
frequently than men.

Pathogenesis: Grave’s disease is an auto-immune disease, caused by the production of multiple
autoantibodies against the TSH receptor. These are as. under:

= Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) - stimulates increased release of thyroid hormone.
= Thyroid growth stimulating immunoglobulins (TGI) - stimulates proliferation of follicular epithelium.
= TSH-binding inhibitor immunoglobulins (TBII) - inhibitory to binding of TSH to its own receptor.

Depending upon its action as inhibitory or stimulatory to follicular epithelium, it may result in alternate
episodes of hypo- and hyperthyroidism.

Morphology:
Macroscopically:
= Symmetrical enlargement of thyroid gland due to diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia of thyroid
follicular epithelial cells.
= Increase in weight to over 80 gm.
* On cut section, the parenchyma has a soft, meaty appearance resembling normal muscle.

Microscopically:
= The follicles are small and are lined by tall columnar epithelium and more crowded than usual.
= There is considerable epithelial hyperplasia and hypertrophy and formation of papillary infoldings
of piled up epithelium into the lumina of follicles.
* The colloid is markedly diminished.
* The stroma shows increased vascularity and accumulation of lymphoid cells; germinal centers are
common.

Fig: Morphology of Graves’ disease.

---

2. Ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos)
3. Dermopathy (scaly thickening and induration of the skin overlying the shins - pretibial myxedema)

Nice to Know:

In Graves ophthalmopathy, the protrusion of the eyeball (exopthalmos) is caused by an increase in the
volume of the retro-orbital connective tissues and extraocular muscles, which occurs for several reasons:

1. Marked infiltration of connective tissue by mononuclear cells, predominantly T cells

2. Inflammation, edema, and swelling of extraocular muscles

3. Accumulation of extracellular matrix components, specifically hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans such
as hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate

4. Increased numbers of adipocytes (fatty infiltration).

These changes not only displace the eyeball but also may interfere with the function of the extraocular
muscles.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1081)

Q. What is goiter? (DU-17Nv,07Ju,06Ja, CU-19Nv) Classify goiter.

Q. Short note: Goiter. (CU-20M)

Ans.

Goiter: The term ‘goitre’ means any enlargement of the thyroid gland, which is caused by compensatory
hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the follicular epithelium in response to thyroid hormone deficiency.

Pathogenesis: Impairment of thyroid hormone synthesis leads to a compensatory rise in the serum TSH level,
which, in turn, causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of thyroid follicular cells and, ultimately, gross
enlargement of the thyroid gland (goiter).

Types of goiter:
1. Diffuse non-toxic (simple) goiter
* Endemic goiter
= Non-endemic / Sporadic goiter

2. Multinodular goiter
= Toxic multinodular goiter
* Non-toxic multinodular goiter.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1082; Harsh Mohan/7"/797)

Hashimoto thyroiditis (under active goiter)
4. lodine deficiency goiter (endemic) — occurs in geographic areas in which the diet is deficient in iodine.

Q. What are the causes of hyperfunctional and hypofunctional goiter? (CMU-24M)

Ans.
Causes_of hyperfunctional goiter (Overactive thyroid): A hyperfunctional goiter is associated with

excessive production of thyroid hormones (hyperthyroidism). Common causes include:

1. Graves’ disease — An autoimmune disorder where antibodies (TSI -  thyroid-stimulating
immunoglobulins) overstimulate the thyroid, causing diffuse toxic goiter and hyperthyroidism.

2. Toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer’s disease) — Multiple nodules in the thyroid become
hyperactive and produce excessive thyroid hormones.

3. Toxic adenoma — A single benign tumor in the thyroid autonomously produces excess thyroid
hormone.

4. Thyroiditis (Subacute or silent thyroiditis) — Inflammation of the thyroid gland, often viral or
autoimmune, can cause transient hyperthyroidism.

5. Excess iodine intake (Jod-Basedow phenomenon) — Occurs when individuals with underlying
thyroid disorders are exposed to excess iodine, triggering excessive thyroid hormone production.

Causes_of hypofunctional goiter _(underactive thyroid): A hypofunctional goiter is associated with
insufficient production of thyroid hormones (hypothyroidism), usually due to:
1. Iodine deficiency — The most common cause worldwide; insufficient iodine leads to decreased thyroid
hormone synthesis, stimulating TSH release and thyroid enlargement.
2. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis — An autoimmune disorder where the immune system attacks the thyroid,
leading to gradual destruction and reduced hormone production.
3. Congenital hypothyroidism — Thyroid hormone deficiency present from birth, often due to thyroid
dysgenesis or enzyme defects.
4. Goitrogenic foods or drugs — Certain foods (e.g., cruciferous vegetables, soy) and drugs (e.g.,
lithium, amiodarone) can inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis.
5. Post-treatment hypothyroidism — Following radioactive iodine therapy, thyroid surgery, or anti-
thyroid drug treatment for hyperthyroidism, the gland may become underactive.

Both hyperfunctional and hypofunctional goiters can present with an enlarged thyroid, but their underlying
causes and systemic effects differ significantly.

Types and causes:
a. Endemic goiter: Goiter occurring with high frequency in iodine-deficient geographic areas.

Q. Enumerate in short about the pathogenesis of thyroid cancer. (CU-08Ja)
Ans.

Pathogenesis of thyroid cancer:

1. Genetic factors: Distinct genetic events are involved in the pathogenesis of the four major histologic
variants of thyroid cancer.

= Papillary carcinomas: Activation of the MAP kinase pathway by rearrangement of the tyrosine
kinase receptors RET or NTRK (neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor), and point mutations in the
BRAF.

* Follicular carcinomas: Mutations in the RAS family of oncogenes.

=" Anaplastic (undifferentiated) carcinomas: Inactivating point mutations in the p53 tumor
suppressor genes.

* Medullary thyroid carcinomas: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN-2) and RET
protooncogenes mutations.

2. Environmental factors: Exposure to ionizing radiation, particularly during the |“ 2 decades of life.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1094)

Q. Short note: Papillary carcinoma of thyroid. (DU-12/04Ja, SUST-21Nv/M, BUP-20Nv/M, RU-
19M)

Ans.

Papillary carcinoma of thyroid:

Most common form of thyroid cancer (80-85%).

They occur throughout life but most often between the ages of 25 and 50.

Found in about three times more frequently in females than in males.

Account for the majority of thyroid carcinomas associated with previous exposure to ionizing

radiation.

Morphology:
Grossly:

= Solitary or multi focal lesions within the thyroid.

= Some tumors are well circumscribed & even encapsulated; others may infiltrate the adjacent
parenchyma with ill-defined margins.

The lesions may contain areas of fibrosis and calcification and are often cystic.
Cut surface sometimes reveals papillary foci that point to the diagnosis.

Microscopically:
= Branching papillae having a fibrovascular stalk covered by a single to multiple layers of cuboidal
epithelial cells.
= Nuclei of the papillary carcinoma cells are optically clear or empty appearance (Ground-glass or
Orphan Annie eye nuclei).

* Concentrically calcified structures termed psammoma bodies are often present within the lesion,
usually within the cores of the papillae.

(N.B: The diagnosis of papillary carcinoma can be made based on these nuclear features, even in the absence
of papillary architecture.)

Q. Enumerate in short about the prognosis of thyroid cancer. (CU-08Ja)

Ans.

Prognosis of thyroid cancer: The prognosis largely depends on several factors including age, extent of
invasion and stage at presentation (presence or absence of distant metastasis).

* Papillary carcinoma: Excellent prognosis, with a 10-year overall survival rate in excess of 95%. 5-
20% of patients have local or regional recurrence, and 10-15% have distant metastases.

= Follicular carcinoma: 10-year overall survival rate 50-70%.

* Medullary carcinoma: Pognosis is excellent if no metastases. It has a late metastases and spread by
lymphatics and blood. 10-year overall survival rate 60-70%.

* Anaplastic carcinoma: There is no effective therapy for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, and the disease
is almost uniformly fatal. Although metastases to distant sites are common, in most cases death occurs
in less than one year as a result of aggressive growth and compromise of vital structures in the neck.
10-year overall survival rate 5-10% and median survival about 2 months.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1086-1092; Harsh Mohan/7"/802)

The Endocrine Pancreas

The endocrine pancreas consists of about | million clusters of cells, the islets of Langerhans, which contain
four major and two minor cell types. The four main types are B, a, 5, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells.
They can be differentiated by the ultrastructural characteristics of their granules, and by their hormone content.

= The £ cells produce insulin, which regulates glucose utilization in tissues and reduces blood glucose
levels, as will be detailed in the discussion of diabetes.

= The a cells secrete glucagon, which stimulates glycogenolysis in the liver and thus increases blood
sugar.

= The 6 cells secrete somatostatin, which suppresses both insulin and glucagon release.

= The PP cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as
stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility. These
cells not only are present in islets but also are scattered throughout the exocrine pancreas.

There are also two rare cell types, D/ cells and enterochromaffin cells.
* DI cells elaborate vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and
hyperglycemia; it also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.
* Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause the
carcinoid syndrome.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1097)

Q. What do you mean by type 1 diabetes mellitus? Give its etiology and pathogenesis.
Q. Write down the pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes mellitus.
Q. Short note: Type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Ans.
Type 1 diabetes (T1D) / Insulin-dependant DM (IDDM) / Juvenile onset DM: Type | diabetes (TID) is an

autoimmune disease characterized by pancreatic B cell destruction and an absolute deficiency of insulin.

It accounts for approximately 5% to 10% of diabetes and is the most common subtype diagnosed in patients
younger than 20 years of age.

Pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes mellitus: Type 1 diabetes is generally considered a T-cell-mediated
autoimmune disease involving destruction of the insulin-secreting B cells in the pancreatic islets.

As in all autoimmune diseases, genetic susceptibility and environmental factors play important roles in the
pathogenesis.

* Autoimmunity: Chronic autoimmune attack on f-cells contributes to B-cell destruction. The
mechanisms of f-cell destruction are-

a. Infiltration of the islets with mononuclear cells containing activated macrophages, CD4+ T helper
cells, CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, NK cells & B lymphocytes. This lesion is called insulitis.

b. Locally produced cytokines such as IFN-y, produced by T cells, and TNF and IL-1, produced by
macrophages damage f-cells.

c. Autoantibodies against islets cells and insulin are produced in 70-80% of patients.
= Genetic susceptibility: HLA-DR3 and DR4 are associated with increased susceptibility to type 1 diabetes.

« Environmental factors: Viruses such as_ coxsackieviruses group B, mumps, measles,
cytomegalovirus, rubella, and infectious mononucleosis.

Q. Write down the pathogenesis of diabetes mellitus. (DU-04M)
Q. Write down the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Ans.
Type 2 diabetes / Non-insulin-dependant DM (NIDDM) / Adult onset DM: Type 2 diabetes is caused by a

combination of peripheral resistance to insulin action and an inadequate secretory response by the pancreatic B
cells (“relative insulin deficiency”).

Approximately 90% to 95% of diabetic patients have type 2 diabetes, and the vast majority of such individuals
are overweight.

Etiopathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus:

1. Genetic factors

2. Obesity

3. Sedentary life style

4. Dietary habit (overeating, especially when combined with obesity and under-activity)
5. Age - Middle aged and elderly (usually above 40 years).

Pathogenesis: Development of T2D involves two key abnormalities-

tissue, and liver, to insulin.

2. B-cell dysfunction: Inadequate insulin secretion in the face of insulin resistance and hyperglycemia
(Ref: Robbin’s/10"/1103; Davidson’s/23"/730)

Q. Describe the effects of diabetes mellitus on kidney.
Ans.

Effects of diabetes mellitus on kidney: The kidneys are prime targets of diabetes. Renal failure is second
only to MI as a cause of death from this disease. Three lesions are encountered:

Q. Short note: Psoriasis of skin. (CMU-24M)
Ans.
Psoriasis of skin: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis that affects about 2% of the population.

Characteristics:

« It usually appears first between the age of 15 and 30 years.

" The lesions are characterised by brownish-red papules and plaques which are sharply demarcated and
are covered with fine, silvery white scales.

* As the scales are removed by gentle scrapping, fine bleeding points appear termed Auspitz sign.

* Commonly involved sites are the scalp, upper back, sacral region and extensor surfaces of the
extremities, especially the knees and elbows.

= In about 25% of cases, peculiar pitting of nails is seen.

* Psoriatic arthritis resembling rheumatoid arthritis is produced in about 5% of cases but rheumatoid
factor is absent.

Histopathology: Following features are observed in fully developed lesions:
* Acanthosis with regular downgrowth of rete ridges to almost the same dermal level with thickening of
their lower portion.
Elongation and oedema of the dermal papillae with broadening of their tips.
Suprapapillary thinning of stratum malpighii.
Absence of granular cell layer.
Prominent parakeratosis.
Presence of Munro microabscesses in the parakeratotic horny layer is diagnostic of psoriasis.

Q. Give the etiology & pathogenesis of basal cell carcinoma.

Q. Give the morphology of basal cell carcinoma / rodent ulcer. (RMU-21M, SU-18M)

Q. Write briefly about basal cell carcinoma. (CU-18Nv)

Q. Short note: Basal cell carcinoma. (DU-10/08Ju, CMU-23M,20Ju,19Nv,16/15Ja,13Ju, 12Ja,11/
10Ju,05Ja, RMU-23M,19/18Nv,12/10/07Ja, BUP-21Nv/M, SU-13Ja)

Q. Short note: Rodent ulcer. (RU-17Nv/Ja)

Ans.

Basal cell carcinoma (Rodent ulcer): Malignant proliferation of basal cell (stem cell) of epidermis.

It is the most common of all malignant skin tumors arising from basal layer of the epidermis & its
appendages. Typically, the basal cell carcinoma is a locally invasive, slow-growing tumour of middle-aged
that rarely metastasises.

Sites: (Important for VIVA)
* Chronic sun-exposed sites in lightly pigmented elderly adults.
* Most commonly on the face (90%), usually above a line from the angle of mouth upto the ear
lobule.

Rodent ulcer

Fig: Common location and macroscopic appearance of basal cell carcinoma (rodent ulcer).

Aetiology:
i) Age: Mostly occur after the age of 40 years.

ii) Race: Lightly skinned races (who have little melanin) are most susceptible than black.
iii) Precancerous conditions: Xeroderma pigmentosum, basal cell nevus syndrome.
iv) Environmental factor: Chronic sun exposure.

Morphology:
Macroscopic:
1, Ulcerated (most common pattern):
* A slow-growing small nodule undergoes central ulceration with pearly, raised rolled margins.
* The tumour enlarges in size by burrowing and by destroying the tissues locally like a rodent and
hence the name ‘rodent ulcer’.

2. Non-ulcerated (less frequent pattern): Pearly and shiny papules often containing dialated
(telangiectatic) vessel.

Fig: Basal cell carcinoma appears as a pearly papule with central ulceration.

Q. Give the morphology of squamous cell carcinoma.

Q. Short note: Squamous cell carcinoma.

Ans.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer): Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common skin

cancer arising on sun exposed sites in older people.

Incidence: Higher incidence in men than in women.

Pathogenesis: The most important cause of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is DNA damage induced by
exposure to UV light. Tumor incidence is proportional to the degree of lifetime sun exposure.

Predisposing factors:
Prolonged sun exposure

Immunosupressive therapy

Industrial carcinogens (tars and oils)

Chronic ulcers and draining osteomyelitis

Old bum scars (Marjolin’s ulcers)

Arsenic exposure

Psoriasis

HIV infection

. Ionizing radiation

10. (In the oral cavity) tobacco and betel nut chewing
11. Precancerous condition- xeroderma pigmentosum, actinic keratosis
12. Human papilommavirus [HPV].

CHOI DAARWNH

Sites: Squamous cell carcinoma may arise on any part of the skin and mucous membranes lined by
squamous epithelium. Most common locations are the face, pinna of the ears, back of hands and
mucocutaneous junctions such as on the lips, anal canal and glans penis.

Morphology:
Macroscopic: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin and squamous-lined mucosa can have one of the
following two patterns:

* More commonly, an ulcerated growth with elevated and indurated margin.
* Less often, a raised fungating or polypoid growth without ulceration.

Microscopic:

* Squamous cell carcinoma in situ is characterized by cells with atypical (enlarged and

hyperchromatic) nuclei involving all levels of the epidermis.

Invasive squamous cell carcinoma shows variable degrees of differentiation, ranging from
tumors composed of polygonal cells arranged in orderly lobules and having numerous large areas

of keratinization, to neoplasms consisting of highly anaplastic cells that exhibit only abortive,
single-cell keratinization (dyskeratosis).

Fig: Malignant melanoma.

Clinical features:
1. Usually asymptomatic
2. Itching or pain may be early manifestations
3. Majority of the lesions are grater than 10 mm in diameter
4. Change in colour, size, or shape in a pigmented lesion are the most consistent clinical signs.

Clinical warning signs:
1. The most important warning signs, sometimes called the ABCDEs of melanoma, are-
Asymmetry
Irregular borders
Change in color
Increasing diameter
Evolution or change over time, especially if rapid.

2. Other features-
* Pigmented lesions > 6 mm in diameter
= Any change in appearance
= New onset of itching or pain.

Growth pattern:
* Radial growth (initial phase): Growth occurs in all directions but is predominantly lateral within the
epidermis and papillary zone of the dermis. During this stage of growth, melanomas do not
metastasize; clinical cure is frequent.

* Vertical growth (later phase): Growth extends into the reticular dermis or beyond. Prognosis varies
with the depth of the lesion. During this phase, lymphatics or hematogenous metastasis may occur.

gray.
* On occasion, zones of white or flesh-colored hypopigmentation also appear.
« The borders of melanomas are irregular and often notched.

Microscopic:
* Individual melanoma cells are larger than normal having large nuclei with irregular contours and
prominent red (eosinophilic) nucleoli.
* The appearance of the tumor cells is similar in the radial and vertical phases of growth.

DEFINITIONS OF MACROSCOPIC TERMS

Excoriation Traumatic lesion breaking the epidermis and causing a raw linear area (i.c., deep scratch);
often self-induced

Lichenification }|Thickened and rough skin characterized by prominent skin markings (as lichen on a tree
trunk); usually the result of repeated rubbing

Onycholysis Separation of nail plate from nail bed

Macule Circumscribed lesion, 5 mm or smaller in diameter, characterized by flatness and
distinguished by coloration (patch is greater than 5 mm)

Papule Elevated dome-shaped or flat-topped lesion 5 mm or less across (nodule is greater than 5 mm)

Plaque Elevated flat-topped lesion, usually greater than 5 mm across (may be caused by
coalescent papules)

Pustule Discrete, pus-filled, raised lesion

Scale Dry, horny, platelike excrescence; usually the result of imperfect cornification

Vesicle Fluid-filled raised Iesion 5 mm or less across (Bulla is greater than 5 mm. Blister is the

DEFINITIONS OF MICROSCOPIC TERMS

Acantholysis Loss of intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes

Acanthosis Diffuse epidermal hyperplasia

Dyskeratosis Abnormal, premature keratinization within cells below the stratum granulosum

Erosion Discontinuity of the skin showing incomplete loss of the epidermis

Exocytosis Infiltration of the epidermis by inflammatory cells

Hydropic swelling Intracellular edema of keratinocytes, often seen in viral infections

(ballooning)

Hypergranulosis Hyperplasia of the stratum granulosum, often due to intense rubbing

Hyperkeratosis Thickening of the stratum corneum, often associated with a qualitative abnormality of
the kfderatin

Lentiginous A linear pattern of melanocyte proliferation within the epidermal basal cell layer

Papillomatosis Surface elevation caused by hyperplasia and enlargement of contiguous dermal
papillae

Parakeratosis Keratinization with retained nuclei in the stratum comeum. On mucous membranes,
parakeratosis is normal.

Spongiosis Intercellular edema of the epidermis

Ulceration Discontinuity of the skin showing complete loss of the epidermis revealing dermis or
subcutis

Vacuolization Formation of vacuoles within or adjacent to cells; often refers to basal cell-basement
membrane zone area

(Ref: Robbins/10°/1135)

Osteomyelitis frequently manifests as a primary solitary focus of disease, but can also be a complication of
any systemic infection. All types of organisms, including viruses, parasites, fungi, and bacteria, can produce
osteomyelitis, but certain pyogenic bacteria and mycobacteria are the most common culprits.

Q Short note: Sequestrum, (DU-18Ja)

Q. What is Brodie’s abscess? (SU-03Ja) (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.
Brodie’s abscess: Brodie’s abscess is a small intraosseous abscess that frequently involves the cortex, and is
walled off by reactive bone. It is sequelae of chronic osteomyelitis.

(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/807)

Or,

Brodie’s abscess is a circumscribed, round/oval cavity containing pus and pieces of dead bone (sequestra)
surrounded by sclerosis.

Q. When acute osteomyelitis turns into chronic form?
Ans.
Turning of acute osteomyelitis into chronic form: In 5-25% cases, acute osteomyelitis fails to resolve and
persists as chronic infection. Chronicity may develop in following cases-
* Delay in diagnosis
Extensive bone necrosis
Inadequate antibiotic therapy
Inadequate surgical debridement
Weakened host defence.

(Ref: Robbins BASIC PATHOLOGY/10"/807)

Q. What do you mean by Pott’s disease?

Q. Short note: Pott’s disease. (DU-19Nv)

Ans.

Pott’s disease: Tuberculous osteomyelitis in the spine (especially the thoracic and lumber vertebra) which is
the most common site of skeletal involvement of TB is known as pott’s disease.

In the spine, infection breaks through intervertebral discs to involve multiple vertebrae and extends into the
surrounding soft tissues, forming abscesses.

Clinical features:
= Localized pain
= Low-grade fever
Chills
= Weight loss.

Complications: Discs and vertebral destruction result in compression fractures that culminate in scoliosis,
kyphosis, and neurologic deficits.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1186)

Ans.
Complications of tuberculous osteomyelitis:
* Permanent compression fracture of discs & vertebra produce severe scoliosis, kyphosis, and
neurologic deficits
* Tuberculous arthritis
* Sinus tract formation
= Psoas abscess
* Amyloidosis.

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/1186)

Q. Short note: Osteosarcoma. (DU-09Ja,07Ju, SMU-23/20M,16Ja, BUP-22M, CMU-
22M, 1 4Ja,12Ju, RU-19M,17/ 16Ju)

Ans. (Very Important for VIVA)

Qsteosarcoma: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant tumor of bone and accounts for
approximately 20% of bone cancers.

Age group: The age distribution of osteosarcoma is bimodal, with 75% occurring before 20 years of age. A
smaller peak occurs in older adults (after 60 years of age), in whom it is frequently associated with
predisposing conditions such as Paget disease of bone, infarcts, and prior radiation (sometimes called
secondary osteosarcomas). Men are affected slightly more often than women (1.6: 1).

Sites of origin: Although any bone can be involved, tumors usually arise in the metaphyseal region of the
long bones; almost 50% are near the knee in the distal femur or proximal tibia.

Fig: Major sites of origin of osteosarcomas.

Morphology:

Gross:
= Osteosarcomas are bulky, gritty, gray-white tumors that often contain hemorrhage and cystic

degeneration.
« The tumours frequently destroy the surrounding cortices and produce soft tissue masses.
= The tumors spread extensively in the medullary canal, and replace hematopoietic marrow.
= Infrequently, they penetrate the epiphyseal plate, or enter the joint.

Microscopic:
= The tomour cells vary in size and shape (pleomorphism) and frequently have large hyperchromatic
nuclei.
* Bizarre tumor giant cells, and abundant mitoses including abnormal (e.g. tripolar) forms are
common.

= Extensive necrosis and intravascular invasion are also common.
* Neoplastic cells can also produce cartilage; if abundant, such tumors are classified as
chondroblastic osteosarcoma.

Clinical features:
1. Painful progressively enlarged mass
2. Pathologic fractures.

Metastases: To the lungs, bones, brain, and elsewhere.
(Ref: Robbins/10'/1188)

(N.B: Radiographically, the enlarging tumor forms a destructive, mixed lytic and blastic mass with
infiltrative margins. The tumor frequently breaks through the cortex and lifts the periosteum, inducing reactive
periosteal bone formation. The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known
radiographically as a Codman triangle, indicates an aggressive tumor.)

(Ref: Robbins/10'"/1188)

Q. Describe the histopathological findings of chondrosarcoma.

Q. Short note: Chondrosarcoma.

Ans.

Chondrosarcoma: Chondrosarcomas are malignant cartilage-producing tumors. After osteosarcoma,
chondrosarcoma is the second most common malignant matrix-producing tumor of bone.

They are subclassified histologically as conventional, clear cell, dedifferentiated, and mesenchymal variants.

Age group: Individuals with chondrosarcoma are usually in their 40s or older, and men are affected twice as
frequently as women.

Sites of origin: Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis, shoulder, and
ribs, but, unlike benign enchondroma, distal extremities are rarely involved.

Morphology:
Gross:
* Conventional chondrosarcomas are large bulky tumors made up of nodules of glistening gray-white,
translucent cartilage, but the matrix is often gelatinous or myxoid and can ooze from the cut surface.
= Spotty calcifications are typically present, and central necrosis may create cystic spaces.
* Tumor spreads through the cortex and into surrounding muscle and fat.

Microscopic:
* The malignant cartilage infiltrates the morrow space & surrounds pre-existing bony trabeculae.

Q. Write down in brief about Ewing sarcoma. (SMU-23M)

Q. Short note: Ewing sarcoma. (DU-17Ja, RU-19/17M,16Ju)

Q. Short note: Ewing tumor. (DU-05Ja)

Ans.

Ewing sarcoma: Ewing sarcoma is a malignant bone tumor characterized by primitive round cells without
obvious differentiation.

It accounts for approximately 6% to 10% of primary malignant bone tumors and the second most common
group of bone sarcomas in children.

Age group: Most affected individuals are 10 to 15 years old, and approximately 80% are younger than 20
years. Boys are affected slightly more frequently than girls.

Sites of origin: Ewing sarcoma usually arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones, especially the femur and
the flat bones of the pelvis and presents as a painful, enlarging mass.

Morphology:

Gross:
* Ewing sarcoma usually arises in the medullary cavity and invades the cortex, periosteum, and soft tissue.
* The tumor is soft, tan-white, and frequently contains areas of hemorrhage and necrosis.

Histology:
* It is composed of sheets of uniform small, round cells with scant cytoplasm that may be clear due to
abundant glycogen.
« The presence of Homer-Wright rosettes (which are rounded cell clusters with a central fibrillary
core) indicates neuroectodermal differentiation.
" Fibrous septae may also be present, but there is little stroma.
* Geographic necrosis may be prominent.

Fig: Ewing tumour in X-ray. Fig: Homer-Wright rosettes cells.

Osteoarthritis (0A): Osteoarthritis (OA), also called degenerative joint disease, is characterized by cartilage

Q. Give in short the pathogenesis (CU-19M) & pathology of rheumatoid arthritis.

Ans.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disorder that principally
attacks the joints, producing a non-suppurative proliferative and inflammatory synovitis.

RA often progresses to articular cartilage destruction and, in some cases, joint fusion (ankylosis).

Extraarticular lesions may involve skin, heart, blood vessels, and lungs, leading to clinical manifestations that
overlap with other autoimmune disorders including systemic lupus erythematosus and scleroderma.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1199)

Rheumatoid arthritts.
(late stage)

Fig: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

Occurrence: RA is three times more common in women than in men. It is most common in those aged 40 to
70, but no age is immune.

Pathogenesis: RA is an autoimmune disease, in which the pathologic changes are mediated by antibodies
against self-antigens and inflammation caused by cytokines, predominantly secreted by CD4+ T cells. CD4+
T helper (T,;) cells initiate the autoimmune response by reacting with an arthritogen, perhaps microbial or a
chemically modified self-antigen.

Continuing autoimmune reaction

#### 📄 Page 361

SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY | 361
TEE —= <= <=

Activation of CD4+ T helper (Ty) cells and other lymphocytes
Local release of inflammatory mediators and cytokines

Destruction of bone and cartilage in joints.

Mediators (cytokines) produced by T-cells and their role in tissue (joint) injury:
« IFN-y from Ty cells activates macrophages and synovial cells.
« IL-17 from Ty17 cells recruits neutrophils and monocytes.
* RANKL expressed on activated T cells stimulates osteoclasts and bone resorption.
* TNF and IL-1] from macrophages stimulate resident synovial cells to secrete proteases that destroy
hyaline cartilage.

Morphology:

1. Joints:

= RA typically affects small joints of the hands and feet.

= The synovium becomes grossly edematous, thickened, and hyperplastic.
= The characteristic histologic features include:

Synovial cell hyperplasia and proliferation.

Dense inflammatory infiltrates (frequently forming lymphoid follicles) of CD4+ helper T
cells, B cells, plasma cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages.

Increased vascularity due to angiogenesis.

Fibrinopurulent exudate on the synovial and joint surfaces.

Osteoclastic activity in subchondral bone, allowing the inflamed synovium to penetrate the
bone and cause periarticular erosions and subchondral cysts.

Pannus formation (exuberant synovium is known as pannus).

2. Tendino-muscular involvement: Focal areas of inflammation in tendons, ligaments and adjacent
skeletal muscle.

3. Skin: Subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules appear in elbows, ulnar aspect of the forearm, occiput, and
lumbosacral area.

4. Blood vessels: A nonspecific acute vasculitis may appear.
5. Eye: Nonspecific conjunctivitis or uveitis.

6. Other organs: Nonspecific inflammatory changes may be found in the lungs, pleura, pericardium,
myocardium and peripheral nerves.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1199; Pocket Companion to Robbins/7"/648,649)

Q. Define meningitis and meningoencephalitis?

Ans.

Meningitis: Meningitis is an inflammatory process of the leptomeninges and CSF within the subarachnoid
space, usually caused by an infection.

It is usually caused by an infection, but may also occur in response to non-bacterial irritant (e.g. chemical
meningitis). Infectious meningitis is broadly classified into acute pyogenic (usually bacterial meningitis)
meningitis, aseptic (usually acute viral meningitis), and chronic (usually tuberculous, sphirochetal, or
cryptococcal) meningitis.

Although infections are the most common causes of meningitis and meningoencephalitis, this reaction may
also occur in response to a nonbacterial irritant introduced into the subarachnoid space (chemical meningitis)
or in the context of a systemic autoimmune disease. Based on the etiology and clinical evolution of the illness,
infectious meningitis is broadly classified into acute pyogenic (usually bacterial), aseptic (usually acute or
subacute viral), and chronic (usually tuberculous, spirochetal, or cryptococcal).

Meningoencephalitis: Meningoencephalitis refers to inflammation of the meninges and brain

parenchyma.
(Ref: Robbins/10'"/1261)

Q. What are the special characteristics of CNS tumors / brain tumours? (CMU-
21Nv,20Nv/M, 19/18/17M,14Ju,10Ja, BUP-22M) (Very Important for VIVA)

Q. Write the peculiarities of CNS tumors. (DU-23Nv, CMU-23Nv, CU-18Nv)
Q. Mention the differences between tumours of the nervous system and tumours of the other

parts of the body.
Ans

Differences between tumours of the nervous system and tumours of the other parts of the body: Tumours

of the nervous system have several unique characteristics that set them apart from neoplastic processes

elsewhere in the body.

First, the clinical course of disease is relatively unique in case of brain tumors. Thus, some glial tumors
with benign histologic features (low mitotic rate, cellular uniformity, and slow growth) may infiltrate large
regions of the brain and lead to serious clinical deficits and poor prognosis.

Second, because of their infiltrative behavior, it is often not feasible to resect glial neoplasms completely

without compromising neurologic function.

Third, any neoplasm can have lethal consequences if it is located in a critical region, as when a benign
meningioma, by compressing the medulla, causes cardiorespiratory arrest.

Finally, the pattern of the spread of primary CNS neoplasms differs from that of other tumours: even the
most highly malignant gliomas rarely metastasize outside the CNS.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1293 + 8'°/1330)
