Q. Mention the types of astrocytoma. (Very Important for VIVA)

Q. Short note: Glioma. (CU-19Nv)

Ans.

Glioma: The term glioma is used for all tumours arising from neuroglia, or more precisely, from
neuroectodermal epithelial tissue. Gliomas are the most common of the primary CNS tumours and
collectively account for 40% of all intracranial tumours.

They include tumours arising:
a. from astrocytes (astrocytomas and glioblastoma multiforme);
b. from oligodendrocytes (oligodendroglioma);
c. from ependyma (ependymoma); and
d. from choroid plexus (choroid plexus papilloma).

Gliomas are disseminated to other parts of the CNS by CSF but they rarely ever metastasise beyond the CNS.

A. Astrocytoma: Most common primary brain tumours. They can be divided based on their infiltration into
the surrounding brain parenchyma.

1. Infiltrating astrocytomas
= Diffuse astrocytoma
* Anaplastic astrocytoma
* Glioblastoma multiforme

2. Non-infiltrating astrocytomas
=  Pilocytic astrocytoma
= Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma
= Brainstem glioma.

B. Oligodendroglioma: Malignant tumor of oligodendrocytes.

« Calcified tumor often involving frontal lobe
= May present as seizures
» Histology shows ‘fired egg’ appearance of tumor cells.

C. Ependymoma: Malignant tumor of ependymal cells usually seen in 4" ventricle.

= Perivascular pseudorosette is characteristic (pseudorosette because the central structure isn’t part of
the tumor. Originally, pseudorosette meant any rosette that didn’t have a truly empty lumen).

* Tumor can result in Aydrocephalous.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1293; BRS Pathology/Sth/383; Pathoma Lecture Notes; Harsh Mohan/7"/879)

features: Astrocytomas have been divided into 4 histologic grades from grade I (low grade) to
grade LV (glioblastoma multiforme) as under.

WHO GRADE I ASTROCYTOMA (also called as diffuse Astrocytoma):
D Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma:
® Grossly, it is usually cystic or solid and circumscribed.
" Microscopically, it is predominantly composed of fusiform pilocytic astrocytes having unusually
long, wavy fibrillary processes.

ij) Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma: It looks histologically pleomorphic and alarming but has
favourable prognosis.

WHO GRADE II (WELL-DIFFERENTIATED) ASTROCYTOMA (also called as fibrillary astrocytoma):
* Grossly, it is a poorly defined, grey-white tumour of variable size. The tumour distorts the underlying
brain tissue and merges with the surrounding tissue.
« Histologically, it is composed of well-differentiated astrocytes separated by variable amount of
fibrillary background of astrocytic processes.

WHO GRADE III (ANAPLASTIC) ASTROCYTOMA:
* Grossly, it may not be distinguishable from the low-grade astrocytoma.
* Histologically, it contains features of anaplasia such as hypercellularity, pleomorphism, nuclear
hyperchromatism and mitoses. Another characteristic feature of anaplastic mvariety of astrocytoma is
the proliferation of vascular endothelium.

WHO GRADE IV ASTROCYTOMA (GLIOBLASTOMA MULTIFORME): It is the most aggressive of
astrocytomas.
a) Grossly, it shows vanegated appearance, with some areas showing grey-white appearance while others
are yellow and soft with foci of haemorrhages and necrosis. The surrounding normal brain tissue is
distorted and infiltrated by yellow tumour tissue.

b) mig sie the features are as under:
It has highly anaplastic and cellular appearance. The cell types show marked variation consisting
of fusiform cells, small poorly-differentiated round cells, pleomorphic cells and giant cells.
Mitoses are quite frequent and glial fibrils are scanty.
* It shows areas of tumour necrosis around which tumour cells may form pseudopalisading.
* Microvascular endothelial proliferation is marked.
(Ref: Harsh Mohan/7"/879)

Q. Short note: Oligodendroglioma.

Ans.

Oligodendroglioma: These are malignant tumors of oligodendrocytes, presents as slow-growing tumor in the
middle-age group often involving frontal lobe of cerebral hemisphere. May present as seizures.

Gross:
* Infiltrative tumors that form gelatinous, gray masses, and may show cysts, focal hemorrhage, and
calcification.

* Closely packed cells with large round nuclei surrounded by a clear halo of cytoplasm (“fried egg”

appearance).
* Tumor divided into groups of cells by delicate capillary strands.

Q. Short note: Meningioma. (DU-07Ja, SU-12Ju, CU-12Ja)

Ans.

Meningioma: This is the second most common primary intracranial neoplasm. Most cases are benign and
slow growing. The neoplasm originates in arachnoidal cells of the meninges; it is external to the brain and
can often be successfully removed surgically. It can cause seizure by compression.

They are uncommon in children (most often occurs after 30 years of age) and show a moderate (3:2) female
predominance.

Molecular genetics: Many show deletion, loss, or mutation in the NF2 locus.

Common sites of involvement:
= Convexities of the cerebral hemispheres

® Dura over the lateral convexity
= Wing of the sphenoid

= Olfactory groove

* Sella turcica

Foramen magnum.

Fig: Meningioma (right).

Morphology:
Gross:
= Usually rounded masses with well defined dural bases that compress underlying brain but are
easily separated from it.
* Extension into the overlying bone may be present.
* Usually encapsulated with thin, fibrous tissue.

Histological:
* Whorled pattern of concentrically arranged spindle cells
* Laminated calcified Psammoma bodies may be present.

Q. Short note: Peripheral nerve sheath tumours. (CU-16Ju)

Ans.

Peripheral nerve sheath tumours: A number of benign and malignant neoplasms are grouped together as
peripheral nerve sheath tumors—all likely arise from cells of Schwann cell lineage.

The three common peripheral nerve sheath tumors:
1. Schwannoma: This benign, slowly growing encapsulated tumor arises from Schwann cells.

2. Neurofibroma: This neoplasm occurs as solitary or multiple tumors of peripheral nerves derived from
Schwann cells that can be subtyped as localized cutaneous, diffuse, or plexiform.

3. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST): Most (approximately 85%) are high-grade
tumors, but low-grade variants are recognized. About half arise in NF1 patients and are assumed to
result from malignant transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma.

Peripheral nerve sheath tumors have association with relatively common familial tumor syndromes,
including neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF 1), neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), and schwannomatosis.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1236; BRS Pathology/5'/385)

Q. Short note: Schwannoma. (CMU-23M, 13Ju)
Ans.

Schwannoma: It is a benign tumour that exhibits Schwann cell differentiation and often arises directly from
peripheral nerves. Schwannomas are a component of NF.

Morphology:
* Schwannomas are well-circumscribed, encapsulated masses that abut the associated nerve without
invading it, a feature that simplifies surgical excision.
* Grossly, these tumours form firm, gray masses.
" Microscopically, they are comprised of an admixture of dense and loose areas referred to as
Antoni-A and Antoni-B areas, respectively.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/1237)

Q. Write in brief about neurofibroma. (CU-20/13Ju)

Q. Short note: Neurofibroma. (CMU-21M,20Nv)
Ans,

Neurofibroma: A neurofibroma is a benign nerve sheath tumor in the peripheral nervous system.
Origin: Neurofibromas arise from nonmyelinating-type Schwann cells.

The neoplastic Schwann cells are admixed with perineurial-like cells, fibroblasts, mast cells, and CD34+
spindle cells. Neurofibromas may be either sporadic or NF] -associated.

Sub-types: Different types of neurofibroma can be distinguished depending on their growth pattern-

Q. Short note: Retinoblastoma. (SU-17M)
Ans.
Retinoblastoma: It is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of children.

Age: Diagnosed usually prior to the 4 years of age.

Pathogenesis of retinoblastoma: Two mutations of the RB gene, located on chromosome 13q14 lead to
neoplastic proliferation of the retinal cells. (Important for VIVA)

Morphology:
1. The pathology of retinoblastoma of both hereditary and sporadic type is identical.

2. Tumours may contain both undifferentiated and differentiated elements.
3. Undifferentiated elements appear as collections of small round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei.
4. Viable tumour cells are found encircling tumour blood vessels with zones of necrosis typically found
in relatively avscular areas.
5. Focal zones of dystrophic calcification are characteristic of retinoblastoma.
(Ref: Robbins/10"/1324)

#### 📄 Page 393

CLINICAL PATHOLOGY | 393
ee ene -- — — ——= ~

IVER FUNCTION TEST
AND JAUNDICE

Liver Function Tests

Q. Enumerate the functions of liver.
Ans.
Functions of liver:

* Secretory function: Formation and secretion of bile.

* Metabolic function (Nutrient & vitamin metabolism): Liver is the main organ for almost all types
of metabolism of glucose and other sugars, amino acids, lipids (fatty acids, cholesterol. hpoproteins).
fat-soluble vitamins & water-soluble vitamins. It is the main site for alcohol metabolism.

= Synthetic function: Synthesis of plasma proteins (except gamma globulins), vitamin-K dependent
clotting factors- (II, VII, IX, X), steroid binding and other hormone-binding protems.

* Excretory function: It excretes drug, alcohol. bilirubin. hormone. cholesterol etc.

= Storage function: Liver stores glycogen, vitamin- A. D, B,:. iron, folic acid etc_

* Detoxification function: Liver detoxifies inactivates toxin, steroids, other hormones, NH: & drugs
such as penicillin, ampicillin, erythromycin etc.

= Haemopoietic function: In first trimester of fetus, liver is the mam site of production of red blood cells

(Ref: Guyton/11°/860-862: Davidson’s/21°/923-925)

Q. Short note: Liver function tests (LFTs). (DU-19M,18Nv,06M, RU-16/08Ju) (V.VI for VIVA)

Ans
ive rction tests: The liver function tests (LFTs) are the biochemical investigations to assess the capacity
of the liver to carry out any of the function it performs.

The major liver function tests are-
1. Tests for excretory function:
a. In blood-
* Serum bilirubin concentration (Normal 0.3-/ mg/dl or 5-17 pmol/L)
* Conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin (in serum, bilirubin is normally almost all unconjugated)
b. In urine- Urinary bilirubin, urobilinogen
c. In stool- Stercobilinogen

Nw

Tests for enzymatic function:
a. Evidence of hepatocellular damage (as in hepatitis):
* Alanine aminotransferase (ALT/ SGPT) [10 - 40 U/L]
* Aspertate aminotransferase (AST/ SGOT) [10 - 35 U/L]

b. Evidence of biliary obstruction (as in obstructive jaundice):
* Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) [40 - 125 U/L]
* y-glutamyl transferase (GGT) [Male: 10 - 55 U/L, Female: 5 - 35 U/L}

3. Tests for synthetic function:

a. Serum albumin level (Normal 4.8 gm/dl) {Range: 3.5 - 5.0 gm/dl} (A falling serum albumin
indicates severity of chronic liver disease & thus it is a bad prognostic sign)
Albumin / globulin ratio (Normal 1|.7 : 1)
Prothrombin time (Normal 12-16 sec) {Jt is a sensitive indicator of both acute and chronic liver
disease)
d. Serum total protein concentration (Normal 6 - 8 gm/dl)

Ss

9

4. Tests for detoxification function: Serum ammonia concentration.

Other biochemical tests:

a. Serum electrolytes (Hyponatraemia may occur in sever liver disease)

b. Blood urea level

c. Serum iron, transferring saturation, serum ferritin level (Hereditary haemochromatosis)
d. Serum & urinary copper (Wilson’s disease)

e. Serum ceruloplasmin (Wilson's disease)

6. Tumour marker: a-fetoprotein (AFP) for hepatocellular carcinoma.
7. Viral markers: Different viral markers for different types of viral hepatitis (A, B, C, D & E).

8. Immunological tests: For autoimmune liver diseases-
a. Anti-mitochondnal antibody (Primary biliary cirrhosis)
b. Antinuclear antibody (Autoimmune hepatitis)
c. Anti-smooth muscle antibody (Autoimmune hepatitis).
(Ref: Lecture SSMC & DMC; Prof. Khaleque/196)

Q Why prothrombin time is more specific than total protein estimation? (DU-09Ja) (Must be
asked in VIVA)

Ans.

Prothrombin time is more specific than total protein estimation: Prothrombin is produced only by liver.
Whereas, some plasma proteins such as immunoglobulins are produced outside the liver (i.e. by plasma cells).
So, total protein concentration in blood does not directly reflect the status of liver function. That’s why
prothrombin time is more specific than total protein estimation.

Q. Which one is more liver specific ALT/AST and why?

Ans.

ALT is more specific for liver damage than AST, as AST is also present in heart, brain, kidney and muscle.
High levels of AST are seen in hepatic necrosis as well as myocardial infarction, congestive cardiac failure and
muscle injury.

Q. Which are the best markers of CLD (chronic liver disease)?
Ans.

Best markers of CLD (chronic liver disease):

a. Total protein and albumin/globulin ratio
b. Prothrombin time (PT).

(N.B: Always remember, PT is better than total protein).

Q. What do you mean by direct and indirect bilirubin?

Q. What is indirect bilirubin? (CU-20/10Ju)

Ans.

Direct bilirubin: Conjugated bilirubin is called direct bilirubin. In aqueous solution, it is water soluble, and
reacts rapidly (within one minute) with the reagent diazotized sulfanilic acid in van den Bergh reaction. That's
why it is called “direct reacting” or direct bilirubin.

Indirect bilirubin: Unconjugated bilirubin is called indirect bilirubin. \t is not soluble in water. In plasma,
it is bound to the albumin. It is obtained by subtracting the ‘direct reacting’ bilirubin from the total bilirubin.
(Ref: Lippincott’s/3"’/283; Prof. Khaleque/194)

Q. State the causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. (CU-16Ja)

Q. Short note: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. (DU-12Ja)

Ans.

Unconjugated _hyperbilirubinemia: It is a clinical condition in which there is increased level of
unconjugated bilirubin in blood.

Cause:
= Excess production of bilirubin (e.g. haemolytic anaemia)
* Reduced hepatic uptake (e.g. Gilbert's syndrome)
* Impaired bilirubin conjugation (e.g. physiological jaundice of the newborn).

Clinical importance: Fraction of unconjugated bilirubin (very small amount) may remain unbound and
diffuse into the tissues particularly in the brain of infants and produce toxic injury (kernicterus).
(Ref: Lecture SSMC; Prof. Khaleque/194)

Predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: Intrahepatic & extrahepatic cholestasis.

B) Clinico-pathological classification:

Haemolytic / pre-hepatic jaundice: It results from excessive breakdown of RBC & excessive
production of unconjugated bilirubin.

Causes:

Congenital defect in RBC e.g. sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia, haemoglobinopathies
Incompatible blood transfusion

Malana

Certain drugs e.g. quinine

Hepatocellular / hepatic jaundice: Damage to the liver cells can cause unconjugated bilirubin
level to increase in the blood as a result of decreased conjugation.

Causes:

Viral hepatitis

Chronic alcoholic hepatitis

Liver cirthosis

Infections e.g. Yellow fever, septicaemia
Poisons e.g. arsenic, CCl,, phosphorus etc.
Paracetamol poisoning

Cardiac failure

Obstructive / post-hepatic jaundice: This is due to an obstruction of the bile duct that prevents
the passage of bile into the intestine. This condition is called cholestasis (i.e. the failure of bile
secretion). The obstruction may be intrahepatic or extrahepatic. The bilirubin in the serum is
conjugated.

Causes: (None will pass without saying this at VIVA)

i) Intra-hepatic cholestasis: This is due to parenchymal liver damage, or excretory dysfunction
of bile canaliculi at a cellular level.

Viral hepatitis

Drugs (e.g. methyltestosterone, estrogen, oral contraceptives)

Primary biliary cirrhosis

Alcoholic hepatitis

Pregnancy

Post-operative.

ii) Extra-hepatic cholestasis: Obstruction in the biliary tract distal to bile canaliculi.
= Stone in common bile duct
* Carcinoma of head of the pancreas or ampulla of vatter
* Metastatic carcinoma of common bile duct
= Stricture of common bile duct

Q. What is acholuric jaundice? (DU-10Ja) (Frequently asked in VIVA)

Choluric jaundice: Jaundice with presence of bilirubin in urine is called choluric jaundice. So, hepatitis and
obstruction of the common bile duct (obstructive jaundice) causes choluric jaundice.

Acholuric jaundice: Jaundice without presence of bilirubin in urine is called acholuric jaundice. Hemolytic
jaundice is acholuric type.

Q. What is physiological jaundice? (DU-14Ja, RU-17Ja)

Q. Short note: Physiological jaundice.

Ans.

Physiological (normal) jaundice: Most infants develop visible jaundice due to clevation of unconjugated
bilirubin concentration during their first week. This common condition is called physiological jaundice ft
generally appears at 2-4 days of age and disappears by | to 2 weeks of age. It is harmless and docen't
usually cause a problem.

This mild jaundice is due to the immaturity of the baby’s liver, which leads to 4 slow processing of bilirubin

Mechanism / reasons: Normally, bilirubin passes through the liver and is excreted as bile through the
intestines. Jaundice occurs when bilirubin builds up faster than a newborn's liver can break it down and pase iI
from the body. Reasons for this include-

1. Newborns make more bilirubin than adults do since they have more turnover of red blood cells

2. A newbom baby’s still-developing liver may not yet be able to remove adequate bilirubin from the
blood

3. Too large an amount of bilirubin is reabsorbed from the intestines before the baby gets rid of it in the stool

Treatment: Treatment is usually not needed. For most babies, jaundice usually gets better without treatment
within 1 to 2 weeks. Sometimes phototherapy is needed for infants whose bilirubin levels are very high

Possible complications: Rare, but serious, complications from high bilirubin levels include:
* Cerebral palsy
* Deafness
* Kernicterus (brain damage from very high bilirubin levels).

Q. Why jaundice appears in premature baby? (RU-15Ja)

Ans.

Causes of jaundice in premature baby: In premature baby liver cannot properly conjugate bilirubin. As a
result, jaundice occurs due to unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. They develop jaundice on or after 2“ or 3”
day of life and resolves by 14 days. The baby is otherwise healthy.

The peak level of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia may be 10-12 mg/dl on the 5® day of life and may rise
to maximum 15 mg/dl, and then falls, the direct fraction is <15% of the total.

Q. Short note: Kernicterus. (DU-1 1Ju)

---

#### 📄 Page 405

CLINICAL PATHOLOGY | 40s
—E EEE ~
Ans.
Kernicterus: Kernictcrus is a neurological syndrome resulting from bilirubin toxicity within the brain —
staining and necrosis of neurons in the basal ganglia, hippocampal cortex, subthalamic nuclei & cerebellum
followed by gliosis of those areas. The cerebral cortex is usually spared.

/ causes:
Prematurity
Hemolytic disease of the newborn
Congenital familial non-hemolytic jaundice
Neonatal hepatitis
Congenital spherocytosis.

Treatment:
1. Appearance of clinical signs suggesting bilirubin toxicity or encephalopathy is an indication for

exchange transfusion at any level of serum bilirubin

| Ans.
3 cardinal features of obstructive jaundice:
1. Conjugated bilirubin
2. Generalized itching
3. Pale stool and urinary bilirubin is present.

Q. Why there is generalized itching in obstructive jaundice? (For Honors Gainers)
Ans.
Cause _of generalized itching in obstructive jaundice: Due to cholestasis, bile salt can not excreted;

accumulation occurs in skin & causes degranulation of mast cell, results in increased release of histamine
resulting in generalized itching.

Q. Why there is pale stool in obstructive jaundice? (For Honors Gainers)
Ans,

Cause of pale stool in obstructive jaundice: No bile — No digestion of fat + Steatorrhoea & ultimately pale
stool.

Q. Why bilirubin is present in urine? (For Honors Gainers)
Ans.

Causes of presence of bilirubin in nurine:
* In obstructive jaundice: Conjugated bilirubin — Water soluble — So, can be excreted through urine.

* In haemolytic jaundice: Unconjugated bilirubin — Not water soluble — Not excreted through urine.

Q. Short note: Casts in urine with interpretation. (RU-13Ju)

Ans.

Casts: These are solidified or coagulated proteins formed in the renal tubules. These are microscopic narrow
cylindrical structures with parallel sides and rounded ends, varying in size and shape. Common casts are
cellular casts (epithelial, RBC, and WBC), granular cast and hyaline cast.

1. Epithelial casts- Found in renal tubular necrosis (RTN)

2. RBC casts- Found in acute glomerulonephritis (it is the hallmark of AGN)
3. WBC casts- Found in pyelonephritis

4. Granular casts- Found in glomerulonephritis

5. Hyaline casts- Normal findings.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/203; Long Cases in Clinical Medicine/1*/376; Lecture SSMC)

Q. Write the microscopic findings of urine in pathological conditions. (SU-14Ju)
Q. Enumerate the diseases that can be diagnosed by urine examination. Explain with clinical
and laboratory findings. (RU-15Ju)
Ans.
Microscopic findings of urine in pathological conditions:
1. RBC: Different causes of haematuria, such as-
Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN)
Acute pyelonephritis
Renal calculi
Renal tuberculosis
Renal cell carcinoma
Neoplasm of ureter, urinary bladder and urethra
Bleeding disorders e.g. haemophilia, thrombocytopenia, DIC
Overdose of anticoagulant therapy
Inflammation: e.g. cystitis, urethritis etc.
Trauma to any part of urinary tract

2. Pus cells: Urinary tract infection.

3. Epithelial cells: Increased epithelial cell signifies contaminated urine, that is not appropriate for
culture.

4. Different casts:
* Epithelial casts- Found in renal tubular necrosis (RTN)

* RBC casts- Found in acute glomerulonephritis (AGN)

or urinary bladder stones.

Q. State the procedure for collection of sample of urine for routine examination. (CU-10Ju)
Ans.
Procedure for collection of sample of urine for routine examination:
= Urine is collected in a clean, dry, sterile pot / sterilized test tube
= For male: Mid-stream urine is normally collected
= For female:
- Before collection, vulva and vestibule must be washed with soap and ringed with dry cloth
- She must unnate keeping vulva apart
- Mid-stream urine is collected
» After collection of urine sample, it should be labeled properly and then submitted for examination
* Fresh urine is to be examined within a few hours (unorganized deposits may appear if left at room
temperature. There is also chance of bacterial contamination).
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/201)

Q. What do you mean by renal clearance test? (DU-07Ju, RU-13Ju,12Ja)
Q. State the importance of renal clearance test.
Q. Short note: Renal clearance test.
Ans.
Renal clearance test: It is the virtual volume of plasma (in ml) that is completely cleared of a particular
substance by both kidneys in each minute.
Or,
Renal clearance may be defined as the virtual volume of plasma which contains the amount of that substance
excreted through urine per minute.

Concentraton of substancein urinex volumeof urine( ml/min)

Renal clearance (ml/ min) = -
Concentraton of substancein plasma(in ml)

Examples:

Renal clearance of inulin (Cinutin) = 125 ml/ min
Renal clearance of creatinine (Creatinine) = 70-140 ml/ min
Renal clearance of urea (Curea) = 60-70 ml/ min

Importance of plasma clearance:

1. It is a good marker of renal function.
2. Assessment of severity of renal impairment.
3. Measurement of GFR, RPF and RBF.

Q. Why serum creatinine level is more specific than serum urea level as a renal function test?
(DU-14Ja,12Ju, RU-17Ju, 1 6Ja)

Q. Why serum creatinine is more specific renal function test? (DU-09/08Ju, RU-13Ja,10Ju)

Q. Why serum creatinine estimation is more valuable test than estimation of blood urea? (DU-07Ju)
Q. Give the clinical importance of serum creatinine. (DU-11Ju,10Ja)

Ans. (Very Important for VIVA)

Serum creatinine level is more specific than serum urea level as a renal function test: Blood urea is a poor
guide to renal excretory function as it varies with protein intake, liver metabolic capacity and renal perfusion.

Serum creatinine is more specific as it is produced from muscle at a constant rate and almost completely filtered
at the glomerulus. If muscle mass remains constant, changes in creatinine concentration reflect changes in GFR.
(Ref: Davidson’s/20"/461)

Q, Short note: 24 hours urinary protein, (CU-13Ju)
Ans,

+ 24-hour urine protein measures the amount of protein released in urine over a 24-
hour period, The test checks the function of the kidneys and detects disease.

#### 📄 Page 418

us| arif's representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Urine samples are collected in one or more containers over a period of 24 hours. The containers are kept ina
cool environment and then sent to a lab for analysis. Specialists then check the urine for protein. The test is
simple and noninvasive

When higher than normal amount of protein are in the urine, it is called proteinuria. Proteinuria is often a sign
of kidney damage and disease.

Normal value: < 80 mg of protein per day.

Indication:

Glomerulonephritis
Uncontrolled diabetes

High blood pressure

SLE

Uninary tract infections (UTIs)
Multiple myeloma
Amyloidosis

Disadvantage:

1. The test does not show what kinds of protein are in the urine.

2. The test also does not show the cause of the protein.

3. Occasionally proteinuria is not a sign of kidney damage (specially for children)

4. Other factors, such as extreme stress, vigorous exercise, dehydration etc. may also influence the test results.

Q. What is microalbumin? Write its importance. (DU-09Ju, RU-12Ja)
Q. Short note: Microalbuminuria? (RU-09Ju)
Ans.

Microalbuminuria: Microalbuminuria describes the urinary excretion of small amounts of normal albumin
protein (30-300 mg/day) which is not detected by conventional methods.

Significance of microalbuminuria:
1. Early sign of diabetes nephropathy

Detection of Bence-Jones protein in urine:

1. Heat test: Bence-Jones proteins have unique behavior in heating. Urine containing Bence-Jones
proteins flocculates when heated slowly to 50-60°C. The flocculated proteins on boiling, and reappears
on cooling below 60°C.

2. Electrophoretic method: The most reliable means for the detection of Bence-Jones proteins is
electrophoresis of a concentrated urine specimen on cellulose acetate. The monoclonal light chains

usually migrate as a marrow band in the globulin region.
(Ref: de Gruchy/5""/306,307)

Q. Short note: Reducing substance in urine. (DU-22Nv, CU-13/12Ja)

Ans.

Reducing substances: Reducing substances are the substances that can reduce Benedict solution.

The most important urinary reducing substances are:
1. Sugar substances: Glucose, lactose, pentose, fructose & galactose.

2. Non-sugar substances:
= Homogentisic acid (present in alkaptonuria)

(N.B: Normally reducing substances are absent in urine, but in certain conditions they are present in urine.
Glycosuria is most common. Lactosuria occurs in pregnancy and during lactation. Pentosuria, fructosuria,
and galactosuria are rare inborn errors of metabolism.)

Rethera’s test: It is the test of detecting ketone bodies in urine.

Procedure:
1. Saturate a few ml (10 ml) of fresh urine taken in a test tube with ammonium sulphate

Q. Short note: Microscopic haematuria. (DU-12Ju)

Ans.

Microscopic haematuria: Haematuria which is invisible by naked eye examination, but detectable under
microscope (due to small number) and on dipstick testing of urine is called microscopic haematuria.

Interpretation of dipstick positive haematuria:
* WBC (suggestive of infection)
* RBC - dysmorphic erythrocytes (phase contrast microscopy) (suggestive of glomerular bleeding)
* RBC casts (suggestive of glomerular bleeding)
* Abnormal epithelial cells (suggestive of tumour).

Glomerular bleeding characteristically causes microscopic haematuria. Whereas macroscopic (visible)
hematuria is more likely to be caused by tumours and severe infections or renal infarction, usually
accompanied by pain.

Management: Management of hematuria depends upon the cause.
(Ref: Davidson’s/21"/478,479)

Q. Short note: Nephrotic syndrome. (DU-15Ja, RU-14Ja, CU-10Ju,09Ja)
Ans

Nephrotic syndrome: It is a glomerular syndrome which is characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5
gnvday), hypoalbuminaemia (plasma albumin level < 3 gm/dl), generalized edema, hyperlipidaemia and
lipiduria (lipid in the urine).

(Ref: Robbins/10'/896,912)

Fig: Patient of nephrotic syndrome.

Causes of nephrotic syndrome: (Very Important for VIVA)
1. Primary glomerular diseases:

* Minimal-change disease (most common in children)
Membranous glomerulonephritis (most common in adults)
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

IgA nephropathy

2. Systemic diseases:
* Diabetes mellitus
* Amyloidosis
* Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
* Drugs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory, penicillamine, heroin)

Q. Short note: Nephritic syndrome (AGN). (CU-04S)

Ans.

Nephritic syndrome / AGN: Nephritic syndrome or acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is a glomerular disease
of kidney which is characterized by inflammation in the glomeruli and is manifested as haematuria (red
blood cells and red cell casts in urine), proteinuria (usually subnephrotic range) with or without edema,
azotemia and hypertension.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/906)

Ans.

Diabetes mellitus (DM): Diabetes mellitus is a clinical syndrome characterised by an increase in plasma blood

Q. Write the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus (as per ADA & WHO). (CMU-
22M,21/20Nv)

Q. Give the WHO diagnostic criteria for diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. (DU-23Nv,21Ja,20Nv/
M,19Nv,14/07Ju, BUP-22Nv,21Nv/M, CU-20M, RU-12Ja)
Ans.

Diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus (as per ADA & WHO): (Very Important for VIVA)

1. A single fasting plasma glucose > 7.0 mmol/L (=126 mg/dl) in symptomatic patients and on two
separate occasions in asymptomatic patients.

2. A random plasma glucose > 11.1 mmol/L (= 200 mg/dl) in an individual with classic sign/ symptoms
of diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia & weight loss) and on two separate occasions in
asymptomatic patients.

3. A2 hours OGTT > 11.1 mmol/L (> 200 mg/dl) after a 75 gm load of glucose.

An HbAIc of = 48 mmol/mol (> 6.5%) is also diagnostic of diabetes.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC; Davidson’s/23"'/727)

(N.B: As HbAlIc reflects the last 2-3 months of glycaemia, it should not be used to diagnose diabetes where
the duration of onset is short, i.e. in someone with suspected type | diabetes or severe symptomatic
hyperglycaemia.)

(Ref: Davidson’s/23"'/727)

Q. Mention the criteria of the patients who should be considered for diabetic testing.
Ans.

Criteria of the patients who should be considered for diabetic testing:

All individuals 45 years of age or older (repeat at 3 years interval)

Persons with classic signs & symptoms of diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, ployphagia & weight loss)
Obesity

History of 1 degree relations with diabetes

Women with gestational diabetes

Individuals with hypertension (> 140/90)

An HDL cholesterol level less than or equal to 35 mg/dl or TG level greater than or equal to 250 mg/dl.
Presence of impaired glucose tolerance on previous testing.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

#### 📄 Page 437

CLINICAL PATHOLOGY | 437
a

Confirmatory biochemical tests for diabetes mellitus:

« Either fasting plasma glucose (FPG) or random plasma glucose (RPG) can be used for the
confirmation of diagnosis. In symptomatic individuals one abnormal plasma glucose measurement in
the diabetic range confirms the diagnosis.

* Asymptomatic individuals with a positive screening test (FPG or RPG) need another abnormal plasma
glucose measurement on another day for the confirmation of the diagnosis.

* OGTT is not recommended for routine use as a confirmatory test.

(N.B: Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 h. Random is defined as any time of day without
regard to time since last meal.)
(Ref: Manual of diabetes mellitus)

Nice to Know:

Screening tests for DM:

* Screening is recommended for all individuals with one or more major risk factors for
developing diabetes mellitus

* FPG (fasting plasma glucose) is the laboratory test recommended for screening of individuals for
diabetes mellitus

* RPG (random plasma glucose) is an alternative test for screening.

* When facilities to do FPG or RPG are not available, CBG (capillary blood glucose) and UG (urinary
glucose) are alternatives screening for patients with classical symptoms of DM.

(Ref: Manual of diabetes mellitus)

1. Target blood glucose level: Fasting blood glucose < 6 mmol/L.

3. Target levels of blood lipids:
© Total cholesterol: < 5.0 mmol/L (approx. 190 mg/dl)
o LDU cholesterol: < 3.0 mmol/L (approx. 115 mg/dl).

Hyperglycaemia sine glycosuria: This is a condition in which the plasma glucose is above the normal renal

Ans.

Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT/ GTT): It is a laboratory test to diagnose diabetes mellitus. When random

blood glucose values are elevated but are not diagnostic of diabetes, glucose tolerance is usually assessed by
the glycemic response to oral ingestion of a glucose load.

It measures the ability of the body to tolerate, or cope with standard dose of glucose. Tolerance is reduced
when insulin is insufficient or absent.

Q. What is IFG? (DU-15Ja,13Ju)

Q. Short note: Impaired fasting glucose (IFG). (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

---

#### 📄 Page 443

CLINICAL PATHOLOGY | 443

NE <<

Impaired fasting glucose (IFG): Impaired fasting glucose (IFG) refers to a condition in which the fasting
blood glucose level is consistently elevated above what is considered normal levels; however, it is not high
enough to be diagnosed as diabetes mellitus.

Or,
IFG is defined as the fasting glucose level between 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L (110 to 125 mg/dL) according to WHO.

Diagnostic criteria: The WHO criteria for impaired fasting glucose (IFG) -

* Fasting plasma glucose = 6.1 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) to 6.9 mmol/L (125 mg/dL)
* 2hrs after OGTT glucose is normal, i.e. <7.8 mmol/L (<140 mg/dl).

Importance:
1. These patients are prone to develop frank diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease.

2. There is a 50% risk over 10 years of progressing to overt diabetes.
3. IFG is a risk factor for mortality due to the serious complications of type-2 diabetes mellitus.

Advice to patients with IFG: The patients are advised for weight reduction about 5 to 10% of their body
weight, regular exercise and follow up. Usually no drug therapy is recommended.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC; Long Cases in Clinical Medicine/1*/610)

Q. What will be the OGTT findings in IGT? (SU-14Ju)

Q. Write the diagnostic criteria for defining impaired glucose tolerance test. (CMU-21M)

Q. Short note: Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT). (DU-15Ju,12Ja) (Very Important for VIVA)
Ans.

Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT): When a random or fasting blood glucose is suggestive but not diagnostic

of DM, that means when the values are above the upper limits of normal but below the values of diagnostic of
diabetes it is called impaired glucose tolerance (IGT).

Or,
When fasting glucose is less than 7 mmol, but during OGTT, 2 hours after the glucose load is 7.8 to 11.0
mmol, it is called IGT.

Diagnostic criteria: The WHO criteria for impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) -

Impaired glucose tolerance
Fasting plasma glucose 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dl)
2 hrs after OGTT 7.8-11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dl)

Advice to patients with IGT: The patient who has IGT are at increased risk of developing frank DM type 2
with time and also macrovascular complications are more (mainly cardiovascular). Lifestyle modification for
type 2 DM and annual check-up for glucose are recommended for this patient. Cardiovascular risk factors
should be treated aggressively.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC; Long Cases in Clinical Medicine/1/610; Davidson’s/23*/726)

Q. What is the significance of HbA;C? (CU-18Nv)

Q. Short note: Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA,C). (DU-21Ja,20Nv/M,16Ju, CMU-21Nv,20Ju,
16Ja,13Ju,11/10/09Ja)

Ans.

Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA,C): Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA,C) is the most widely used measure
of long-term glycaemic control in diabetes mellitus. It is produced by the glycosylation of hemoglobin at a rate
proportional to the glucose concentration.

(N.B: Slow non-enzymatic covalent attachment of glucose to hemoglobin is called glycosylation of
hemoglobin.)

Normal value: 4.0 - 6.0% of total Hb.

Importance:
1. Glycosylated haemoglobin provides an accurate and objective measure of glycaemic control over a

period of weeks to months.

Q. What are the ketone bodies? (DU-1 1 Ju, 10Ja, RU-17/16Ja)

Q. Define ketonuria. How it is formed?

Ans.

Ketonuria: Acetoacetate, B-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone are collectively called ketone bodies or ketones.
Excretion of more than a trace of these substances in the urine is called ketonuria.

Mechanism of formation of ketonuria: Glucose provides energy to our body. If intake is insufficient or
metabolism defective due to lack of insulin as in untreated or uncontrolled diabetes, body obtains energy by
breaking down fats & ketones. Ketones are toxic to brain and can cause coma found in diabetic ketoacidosis.
In ketoacidosis, ketonuria is always present. Urine ketone test detect acetoacetate and acetone only.

(Ref: Lecture SSMC)

Q. How ketoacidosis develops in cases of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus? (DU-24Nv, 1 1Ju,10Ja,

O8Ju)

Ans.

Ketoacidosis / diabetic ketoacidosis: Over production of ketone bodies in long-standing uncontrolled or
poorly controlled diabetes mellitus exceeds buffering capacity of blood. As a result, blood pH is decreased and
acidosis is produced which is called ketoacidosis.

Q. Define gestational diabetes mellitus. (DU-09Ja, RU-20Nv,18Ja)

Q. Short note: Gestational diabetes mellitus. (/mportant for VIVA)

Ans.

Gestational diabetes mellitus: Glucose metabolism changes during normal pregnancy. Gestational diabetes is
defined as diabetes with first onset or recognition during pregnancy.

WHO suggests that all women meeting criteria for impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes after a 75 gm OGTT
should be classified as having gestational diabetes.

Risk factors for gestational diabetes:

Obesity

2. Family history of type 2 diabetes

3. Previous glucose abnormality in pregnancy
4. Previous macrosomia

—_

Complications of gestational diabetes:
Gestational diabetes is associated with an increased risk of later development of type 2 diabetes.

1.
2. Maternal hyperglycemia is associated with increased fetal size (fetal macrosomia) & obstructed labour,

Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus: The European criteria of diagnosis of gestational diabetes are:

= Venous plasma glucose in the fasting state: > 5.5 mmol/L (99 mg/dl)
=» 2 hours after a glucose load: > 9 mmol/L (162 mg/dl).

(Ref: Davidson’s/23"/752)

Indication of semen analysis: (Very Important for VIVA)

Follow up after vasectomy

Artificial insemination

Paternity test (forensic medicine purpose)

In suspected rape case - for identification of the accused.

wren

Q. How semen is collected for analysis? (DU-15Ja)
Ans

Semen collection procedure:

1. Preparation of the patient:
* Patient should be instructed to collect semen with a sexual abstinence of 3-5 days.
* Should be obtained by masturbation (self-stimulation) or collect at home during the act of
intercourse (by coitus interruptus). Condom should be avoided, as it contains spermicidal agent.
* Patient should evacuate his bladder before ejaculation.
= Patient must wash hands before collection.

2. Collection of specimen and transport:

* Should be collected in a dry, clean plastic container provided by the laboratory.

* Condom collection is unacceptable.

=  Patient’s name, age, date and time of collection should be recorded.

* Sample should be taken to the laboratory within 1 hour of collection and kept at body temperature.
(Ref: Lecture SSMC, BSMMU Lab. Medicine & AFIP Clinical Pathology)

Q. Short note: Normozoospermia. (RU-18M)
Ans.

Semen analysis: Semen analysis measures the quality and quantity of the fluid secreted during ejaculation. It
evaluates both liquid portion called semen or seminal fluid, and microscopic moving cells called sperm.
It is often used to study the fertility status of a male.

Basic semen analysis measures:
1. Semen volume
2. Sperm concentration
3. Sperm motility
4. Sperm morphology

Additional pH & fructose levels (absence of fructose or high pH may be associated with ejaculatory, tract,
obstruction or seminal vesicle dysfunction) & WBC counts within semen can also be done.

Normal findings of semen analysis: (Please read this at least 10 times for VIVA)

1. Appearance Opalescent / Opaque

2. Colour Grayish white

3. Volume 2-5 ml / ejaculation

4. Viscosity High

5. Consistency Thick

6. Odour Musty / fishy

7. pH range ice 7.8 a

3. Sperm morphology _ >50% sperms are morphologically normal (normal head, body & tail)
4. Sperm viability >75% sperms are viable

5. _Leucocytes <1 million / ml

Q. Short note: Oligoasthenozoospermia. (BUP-21N/M)
Ams.
Ofigeasthenozoospermia: It is a sperm disorder that involves two disorders at the same time-

a) Oligospermia: Low sperm count.

b) Asthenozoospermia: Abnormal sperm motility with more than 60% of sperm being immotile or
unable to move in a straight direction.

Causes:
a) In most cases causes are unknown / idiopathic.
b) Testicular diseases e.g. orchitis.
c) Some genetic disorders e.g. Klinefelter’s syndrome, immotile cilia syndrome.
4) Immunologic.

Treatment: Treatment of reversible cause, if any.

Q. Define pseudocyesis. (RMU-23M, 19Nv)

Ans.

Pseudocyesis (false pregnancy): Pseudocyesis is a syndrome when a woman shows all the symptoms of being
pregnant except for the presence of a fetus.

Their belly grows like a pregnant woman, and they can even go into false labour.

Q. How will you proceed to diagnose a case of male (RU-15/13Ju) and female infertility? (RU-13Ju)
Q. Short note: Infertility test.

Ans.

Infertility test: Infertility test are meant to establish the reason why a couple is not able to conceive naturally.
Overall, 20-30% of the cases of infertility are due to a problem with the male partner.

Diagnosis of male infertility:

1. Medical, sexual and social history
2. General physical examination (including an examination of genitals)

3. Specific fertility tests:
= Semen analysis
- Physical, chemical and microscopic test
- Immunological assay
- Anti-sperm antibody test
- Sperm function test
- Post ejaculatory urine analysis
= Hormone testing (testosterone and other male hormones)
*  Transrectal and scrotal ultrasound
= Genetic testing

Diagnosis of female infertility:
1. Medical, sexual and social history
2. General physical examination (including a regular gynaecological examination)
3. Specific fertility tests:

---

#### 📄 Page 455

CLINICAL PATHOLOGY | 455

Hormone assay (LH, FSH, estradiol, progesterone, prolactin, thyroid & pituitary hormone)

Hysterosalpingography (a special X-ray test to locate blockage or other problems in the uterus
and fallopian tube)

Ovulation testing (blood test to measure hormone levels to determine whether the patient is
ovulating or not)

Ovarian reserve test (this test helps to determine the quality and quantity of the eggs available
for ovulation)

Diagnostic laparoscopy (this can identify endometriosis, scarring, blockages or irregularities of
the fallopian tubes, and problems with the ovaries and uterus)

Imaging tests (e.g. pelvic ultrasound, hysterosonography, hysteroscopy etc.)
Endometrial biopsy (to verify ovulation and inspect the lining of the uterus)
Pap’s smear
Genetic testing (to determine whether there is a genetic defect causing infertility).
(Ref: Lecture SSMC, BSMMU Lab. Medicine & AFIP Clinical Pathology)

Q. What are the tests done in CSF examination? (DU-04S)

Ans.
Tests done in CSF examination:

1. Physical examination:

Quantity or volume

Colour

Appearance

Pressure

Specific gravity

Presence of blood

Clot formation (CSF is normally clear and colorless)

* VDRL for syphilis

Q. What is pleocytosis? (DU-10Ju)

Ans.

Pteocytosis: Pleocytosis is a term used to describe an increased cell count (Gk. pleion = more), usually
referring to an increase in white blood cell (WBC) count in a bodily fluid, such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). It
is often defined specifically as an increased WBC count in CSF.

Importance: It is indicative of an inflammatory, infectious, or malignant condition.

Q. A patient with pyogenic meningitis comes to you, but CSF finding shows that CSF glucose is
high. How it can be possible?

Ans.
The patients has uncontrolled DM.

We know,

CSF glucose = 60% of blood glucose level

If blood glucose level = 100 mg /dl

Then, normal CSF = 60 mg/dl

If the patient has > 200 mg/dl blood glucose level
Then his normal CSF level will be > 120 mg/dl.

So, although this patient has pyogenic meningitis, CSF glucose will be higher than normal.

Q. Mention the hallmark of meningitis caused by Neisseria.

Ans.
Meningococcal skin rash.

Q. Mention two important physical sign in meningitis.
Ans.
1. Neck rigidity
2. Kemnig’s sign (extension at the knee with the hip joint flexed causes spasm in the hamstring muscles)
3. Brudzinski’s sign (passive flexion of the neck causes flexion of the hips and knees).
(Ref: Davidson’s/23™/1019)
Q. Why CSF looks cloudy or turbid?
Ans.
Due to excess amount of protein.

Q. Why protein is increased in all types of meningitis?

Ans.
Because it is an inflammation and in every inflammation, there is exudate formation, which contains much

more protein.

Q. Why CSF sugar is markedly reduced in pyogenic meningitis? (DU-23Nv)

Ans.
Because every pyogenic bacteria consumes glucose as their food and energy.

Q. Why glucose is normal in viral meningitis?
Ans.
Because virus dose not consume glucose.

Q. What do you mean by asceptic meningitis?
Ans.
It usually refers to viral meningitis.

Ans.
ADA test.

The fluid which is present in pleural cavity is called pleural fluid. Normal amount: |-10 ml. Abnormal

Q Mention the significance of pleural fluid study. (CU-08Ju)
ARs.
Sgaificance of pleural fluid study: By studying pleural fluid, we can detect the following diseases-

Exedative pleural fluid: (High protein content)
1) Pulmonary tuberculosis

2) Pneumonia (para-pneumonic effusion)

3) Bronchial carcinoma

4) Pulmonary infarction

5) Collagen disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis)
6) Lymphoma

Transudative pleural fluid: (Low protein content)
1) Congestive cardiac failure

2) Nephrotic syndrome

3) Cirrhosis of liver

4) Malnutrition

5) Hypothyroidism

6) Meig’s syndrome (ovarian fibroma, ascites and right sided pleural effusion)
7) Acute rheumatic fever.

The cause of majority of the pleural effusions can usually be identified through a thorough history, clinical

examination and relevant investigations.
(Ref: Davidson’s/23"/563)

Q. Short note: Ascitic fluid study. (CMU-22M, 13Ja,12Ju)

Ans.

Ascitic fluid study: Ascitic fluid should undergo gross inspection as well as laboratory analysis. Routine
laboratory test include:

= Differential cell count

= Albumin assay
= Cultures.

Inspection: Ascitic fluid is typically translucent and yellow. Fluid of other colour or consistency may reflect
specific underlying disease processes-

Disease Ascitic Muid appearance

Cirrhosis Straw-coloured, or bile stained

Neoplasm Straw-coloured, hemorrhagic, mucinous, or chylous
Tuberculous peritonitis Clear, turbid, hemorrhagic, or chylous

Pyogenic peritonitis Turbid, or purulent

Congestive heart failure Straw-coloured

Nephrosis Straw-coloured, or chylous

Pancreatic ascites (pancreatitis, pseudocyst) Turbid, hemorthagic, or chylous

(Ref: School of Medicine, Queen’s university)
Cell count: Several millileters of ascitic fluid is sufficient to obtain a differential cell count.

Albumin:

Evudative ascetic fluid Pransudative ascetic Muid

(Iheh protem content)
* Peritoneal tuberculosis = Heart failure
* Pancreatitis = Cirthosis of liver
* Malignancy involving peritoneum = Nephrotic syndrome

(Low protem content)

## Arif's Pathology & Haematology — Electrolyte and Acid-Base Balance

> **Source:** `Arif Pathology guide 2025 [2].pdf` · **Pages 470–479** (10 extracted) · **UNIT-II : CLINICAL PATHOLOGY**
#### 📄 Page 470

470 | arif's representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

ACID-BASE
BALANCE

Electrolytes

Q. What are the electrolytes that are done to evaluate a patient? Give their normal levels. (DU-
16Ja)

Q. Give the normal level of serum electrolytes. (DU-15Ja) Mention the clinical importance of
serum electrolytes. (SU-19Nyv,17M)

Q. Write down the components of electrolytes with their normal values. (CMU-21M)

Q. Give the normal serum levels of Na’, K*, Cl HCO; and Ca’*. (DU-05Ja)

Q. Short note: Serum electrolytes. (CU-15Ja)

Ans.

Serum electrolytes: Serum electrolytes are the salts and metallic components that are dissolved within the
blood serum (serum is the liquid portion of blood).

Electrolytes carry an electrical charge, either negative or positive. The negatively charged electrolytes are
balanced by the positively charged electrolytes.

Normal level of serum electrolytes:

Electrolytes Reference range (mmol/L or meq/L)
Na” 135 - 145

K* 3.6 -5.1

cr 95 - 107

HCO, 21-29

Ca” 2.1 - 2.6 (9-11 mg/dl)

(Ref: Davidson’s/21*/1294,1296)

Importance of serum electrolytes: Electrolytes are involved in most of the body’s daily functions. For
example, electrolytes are required for:

Proper nerve conduction

Heart and skeletal muscle contraction
Maintenance of proper hydration status
Maintenance of proper blood pH.

Q. Short note: SGPT & SGOT. (CU-09Ja)
Ans.

SGPT & SGOT: Aspartate transaminase (AST / SGOT) & alanine transaminase (ALT / SGPT) function
normally to transfer the amino group from an amino acid, alanine in the case of ALT and aspartate in the case
of AST, to a ketoacid, producing pyruvate and oxaloacetate respectively.

Both SGOT & SGPT arc located in the cytoplasm of the hepatocyte. Although both transaminase enzymes are
widely distributed in other tissues of the body, the activities of ALT outside the liver are low, and therefore this
enzyme is considered more specific for hepatocellular damage.

(Ref: Davidson’s/20"/940)

Normal values and conditions where SGPT & SGOT are increased: Please write from above.

Ans.

Cardiac markers: These are intracellular enzymes or proteins released to blood following cardiac muscle

damage due to ischemia (e.g. myocardial infarction) or other assaults and shows serial change in plasma
concentration with an initial rise followed by a fall.

Types of cardiac markers: Two types-
Enzymes:
1. Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) / Creatine kinase (CK)
2. Aspertate transaminase (AST/ SGOT)
3. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
4. y-Glutamyl transpeptidase (y-GTP)
Other proteins:
1) Troponins
2) Myoglobin.

Q. Why troponin T & I are the best indicator for MI? (DU-08Ja)

#### 📄 Page 484

484 arvif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

Q. Mention the clinical importance of troponin-I. (RU-15Ja)

Q. Short note: Troponin. (DU-06Ja)

Ans.

Troponin: Troponins are proteins that regulate calcium-mediated contraction of cardiac and skeletal muscle.

Types:
* Troponin I (Tn): It is totally cardio-specific, hence it is called cardio-specific troponin-I (cTn-I).
* Troponin T (TnT): It is not totally cardio-specific.
* Troponin C (TnC): It is not used as a cardiac marker.

Clinical importance: Troponin I (TnI) and troponin T (TnT) are structural cardiac muscle proteins that are
released during myocyte damage and necrosis, and represent the best indicator for diagnosis of acute MI,
because these markers have nearly complete cardiac tissue specificity and high sensitivity.

Troponin I (TnI) and Troponin T are not normally detectable in the circulation, but following acute MI, levels
of both cardiac troponins rise at 4 to 6 hours and peak at 24-48 hours. Troponin levels remain elevated for 5
to 14 days after the acute event.

(Ref: Robbin’s/10"/550; Davidson’s/23"/450)

(N.B: The troponins level may also be elevated in minor degrees of myocardial damage, pulmonary embolus,
septic shock and pulmonary oedema).
(Ref: Davidson’s/23"/450)

Q. Short note: CPK. (CU-10Ju)
Q. Short note: CK. (DU-04S)
Ans.
Creatine kinase (CK) or creatine phosphokinase (CPK): Creatine kinase is an enzyme that is highly
concentrated in brain, myocardium, and skeletal muscle and is composed of two dimers, designated “M” and “B”.
(Ref: Robbin’s/7'"/583)
Types / Isoforms:
=" (CK-M®M): Found in skeletal muscle
= (CK-MB): Found in cardiac muscle
= (CK-BB): Found in brain.
(Ref: Davidson’s/20"/1075; Robbin’s/10'"/550)
Normal value:
Male: 55-170 U/L
Female: 30-135 U/L
(Ref: Davidson’s/23"/1360)

Myocardial infarction

Inflammatory myositis + vasculitis

Trauma, strenuous exercise
Hypothyroidism, metabolic myopathy.

Rmeangp

(Ref: Davidson’s/21"/1064)

Q. A male of 56 years of age presented to you with excruciating left sided chest pain and
sweating, not relieved by taking rest and nitroglycerine sublingually. What is your
provisional diagnosis? What are the investigations you should advice and their expected
clinical results? (DU-11Ja)

Ans,

Provisional diagnosis: Acute myocardial infarction.

Investigations with expected results:
i) ECG —ST segment elevation, Pathological Q-wave formation, T-wave inversion.
ii) CK-MB - Markedly raised. It starts to rise within 4-6 hours and remains elevated up to 48 to 72
hours.
iii) Troponin-I — Markedly raised. It starts to rise within 4-6 hours and remains elevated up to 5 to 14
days.

Q. Name two enzymes acting as tumour marker. (RU-13Ja)
Ans.
Two enzymes acting as tumour marker:

1. Acid phosphatase: Marker for carcinoma of prostate and metastatic tumour of bone.
2. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP): Marker for metastatic tumour of bone.

Q. Write the clinical importance of PSA. (DU-10/08Ja)
Ans.
Clinical importance of PSA:

1. Measurement of PSA is the most important test used in the diagnosis and management of prostate
cancer.
20-40% of patients with a serum PSA > 4.0 ng/ml will have prostate cancer on biopsy.
High levels of serum PSA (> 100 ng/ml) almost always indicate distant bone metastases.
PSA is most useful for monitoring response to treatment and disease progression.
It is also a tumour marker of some breast cancers.

(Ref: Robbins/10"/981; Davidson’s/23"¢/439,1322,1324)

Q. A 51 year old, chronic alcoholic man was admitted with central abdominal pain radiating
to back. His serum amylase was 12000 U/L (Normal <300 U/L). What will be your
provisional diagnosis? What type of necrosis will be observed in the peritoneum? (DU-13Ja)
Ans

Provisional diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis.

Type of necrosis in the peritoneum: Enzymatic fat necrosis.

Q. Short note: ADA. (SU-17M)
Ans.

ADA: Adenosine deaminase (also known as adenosine aminohydrolase, or ADA) is an enzyme involved
in purine metabolism. It is needed for the breakdown of adenosine from food and for the turnover of nucleic
acids in tissues.

Importance: Its primary function in humans is the development and maintenance of the immune system. —
However, ADA association has also been observed with epithelial cell differentiation, neurotransmission, —
and gestation maintenance.

Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to pulmonary fibrosis.
(Ref: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_deaminase) _

apoproteins) means for transport of lipid in blood.

Classification of lipoproteins: Four major groups of plasma lipoproteins have been identified-
1. Chylomicrons
2. Very-low density lipoproteins (VLDL) or, pre-B-Lipoproteins
3. Low-density lipoproteins (LDL) or, B-Lipoproteins
4. High-density lipoproteins (HDL) or, a-Lipoproteins.

Structure of lipoprotein: A typical lipoprotein consists of-

1. A lipid core-containing non polar triglyceride and cholestery! ester.

2. A single surface layer of phospholipid, free cholesterol and apoproteins. Phospholipid and

cholesterol are so oriented that their polar groups face outward to the aqueous medium, making the
particle water soluble.

Fig: Structure of a lipoprotein.

Functions of lipoproteins: Since lipids are insoluble in water, they cannot alone travel in the aqueous blood
plasma. Lipoproteins are water soluble. So lipids can easily travel in blood as lipoprotein. So lipoproteins act
as transport vehicle for lipid in plasma.

1. Chylomicrons: Transport exogenous TAG from intestine to liver & peripheral tissue.

2. VLDL:

= Transport endogenously synthesized TAG from liver to peripheral tissue.
= Acts as precursor of LDL

3. LDL: Transport cholesterol from liver to peripheral tissue.

HDL: Transport cholesterol from peripheral tissues to liver for its degradation and excretion
(Reverse cholesterol transporter).

Blood levels of lipoproteins:

Type of lipoprotein Origin Main lipid content Blood level (mg/dl)

Chylomicron Intestine TAG 100 - 200
VLDL Liver TAG < 40
LDL From VLDL in blood | Cholesterol < 130
HDL Liver and intestine Phospholipids > 40

Clinical importance:
1. High LDL level causes increased cholesterol deposition in arterial wall resulting in atherosclerosis.

2. HDL removes cholesterol from peripheral tissues and thus prevents formation of atherosclerosis.
3. Imbalance in the rate of TG formation in liver and in VLDL secretion leads to fatty liver.
(Ref: Harper’s/28"/213-215; Lippincott’s/5"/227,228)

Q. Name the anti-atherogenic lipoproteins. Describe the role of HDL-cholesterol.
Q. What is the clinical importance of HDL? (CU-09Ja)

Q. Why HDL is beneficial for our health, explain? (DU-22Nv)

Ans.

Anti-atherogenic lipoprotein: HDL.

Role of HDL-cholesterol: HDL transports cholesterol form the peripheral tissue to the liver. In the liver,
this cholesterol can be either repackaged into lipoproteins, converted into bile acids or secreted into the bile in
unchanged form for removal from the body. So, the more the HDL-cholesterol, the less the cholesterol

deposition in peripheral tissue and the Jess chance of atherosclerosis. That is why HDL is known as anti-
atherogenic or, sometimes called “good cholesterol”.

A high level of HDL-C seems to protect against cardiovascular diseases, and low HDL cholesterol levels (less
than 40 mg/dL) increase the risk for heart disease. So, HDL particle is considered as protection to the body’s
cardiovascular health. So it is good / beneficial for health.

(Ref: Harper’s/29"/242; Lippincott’s/5"/234-237)

Q. Short notes: HDL. (RU-09Ju)
Ans

HDL: It is a lipoprotein having highest density.
Synonym: a-lipoprotein.

Role of HDL-cholesterol: HDL transports cholesterol form the peripheral tissues to the liver (Reverse
cholesterol transporter). \n the liver, this cholesterol can be either repackaged into lipoproteins, converted into
bile acids or secreted into the bile in unchanged form for removal from the body. So, the more the HDL-
cholesterol, the less the cholesterol deposition in peripheral tissue and the less chance of atherosclerosis. That
is why HDL is known as anti-atherogenic or, sometimes called “good cholesterol”.

A high level of HDL-C seems to protect against cardiovascular diseases, and low HDL cholesterol levels (less
than 40 mg/dL) increase the risk for heart disease. So, HDL particle is considered as protection to the body’s
cardiovascular health.

(Ref: Harper’s/29""/242; Lippincott’s/5"/234-237)

Q. What is good and bad cholesterol? Why they are called so? (BUP-21 Nv/M)

Q. Why HDL is called good cholesterol (BUP-22M) and LDL is bad cholesterol? (DU-
23Nv,08Ja)

Ans.

HDL is called good cholesterol and LDL is bad cholesterol: HDL is called good cholesterol, because HDL
removes cholesterol from the peripheral tissues to the liver where it is metabolized and excreted in bile, thus it

reduces tissue atherogenecity.
On the other hand, LDL is called bad cholesterol, because LDL carries cholesterol from the liver to the

peripheral tissues, thus it increases tissue atherogenecity.
(Ref: Davidson’s/21°'/451)

Q. Short note: Occult blood test (OBT). (DU-06S, BUP-22Nv, RU-19/18/17Nv, 16/14Ju,13/12Ja,
SU-17M, 1 1Ja,09Ju, CU-16Ju,07Ja)
Ans.

Occult blood test: The test is done to detect altered blood or trace amount of blood which is not visible.
Methods:

1. Orthotoluidine test
2. Hema-Check slide test

A. Orthotoluidine test:
Procedure:

1) Make an emulsion of the stool (size of a pea) in distilled water in a test tube.
2) Boil for 5 minutes and cool.

3) Place 4 drops of orthotoluidine and 1 drop of H,0, in a clean test tube, and leave for 1 minute.

---

#### 📄 Page 496

496 arif’s representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

4) Add | drop of stool suspension.

Interpretation: A green colour within | minute indicates positive result.

A false positive reaction may occur due to the presence of meet or green vegetable products in the
sample of stool. So the individual must not take meet or green vegetables for three days prior to the
test to make the test significant.

B. Hema-Check slide test: Test paper (slide) is used.
Conditions where occult blood test may be positive:

1. Bleeding peptic ulcer disease
2. Carcinoma of stomach
3. Carcinoma of colon
4. Ulcerative colitis.
(Ref: Prof. Khaleque/378-379)

Ans.

= Ascaris lumbricoides

= Trichuris trichiura

= Enterobius vermicularis.

Q. What is melaena? What are the causes of melaena?
Ans.

Melaena: Melaena is the passage of black, tarry stools containing altered blood which is usually caused by
bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract.

Causes of bleeding from upper gastrointestinal tract (melaena):
1) Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) (H. Pylori, NSAIDs)
2) Gastric erosion (NSAIDs, Alcohol)
3) Oesophageal varices due to liver diseases with portal vein thrombosis
4) Cancer of stomach and esophagus
5) Esophagitis with hiatus hemia
6) Vascular malformation
7) Mallory-Weiss tear.

(Ref: Davidson’s/23"'/781)

Q. Write four causes of fresh blood in stool.

Ans.

Causes of fresh blood in stool (haematocazia): It may be found in bleeding from lower G.I. tract.
= Dysentery

Bleeding piles

Malignant disease (Ca. rectum, Ca. colon)

Ulcerative colitis

Crohn’s disease

Anorectal fissure, haemorrhoids

Meckel’s diverticulum.

(Ref: Davidson’s/23"*/782; Lecture SSMC & DMC)

Q. How sputum is collected? Write the tests for sputum examination. (SU-14Ju)
Y. Short note: Sputum collection and examination. (CU-14/12Ju)

Q. Short note: Sputum examination. (RU-13Ju, SU-10Ju)

Ans.

Sputum examination: (Sputum is mucus that is coughed up from the lower airways)

Collection of sputum: Sputum should be collected in a clean, dry, wide necked container. For culture it
should preferably be collected in sterile container. Sputum is best collected in the morning before any mouth
washed is used. The person should cough deeply to produce a sputum specimen.

Examinations:

1. NACKED EYE EXAMINATION:
a. Presence of blood (hemoptysis):

Pulmonary tuberculosis

Bronchiectasis

Mitral stenosis

Pneumonia

Lung abscess

Bronchogenic carcinoima

b. Amount
« Scanty in bronchitis, bronchial asthma, early stage of pneumonia.
= Copious in pulmonary edema, lung abscess, advanced TB.

c. Colour
= White & mucoid in bronchitis, bronchial asthma.
= Rusty in pneumonia.
« Yellow or green in purulent state.
= Pink frothy in pulmonary edema.
» Blood-stained in hemoptysis.

---

#### 📄 Page 498

| arif's representation on PATHOLOGY & HAEMATOLOGY

d.

Consistency

* Mucoid in chronic bronchitis, early TB.

* Purulent in acute and chronic bronchitis, bacterial pneumonia & bronchopneumonia, lung
abscess.

* Mucopurulent in all bacterial infection of upper respiratory tract.

* Viscid and rusty in pneumonia.

* Frothy sputum in pulmonary edema.

« Anchovy sauce in amoebic abscess.

Odour
= Sputum is usually odourless. It is offensive or putrid (foul smelling) in bronchiectasis, lung

abscess and gangrene.

MICROSCOPIC EXAMINATION:

Ziehl-Neelsen staining: Done for demonstration of tubercle bacilli.

Gram staining: Done for demonstration of common bacteria, actinomyces and fungi.

Leishman staining: It is done to identify eosinophils and other leukocytes and pus cells.
Unstained cover slip preparation: Done for demonstration of Entamoeba histolytica, hydatid
cyst etc.

KOH preparation: Done for demonstration of Aspergillus species.

Demonstration of malignant cells: Papinicolaou stain, or haematoxylin and eosin stain is used.

CULTURE OF THE SPECIMEN.

Q. Short note on: VDRL test. (DU-03M)
Ans.
VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) test:
* It is mostly used simple and rapid test for syphilis.
* It is non-specific but a useful screening test.
« It becomes positive within 3-4 weeks or primary infection.
* It generally becomes negative by 6 months after treatment.

Advantage:
ii) Simple and easy to perform.
ili) Inexpensive.
iv) It is suitable as screening test and is positive in about 70% of primary and 98% of secondary syphilis.

Disadvantage:
i) Non-specific, false positive results may occur in some diseases like malaria, measles, infectious
mononucleosis, leprosy, SLE, rheumatic disorders etc.
ii) May also become negative in late latent stage.
ili) The VDRL antigen must be prepared fresh daily.
(Ref: Prof. Akram/3"/241,242)

4. Increased protein loss: Nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis (AGN)
